Appendix.title: ABI and object layout
Appendix.Content: ABI and object layout
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: C003 · Latest development: C007
Definition and mechanism

C++23 preserves declaration order for nonzero-size non-variant data members even across different access labels; earlier standards had weaker ordering guarantees. alignas can request supported stronger alignment, increasing stride. Standard-layout and trivial copyability are distinct; offsetof is guaranteed for standard-layout types, while use on others is conditionally supported. Verify CPU/upload/shader offsets separately.

An application binary interface (ABI) specifies implementation-level calling and data-layout conventions. Member offsets, complete size/alignment, and calling conventions affect binary compatibility. sizeof/alignof/offsetof inspect a standard-layout record; they do not define a portable file schema. Assume stated target rules before deriving 0/4/8 offsets.
Prerequisites

ListItem.Content: Alignment and padding — Address divisibility determines legal placement and layout holes.
Fixed-width integer types — The representation width fixes byte count and valid shift range.

Appendix.title: ASLR
Appendix.Content: ASLR
Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C003 · Latest development: C003
Definition and mechanism

Address-space layout randomization varies mapping locations to make fixed-address assumptions less reliable and support exploitation resistance. It does not alter C++ member offsets or grant pointer validity. A pedagogical stack/heap/data/text ordering is not a guaranteed live map.
Prerequisites

ListItem.Content: Process isolation and page permissions — The mapping context and permissions constrain which accesses proceed.

Appendix.Content: Used by
Update downstream uses when later chunks build on this concept.
Recall and next depth
Distinguish randomized mapping base from fixed member-relative offset.
Pending: Entropy, loader/ABI rules and platform security limits.
Source and navigation
C003 teaching chapter · Part definitions · Dependency Map
Reconstruction depth

Address Space Layout Randomization changes where executable images, shared libraries, stacks, heaps and other mappings are placed between process runs. The security goal is to make an attacker’s guessed code or data address less reliable; it is not memory encryption and it does not prevent a program from using valid pointers after the loader establishes mappings.

For engine code, the important consequence is that a virtual address is process-instance state, not durable identity. Serializing a raw pointer, hashing it as an asset identifier, or expecting the same module base across runs is invalid even before ASLR is considered; ASLR makes the mistake obvious.

Position-independent code and relocation machinery allow code and data references to work when the loader chooses a different base. Debuggers and crash reports therefore resolve addresses against the exact module build and load map rather than treating an absolute address as a universal source location.

A practical test is to run a tiny program multiple times and record stack, heap, function and shared-library addresses while keeping the binary unchanged. Values may vary, while relationships required by the program remain valid. ASLR strength and platform policy are operating-system evidence, not something portable C++ can infer from one run.

Appendix.Content: Absolute and relative error

Appendix.title: Accumulated rounding error
Appendix.Content: Accumulated rounding error
Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C005 · Latest development: Phase 10
Definition and mechanism

Appendix.Content: Addresses and virtual memory
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: C002 · Latest development: C003
Definition and mechanism

An address identifies a location in an address space. User-space object addresses are normally virtual, translated through per-process mappings to physical frames with permissions. A page translation preserves offset; VA 12345ABC mapping VPN 12345 to PFN 987 yields PA 987ABC with 4-KiB pages. Adjacent virtual pages may have scattered physical backing. Appendix.title: Alignment and padding
Appendix.Content: Alignment and padding
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: C002 · Latest development: C003

Appendix.title: Allocator fragmentation
Appendix.Content: Allocator fragmentation
Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C003 · Latest development: C003
Definition and mechanism

Internal fragmentation is unused space inside an allocated block, e.g. 37 bytes requested in a 48-byte class leaves 11. External fragmentation is free space split into holes incapable of satisfying one contiguous request, e.g. three separated 20-byte holes cannot supply one 60-byte block. Metadata overhead is an additional cost.
Prerequisites

ListItem.Content: Dynamic allocation and heap — Allocated buffers/blocks supply the storage whose ownership and fragmentation matter.

Appendix.Content: Used by

ListItem.Content: Huge pages and TLB reach — uses this mechanism as stated in its prerequisites.

Appendix.Content: Recall and next depth
Distinguish slack, metadata, and separated holes.
Pending: Coalescing, size classes, virtual commitment and measured overhead.
Source and navigation
C003 teaching chapter · Part definitions · Dependency Map
Reconstruction depth

Fragmentation is wasted allocation capacity caused by request shapes and allocator policy. Internal fragmentation is unused space inside an allocated block because of alignment, size classes or rounding. External fragmentation is free memory split into pieces that cannot satisfy a larger request even when total free bytes are sufficient.

A game or graphics workload amplifies the issue because lifetimes are structured: per-frame temporaries, long-lived assets, streaming resources and transient staging data behave differently. Using one general heap for all of them can mix lifetimes and make reuse less predictable.

A useful experiment records requested bytes, committed bytes, peak live bytes, largest free span, allocation count and reuse over time. Frame arenas eliminate external fragmentation inside a frame by resetting wholesale; pools trade generality for fixed-size reuse; free lists require split and coalesce policy.
Fragmentation is not measured by the process uses a lot of memory alone. Residency, allocator metadata, page commitment and application-owned slack must be separated before choosing a remedy.

Appendix.Content: Arithmetic policies
Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C002 · Latest development: C002
Definition and mechanism
Modular, checked, widened, saturated, and arbitrary-precision arithmetic define different outcomes when a mathematical result does not fit.

A policy states the intended response to an unrepresentable answer: wrap modulo a base, report checked failure, widen storage, clamp to an endpoint, or grow arbitrary precision. Choose by subsystem meaning. Color-byte output and hash arithmetic need different policies.

Appendix.title: Atomic operations and write contention
Appendix.Content: Atomic operations and write contention
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: C001 · Latest development: C005
Definition and mechanism
Independently meaningful fields sharing a word can require coordinated read-modify-write and can cause unrelated writers to contend.

An atomic update is indivisible to other participating accesses under its specified memory ordering. Packed independent flags may share one read-modify-write location: writers can overwrite each other without coordination. Contention means accesses compete for ownership or serialization.

Atomic additions can prevent lost writes without fixing addition order. Different valid schedules can produce different rounded sums; deterministic reduction requires a defined tree as well as safe synchronization.
Prerequisites

ListItem.Content: Bit packing — Packing places several constrained values into a carrier.
Machine word — A processor’s natural integer processing width is often called its word width, but the term is architecture dependent.

Appendix.Content: Used by

ListItem.Content: Numerical reproducibility — Indivisible updates do not impose a unique schedule-independent ordering.

Appendix.title: Atomic publication and durability
Appendix.Content: Atomic publication and durability
Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C003 · Latest development: C003
Definition and mechanism

Publishing a prepared temporary file by replacement concerns observers of the filesystem namespace. Crash durability concerns whether contents and namespace updates survive failures; it needs a specified platform/filesystem protocol. Neither follows from building a vector of bytes. The supplied AtomicFile excerpt is an unverified repository claim, not a tested durability guarantee.
Prerequisites

ListItem.Content: Serialization — Publication persists already-specified bytes, rather than defining their format.
Ownership and non-owning views — A mapping or publication pipeline must keep referenced bytes valid.

Appendix.Content: Used by
Update downstream uses when later chunks build on this concept.
Recall and next depth

Pending: Platform replacement semantics, flush ordering, recovery and cross-volume limits.
Source and navigation
C003 teaching chapter · Part definitions · Dependency Map
Executed POSIX durability sequence
The durability contract now has an actual syscall-level witness in tools/labs/atomic_publication_durability_lab.cpp.

The reference creates a staging file with exclusive creation, writes the complete payload, calls fsync on the file, closes it, renames it within the same directory, opens the containing directory, and calls fsync on that directory before treating publication as complete. It then verifies the final bytes and absence of the staging name. Separate tests reject a pre-existing staging file and a traversal-style final name.

This is stronger than “write temp then rename,” because rename atomicity and durable persistence are different properties. The file sync requests persistence of file contents/metadata; the directory sync requests persistence of the directory-entry change. Successful calls on CI are evidence that the operating-system/filesystem accepted that ordering. They are not a laboratory power-cut test and cannot promise identical persistence guarantees on every filesystem, storage controller, Windows API, network filesystem or production asset pipeline.

Appendix.title: Basis coordinates and dimension
Appendix.Content: Basis coordinates and dimension
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase6 · Latest development: Phase7
Definition and mechanism

Phase 7 stores basis images as matrix columns and derives coordinate conversion <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">[</mo> <mi>v</mi> <msub> <mo stretchy="false">]</mo> <mi>C</mi> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <msup> <mi>C</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>−</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msup> <mi>B</mi> <mo stretchy="false">[</mo> <mi>v</mi> <msub> <mo stretchy="false">]</mo> <mi>B</mi> </msub> </math>. The endpoint bases and whether motion is active or passive determine the product; row-major storage does not. Reconstruction and active/passive example.

A basis is an ordered independent spanning set. Independence makes coordinates unique; spanning makes every vector reachable. Dimension counts basis elements over the chosen field, not stored components or bytes. A basis change alters coordinates without necessarily moving the physical vector.

<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>3</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>2</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>+</mo> <mn>2</mn> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math>, so its slanted-basis coordinates are <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>2</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math>. A plane inside three-dimensional coordinates still has dimension two.

Appendix.title: Bfloat16
Appendix.Content: Bfloat16
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: C006 · Latest development: C006
Definition and mechanism
BF16 has1/8/7 fields, bias127 and8 normal precision bits. It keeps broad exponent range at coarse spacing2^-7 above1. A nearest-even conversion must handle NaNs separately from finite rounding.
Prerequisites

ListItem.Content: IEEE-754 floating point — supplies the representation or validity rule used above.
Rounding to nearest ties to even — supplies the representation or validity rule used above.

Recall and next depth

Pending: Target flushing, payload conventions and accumulation instructions require independent checks.
Source and navigation
Continuous teaching story · Source coverage ledger · Dependency Map
Range is preserved more than precision

Bfloat16 keeps the 8-bit exponent width of binary32 but stores only 7 explicit fraction bits. A normal value therefore has 8 bits of significand precision including the hidden leading one. Compared with IEEE binary16, bfloat16 sacrifices substantial local precision to retain a binary32-like exponent range.

That trade is useful for ML tensors whose dynamic range matters more than fine per-value precision. It is poor for algorithms where small relative changes accumulate over many steps. Common mixed-precision kernels store operands in bfloat16 but accumulate products in binary32.

Conversion is not merely truncation if the implementation promises round-to-nearest behavior. Correct rounding must account for discarded bits and tie policy; NaN payloads and infinities need explicit handling. Tests should inspect bit-level round trips, halfway cases, overflow/underflow, NaNs, and error growth in dot products accumulated in bfloat16 versus binary32.

Appendix.title: Big endian
Appendix.Content: Big endian
Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C003 · Latest development: C003
Definition and mechanism

The lowest address holds the most-significant octet. For 0x12345678, offsets 0–3 hold 12/34/56/78. A decoder repeatedly multiplies its prefix by 256 and adds the next octet. Integer value is independent of host order.
Prerequisites

ListItem.Content: Endianness — Byte order tells how digit significance maps to sequence positions.
Positional notation — Base-256 weighted digits give the codec’s numeric meaning.

C003 teaching chapter · Part definitions · Dependency Map
Reconstruction depth
Big-endian byte order stores the most-significant byte of a multibyte integer at the lowest address. For the 32-bit value
Appendix.RawBlock: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"> <mn>0</mn> <mi>x</mi> <mn>12345678</mn> <mo>,</mo> </math>
Appendix.Content: the four bytes in increasing address order are
Appendix.RawBlock: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"> <mn>12</mn> <mstyle scriptlevel="0"> <mspace width="0.278em" /> </mstyle> <mn>34</mn> <mstyle scriptlevel="0"> <mspace width="0.278em" /> </mstyle> <mn>56</mn> <mstyle scriptlevel="0"> <mspace width="0.278em" /> </mstyle> <mn>78.</mn> </math>
Appendix.Content: Endianness describes byte ordering, not bit ordering inside a byte and not the abstract value of the integer. Arithmetic on a correctly loaded integer is independent of whether its bytes arrived in big- or little-endian form.

The engineering boundary is serialization. A file or network protocol must declare byte order explicitly, because dumping a host struct makes the external format depend on machine layout, padding and host endianness. Network protocols traditionally use big-endian network byte order, but a custom format may choose either convention as long as decoding is explicit.

A reliable parser reads bytes, validates length, reconstructs the integer with shifts or standardized byte-swap facilities, and tests known byte sequences. The failure to avoid is double-swapping: once bytes have been converted into host numeric value, downstream code should not keep carrying an ambiguous network-order integer type unless the API makes that distinction explicit.

Appendix.title: Binary conversion
Appendix.Content: Binary conversion
Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C001 · Latest development: C001
Definition and mechanism
Repeated division emits low-to-high binary digits; weighted sums or Horner evaluation decode them.

Euclidean division writes n = 2q + r, where q is the integer quotient and r is 0 or 1. Repeated remainders give bits from least to most significant. Zero must be represented explicitly as 0. Horner evaluation reads left to right: accumulator = 2×accumulator + next bit.
Prerequisites

ListItem.Content: Positional notation — A base is the number of available digits.

Definition and mechanism

Shift dividend bits into a remainder, compare/subtract the divisor, and emit quotient bits while maintaining <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>D</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mi>Q</mi> <mi>d</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mi>R</mi> </math>.

At each dividend bit, form remainder=2×remainder+bit. If it reaches the divisor, subtract and emit quotient bit 1; otherwise emit 0. For 13/3, quotient 4 and remainder 1 satisfy 13=4×3+1. A wider temporary may be needed for shifted remainder.

Reconstruction depth

IEEE binary16 uses 1 sign bit, 5 exponent bits and 10 stored fraction bits. Normal numbers have an implicit leading one, giving 11 bits of significand precision. The narrow exponent and significand make half precision cheaper to store and move than binary32, but not a drop-in replacement for every intermediate.

Around magnitude 1, adjacent normal values are roughly <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msup> <mn>2</mn> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>−</mo> <mn>10</mn> </mrow> </msup> </math> apart. As magnitude grows, spacing grows with the exponent. Subnormals extend representable values toward zero with reduced precision, while exponent all-ones encodes infinities and NaNs.

A graphics or ML pipeline should distinguish storage precision from accumulation precision. Vertex attributes, textures or weights may be stored as binary16 while dot products and reductions accumulate in binary32. This often preserves bandwidth savings without accepting catastrophic accumulation error.

Tests should include exact endpoints around 1, overflow to infinity according to conversion rules, underflow and subnormals, signed zero and NaN propagation policy. Hardware may flush subnormals or use mixed-precision instructions, so performance behavior requires target-specific evidence.

Appendix.title: Binary64
Appendix.Content: Binary64
Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C004 · Latest development: C004
Definition and mechanism
A 64-bit binary interchange format with 1/11/52 fields, 53 significant normal bits and bias 1023. Normal exponent range is −1022 through 1023. Word 3FF0000000000000 means 1.
Prerequisites

Precision, exponent range, and the integer-exact region

IEEE-754 binary64 uses 1 sign bit, 11 exponent bits, and 52 stored fraction bits. Normal values have an implicit leading one, giving 53 bits of significand precision. Around magnitude one, the gap between adjacent values is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msup> <mn>2</mn> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>−</mo> <mn>52</mn> </mrow> </msup> </math>.

Every integer with magnitude up to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msup> <mn>2</mn> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mn>53</mn> </mrow> </msup> </math> is exactly representable, but beyond that boundary adjacent integers begin sharing the same floating representation. This matters when timestamps, IDs, byte counts or large counters are moved through a double-based API: an integer may be within the exponent range yet still lose unit precision.

Binary64 dramatically reduces rounding error compared with binary32 but doubles storage/bandwidth and does not cure unstable algorithms. Coordinate systems for large worlds often use double on the CPU and camera-relative float on the GPU, making the conversion boundary part of the design.

Tests should cover adjacent values around <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msup> <mn>2</mn> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mn>53</mn> </mrow> </msup> </math>, normal/subnormal transitions, overflow, signed zero, infinities/NaNs, and cancellation cases that remain ill-conditioned even at 64-bit precision.

Appendix.title: Build graph usage requirements
Appendix.Content: Build graph usage requirements

A build target has two interfaces at once. Its source code exposes a programming interface, while its build-system target exposes the information consumers need to compile and link against that interface.
In CMake terminology, PRIVATE, PUBLIC and INTERFACE describe propagation of usage requirements. They do not correspond to private/public members in C++.
A PRIVATE requirement is needed to build the target itself but should not be inherited by ordinary consumers.
A PUBLIC requirement is needed both by the target and by consumers because the target’s public interface depends on it.
An INTERFACE requirement is consumed by downstream targets but is not used to compile the target’s own sources.
Why public headers force propagation

Suppose library EngineMath has a public header that includes ThirdParty/Vec.hpp. A consumer compiling only its own source plus EngineMath’s public include path still needs the third-party include directory. Marking that dependency PRIVATE may let EngineMath build while every independent consumer fails.
The same reasoning applies to compile features, preprocessor definitions, generated headers and transitive link dependencies whose symbols appear in the public ABI.
The test should therefore be from the consumer’s perspective: can a tiny program include the advertised public header and link using only the public target?
Build graph versus include graph

A textual include graph and a target dependency graph answer different questions. A source file can include a header without the build graph correctly propagating its location. Conversely, linking to a library can be required even when no source file directly includes one of its headers.
Imported targets and namespaced targets are preferable to global compiler/linker flags because the dependency becomes attached to the thing that owns it.
Cycles and architecture

A cycle in target dependencies is often an architecture smell. Static-library cycles can also produce linker-order problems. Dependency inversion, interface targets or extracting a lower-level common module can make the ownership direction explicit.
Evidence

A strong build-interface test creates a minimal consumer target in a separate directory, links only the exported target, and compiles with no accidental include directories from the main project. Installation/export tests should repeat this against the installed package so the build tree cannot hide missing usage requirements.
Read the connected explanation in Continuous Notes/Computing Foundations - From Bits to C++ and Systems APIs#The build graph becomes another interface.
Related: C++ modules and reachability, ABI and object layout, Interface contracts and publication.

Why clipping a contribution changes the estimator
A capped weighted update replaces an unbounded contribution <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>w</mi> <mi>x</mi> </math> with something like
Appendix.RawBlock: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mover> <mi>w</mi> <mo stretchy="false">~</mo> </mover> </mrow> <mo>=</mo> <mo data-mjx-texclass="OP" movablelimits="true">min</mo> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>w</mi> <mo>,</mo> <msub> <mi>w</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mi>m</mi> <mi>a</mi> <mi>x</mi> </mrow> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>,</mo> <mstyle scriptlevel="0"> <mspace width="2em" /> </mstyle> <mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mover> <mi>w</mi> <mo stretchy="false">~</mo> </mover> </mrow> <mi>x</mi> <mo>.</mo> </math>
Appendix.Content: The cap protects an online system from one extreme weight dominating state, overflowing finite precision, or creating intolerable variance. But unless the cap is part of the intended mathematical model, it introduces bias: contributions above the threshold are deliberately underrepresented.

This trade appears in importance weighting, robust online statistics, adaptive reconstruction and control. The correct question is not “does clipping stabilize it?” but how bias changes as the cap moves and whether the uncapped tail is real signal, model mismatch, or corrupted data.

A useful experiment sweeps <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>w</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mi>m</mi> <mi>a</mi> <mi>x</mi> </mrow> </msub> </math>, records variance, bias against an uncapped/high-precision reference, effective sample size and downstream failure rate. Tests should include weights exactly at the cap, negative/invalid weights when the domain forbids them, and extreme values that would overflow the uncapped path.

Appendix.title: Carry and borrow
Appendix.Content: Carry and borrow
Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C002 · Latest development: C002
Definition and mechanism
Carry is information leaving the high end of unsigned addition; borrow records an unmet subtraction at a bit position. Architecture subtraction flags may encode borrow or no-borrow.

For N-bit unsigned addition, carry-out means the exact sum exceeds 2ᴺ−1. A borrow means a subtraction needs value from a higher position. In an ordinary unsigned subtract, A<B implies borrow. Some architectures expose the complement, no borrow, in their carry flag.
Prerequisites

Boolean algebra — The logical domain is false/true.

Appendix.title: Carry, overflow, negative, and zero flags
Appendix.source: Concepts/Carry, overflow, negative, and zero flags.md
Appendix.Content: Carry, overflow, negative, and zero flags
Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C002 · Latest development: C002
Definition and mechanism
C reports unsigned carry, V signed-range failure, N the result’s sign bit, and Z an all-zero architectural result.

For eight-bit addition, C tests exact sum>255; V tests signed sum outside [−128,127]; N is result bit 7; Z tests low result==0. 7F+01 gives 0,1,1,0; FF+01 gives 1,0,0,1 in C,V,N,Z order. These are binary arithmetic flags, not decimal-mode behavior.
Prerequisites

ListItem.Content: Two's complement — For raw unsigned value u in N bits, signed decoding is u when u<2ᴺ⁻¹, otherwise u−2ᴺ.
Full adder — A full adder adds A, B, and carry-in.

Appendix.title: Checksums CRCs and hashes
Appendix.Content: Checksums, CRCs, and hashes
Curriculum depth: Reference implemented and known-answer tested · First seen: C006 · Latest development: Phase 28 repair
A checksum or digest maps an arbitrary byte sequence to a smaller fixed-size value. Different families make different promises.
An additive checksum is mainly an accidental-error detector and is weak against structured changes such as reordering or compensating byte modifications.

A CRC interprets bits as a polynomial over <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>G</mi> <mi>F</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>2</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math> and computes a remainder under a declared generator polynomial and parameter set. CRCs are excellent for many transmission/storage error patterns, but they are not cryptographic authenticators.

A cryptographic hash such as SHA-256 is designed so that finding collisions or preimages is computationally hard under the security assumptions of the primitive. A hash still does not authenticate a file when an attacker can replace both the file and the untrusted hash value.
SHA-256 compression structure

SHA-256 pads the message with a one bit, enough zero bits to leave 64 bits at the end of the final 512-bit block, and then the original message length modulo <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msup> <mn>2</mn> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mn>64</mn> </mrow> </msup> </math>. Each 512-bit block expands sixteen 32-bit words into a 64-word schedule and updates an eight-word chaining state through 64 rounds.

The important learning boundary is representation: message words are interpreted in the algorithm’s specified byte order. Reinterpreting native host integers without explicit conversion can produce a platform-specific hash implementation.
Known-answer evidence

tools/labs/crypto_primitives_lab.cpp implements SHA-256 directly and validates the standard digest of “abc” and the empty message. The same SHA-256 implementation is then used by HMAC, HKDF and a domain-separated Merkle tree.

This raises the evidence above “definition present,” but the implementation is educational. It is not reviewed for constant-time behavior, hardware acceleration, fault attacks, side channels or production cryptographic use.
What to use for what
Use a checksum/CRC when the threat is accidental corruption and the protocol specifies the polynomial/parameters.
Use a cryptographic hash when content identity or collision/preimage resistance is required.
Use a MAC such as HMAC when a party holding a secret key must authenticate content.
Use a digital signature when verification must be possible without sharing the signing secret.
Prerequisites
Bitwise XOR, Serialization, Endianness.
Used by
Integrity and authenticity, HMAC and HKDF, Merkle trees and authenticated structure, Production manifests and transactional publication.

Appendix.title: Conditioning and singularity
Appendix.Content: Conditioning and singularity
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: C004 · Latest development: Phase7
Definition and mechanism

Conditioning measures sensitivity to input perturbation. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>A</mi> <mo>=</mo> <msup> <mn>10</mn> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>−</mo> <mn>4</mn> </mrow> </msup> <msub> <mi>I</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msub> </math> has determinant <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msup> <mn>10</mn> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>−</mo> <mn>8</mn> </mrow> </msup> </math> but condition number one in the 2-norm. Uniform scaling changes determinant magnitude without changing this conditioning measure.

Phase 7 develops <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>κ</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>A</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>=</mo> <mo data-mjx-texclass="ORD" fence="false" stretchy="false">‖</mo> <mi>A</mi> <mo data-mjx-texclass="ORD" fence="false" stretchy="false">‖</mo> <mo data-mjx-texclass="ORD" fence="false" stretchy="false">‖</mo> <msup> <mi>A</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>−</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msup> <mo data-mjx-texclass="ORD" fence="false" stretchy="false">‖</mo> </math>, near-parallel-column sensitivity, pivoted elimination and inverse residuals. Equal determinants can conceal very different stretch ratios: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>diag</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msup> <mn>10</mn> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>−</mo> <mn>10</mn> </mrow> </msup> <mo>,</mo> <msup> <mn>10</mn> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>−</mo> <mn>10</mn> </mrow> </msup> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>diag</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>,</mo> <msup> <mn>10</mn> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>−</mo> <mn>20</mn> </mrow> </msup> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math> both have determinant <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msup> <mn>10</mn> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>−</mo> <mn>20</mn> </mrow> </msup> </math> but conditions one and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msup> <mn>10</mn> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mn>20</mn> </mrow> </msup> </math>. Subtraction of nearby inputs exposes input uncertainty relative to a small difference. Sensitivity belongs to the problem; exact subtraction of stored operands cannot recover information lost when those inputs were rounded.

Appendix.title: Copy-on-write
Appendix.Content: Copy-on-write
Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C003 · Latest development: C003
Definition and mechanism

COW initially shares physical contents while deferring private copies. A permitted write to a COW-protected mapping faults; OS allocates/copies a frame, updates the writer’s mapping, and retries. Other mappings retain old contents. Not every read-only page is COW, so not every write fault is recoverable.
Prerequisites

ListItem.Content: Page faults and demand paging — Deferred private copying is implemented through a recoverable write fault.

Appendix.Content: Used by
Update downstream uses when later chunks build on this concept.
Recall and next depth
Show frame identity before and after one process writes.
Pending: Fork behavior, mapping flags, reference tracking and costs.
Source and navigation
C003 teaching chapter · Part definitions · Dependency Map
Reconstruction depth

Copy-on-write delays physical copying until shared data is actually modified. At the virtual-memory level, two address spaces may initially map the same physical page as read-only. A write triggers a protection fault; the operating system allocates a private page, copies old contents, updates the writer’s page table and resumes the instruction.

The key invariant is logical independence after a write, even though physical storage was shared before it. This is why process creation can be cheap initially without eagerly duplicating every writable page.

COW has costs that disappear in a high-level description: the first write can incur a page fault and page copy, dirty-page accounting changes, and large working sets can turn an initially cheap clone into substantial later memory traffic. Huge pages and NUMA placement make those costs workload-dependent.

Do not generalize OS page COW into a recommendation for C++ value types. Library-level copy-on-write strings or containers complicate iterator/reference validity, threading and mutation semantics. The mechanism is useful when ownership and fault or copy behavior are explicit.

Source and navigation
Continuous explanation · Coverage and source gap · Sources and verification
University course development

Computational geometry often decides whether points are left or right of a directed line, whether three points are collinear, or whether a point lies inside a circle. These decisions reduce to determinant signs. For points <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>a</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>b</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>c</mi> </math> in 2D, the signed area determinant classifies orientation. If its exact value is near zero, floating-point rounding can change the sign and make neighboring algorithms disagree, creating flipped triangles or invalid topology. Robust predicates evaluate a fast approximate determinant with an error bound; if the sign is certain they stop, and if uncertain they recompute with higher precision. This adaptive strategy spends extra work only near degeneracy. It does not make constructed intersection coordinates exact, but it protects discrete branching decisions that must be globally consistent in triangulation, mesh repair, and ray-edge intersection.

Appendix.title: Deterministic reduction tree
Appendix.Content: Deterministic reduction tree
Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C005 · Latest development: C005
Definition and mechanism

A reduction fixes input order, partition and merge topology so scheduling cannot change the arithmetic grouping. Midpoint recursive splitting is one such tree. Different SIMD widths or partitions can otherwise change it.
Prerequisites

ListItem.Content: Compensated and pairwise summation — A fixed pairwise topology specifies the additions a deterministic reduction performs.

Appendix.Content: Used by

ListItem.Content: Numerical reproducibility — uses this mechanism to establish its numerical contract.

Appendix.Content: Recall and next depth
Reconstruct the definition’s example and name the assumptions that make it valid.
Pending: Cross-platform identity also requires compatible operation semantics, precision, libraries and environment.
Source and navigation
M005 teaching chapter · Part definitions · Dependency Map
Reconstruction depth

Floating-point addition is not associative, so a parallel reduction can change low bits when thread count, work partition or scheduling changes. A deterministic reduction tree fixes grouping order independently of which worker finishes first.

For eight values, a balanced tree can always compute <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mn>0</mn> </msub> <mo>+</mo> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mn>1</mn> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>+</mo> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msub> <mo>+</mo> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mn>3</mn> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>+</mo> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mn>4</mn> </msub> <mo>+</mo> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mn>5</mn> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>+</mo> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mn>6</mn> </msub> <mo>+</mo> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mn>7</mn> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math>. The balanced tree can also reduce error growth compared with some highly unbalanced orders, although it is not equivalent to exact or compensated summation.

Determinism costs constraints: the implementation may need stable chunk boundaries, temporary partials and an ordered merge. On GPUs, subgroup width and dispatch shape can otherwise change the effective tree.

Tests should permute scheduling while preserving logical indices and require identical result bits for the deterministic path. A separate accuracy test should compare against a higher-precision or compensated reference; repeatability and numerical accuracy are related but distinct properties.

Appendix.title: Endianness
Appendix.Content: Endianness
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: C001 · Latest development: C003
Definition and mechanism

Byte order maps numeric significance to ascending addresses without changing the value. Little endian emits the low octet first; big endian emits the high octet first. The 32-bit value 0x12345678 becomes 78/56/34/12 or 12/34/56/78 respectively. It does not specify intra-byte bit order. Explicit unsigned shifts/masks define an external representation independent of native host order.
Prerequisites

ListItem.Content: Byte and octet — Byte units define both storage offsets and significance digits.
Bit significance — Distinguish byte significance from where it is stored.

Appendix.title: Exclusive and shared smart-pointer ownership
Appendix.Content: Exclusive and shared smart-pointer ownership
Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C010 · Latest development: C010
Definition and mechanism

std::unique_ptr<T, D> is a move-only exclusive owner whose deleter D defines disposal. get() exposes a borrow; release() transfers the responsibility without deleting. std::shared_ptr<T> joins a shared ownership group represented by a control block; the managed object is destroyed when the last strong owner is released. The control block can outlive the object while weak observers remain. The stored pointer and the object whose destruction the control block arranges can differ (for example, aliasing ownership).

Shared ownership is not pointee synchronization. Concurrent operations on distinct smart-pointer handles do not automatically make concurrent access to T safe. Use sharing only when several independent parties truly retain the same lifetime.
Prerequisites

ListItem.Content: Ownership and non-owning views — Access-only views and ownership responsibilities are different contracts.
RAII and resource handles — Smart pointers are standard resource owners built around lifetime-bound cleanup.

Appendix.title: Exhaustive finite-state testing
Appendix.Content: Exhaustive finite-state testing
Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C002 · Latest development: C002
Definition and mechanism

Small fixed domains can be enumerated completely; eight-bit add-with-carry has <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mn>256</mn> <mo>×</mo> <mn>256</mn> <mo>×</mo> <mn>2</mn> <mo>=</mo> <mn>131,072</mn> </math> inputs.

Exhaustive testing enumerates every input in a chosen finite domain. Two bytes and carry give 256×256×2=131072 inputs. Use an independent signed-range oracle instead of restating the same overflow formula; complete arithmetic inputs do not cover all emulator state.
Prerequisites

ListItem.Content: Interpretation contract — For 0xAD, unsigned interpretation gives 173; eight-bit two’s complement gives −83.
Boolean algebra — The logical domain is false/true.

Appendix.Content: Fixed-point range and resolution
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: C006 · Latest development: C006

Reconstruction depth

A fixed-point value stores an integer <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>q</mi> </math> together with an implied scale <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>s</mi> </math>, so the represented real quantity is
Appendix.RawBlock: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"> <mi>x</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mi>q</mi> <mstyle scriptlevel="0"> <mspace width="0.167em" /> </mstyle> <mi>s</mi> <mo>.</mo> </math>
Appendix.Content: For a binary fractional format with <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>F</mi> </math> fractional bits, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>s</mi> <mo>=</mo> <msup> <mn>2</mn> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>−</mo> <mi>F</mi> </mrow> </msup> </math>. Increasing <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>F</mi> </math> improves resolution but consumes integer range because storage width has not changed. For signed <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>N</mi> </math>-bit two’s-complement storage, the approximate real range is
Appendix.RawBlock: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"> <mo stretchy="false">[</mo> <mo>−</mo> <msup> <mn>2</mn> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mi>N</mi> <mo>−</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msup> <mi>s</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msup> <mn>2</mn> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mi>N</mi> <mo>−</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msup> <mo>−</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mi>s</mi> <mo stretchy="false">]</mo> <mo>.</mo> </math>
Appendix.Content: This makes format choice an error-budget decision rather than a syntax decision. Position data may need large range; normalized coefficients may need fine local resolution. Multiplication temporarily doubles the number of fractional bits, so a production operation needs a widened intermediate or a deliberate rescale, round and saturate policy.

Tests should exercise representable endpoints, half-step rounding, overflow, negative values, multiplication rescaling and accumulation. A format can be perfectly deterministic and still be numerically unsuitable if its step size exceeds the physical or visual tolerance of the subsystem using it.

Appendix.title: Fixed-width integer types
Appendix.Content: Fixed-width integer types
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: C002 · Latest development: C008
Definition and mechanism
Native bool is not a portable wire/GPU field; validate an explicit zero/one encoding. Floating type names do not guarantee exact IEEE formats; is_iec559 alone does not identify binary32.

int need not be32 bits; sizeof(char)==1 measures a C++ byte and CHAR_BIT is at least8. Plain char is distinct from signed/unsigned char and its signedness is implementation-defined. size_t represents object sizes, not a stable serialized field. Query numeric_limits for digits, lowest, max and floating capabilities. A container’s size_type is not universally required to be exactly size_t.
<cstdint> exact-width types express binary layout contracts; least and fast families have different portability goals.

When supplied, std::uint32_t has exactly 32 bits; uint_least32_t has at least 32; uint_fast32_t is chosen for speed with at least 32. Exact-width typedefs are optional on implementations lacking suitable types. size_t represents object sizes and ptrdiff_t differences.
Prerequisites

ListItem.Content: Machine word — A processor’s natural integer processing width is often called its word width, but the term is architecture dependent.
Byte and octet — An octet is exactly eight bits.

Appendix.title: Floating-point infinities
Appendix.Content: Floating-point infinities
Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C004 · Latest development: C004
Definition and mechanism
All-one exponent and zero fraction encode signed infinity. This is not maximum finite. Infinity minus itself is NaN; overflow’s result also depends on rounding direction.

Reconstruction depth

IEEE-754 infinities represent values beyond the finite exponent range and results such as nonzero finite division by signed zero. They participate in arithmetic according to defined extended-real-like rules. Adding a finite value to positive infinity stays positive infinity, while indeterminate forms such as infinity minus infinity produce NaN.

Infinity can be useful as a sentinel in algorithms, such as an initial shortest-path distance, because comparisons with finite positive values behave naturally. But it is not automatically a valid physical or engine state. A transform position, mass, texture coordinate or timestamp becoming infinite usually signals overflow or invalid input and should be caught at a subsystem boundary.

A robust numeric API distinguishes the floating type can encode infinity from this domain accepts infinity. Tests should exercise overflow, division by zero under the active floating environment, comparisons, finite-value validation and serialization behavior. Fast-math modes may weaken exceptional-value assumptions, so production guarantees must match compile configuration.

Appendix.title: Forward and backward error
Appendix.Content: Forward and backward error
Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C005 · Latest development: C005
Definition and mechanism

Forward error measures output discrepancy. Backward error measures how much the input must change for the computed output to be exact. Stability concerns algorithm errors; conditioning concerns problem sensitivity. Small backward error can coexist with large forward error.
Prerequisites

ListItem.Content: Absolute and relative error — Discrepancy, magnitude and reference units define sensitivity and threshold significance.

Appendix.title: Full adder
Appendix.Content: Full adder
Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C002 · Latest development: C002
Definition and mechanism

Adds <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>A</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>B</mi> <mo>,</mo> <msub> <mi>C</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mi>i</mi> <mi>n</mi> </mrow> </msub> </math>; sum is three-way XOR and carry is the majority of its inputs.

A full adder adds A, B, and carry-in. Sum is their parity; carry-out is 1 when at least two inputs are 1. Build it from two half adders: add A,B, then add that sum to carry-in, then OR the two carry outputs.
Prerequisites

ListItem.Content: Half adder — A half adder adds two bits with sum S=A XOR B and carry C=A AND B.
Carry and borrow — For N-bit unsigned addition, carry-out means the exact sum exceeds 2ᴺ−1.

Appendix.title: GGUF binary model loading
Appendix.Content: GGUF binary model loading

GGUF is a binary container used by GGML-family inference runtimes. Treating it as “a file full of weights” is too vague for a safe loader. A loader must first establish a byte-level contract: magic, format version, tensor count, metadata count, typed metadata records, tensor descriptors, alignment, tensor-data offsets, and bounds. Only after those checks can tensor bytes become runtime values.

The first four bytes identify the format as GGUF. Multi-byte fields must be decoded according to the file format instead of reinterpreting an arbitrary file buffer as a C++ struct. Native C++ structs inherit compiler padding, alignment and host-representation assumptions that a binary file does not owe the process reading it.
A useful loading pipeline is:

ListItem.Content: Read and validate the fixed prefix.
Parse metadata key/value records with checked lengths.
Parse tensor descriptors: name, rank and shape, data type, and relative data offset.
Compute the aligned start of the tensor-data section.
Validate every tensor interval against file length and arithmetic overflow.
Keep file or mapping ownership alive for every lazy tensor view.
Convert the file tensor type into an internal runtime type only after the descriptor is validated.
Dispatch dequantization or quantized kernels from that internal type rather than from filename assumptions.

Appendix.Content: The official GGUF documentation describes the format as a single-file, extensible model container and defines architecture metadata, tensor data layout information, and attention metadata such as head counts and key/value dimensions. Those metadata values affect runtime shape contracts; they are not merely labels.
Primary reference: https://github.com/ggml-org/ggml/blob/master/docs/gguf.md
Prefix witness

tools/labs/phase29_ml_runtime_lab.cpp parses the GGUF magic, version, tensor count and metadata count from an explicit byte vector using checked little-endian reads. It has a negative case for invalid magic.

That witness intentionally stops at the prefix. It proves that the repository now owns the boundary between raw bytes and validated scalar header fields; it does not pretend that the entire GGUF metadata type system or quantized tensor catalog has already been implemented.
What a full loader must prove

A production reader must defend against truncated strings, absurd ranks, shape-product overflow, unsupported quantization types, alignment overflow, tensor intervals outside the file, duplicate or contradictory metadata, offsets that alias unintentionally, and files whose declared architecture cannot be executed by the runtime.

For memory mapping, “the pointer is valid” is not enough. The mapping object and file lifetime must outlive every lazy tensor view. Page faults also become part of performance: a model that technically maps instantly can still stall during first use if access order faults pages unpredictably.
Quantized execution boundary

GGUF storage type and execution type are separate decisions. A block-quantized format normally stores scale or other metadata together with packed codes. A portable reference path should decode or dot-product those blocks in a simple scalar implementation first. SIMD or Metal kernels then have an independent oracle. If the optimized path disagrees, the scalar path is evidence; if both paths share the same unpacking bug, the test is not independent enough.
Related: Tensor runtime layout and views, Quantized matvec and dequantization, Transformer attention and KV cache runtime, Binary format contracts.
Metadata and tensor-descriptor witness

The earlier prefix-only boundary has now been extended by tools/labs/gguf_metadata_tensor_lab.cpp. The subset parser validates GGUF v3 magic and counts, parses typed UINT32 and STRING metadata, consumes general.alignment, reads tensor names/ranks/dimensions/type IDs/relative offsets, computes the aligned tensor-data start, and rejects truncation or invalid alignment.

The parser remains deliberately incomplete rather than permissive. Unsupported metadata types are rejected instead of skipped with guessed sizes. It does not yet implement arrays, every GGUF value type, every GGML quantized tensor block, tokenizer metadata, endian conversion for big-endian files, or payload interval validation for all tensor types. That is the correct boundary for an independent reference: a small loader should fail loudly outside the subset it actually understands.

Appendix.title: GPU workgroups and synchronization
Appendix.Content: GPU workgroups and synchronization

GPU execution has several scopes that must not be collapsed into the word “thread.” An invocation executes one logical shader instance. Invocations are grouped into workgroups for explicitly shared local memory and workgroup barriers. Hardware may execute smaller subgroup or SIMD groups inside a workgroup. Many workgroups make up a dispatch.

A workgroup barrier can coordinate invocations that participate in that workgroup. It cannot create a global barrier across arbitrary workgroups in the same dispatch. If an algorithm requires all blocks to finish phase A before any block begins phase B, use a mechanism that establishes that dependency: usually separate dispatches/commands with API synchronization, or a carefully designed device-wide primitive supported by the target model.
Execution barrier versus memory visibility

“Everyone reached the same point” and “everyone can now observe the required writes” are related but distinct contracts. APIs and shading languages expose memory scopes and semantics because a control barrier alone is not a universal cache flush.
The producer/consumer question is always:

ListItem.Content: what operation produced the bytes?
what later operation consumes them?
which execution scopes must be ordered?
which memory accesses must become visible?
which resource/subresource is covered?

Appendix.Content: Subgroups

Subgroup collectives can exchange values and perform ballots, reductions and scans without workgroup shared memory. They are fast but require care around subgroup width, inactive lanes and portability. An algorithm that silently assumes 32 lanes can break on hardware using a different subgroup size.
Shared memory and bank conflicts

Workgroup memory is physically optimized for cooperation but has finite capacity and bank structure. Tiling can reduce global bandwidth, yet an unfortunate address pattern can serialize accesses through bank conflicts. Register pressure and shared-memory allocation also constrain occupancy, so increasing tile size is not free.
Evidence boundary

The canonical notes now distinguish CPU semantic models from native hardware evidence. A CPU prefix-scan or render-graph test can prove dependency logic but cannot prove Vulkan visibility, Metal hazard behavior, subgroup width or driver performance. Hardware claims require validation layers, GPU capture/counters, and device-specific results.
Teach and reconstruct: Continuous Notes/Computing Foundations - From Bits to C++ and Systems APIs#Let many invocations cooperate without inventing a global clock.
Related: Prefix scan and stream compaction, Shader buffer ABI.

Appendix.title: Groupwise quantization and metadata
Appendix.Content: Groupwise quantization and metadata
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: C006 · Latest development: C006
Definition and mechanism
Local groups share a scale, improving adaptation at a metadata cost. Symmetric INT4 calibration maxAbs/7 reconstructs codes around [-7,7]; float scales add about 32/G bits per value for full groups.
Prerequisites

ListItem.Content: Affine quantization and zero point — supplies the representation or validity rule used above.
Bit packing — supplies the representation or validity rule used above.

Appendix.Content: Used by
Connect later dependent concepts here when their explanations use this mechanism.
Recall and next depth
Reconstruct the example and identify the condition that would invalidate it.
Pending: No task-accuracy or throughput benchmark was run.
Source and navigation
Continuous teaching story · Source coverage ledger · Dependency Map
Reconstruction depth

Groupwise quantization divides a tensor into blocks and assigns quantization parameters per block rather than per entire tensor. For affine quantization, a group may store scale <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>s</mi> </math> and zero point <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>z</mi> </math> so that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mover> <mi>x</mi> <mo stretchy="false">^</mo> </mover> </mrow> <mo>=</mo> <mi>s</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>q</mi> <mo>−</mo> <mi>z</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math>.

The group size controls a three-way trade: smaller groups follow local distributions more accurately but increase metadata bandwidth and reduce the work sharing one scale; larger groups amortize metadata and simplify vector kernels but increase approximation error when values have heterogeneous ranges.

Metadata is part of the runtime format. A decoder needs the exact grouping axis and order, group length, code width, scale type, zero-point type, tail policy, alignment and byte order. A mismatch can produce plausible but entirely wrong model outputs.

Benchmarking should report payload plus metadata bytes and measure the real dequantized dot-product kernel rather than only offline reconstruction error. The best group size depends on cache behavior, SIMD width, memory bandwidth and model sensitivity.

Appendix.Content: Guard round and sticky bits
Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C004 · Latest development: C004
Definition and mechanism
Guard is first discarded bit, round the next, sticky ORs all remaining bits. With retained low bit L, nearest-even increments when G AND (R OR sticky OR L). Sticky summarizes any nonzero tail.
Prerequisites

ListItem.Content: Boolean algebra — The rounding increment condition combines one-bit guard, round, sticky and parity inputs.
Rounding to nearest ties to even — Midpoint parity determines discarded-tail decisions and the normal relative-error bound.

Appendix.title: Guest and host integer domains
Appendix.Content: Guest and host integer domains
Curriculum depth: Forward · First seen: C002 · Latest development: C002
Definition and mechanism

An emulator may compute an <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>N</mi> </math>-bit guest operation in a wider host type so carry and other discarded architectural information remain observable.

Guest means the machine being emulated; host means the implementation platform. An eight-bit guest addition can use a host temporary holding 0–511, extract carry, then narrow to 0–255. Host signed overflow must never be used to imitate guest wrap.
Prerequisites

ListItem.Content: Fixed-width integer types — When supplied, std::uint32_t has exactly 32 bits; uint_least32_t has at least 32; uint_fast32_t is chosen for speed with at least 32.
Carry, overflow, negative, and zero flags — For eight-bit addition, C tests exact sum>255; V tests signed sum outside [−128,127]; N is result bit 7; Z tests low result==0.

Appendix.title: HMAC and HKDF
Appendix.Content: HMAC and HKDF
HMAC authenticates a message under a shared secret key. HKDF uses HMAC to turn input keying material into one or more pseudorandom-looking keys with explicit context separation.
Extract then expand
HKDF has two conceptual stages.
Extract computes a pseudorandom key:
Appendix.RawBlock: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"> <mi>P</mi> <mi>R</mi> <mi>K</mi> <mo>=</mo> <msub> <mi>HMAC</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mi>s</mi> <mi>a</mi> <mi>l</mi> <mi>t</mi> </mrow> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>I</mi> <mi>K</mi> <mi>M</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>.</mo> </math>
Appendix.Content: Expand derives output keying material in blocks:
Appendix.RawBlock: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"> <mi>T</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>=</mo> <msub> <mi>HMAC</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mi>P</mi> <mi>R</mi> <mi>K</mi> </mrow> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>i</mi> <mi>n</mi> <mi>f</mi> <mi>o</mi> <mstyle scriptlevel="0"> <mspace width="0.167em" /> </mstyle> <mo data-mjx-texclass="ORD" fence="false" stretchy="false">‖</mo> <mstyle scriptlevel="0"> <mspace width="0.167em" /> </mstyle> <mn>0</mn> <mi>x</mi> <mn>01</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>,</mo> </math>

<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"> <mi>T</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>i</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>=</mo> <msub> <mi>HMAC</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mi>P</mi> <mi>R</mi> <mi>K</mi> </mrow> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>T</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>i</mi> <mo>−</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mstyle scriptlevel="0"> <mspace width="0.167em" /> </mstyle> <mo data-mjx-texclass="ORD" fence="false" stretchy="false">‖</mo> <mstyle scriptlevel="0"> <mspace width="0.167em" /> </mstyle> <mi>i</mi> <mi>n</mi> <mi>f</mi> <mi>o</mi> <mstyle scriptlevel="0"> <mspace width="0.167em" /> </mstyle> <mo data-mjx-texclass="ORD" fence="false" stretchy="false">‖</mo> <mstyle scriptlevel="0"> <mspace width="0.167em" /> </mstyle> <mi>i</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>.</mo> </math>
Appendix.Content: Concatenate blocks until the requested output length is reached.

The info field is not decoration. It lets the same root keying material derive separate keys for different purposes, versions, peers or directions. Domain separation reduces accidental cross-protocol key reuse.
A salt can improve extraction and should follow the protocol design. HKDF does not create entropy that is absent from the input keying material.
Evidence
tools/labs/crypto_primitives_lab.cpp validates HMAC-SHA256 against RFC 4231 and HKDF-SHA256 extract/expand against RFC 5869 test vectors.
That proves the bit-level reference on those vectors. It does not establish side-channel resistance, secret erasure, key storage, protocol context selection or application security.
Primary standards: RFC 2104 / RFC 4231 for HMAC testing and RFC 5869 for HKDF.
Related: Integrity and authenticity, Checksums CRCs and hashes.

Appendix.title: Half adder
Appendix.Content: Half adder
Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C002 · Latest development: C002
Definition and mechanism

Adds two bits with <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>S</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mi>A</mi> <mo>⊕</mo> <mi>B</mi> </math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>C</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mi>A</mi> <mo>∧</mo> <mi>B</mi> </math>, but accepts no incoming carry.

A half adder adds two bits with sum S=A XOR B and carry C=A AND B. Inputs 1,1 produce binary 10: low sum 0, carry 1. It cannot consume a carry from a previous position, which motivates the full adder.
Prerequisites

ListItem.Content: Bitwise XOR — XOR returns 1 when inputs differ.

Appendix.Content: Used by

ListItem.Content: Full adder — uses half adder as part of its representation or reasoning.

Appendix.Content: Recall and next depth

C002 teaching chapter · Part definitions and mechanisms · Dependency Map
From truth table to gate delay
A half adder adds two one-bit inputs <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>a</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>b</mi> </math>. The sum bit is XOR and the carry bit is AND:
Appendix.RawBlock: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"> <mi>s</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mi>a</mi> <mo>⊕</mo> <mi>b</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mstyle scriptlevel="0"> <mspace width="2em" /> </mstyle> <mi>c</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mi>a</mi> <mo>∧</mo> <mi>b</mi> <mo>.</mo> </math>
Appendix.Content: The truth table is not just a memorization device; it proves why one output bit cannot encode all four input sums. Input <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mn>1</mn> <mo>+</mo> <mn>1</mn> </math> produces binary <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mn>10</mn> </math>, requiring a second bit for carry.

A half adder has no carry-in, so it cannot by itself build every bit position of a multi-bit integer addition. A full adder incorporates carry-in and can be composed into ripple-carry or faster prefix structures. The important systems connection is dependency depth: in a ripple chain, each bit may wait for the previous carry, whereas parallel-prefix adders reorganize generate/propagate information to reduce critical path.
A reconstruction exercise should derive XOR/AND from the four rows, compose two half adders into a full adder, then explain why gate count and propagation depth are different optimization targets.

Appendix.title: Hessians and local curvature
Appendix.Content: Hessians and local curvature
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 9 · Latest development: Phase 9
Definition and mechanism

The Hessian collects second partial derivatives of a scalar objective. It describes how the gradient changes and supplies the quadratic term in a local Taylor model. For a smooth scalar field, the Hessian is symmetric under the usual equality-of-mixed-partials assumptions. Its eigenvectors indicate local curvature directions: positive eigenvalues give upward curvature, negative values downward curvature, and near-zero values weakly constrained directions. A positive-definite Hessian supports a strict local minimum in the unconstrained setting, while an indefinite Hessian signals a saddle-like local model. The Hessian is not the same as the curvature of an embedded geometric surface, though both involve second-order change. In optimization, exact Newton steps solve with the Hessian; practical methods may regularize or approximate it because conditioning, cost, or indefiniteness can make direct steps unreliable.
Prerequisites
Used by

Content.Link: Nonlinear least squares: Gauss-Newton and Levenberg-Marquardt

Appendix.title: Hexadecimal
Appendix.Content: Hexadecimal
Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C001 · Latest development: C001
Definition and mechanism
Base 16 maps one digit to four bits, preserving visible bit structure compactly.

Hex digits 0–9 and A–F represent values 0–15. A nibble is four bits, so 1010 1101₂ is AD₁₆. Group from the right and pad only the left when needed. Human digit order does not determine array packing order.
Prerequisites

Bit significance — LSB means least significant bit, normally position 0 with weight 1.

Appendix.title: Huge pages and TLB reach
Appendix.Content: Huge pages and TLB reach
Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C003 · Latest development: C003
Definition and mechanism

A larger page covers more bytes per translation. With T same-size cached entries, illustrative reach is T×P bytes. One GiB requires 262144 pages at 4 KiB versus 512 at 2 MiB. Larger pages trade flexibility, availability, fragmentation and fault granularity; the counts alone do not prove performance improvement.
Prerequisites

ListItem.Content: TLB — Larger pages change the amount of memory covered by cached translations.
Allocator fragmentation — Coarser allocation granularity introduces space/availability trade-offs.

Appendix.Content: Used by
Update downstream uses when later chunks build on this concept.
Recall and next depth
Calculate page counts without asserting a universal speedup.
Pending: Mixed page sizes, workloads, benchmarks and OS policy.
Source and navigation
C003 teaching chapter · Part definitions · Dependency Map
Reach, fragmentation, and measurement

TLB reach is approximately the number of cached translations multiplied by the page size. If a TLB can hold <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>N</mi> </math> translations, switching from 4 KiB pages to 2 MiB huge pages can increase the bytes covered by those translations by a factor of 512.

That does not make huge pages universally faster. They can increase internal fragmentation, make allocation/compaction harder, change NUMA placement behavior and waste memory when only small portions of each huge page are touched. Transparent Huge Pages may also promote or split mappings asynchronously, so an application should not infer actual page size from its allocation API alone.

The right benchmark holds the useful computation fixed while varying working-set size and access stride, then observes TLB/page-walk counters where available. A speedup from huge pages should correlate with translation pressure rather than simply with a different allocator or cache footprint.
For engines, huge pages are most plausible for stable, large, densely accessed arenas—not as a default for every allocation.

Appendix.title: IEEE-754 floating point
Appendix.Content: IEEE-754 floating point
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: C001 · Latest development: C005
Definition and mechanism

IEEE-754 specifies floating formats and behavior including representation classes, rounding directions and exception conditions. A finite bit pattern is interpreted through sign, exponent and significand rules, not as a two’s-complement integer.

Binary32 has 1/8/23 stored fields and 24-bit normal precision; binary64 has 1/11/52 fields and 53-bit normal precision. Word 412A0000 encodes 10.625 in binary32. Exponent-zero and all-one fields distinguish zero/subnormal and infinity/NaN. Normal spacing expands with exponent; nearest-even and directed modes choose representable results under explicit rules. These format names do not prove every C++ float/double has those representations.
M005 develops alignment, cancellation, FMA and accumulated error. Numeric equality is not representation identity, and moving rounding points can change the computed result.
Prerequisites

ListItem.Content: Bit field — A field is a declared range with offset s and width w, not automatically a C++ language bit-field member.
Interpretation contract — For 0xAD, unsigned interpretation gives 173; eight-bit two’s complement gives −83.

Appendix.Content: Used by

Bfloat16 — uses this mechanism to define its representation, error or validation contract.

Appendix.title: Integral promotion
Appendix.Content: Integral promotion
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: C001 · Latest development: C002
Definition and mechanism
Narrow integral operands promote to int when it represents their entire range, otherwise to unsigned int; the operator acts at that promoted width.

Narrow integer types become int if int represents every original value; otherwise they become unsigned int. Promotion happens before the operation, not only on assignment. On the usual host, uint8_t{250}+uint8_t{10} is int 260; converting afterward to uint8_t yields 4.
Prerequisites

Interpretation contract — For 0xAD, unsigned interpretation gives 173; eight-bit two’s complement gives −83.

Appendix.title: Integrity and authenticity
Appendix.Content: Integrity and authenticity
Curriculum depth: Derived with executable primitive witnesses · First seen: C006 · Latest development: Phase 28 repair
Integrity means detecting unauthorized or accidental modification relative to a trusted reference. Authenticity additionally answers who or what was authorized to create the message.
Hashing a file and storing the digest beside it protects against accidental corruption only when the digest itself is trusted. An attacker able to replace both can recompute the hash.
A message authentication code solves a different problem: parties share a secret key <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>K</mi> </math> and compute a tag such as
Appendix.RawBlock: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"> <msub> <mi>HMAC</mi> <mi>K</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>m</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>.</mo> </math>
Appendix.Content: Someone without the key should not be able to forge a valid tag for a modified message under the security assumptions of HMAC and the underlying hash.

A digital signature separates signing and verification keys and supports different trust models. The choice between MAC and signature is therefore architectural, not a matter of which API call is available.
HMAC construction
For hash block size <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>B</mi> </math>, normalize key <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>K</mi> </math> to one block, then compute

Appendix.Content: The inner and outer domains prevent the construction from being equivalent to a naive hash of key concatenated with message.
tools/labs/crypto_primitives_lab.cpp checks HMAC-SHA256 against an RFC 4231 known-answer vector.
Key management is part of authenticity
A mathematically correct MAC does not help if:

ListItem.Content: the key is embedded publicly in the executable;
keys are reused across incompatible protocols without domain separation;
a compromised key is never rotated;
comparison leaks useful timing information in an adversarial environment;
replayed old authenticated messages are accepted without nonce/counter/version policy.

Appendix.Content: Cryptographic primitives are building blocks, not complete protocols.
Production boundary

The educational implementations in this repository exist to make the bytes/rounds/contracts reconstructable. Production systems should use vetted cryptographic libraries and platform key-storage facilities rather than treating a teaching SHA/HMAC implementation as hardened security code.
Related: Checksums CRCs and hashes, HMAC and HKDF, Merkle trees and authenticated structure, Shamir secret sharing.

Appendix.title: Interface contracts and publication
Appendix.Content: Interface contracts and publication
An interface contract says more than which function name to call. It defines the states in which an operation is valid and what becomes true when it succeeds.
A complete contract should state:

ListItem.Content: valid input domain and units;
ownership and lifetime of arguments/results;
mutation and aliasing;
failure representation and exception/error guarantees;
thread/concurrency rules;
timing: immediate, deferred or asynchronous;
invalidation;
observability/publication point.

Appendix.Content: Publication is a state transition

A producer may construct a resource privately and then publish it so consumers can rely on it. Before publication, partial state can remain invisible. After publication, every documented invariant must hold.
For CPU concurrency, release/acquire synchronization is one possible publication mechanism when the memory model requirements fit the data structure.
For asynchronous assets, “decode finished” does not mean “GPU resource is safe to sample.” A useful state machine may distinguish:
requested → decoded → upload recorded → submitted → GPU-ready → published.
Similarly, an obsolete request must not publish after a newer generation has replaced it. Generation IDs or request tokens protect the destination identity.
Ownership versus readiness

A reference can be alive but not ready. A GPU buffer wrapper can exist while its upload is still in flight. Conversely, a resource can be GPU-ready while the CPU owner is about to destroy it unless retirement is deferred until all GPU use completes.
Lifetime and synchronization are independent axes.
Failure guarantees

If publication is atomic, consumers should observe either the old valid version or the new valid version, not a half-updated mixture. That promise requires implementation evidence appropriate to the domain: atomics/locks for CPU state, transaction/staging for files, semaphore/fence/queue dependencies for GPU work.
Evidence

tools/labs/threaded_asset_publication_lab.cpp and tools/labs/production_pipeline_contract_lab.cpp exercise two different publication domains: concurrent asset decoding/publication and deterministic staged production publication.
Read the connected explanation in Continuous Notes/Computing Foundations - From Bits to C++ and Systems APIs#An API is a promise about an operation.
Related: Atomic publication and durability, Production manifests and transactional publication, Vulkan synchronization2 and resource transitions.

Appendix.title: Internal and tail padding
Appendix.Content: Internal and tail padding
Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C003 · Latest development: C003
Definition and mechanism

Internal padding fills holes before members to satisfy alignment. Tail padding follows the final member so array stride preserves complete-object alignment. Under 1/4/1 rules, byte–uint32–byte occupies offsets 0/4/8 with end nine and size 12. Padding is not a semantic format field and cannot be relied on as stable encoded content.

Appendix.title: Interpretation contract
Appendix.Content: Interpretation contract
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: C001 · Latest development: C003

The width, layout, type, and conventions that turn an otherwise ambiguous bit pattern into data.

Appendix.title: Jacobians, pushforwards, and pullbacks
Appendix.Content: Jacobians, pushforwards, and pullbacks
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 9 · Latest development: Phase 9
Definition and mechanism

The Jacobian is the matrix of first derivatives of a vector-valued function. It maps a small input displacement to a first-order output displacement, a forward sensitivity often called a pushforward or Jacobian-vector product. Gradients transform in the reverse direction by the transpose Jacobian, the pullback used in reverse-mode differentiation. These operations differ because vectors and covectors have different transformation rules. Jacobians compose by matrix multiplication and their determinants describe local volume changes. A Jacobian is local: it does not replace a nonlinear transformation globally. At singular points it can lose rank or become ill-conditioned, affecting inverse sensitivity, uncertainty propagation, and optimizer steps. State coordinate ordering and column-vector conventions before interpreting signs or multiplication order.

Appendix.title: Little endian
Appendix.Content: Little endian
Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C003 · Latest development: C003
Definition and mechanism

The lowest address holds the least-significant octet. For 0x12345678, offsets 0–3 hold 78/56/34/12. Writer byte i selects bits 8i through 8i+7; a matching reader restores the same weights. This is byte order, not bit reversal.
Prerequisites

ListItem.Content: Endianness — Byte order tells how digit significance maps to sequence positions.
Shift operations — Shifts relocate a selected byte or address field to its significance position.

Appendix.Content: Used by
Update downstream uses when later chunks build on this concept.

Pending: Mixed-endian cases and protocol integration.
