C003 teaching chapter · Part definitions · Dependency Map
Reconstruction depth
Little-endian byte order stores the least-significant byte first. The 32-bit integer
Appendix.RawBlock: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"> <mn>0</mn> <mi>x</mi> <mn>12345678</mn> </math>
Appendix.Content: appears in increasing memory addresses as
Appendix.RawBlock: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"> <mn>78</mn> <mstyle scriptlevel="0"> <mspace width="0.278em" /> </mstyle> <mn>56</mn> <mstyle scriptlevel="0"> <mspace width="0.278em" /> </mstyle> <mn>34</mn> <mstyle scriptlevel="0"> <mspace width="0.278em" /> </mstyle> <mn>12.</mn> </math>
Appendix.Content: That layout is useful only after the interpretation contract is known: the same four bytes could be part of an integer, float, packed header or text. Endianness never supplies the type by itself.

Most contemporary desktop CPUs are little-endian, but that is not permission to encode a durable binary format with raw object bytes. A format needs explicit field widths, byte order, versioning and bounds checks. If a file is defined little-endian, decode each field as little-endian even on a little-endian host; the explicit operation documents the contract and preserves portability.

Tests should use byte arrays whose numeric values are obvious, include unaligned offsets, and verify both read and write paths. For floating point, byte order and IEEE-754 representation are separate assumptions.

Appendix.title: Logical versus bitwise operators
Appendix.Content: Logical versus bitwise operators
Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C001 · Latest development: C001
Definition and mechanism
Logical operators reduce operands to conditions; bitwise operators transform corresponding representation lanes.

Built-in &&, ||, and ! convert operands to truth conditions. &, |, ^, and ~ operate on integer representation bits. For 10 and 12, 10 & 12 is 8 whereas 10 && 12 is true. Overloaded operators may have additional semantics.
Prerequisites

Bitwise OR — Per lane: only 0|0 is 0; the other three cases are 1.

Appendix.title: Machine epsilon
Appendix.Content: Machine epsilon
Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C004 · Latest development: C004
Definition and mechanism
For these binary types epsilon is upward spacing at 1: 2^-23 for binary32 and 2^-52 for binary64. It is neither minimum positive value nor a physical threshold.
Prerequisites

ListItem.Content: Significand and hidden bit — Fraction weights and effective precision determine value and the smallest retained position.

Appendix.Content: Used by

M004 teaching chapter · Per-part definitions · Dependency Map
Epsilon is local to one magnitude

For a floating type, machine epsilon is commonly defined as the distance from <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mn>1</mn> </math> to the next representable number greater than <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mn>1</mn> </math>. For binary precision <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>p</mi> </math>, that spacing is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msup> <mn>2</mn> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mn>1</mn> <mo>−</mo> <mi>p</mi> </mrow> </msup> </math>. It describes one location in the representable lattice; it is not a universal comparison tolerance.
Floating spacing scales with exponent. Near a large world coordinate, one ULP can be much larger than epsilon; near zero, subnormal spacing follows a different regime. Therefore testing
for arbitrary geometric or physical quantities is usually unjustified.

A defensible comparison begins with the domain: absolute tolerance for quantities near zero, relative tolerance when scale matters, ULP bounds when representation-level proximity is intended, or an exact predicate when the algorithm can provide one. Tests should include values near 1, large magnitudes, tiny normals/subnormals and adjacent representable values using nextafter.

Appendix.title: Merkle trees and authenticated structure
Appendix.Content: Merkle trees and authenticated structure

A Merkle tree hashes data into leaves and repeatedly hashes child digests into parent digests until one root remains. The root commits to the entire ordered leaf set under the collision-resistance assumptions of the hash and the tree encoding.
A safe design domain-separates leaves from internal nodes, for example:
Appendix.RawBlock: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"> <msub> <mi>L</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <mi>H</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mi>x</mi> <mn>00</mn> <mstyle scriptlevel="0"> <mspace width="0.167em" /> </mstyle> <mo data-mjx-texclass="ORD" fence="false" stretchy="false">‖</mo> <mstyle scriptlevel="0"> <mspace width="0.167em" /> </mstyle> <mi>d</mi> <mi>a</mi> <mi>t</mi> <msub> <mi>a</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>,</mo> </math>

<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"> <mi>P</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mi>H</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mi>x</mi> <mn>01</mn> <mstyle scriptlevel="0"> <mspace width="0.167em" /> </mstyle> <mo data-mjx-texclass="ORD" fence="false" stretchy="false">‖</mo> <mstyle scriptlevel="0"> <mspace width="0.167em" /> </mstyle> <mi>l</mi> <mi>e</mi> <mi>f</mi> <mi>t</mi> <mstyle scriptlevel="0"> <mspace width="0.167em" /> </mstyle> <mo data-mjx-texclass="ORD" fence="false" stretchy="false">‖</mo> <mstyle scriptlevel="0"> <mspace width="0.167em" /> </mstyle> <mi>r</mi> <mi>i</mi> <mi>g</mi> <mi>h</mi> <mi>t</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>.</mo> </math>
Appendix.Content: Without an unambiguous encoding, different logical tree structures can accidentally serialize to the same byte concatenation before hashing.
Inclusion proof

To prove that one leaf belongs to a tree, provide the sibling hash at each level and the left/right ordering bits. The verifier starts from the leaf hash and reconstructs the root. Proof size is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>O</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>log</mi> <mo data-mjx-texclass="NONE">⁡</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math> for a balanced binary tree.
The trusted root must come from a trusted channel or authenticated record. A Merkle proof checked against an attacker-provided root proves nothing about authenticity.
Odd leaf policy
When a level has an odd number of nodes, the format must specify what happens: duplicate the last node, promote it, or use another encoding. Different policies create different roots.

tools/labs/crypto_primitives_lab.cpp uses an explicit domain-separated construction and duplicates the last digest on odd levels. The test proves determinism and that changing one sample leaf changes the root in the exercised case.
Related: Checksums CRCs and hashes, Integrity and authenticity.

Appendix.title: Metric gradients and differential measurements
Appendix.Content: Metric gradients and differential measurements
The differential of a scalar function is a linear measurement of displacement. The gradient is the vector that represents that measurement after an inner product or metric has been chosen.
At a point, let coordinate derivative coefficients be collected in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>g</mi> </math>. Then

Appendix.title: Minimum signed value
Appendix.Content: Minimum signed value
Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C002 · Latest development: C002
Definition and mechanism
Two’s-complement range has one extra negative value, so INT_MIN cannot be negated or represented by same-type absolute value.

N-bit two’s complement spans −2ᴺ⁻¹ through 2ᴺ⁻¹−1. Eight-bit minimum is −128, whose positive counterpart 128 does not fit. Negating int minimum or dividing it by −1 overflows the operation type. Narrow int8_t operands may promote first, so the original storage width alone does not establish UB.
Prerequisites

ListItem.Content: Two's complement — For raw unsigned value u in N bits, signed decoding is u when u<2ᴺ⁻¹, otherwise u−2ᴺ.

Appendix.Content: Used by

ListItem.Content: Fixed-point rescaling — uses this mechanism to define its representation, error or validation contract.
Signed integer overflow — uses minimum signed value as part of its representation or reasoning.

Appendix.title: Mixed signedness
Appendix.Content: Mixed signedness
Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C002 · Latest development: C002
Definition and mechanism
A negative signed operand can convert to a large unsigned value; choose semantic types consistently or use std::cmp_*, std::in_range, or std::ssize where appropriate.

int −1 compared with unsigned int 1 converts to a large unsigned value on the usual host, so the comparison is false. std::cmp_less preserves mathematical ordering. A valid index still needs a lower bound: index>=0 && std::cmp_less(index,size).
Prerequisites

ListItem.Content: Usual arithmetic conversions — After promotions, equal-signedness operands use the higher-ranked type.

Appendix.title: Mixed-precision state updates
Appendix.Content: Mixed-precision state updates
Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C005 · Latest development: C005
Definition and mechanism

Finite binary32 promotes exactly to binary64, but lost bits are not recovered. Double update arithmetic followed by float persistent storage rounds each step. A three-sample mean near 0.5 distinguishes float from double state despite double intermediates.
Prerequisites

ListItem.Content: Binary32 — Its finite significand/exponent makes each stored finite value a dyadic rational.
Binary64 — A wider format can represent finite binary32 values exactly but not recover earlier loss.
Rounding to nearest ties to even — Midpoint decisions determine separate/fused results and narrowed persistent state.

Appendix.title: Move casts and forwarding references
Appendix.Content: Move casts and forwarding references
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: C008 · Latest development: C009
Definition and mechanism

Consumer constructors/assignments now distinguish the cast from actual resource transfer. Const can force copying, return std::move(local) can prevent NRVO, and move_if_noexcept selects a path based on usable construction properties.

std::move is an xvalue cast preserving constness, not a resource transfer. A deduced cv-unqualified T&& parameter can be a forwarding reference: lvalue arguments deduce T& and collapse to an lvalue reference. std::forward restores the category encoded by deduction.
Prerequisites

ListItem.Content: Auto decltype and reference collapsing — Deduction and collapsing encode the caller category forwarding restores.
Value categories and materialization — Expression category determines viable binding and whether temporary identity is needed.

Appendix.Content: Move operations and moved-from states

Move construction creates a destination; move assignment also handles a prior target resource. Ownership transfer must repair the surviving source’s documented state. Valid-but-unspecified is not destroyed/uninitialized, and custom types must maintain their own invariants.

Appendix.title: Multilevel pointer qualification
Appendix.Content: Multilevel pointer qualification
Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C008 · Latest development: C008
Definition and mechanism

int** cannot implicitly become const int**: that would permit injection of an actually const object’s address into an original int*. int** can become const int* const*, whose intermediate read-only pointer blocks that assignment.
Prerequisites

ListItem.Content: Const qualification and shallow constness — Access-path qualification constrains nested conversions and member writes.

Appendix.Content: Used by
Later sources will deepen this same node; no empty dependent nodes are created.
Recall and next depth
Rebuild the hypothetical pointer injection step by step. Pending: qualification decomposition at further levels. Written coverage does not establish learner mastery.
Source and navigation
Teaching explanation and examples · Exact coverage · Dependency Map
Const applies at each indirection level

For a pointer chain, qualification is attached to a particular level rather than to the whole expression. const T* means the pointed-to T is not writable through that path; T* const means the pointer object itself cannot be reseated; const T* const combines both.

The distinction becomes safety-critical at multiple levels. Converting T** to const T** is not generally safe: if it were allowed, code could store a pointer-to-const object into the outer pointer and later write through the original T*, violating const protection. Qualification conversions therefore follow stricter rules than the familiar T* -> const T* case.

Engine APIs should avoid raw multi-level pointer mutation unless the ownership/indirection contract truly requires it. Spans, references to containers, output wrappers or typed handle arrays often express the real intent more clearly. A reconstruction exercise should explain each const position and demonstrate the classic unsafe hypothetical conversion.

Appendix.title: NaNs and payloads
Appendix.Content: NaNs and payloads
Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C004 · Latest development: C004
Definition and mechanism

All-one exponent with nonzero fraction encodes a non-numerical, unordered NaN. Quiet and signaling classes differ; fraction bits can carry payload information. Ordinary NaN equality is false; use isnan. Raw words can be classified without consuming signaling NaNs as floating values.
Prerequisites

ListItem.Content: Binary32 — The concrete fields provide the representation used in this mechanism.

Appendix.title: Named members versus array elements
Appendix.Content: Named members versus array elements
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: C007 · Latest development: C008
Definition and mechanism
The x member’s one-past pointer is not an authorized y access. A span describes an already-valid range; adjacency cannot create that range.

Adjacent x/y/z fields are separate subobjects, not T[3]. A pointer to x supports one-element-array pointer arithmetic; one-past cannot be dereferenced to access y. span(&x,3) does not create an array. Use explicit member dispatch or actual array storage; a ToArray result is a copy.
Prerequisites

ListItem.Content: Pointer arithmetic and provenance — Array-relative pointer bounds explain why adjacency of separate members cannot authorize indexing.

Appendix.title: Noexcept and transfer selection
Appendix.Content: Noexcept and transfer selection
Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C009 · Latest development: C009

noexcept is an escaping-exception contract; violation terminates. move_if_noexcept selects const T& when a throwing move and usable copy make rollback safer, otherwise T&&. It casts rather than transfers, and non-copyable throwing moves may weaken operation-specific guarantees.

Appendix.title: Norms, dual norms and error budgets
Appendix.source: Concepts/Norms, dual norms and error budgets.md
Appendix.Content: Norms, dual norms and error budgets
A norm defines a size rule. Its dual norm measures the largest scalar response a linear measurement can produce over the unit ball of that norm.
For a covector represented by coefficients <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>a</mi> </math>,
Appendix.RawBlock: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"> <mo data-mjx-texclass="ORD" fence="false" stretchy="false">‖</mo> <mi>a</mi> <msub> <mo data-mjx-texclass="ORD" fence="false" stretchy="false">‖</mo> <mo>∗</mo> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <munder> <mo data-mjx-texclass="OP" movablelimits="true">max</mo> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo data-mjx-texclass="ORD" fence="false" stretchy="false">‖</mo> <mi>e</mi> <mo data-mjx-texclass="ORD" fence="false" stretchy="false">‖</mo> <mo>≤</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </munder> <msup> <mi>a</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mi mathvariant="sans-serif">T</mi> </mrow> </mrow> </msup> <mi>e</mi> <mo>,</mo> </math>
Appendix.Content: and therefore
Appendix.RawBlock: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"> <mo stretchy="false">|</mo> <msup> <mi>a</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mi mathvariant="sans-serif">T</mi> </mrow> </mrow> </msup> <mi>e</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo stretchy="false">|</mo> </mrow> <mo>≤</mo> <mo data-mjx-texclass="ORD" fence="false" stretchy="false">‖</mo> <mi>a</mi> <msub> <mo data-mjx-texclass="ORD" fence="false" stretchy="false">‖</mo> <mo>∗</mo> </msub> <mstyle scriptlevel="0"> <mspace width="0.167em" /> </mstyle> <mo data-mjx-texclass="ORD" fence="false" stretchy="false">‖</mo> <mi>e</mi> <mo data-mjx-texclass="ORD" fence="false" stretchy="false">‖</mo> <mo>.</mo> </math>
Appendix.Content: This turns an error budget into a sensitivity bound. The choice of norm matters because different “allowed error shapes” have different worst cases. A Euclidean ball is self-dual: the dual of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>ℓ</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msub> </math> is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>ℓ</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msub> </math>. A componentwise box uses <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>ℓ</mi> <mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi> </msub> </math> for the error and has <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>ℓ</mi> <mn>1</mn> </msub> </math> as the dual measurement norm. An <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>ℓ</mi> <mn>1</mn> </msub> </math> error budget has <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>ℓ</mi> <mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi> </msub> </math> dual sensitivity.

Example: if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>a</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>2</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mo>−</mo> <mn>3</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo data-mjx-texclass="ORD" fence="false" stretchy="false">‖</mo> <mi>e</mi> <msub> <mo data-mjx-texclass="ORD" fence="false" stretchy="false">‖</mo> <mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi> </msub> <mo>≤</mo> <mn>0.01</mn> </math>, then
Appendix.RawBlock: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"> <mo stretchy="false">|</mo> <msup> <mi>a</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mi mathvariant="sans-serif">T</mi> </mrow> </mrow> </msup> <mi>e</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo stretchy="false">|</mo> </mrow> <mo>≤</mo> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo stretchy="false">|</mo> </mrow> <mn>2</mn> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo stretchy="false">|</mo> </mrow> <mo>+</mo> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo stretchy="false">|</mo> </mrow> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>−</mo> <mn>3</mn> </mrow> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo stretchy="false">|</mo> </mrow> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mn>0.01</mn> <mo>=</mo> <mn>0.05</mn> <mo>.</mo> </math>
Appendix.Content: This is more informative than a generic epsilon because it says what perturbations are permitted and what scalar quantity is being protected.

Error budgets in graphics and simulation should also carry units. A state vector mixing metres, radians, exposure values and normalized texture coordinates does not acquire a physically meaningful Euclidean norm merely because the values are stored in one array. The metric or scaling must state what “one unit of error” means in each subspace.

Appendix.title: Null pointers and optional access
Appendix.Content: Null pointers and optional access
Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C008 · Latest development: C008
Definition and mechanism

A null pointer designates no object/function; nullptr_t converts to appropriate null pointer values without choosing an integer overload. A non-null pointer is not a lifetime or bounds proof. Deleting a typed null object pointer is valid, but bare delete nullptr is ill-formed.
Prerequisites

ListItem.Content: Pointer arithmetic and provenance — Storage relationships, bounds and lifetime distinguish valid access from a non-null value.

Appendix.Content: Used by
Later sources will deepen this same node; no empty dependent nodes are created.
Recall and next depth
Explain absence, stale access and one-past access separately. Pending: optional/reference wrapper APIs and owning-pointer policies. Written coverage does not establish learner mastery.
Source and navigation
Teaching explanation and examples · Exact coverage · Dependency Map
Absence must be part of the type or contract

A null pointer represents “no object at this address-bearing interface”; dereferencing it is invalid. That makes raw pointer nullability an API question. If a parameter must always designate an object, a reference or explicitly non-null wrapper communicates more than a nullable pointer plus a comment.

Optional ownership and optional observation are different. A std::unique_ptr<T> may be empty while also owning when nonempty; T* may be nullable but usually says nothing about ownership; std::optional<T> stores an optional value without indirection. Choosing among them should follow lifetime and absence semantics rather than syntax convenience.
Null checks also do not prove lifetime. A non-null dangling pointer is still invalid, and a pointer can become logically stale even if its numeric address is later reused for a different object.

Tests for optional APIs should cover absent state, present state, transitions between them, moved-from ownership and invalid external identifiers. Avoid sentinel pointer values other than the language-defined null representation unless a low-level ABI explicitly owns that convention.

Appendix.title: Numerical error budgets
Appendix.Content: Numerical error budgets
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 10 · Latest development: Phase 10
Definition and mechanism

A computed result can differ from a target because of model assumptions, discretization, solver termination, arithmetic, sampling, or uncertain reference data. These contributions may interact, so an additive budget is a diagnostic model rather than a universal identity. First identify which errors are deterministic bounds, which are observed estimates, and which are stochastic uncertainty. For example, a ray-traced pixel can combine approximation of geometry, finite sample variance, floating-point accumulation, and an imperfect reference image. Allocate effort where the dominant contribution lies: extra precision cannot fix model bias, and more samples cannot repair an incorrect PDF. Report units and assumptions with every tolerance.

Appendix.title: Numerical tolerance policies
Appendix.Content: Numerical tolerance policies
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: C004 · Latest development: C005
Definition and mechanism

Tolerance is a task-chosen allowed discrepancy: absolute in original units, relative to scale, or representable-step based. Machine epsilon is not automatically a norm cutoff. Handle non-finite values and validate tolerances before formulas.

M005 distinguishes absolute tolerance in the quantity’s units from dimensionless relative tolerance. Validate policy parameters and classify non-finite values before arithmetic; approximate closeness is not transitive.
Prerequisites

ListItem.Content: Machine epsilon — Spacing near one supplies a reference precision scale, not a universal local gap or tolerance.
ULP and representable spacing — Adjacent representable points define rounding candidates, errors and step distances.
Floating-point infinities — Non-finite operands and overflowing intermediates need branches before ordinary finite formulas.
NaNs and payloads — Unordered comparisons and payload distinctions require explicit metric, comparison and serialization policy.

Appendix.title: ONNX graph import and lowering
Appendix.Content: ONNX graph import and lowering

ONNX is a graph interchange format, not a command stream to execute blindly. Import therefore has two separate responsibilities: decode the normative serialized model, then lower its graph semantics into the engine’s own validated intermediate representation.

The ONNX IR describes a graph as a side-effect-free computation containing model parameters and a topologically ordered list of nodes. Node outputs obey single-static-assignment: an output value name is produced once. Inputs, outputs and initializers have declared types and shapes, and symbolic dimensions can constrain values across the graph.
Primary reference: https://onnx.ai/onnx/repo-docs/IR.html
Import pipeline
Parse. Decode Protocol Buffers into ONNX model objects. Reject malformed serialization before graph reasoning begins.
Validate names and versions. Check IR version, opset imports, graph name, duplicate names and unsupported domains.
Resolve value contracts. Establish element type, rank and known or symbolic dimensions for graph inputs, outputs, initializers and intermediate values.
Validate graph order and SSA. Every consumed value must either be a graph input, initializer or output of an earlier node; every node output must be unique in its namespace.
Normalize operators. Convert ONNX attributes and optional inputs into an internal operator description whose defaults are explicit.
Infer and verify shapes. Propagate shapes where operator rules permit it, while keeping an unknown dimension distinct from an invented concrete dimension.
Lower. Translate supported operators into backend-neutral internal nodes. Unsupported operations must produce a deterministic diagnostic, not fall through to an unrelated kernel.
Plan execution. Topologically schedule nodes, assign storage and lifetimes, select kernels by capabilities, and insert device transfers or fallback boundaries deliberately.
Why an internal IR matters

If Vulkan, Metal and CPU code each interpret ONNX attributes independently, the repository effectively owns multiple importers with multiple chances to disagree. The importer should instead produce one small semantic IR: tensors, operators, attributes, shapes, constants and explicit capability requirements. Backends lower that IR.

This creates a testable seam. A CPU reference kernel and a Metal kernel can receive the same normalized MatMul or Softmax node. Their numerical agreement can then be tested without re-testing protobuf parsing.
Executable graph contract

tools/labs/phase29_ml_runtime_lab.cpp does not parse protobuf and labels that limitation explicitly. It models the post-decode internal graph boundary and verifies that inputs and initializers are available before use and that node outputs satisfy SSA uniqueness. Negative cases reject use-before-definition and duplicate outputs.

That is deliberately narrower than ONNX support. Full support requires actual protobuf decoding, opset semantics, operator-specific validation, shape inference and numerical parity against a trusted runtime.
Related: Tensor runtime layout and views, Transformer attention and KV cache runtime, Interface contracts and publication.
Real protobuf and official reference-runtime witness

The internal graph contract is now complemented by tools/ml/onnx_contract.py, which uses the official ONNX package instead of modeling the interchange format by hand. The witness builds a ModelProto with MatMul → Add → Relu, named initializers and symbolic batch dimension, serializes it to a real .onnx protobuf, reloads it, runs the official model checker, invokes shape inference, and executes the graph with ONNX’s reference evaluator.

The expected numerical result is independently computed with NumPy before comparison. A second deliberately invalid model reuses a node-output name and must be rejected by the official checker, exercising the SSA constraint at the actual interchange boundary.

This changes the evidence level for the ONNX file/IR boundary, not for a production inference backend. Dynamic control flow, nested subgraphs, arbitrary opsets, external tensor data, quantized operators, custom domains, ONNX Runtime/device execution and current KairoONNX lowering still need separate proofs.

Appendix.title: Object construction and storage reuse
Appendix.Content: Object construction and storage reuse
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: C007 · Latest development: C010
Definition and mechanism

Initialization creates an occupant whereas assignment replaces an existing occupant’s state. Ordinary constructor failure and post-target delegation failure have different complete-object cleanup behavior.

Storage needs sufficient size/alignment before object initialization can complete and start an ordinary lifetime. construct_at and destroy_at separate object life from backing storage. A cast alone does not construct arbitrary types. Some specified operations implicitly create implicit-lifetime objects; replacement and launder have additional preconditions.

M010 adds the resource-management view: placement construction or construct_at uses already-provided storage; it does not allocate that storage. destroy_at ends the occupant’s lifetime, while an arena separately decides when to reuse or release its bytes. Explicit destruction is safe only inside a protocol that prevents accidental second destruction. See Placement construction and explicit lifetime management.
Prerequisites

ListItem.Content: Storage duration and object lifetime — Backing-storage duration must be distinguished from the occupant’s start, destruction and replacement.

Appendix.Content: Used by

ListItem.Content: Object identity and generation handles — uses this prerequisite to establish its entity, lifetime, representation or lookup contract.

Content.Link: Placement construction and explicit lifetime management

Appendix.title: Octal
Appendix.Content: Octal
Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C001 · Latest development: C001
Definition and mechanism
Base 8 maps one digit to three bits; it survives in permissions and legacy literal syntax.

Octal digits run from 0 through 7. Group binary from the right in threes: 010 101 101₂ = 255₈. In C++, 0255 is octal 173; decimal 255 is a different value. Permission triples such as rwx map naturally onto three bits.
Prerequisites

ListItem.Content: Positional notation — A base is the number of available digits.

Appendix.Content: Used by
Connect later chunks here when they use this concept.
Recall and next depth
Explain octal without the label, work the example above, then state the assumption whose removal would change the result.
Pending: Unix permission semantics.
Source and navigation
C001 teaching chapter · Part definitions and mechanisms · Dependency Map
Why octal still matters

Octal groups binary digits in threes. Each octal digit therefore represents exactly three bits, so a binary field such as 111 101 010 maps directly to 752₈ without repeated division. Hexadecimal dominates modern memory dumps because bytes align naturally to two hex digits, but octal survives in domains whose historical or semantic fields are three-bit groups.

POSIX permission notation is the canonical example: read/write/execute are bit values <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mn>4</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>2</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>1</mn> </math>, so permission 0754 means owner 111, group 101, other 100. The leading zero in C/C++ source historically denotes an octal integer literal, which creates a real parsing hazard: 010 is eight, not ten. Modern code should prefer explicit intent and avoid visually ambiguous numeric literals.

A reconstruction test should convert binary↔octal by bit grouping, explain why each digit is 0–7, decode a permission triple, and identify the literal-syntax hazard. Octal is not a different storage representation in memory; it is a textual interpretation of the same integer bits.

Appendix.title: Offset-binary coding
Appendix.Content: Offset-binary coding
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: C006 · Latest development: C006
Definition and mechanism
A bias turns signed levels into unsigned codes. For the source-shaped INT4 convention c=q+8, -3 becomes nibble0101, not the two’s-complement nibble1101.
Prerequisites

ListItem.Content: Unsigned modular arithmetic — supplies the representation or validity rule used above.
Interpretation contract — supplies the representation or validity rule used above.

Appendix.Content: Used by
Connect later dependent concepts here when their explanations use this mechanism.
Recall and next depth
Reconstruct the example and identify the condition that would invalidate it.
Pending: Do not assume an INT4 label defines offset versus two’s-complement storage.
Source and navigation
Continuous teaching story · Source coverage ledger · Dependency Map
Ordering and bias
Offset-binary represents signed values by adding a fixed bias before storing an unsigned code:
Appendix.RawBlock: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"> <mi>q</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mi>x</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mi>B</mi> <mo>.</mo> </math>
Appendix.Content: With an <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>n</mi> </math>-bit field and the common midpoint bias <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>B</mi> <mo>=</mo> <msup> <mn>2</mn> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mi>n</mi> <mo>−</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msup> </math>, the smallest signed value maps near code zero and the largest maps near the all-ones code. Unlike two’s complement, the unsigned lexical order of codes then matches the numeric order of represented values. That property is useful in some exponent fields, ADC outputs, sortable binary formats and hardware interfaces.

The bias is part of the format contract. Decoding with the wrong bias shifts every value while still producing plausible numbers. The IEEE-754 exponent field is related but reserves all-zero and all-one exponent codes for subnormals/zero and infinities/NaNs, so it is not simply an unrestricted offset-binary integer.
Tests should check both endpoints, the code corresponding to numeric zero, monotonic ordering, and rejection or handling of reserved codes when the surrounding format defines them.

Appendix.title: One Definition Rule
Appendix.Content: One Definition Rule
Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C007 · Latest development: C007
Definition and mechanism

ODR requires coherent definitions. A non-inline externally linked function normally needs one program definition when odr-used. Certain class, template and inline definitions can appear in multiple translation units only under the rule’s conditions, including matching tokens and lookup; named-module attachment changes the permitted cases. Header guards operate within one translation unit, not across the program.
Prerequisites

ListItem.Content: Declarations and definitions — Agreement about which declarations define entities is necessary to state the one-definition constraint.

Appendix.title: One's complement
Appendix.Content: One’s complement
Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C002 · Latest development: C002
Definition and mechanism
Negation inverts every bit, leaving two zeros and requiring end-around carry for ordinary addition.

Negative x is the N-bit complement of positive x. Eight-bit −5 is 11111010; zeros are all zeros and all ones. Adding 5 and encoded −3 gives a carry plus low value 1; end-around carry adds that carry back to yield 2.
Prerequisites

ListItem.Content: Bitwise NOT — Complement must specify width: eight-bit complement of 0x0F is 0xF0, while sixteen-bit complement is 0xFFF0.
Signed magnitude — The high bit holds sign and the remaining bits hold magnitude.

Appendix.title: One-bit centroid quantization
Appendix.Content: One-bit centroid quantization
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: C006 · Latest development: C006
Definition and mechanism
One sign label selects one of two row means. Row [-1,-3,2,4] reconstructs [-2,-2,3,3], with RMSE one. Two float32 centroids cost 64 additional bits per row.
Prerequisites

ListItem.Content: Quantization and compressed weights — supplies the representation or validity rule used above.

Appendix.Content: Used by
Connect later dependent concepts here when their explanations use this mechanism.
Recall and next depth
Reconstruct the example and identify the condition that would invalidate it.
Pending: Empty-side, zero and non-finite policies must be explicit in a production codec.
Source and navigation
Continuous teaching story · Source coverage ledger · Dependency Map
Reconstruction depth

One-bit centroid quantization does not merely store a sign. A group of source values is partitioned into two reconstruction levels, often centroids <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>c</mi> <mn>0</mn> </msub> </math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>c</mi> <mn>1</mn> </msub> </math>, and each element stores one membership bit. Decoding is therefore
Appendix.RawBlock: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"> <msub> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mover> <mi>x</mi> <mo stretchy="false">^</mo> </mover> </mrow> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <msub> <mi>c</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <msub> <mi>b</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> </mrow> </msub> <mo>,</mo> <mstyle scriptlevel="0"> <mspace width="2em" /> </mstyle> <msub> <mi>b</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>∈</mo> <mo fence="false" stretchy="false">{</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo fence="false" stretchy="false">}</mo> <mo>.</mo> </math>
Appendix.Content: If the centroids are fixed to symmetric values such as <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo fence="false" stretchy="false">{</mo> <mo>−</mo> <mi>a</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mo>+</mo> <mi>a</mi> <mo fence="false" stretchy="false">}</mo> </math>, metadata becomes cheaper but the representation loses the ability to follow asymmetric distributions. If they are fitted per group, metadata cost increases but reconstruction error can fall.
The useful engineering quantity is total cost, not bits-per-weight in isolation:
Appendix.RawBlock: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"> <mtext>effective bits/value</mtext> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>+</mo> <mfrac> <mtext>centroid metadata bits</mtext> <mtext>group size</mtext> </mfrac> <mo>.</mo> </math>
Appendix.Content: Small groups adapt better but pay more metadata and may reduce SIMD efficiency. Large groups amortize metadata but force unrelated values to share two reconstruction levels.

A correct implementation tests deterministic centroid selection, empty-cluster handling, tie policy, bit packing order, group tails, finite decoded values, and error against a declared metric. For inference, the important next question is whether the binary code can participate directly in a dot-product kernel or must be expanded first; that determines whether compression actually saves bandwidth.

Appendix.title: Packed structures and misaligned access
Appendix.Content: Packed structures and misaligned access
Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C003 · Latest development: C003
Definition and mechanism

Compiler packing extensions can weaken aggregate/member alignment and remove holes. A uint32 member at offset one may be misaligned. Direct extension-aware member access may receive special code generation; extracting an ordinary typed pointer can lose that treatment. Hardware tolerance does not establish legal C++ access. Explicit codecs avoid alignment, lifetime, and host-layout assumptions.
Prerequisites

ListItem.Content: Alignment and padding — Address divisibility determines legal placement and layout holes.
Internal and tail padding — The position and amount of unused layout space determine reordering/packing effects.
Undefined behavior — Hardware completion does not prove a language-level operation legal.

Appendix.title: Page faults and demand paging
Appendix.Content: Page faults and demand paging
Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C003 · Latest development: C003
Definition and mechanism

A memory fault requires OS intervention when current translation/protection state cannot satisfy access. Valid demand loading, zero-fill, or copy-on-write may install/alter mapping then retry. Invalid addresses or denied permissions may fail instead. A fault need not perform disk I/O; a TLB miss need not fault at all.
Prerequisites

ListItem.Content: Page tables and MMU — Cached or faulting translation starts from the mapping/protection mechanism.

Appendix.Content: Used by

Memory-mapped files — uses this mechanism as stated in its prerequisites.

Appendix.title: Page tables and MMU
Appendix.Content: Page tables and MMU
Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C003 · Latest development: C003
Definition and mechanism

The memory management unit (MMU) translates/protects accesses using mapping information. Page tables hold virtual-page→physical-frame mappings plus permissions/state, often hierarchically. A permitted VPN 12345→PFN 987 with offset ABC produces PA 987ABC. This model is architecture-neutral, not a specific entry format.
Prerequisites

ListItem.Content: Pages and page offsets — Page identity is translated while within-page position is preserved.
Process isolation and page permissions — The mapping context and permissions constrain which accesses proceed.

Appendix.Content: Used by

ListItem.Content: TLB — uses this mechanism as stated in its prerequisites.
Page faults and demand paging — uses this mechanism as stated in its prerequisites.

Appendix.title: Pages and page offsets
Appendix.Content: Pages and page offsets
Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C003 · Latest development: C003
Definition and mechanism

A page is a virtual address block; a frame is page-sized physical backing. With page size P=2^k, divide VA into VPN=floor(VA/P) and offset=VA mod P. Translation substitutes frame identity while preserving offset. The 4-KiB examples use k=12; actual supported sizes are platform-dependent.
Prerequisites

ListItem.Content: Addresses and virtual memory — Mappings give numeric locations their process-specific storage identity.
Bit mask — A low-bit mask isolates the within-page offset.
Shift operations — Shifts relocate a selected byte or address field to its significance position.

Appendix.Content: Used by

ListItem.Content: Page tables and MMU — uses this mechanism as stated in its prerequisites.
Virtual and physical contiguity — uses this mechanism as stated in its prerequisites.

Appendix.title: Parameter passing and sink contracts
Appendix.Content: Parameter passing and sink contracts
Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C009 · Latest development: C009
Definition and mechanism

A by-value parameter is an object initialized from the argument expression: lvalues ordinarily copy, xvalues can move, and appropriate prvalues construct directly. References borrow; a pointer parameter copies its pointer value. A sink intentionally retains or consumes a value, not merely observes it.
Prerequisites

ListItem.Content: References and aliases — Parameter access differs according to whether a new object is created or an existing referent is borrowed.
Const qualification and shallow constness — A read-only parameter path does not establish global immutability or ownership.

Appendix.title: Physical and logical binary states
Appendix.Content: Physical and logical binary states
Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C001 · Latest development: C001
Definition and mechanism
Physical ranges or stored states are classified as logical 0 or 1; noise tolerance comes from accepting ranges rather than exact values.

A threshold is a boundary used to classify a measured physical quantity. A noise margin is the distance between a valid signal level and a boundary: variation inside that margin does not change the interpreted bit. A storage element retains state; combinational logic computes an output from current inputs. Exact voltage limits depend on the device.
Prerequisites
No prior curriculum concept is required; this is a starting point.
Used by

ListItem.Content: Bit — uses physical and logical binary states as part of its representation or reasoning.

Appendix.title: Placement construction and explicit lifetime management
Appendix.source: Concepts/Placement construction and explicit lifetime management.md
Appendix.Content: Placement construction and explicit lifetime management
Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C010 · Latest development: C010
Definition and mechanism

Placement new or std::construct_at initializes an object in storage already provided by the caller; it does not allocate that backing storage. The storage must have adequate size and alignment. std::destroy_at ends an object’s lifetime but does not release the storage. A pool/container must track occupancy, partial construction, exactly-once destruction, and when reuse is permitted. Transparent replacement and std::launder have detailed preconditions; launder neither constructs nor revives an object.
Prerequisites

ListItem.Content: Object construction and storage reuse — An object’s lifetime is not the same as backing storage availability.
RAII and resource handles — Low-level storage protocols still need one responsible owner.

Appendix.Content: Used by
Recall and next depth
Sketch Empty → Live(A) → Empty → Live(B) → Released. State the operation and precondition on every edge. Pending: implicit-lifetime operations, allocator traits, and container exception guarantees.

Appendix.title: Pointer arithmetic and provenance
Appendix.Content: Pointer arithmetic and provenance
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: C003 · Latest development: C008
Definition and mechanism

M008 adds null/object/one-past distinctions, same-array representable subtraction and round-trip limits. Provenance proposals are research, not adopted C++23 rules; byte inspection differs from arbitrary typed access.

A scalar member behaves as a one-element array for pointer arithmetic, not as an array containing adjacent sibling members. &x+1 can be a one-past pointer but cannot be dereferenced to access y. Actual array storage supports traversal; a span only views an already-valid range. Layout/size assertions do not authorize sibling traversal.

A pointer is a typed access path constrained by array bounds, alignment, and object lifetime, not merely an integer. Within an array, p+i advances i elements; one-past is permitted for traversal but not dereference. Byte views inspect representations; uintptr_t, when provided, is an integer conversion facility, not permission to access arbitrary storage.
Prerequisites

ListItem.Content: Addresses and virtual memory — Mappings give numeric locations their process-specific storage identity.
Storage duration and object lifetime — Access requires an object and backing storage that are still valid.

Appendix.Content: Used by

ListItem.Content: Named members versus array elements — uses this prerequisite to establish its entity, lifetime, representation or lookup contract.
GPU vertex specification ## Recall and next depth

Appendix.Content: Explain p+1 for int versus byte and why a numeric address is insufficient.

Appendix.title: Positional notation
Appendix.Content: Positional notation
Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C001 · Latest development: C001
Definition and mechanism

Digits receive powers-of-base weights; binary uses base two and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>V</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mo data-mjx-texclass="OP">∑</mo> <msub> <mi>b</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <msup> <mn>2</mn> <mi>i</mi> </msup> </math>.

A base is the number of available digits. Position i contributes digit × baseⁱ; the rightmost position is i=0. For 1011₂, the weights 8,4,2,1 give 8+2+1=11. The number of states is 2ᴺ, while the maximum unsigned value is 2ᴺ−1.
Prerequisites

ListItem.Content: Bit — A bit has two possible logical states.

Appendix.Content: Used by

ListItem.Content: Terminating fractions and dyadic rationals — Finite fractional digits correspond to an integer over a power of the base.
Significand and hidden bit — uses positional notation to establish this mechanism’s representation or policy.

Appendix.title: Prefix scan and stream compaction
Appendix.Content: Prefix scan and stream compaction
A prefix scan turns local counts into globally consistent offsets. For an exclusive sum scan of input <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>x</mi> </math>,
Appendix.RawBlock: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"> <msub> <mi>y</mi> <mn>0</mn> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mstyle scriptlevel="0"> <mspace width="2em" /> </mstyle> <msub> <mi>y</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <munderover> <mo data-mjx-texclass="OP">∑</mo> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mi>j</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>0</mn> </mrow> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mi>i</mi> <mo>−</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </munderover> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mi>j</mi> </msub> <mo>.</mo> </math>
Appendix.Content: If each element says how many output records it will emit, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>y</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> </math> is the first output slot owned by element <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>i</mi> </math>. This converts a race-prone global append into deterministic non-overlapping regions.

For Boolean compaction, let predicate <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>b</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>∈</mo> <mo fence="false" stretchy="false">{</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo fence="false" stretchy="false">}</mo> </math>. Scan <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>b</mi> </math> to obtain offsets. Every active element with <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>b</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> </math> writes itself to output[scan[i]]. The final output count is scan[n-1] + b[n-1].
Parallel structure

The naive parallel scan that repeatedly doubles an offset performs <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>O</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mi>log</mi> <mo data-mjx-texclass="NONE">⁡</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math> work. A work-efficient tree scan performs an up-sweep/reduction followed by a down-sweep and uses <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>O</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math> work with <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>O</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>log</mi> <mo data-mjx-texclass="NONE">⁡</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math> depth.
On a GPU, a practical large-array scan normally has several levels:

ListItem.Content: scan each workgroup block into local output;
record each block total;
scan the block totals;
add each scanned block offset back into that block’s local results.

Appendix.Content: Every phase has a dependency. Dispatching all phases without establishing visibility/order is not a valid scan merely because each shader is individually correct.
Shared-memory bank conflicts and subgroup width affect performance, while workgroup barriers only synchronize participating invocations in that workgroup.
Stream compaction as an allocation proof

Compaction is useful beyond filtering visible objects. It appears in GPU-driven draw generation, BVH construction, particle survival, tiled light lists, Gaussian tile duplication and sparse work queues.
The scan proves that each surviving producer owns a distinct range before any scatter writes occur.
Evidence boundary

The current repository has CPU-side scan/compaction reasoning in the canonical volumes but does not yet claim a native Vulkan/Metal scan kernel benchmark. The next hardware proof should compare a scalar CPU oracle, a workgroup implementation, multi-workgroup hierarchy, adversarial non-power-of-two sizes, and captured GPU timing.
Primary background: NVIDIA GPU Gems 3, Chapter 39, “Parallel Prefix Sum (Scan) with CUDA.”
Teach and reconstruct: Continuous Notes/Computing Foundations - From Bits to C++ and Systems APIs#Scan turns local counts into nonoverlapping output regions.

Appendix.title: Process isolation and page permissions
Appendix.Content: Process isolation and page permissions
Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C003 · Latest development: C003
Definition and mechanism

An address-space mapping context determines which physical frame a virtual number names and whether read/write/execute access is permitted. Two processes may use VA 0x400000 for different frames; shared mappings can deliberately use one frame. Permission checks belong to mapping state, not to the apparent numerical validity of a pointer.

Appendix.title: Quantization error metrics
Appendix.Content: Quantization error metrics
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: C006 · Latest development: C006
Definition and mechanism

For N>0, RMSE is sqrt(sum squared discrepancies/N), MAE is mean absolute discrepancy, and max error is the largest observed magnitude. Promote float operands before subtraction when measuring in double.
Prerequisites

ListItem.Content: Absolute and relative error — supplies the representation or validity rule used above.
Quantization and compressed weights — supplies the representation or validity rule used above.

Appendix.Content: Used by
Connect later dependent concepts here when their explanations use this mechanism.
Recall and next depth
Reconstruct the example and identify the condition that would invalidate it.
Pending: Representation error alone does not establish downstream task correctness.
Source and navigation
Continuous teaching story · Source coverage ledger · Dependency Map
A metric must match what the consumer loses

Quantization error is the difference <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>e</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mi>x</mi> <mo>−</mo> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mover> <mi>x</mi> <mo stretchy="false">^</mo> </mover> </mrow> </math> between source and reconstruction, but one scalar summary cannot answer every engineering question. Mean squared error emphasizes large deviations; mean absolute error is less sensitive to outliers; maximum absolute error exposes worst-case bounds; relative error becomes useful when scale varies but is unstable near zero.

For tensors, per-tensor MSE can hide one badly damaged channel or group. Diagnostics should often include per-group distributions, saturation counts, scale histograms, and downstream task error. A quantizer that minimizes weight MSE is not guaranteed to minimize model-output error because layers amplify directions differently.

Signal metrics also depend on representation. Comparing gamma-encoded RGB with ordinary squared error is not the same as comparing linear-light energy. Normals may need angular error rather than component MSE.

A useful quantization benchmark therefore reports storage cost together with several reconstruction metrics and one consumer-level metric. The metric is part of the experiment hypothesis, not a decorative number added after compression.

Appendix.title: Quantized matvec and dequantization
Appendix.Content: Quantized matvec and dequantization

Quantization trades representation precision for storage and bandwidth. The runtime question is not merely “how many bits per weight?” It is what mathematical value each stored code represents, where its scale or zero-point metadata lives, and how the dot product is accumulated without silently changing the model.
For a simple symmetric per-row signed 8-bit scheme,
Appendix.RawBlock: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"> <mi>s</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mfrac> <mrow> <munder> <mo data-mjx-texclass="OP" movablelimits="true">max</mo> <mi>i</mi> </munder> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo stretchy="false">|</mo> </mrow> <msub> <mi>w</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">|</mo> </mrow> <mn>127</mn> </mfrac> <mo>,</mo> <mstyle scriptlevel="0"> <mspace width="2em" /> </mstyle> <msub> <mi>q</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <mi>round</mi> <mstyle scriptlevel="0"> <mspace width="-0.167em" /> </mstyle> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="INNER"> <mo data-mjx-texclass="OPEN">(</mo> <mfrac> <msub> <mi>w</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mi>s</mi> </mfrac> <mo data-mjx-texclass="CLOSE">)</mo> </mrow> <mo>,</mo> </math>
Appendix.Content: with clamping to the representable range. The reconstructed value is
Appendix.RawBlock: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"> <msub> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mover> <mi>w</mi> <mo stretchy="false">^</mo> </mover> </mrow> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <mi>s</mi> <msub> <mi>q</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>.</mo> </math>
Appendix.Content: A reference matrix-vector product can therefore compute
Appendix.RawBlock: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"> <mi>y</mi> <mo>=</mo> <munder> <mo data-mjx-texclass="OP">∑</mo> <mi>i</mi> </munder> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>s</mi> <msub> <mi>q</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>.</mo> </math>
Appendix.Content: That scalar implementation is not necessarily fast, but it creates an oracle for SIMD or GPU fused dequantization-and-dot kernels.

Before clamping, the scalar reconstruction error for ordinary round-to-nearest is bounded by roughly half a quantization step. The output error is workload-dependent because the dot product combines weight errors with input magnitudes. An accuracy report therefore needs representative activations or a model-level metric, not only weight reconstruction error.
Zero rows and exceptional values

When all weights in a block are zero, dividing by the maximum absolute value would produce an invalid scale. The format and runtime need an explicit zero-block representation. Non-finite input weights should be rejected or handled by a documented conversion policy instead of entering integer casts accidentally.

Groupwise 4-bit formats add another trade-off. Smaller groups let the scale adapt more locally but spend more bytes on metadata and may increase metadata bandwidth. Larger groups reduce metadata overhead but make each scale describe a wider distribution.
Reference versus optimized execution

tools/labs/phase29_ml_runtime_lab.cpp implements a checked per-row Q8 reference and compares its dot product against the original floating-point row under a stated error budget. The point is not to advertise Q8 as the final format; it is to establish the proof pattern:
stored codes plus metadata → scalar interpretation → reference result → optimized kernel → measured error and performance.

A Metal or SIMD kernel should be judged against that reference on adversarial widths, tails, zero blocks, extreme scales and random vectors. SIMD lane packing is an implementation detail; the dequantized mathematical contract remains the same.
Related: Quantization and compressed weights, GGUF binary model loading, Tensor runtime layout and views.

Appendix.title: Quaternion algebra and Hamilton product
Appendix.Content: Quaternion algebra and Hamilton product
Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: Phase7 · Latest development: Phase7
Definition and mechanism

A quaternion has scalar w and vector u. Hamilton multiplication combines scalar product w_a w_b minus dot(u_a,u_b), and vector w_a u_b plus w_b u_a plus cross(u_a,u_b). It is associative and generally noncommutative; component order is a separate interface convention.
Reconstruction cue: i times j equals k, while j times i equals minus k.

Appendix.Content: Quaternion interpolation and shortest paths

Definition and mechanism

Quaternion interpolation must account for the double cover. Flip one endpoint when their dot is negative for the usual shortest rotational path, then use NLERP or SLERP. NLERP changes angular speed; SLERP follows a great-circle arc with a small-angle fallback.

Appendix.title: Quaternion rotation and double cover
Appendix.Content: Quaternion rotation and double cover
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase7 · Latest development: University courses
Definition and mechanism

For a unit quaternion q, the sandwich q(0,v)conjugate(q) rotates v. q and minus q give the same physical rotation. Every nonzero quaternion also rotates without scale if its true inverse is used; substituting conjugate for inverse off the unit sphere scales by the squared norm.
Reconstruction cue: The scalar-first quaternion (sqrt(1/2),0,0,sqrt(1/2)) rotates the X axis to Y.
Prerequisites
Used by
Recall and next depth
Reconstruct the example, state its conventions and find an input that violates its preconditions. Deeper algorithms and measured production performance remain separate from the present model.
Source and navigation
Continuous explanation · Coverage and source gap · Sources and verification
University course development

Extend the existing quaternion note with interpolation and sign handling in animation. A unit quaternion represents a 3D rotation, but <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>q</mi> </math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo>−</mo> <mi>q</mi> </math> encode the same physical orientation. If two endpoint quaternions have a negative dot product, negate one endpoint before interpolation so the path follows the shorter arc on the unit four-dimensional sphere. Linear interpolation followed by normalization is inexpensive and often adequate for close orientations; spherical linear interpolation travels at constant angular speed for widely separated rotations. Quaternion interpolation acts on orientation, while translation and scale need their own rules. This matters in camera paths and articulated characters: interpolating four components without handling the double cover can create an unnecessary long spin, while interpolating Euler angles can encounter a gimbal singularity. Validate unit length after operations subject to floating-point drift.
Coordinate frames, transformations, and pose · Scene graphs and articulated geometry · Animation curves and motion paths

Appendix.title: RAII and resource handles
Appendix.Content: RAII and resource handles
Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C010 · Latest development: C010
Definition and mechanism

Resource Acquisition Is Initialization (RAII) ties a cleanup responsibility to a well-defined object’s lifetime. A resource handle acquires or adopts responsibility, preserves the release protocol through moves/composition, and performs matching cleanup on scope exit—including ordinary exception unwinding. The resource can be a memory allocation, lock, file, socket, native GPU object, or other paired protocol. RAII does not itself prove that an external asynchronous user has finished; it must trigger the correct deferred-release protocol.

Construction failure cleans completed subobjects, so each acquired responsibility should enter an owner immediately. A raw native handle is not an owner unless its release contract is implemented and documented.
Prerequisites

ListItem.Content: Storage duration and object lifetime — Object scope and resource lifetime must be distinguished.
Destruction and partial construction — Completed owner subobjects clean up during failure.

Appendix.Content: Used by

Appendix.title: Read-only data and code
Appendix.Content: Read-only data and code
Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C003 · Latest development: C003
Definition and mechanism

Executable text commonly holds machine instructions; read-only mappings often hold literals/constants. W^X (writable or executable) policy discourages simultaneously writable executable storage, with platform/JIT qualifications. Modifying a string literal is undefined behavior regardless of whether hardware protection catches it. const automatic objects need not be in read-only mappings.

Appendix.title: Reciprocal bases and coordinate measurements
Appendix.Content: Reciprocal bases and coordinate measurements
A basis reconstructs vectors; a reciprocal basis measures their coefficients. Those are different jobs when the basis is not orthonormal.

Let basis vectors <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>b</mi> <mn>1</mn> </msub> <mo>,</mo> <mo>…</mo> <mo>,</mo> <msub> <mi>b</mi> <mi>n</mi> </msub> </math> form the columns of matrix <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>B</mi> </math>. Coordinates <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>c</mi> </math> reconstruct a vector by
Appendix.RawBlock: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"> <mi>v</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mi>B</mi> <mi>c</mi> <mo>.</mo> </math>

The rows of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msup> <mi>B</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>−</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msup> </math> are the coordinate-measurement covectors. In Euclidean coordinates, their vector representatives are the columns of
Appendix.RawBlock: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"> <msup> <mi>B</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>−</mo> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mi mathvariant="sans-serif">T</mi> </mrow> </mrow> </msup> <mo>.</mo> </math>
Appendix.Content: These reciprocal vectors <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msup> <mi>b</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msup> </math> satisfy
Appendix.RawBlock: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"> <msup> <mi>b</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msup> <mo>⋅</mo> <msub> <mi>b</mi> <mi>j</mi> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <msubsup> <mi>δ</mi> <mi>j</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msubsup> <mo>.</mo> </math>
Appendix.Content: For the slanted basis <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>b</mi> <mn>1</mn> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math>, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>b</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math> and vector <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>v</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>3</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>2</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math>, directly dotting with the basis vectors gives <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>3</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>5</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math> and is wrong as a coordinate recovery rule. The reciprocal basis is
Appendix.RawBlock: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"> <msup> <mi>b</mi> <mn>1</mn> </msup> <mo>=</mo> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mo>−</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>,</mo> <mstyle scriptlevel="0"> <mspace width="2em" /> </mstyle> <msup> <mi>b</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msup> <mo>=</mo> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>,</mo> </math>
Appendix.Content: so the measurements are <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msup> <mi>b</mi> <mn>1</mn> </msup> <mo>⋅</mo> <mi>v</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> </math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msup> <mi>b</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msup> <mo>⋅</mo> <mi>v</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>2</mn> </math>, exactly the coefficients that reconstruct <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>v</mi> <mo>=</mo> <msub> <mi>b</mi> <mn>1</mn> </msub> <mo>+</mo> <mn>2</mn> <msub> <mi>b</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msub> </math>.

A reciprocal basis is therefore a concrete bridge from vectors to covectors. It also explains why normal transformation uses an inverse transpose: normals are measurements that must continue to annihilate tangent directions after the tangent basis changes.
In numerical code, do not build a matrix inverse merely to solve one coordinate problem. Use a factorization or direct solve appropriate to the matrix structure and condition.

Value-returning temporary accessors provide an owning result through direct construction or member movement. Both const and mutable rvalue policies remain required; the shorter M009 source example does not replace the four-way safe design.

Member &/&& qualifiers constrain the caller’s object category. Borrowed getters suit persistent owners; temporary getters can return owning values or be deleted. Appendix.title: Ripple-carry addition
Appendix.Content: Ripple-carry addition
Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C002 · Latest development: C002
Definition and mechanism
Each full adder feeds its carry to the next position, making worst-case circuit propagation depth grow with word width.

Connect carry-out at bit i to carry-in at i+1. For 01111111 + 1, a carry traverses the low seven stages. Circuit delay grows with width in this simple design; fixed-width software addition still counts as O(1) with respect to input size.

Appendix.title: Rules of Three Five and Zero
Appendix.source: Concepts/Rules of Three Five and Zero.md
Appendix.Content: Rules of Three Five and Zero
Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C009 · Latest development: C009
Definition and mechanism

Three coordinates destruction/copy construction/copy assignment; Five adds both moves. These are semantic design decisions, not requirements to implement copying. Appendix.title: Saturating arithmetic
Appendix.Content: Saturating arithmetic
Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C002 · Latest development: C002
Definition and mechanism
Clamp unrepresentable results to range boundaries instead of wrapping; useful for bounded media values but generally non-associative.

Saturation clamps a mathematical result to a permitted interval: unsigned-byte 250+20 becomes 255 instead of 14. Clamp a widened result. Signed saturation is not associative: saturating (100+100)−100 yields 27 while 100+saturating(100−100) yields 100.

Signed integer overflow — Overflow concerns the operation’s signed type after promotions.

Appendix.title: Scopes and name lookup
Appendix.Content: Scopes and name lookup
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: C007 · Latest development: C008
Definition and mechanism

Lookup precedes overload resolution. A derived overload can hide base overloads; using Base::name restores candidates. A local int x=x reads the newly declared uninitialized local, not an outer integer.

Scope locates a name’s binding; lookup resolves a spelling to declarations. A local x can hide ::x without destroying it. A block-scope static has a local name but persistent storage. Qualified lookup names a namespace or class explicitly.

Appendix.title: Serialization
Appendix.Content: Serialization
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: C001 · Latest development: C006
Definition and mechanism

Serialization maps semantic fields to a specified byte sequence; decoding validates and reconstructs them. Width, order, version, bounds, and padding policy belong to that contract. A U8/U32-LE/U64-LE header occupies 13 bytes at offsets 0/1/5, independently of a native record’s possible 16-byte ABI layout. Packing removes some holes, not host dependencies. Publication and durability are subsequent operations.

M004 extension: a binary32 representation word such as 3F800000 can be serialized as little-endian bytes 00 00 80 3F. Raw-bit preservation retains signed-zero and NaN-payload differences; canonicalization deliberately merges them. Numeric equality does not imply byte identity. This is a format policy, not permission to change existing files.

M006 adds explicit schema/version/identity contracts, overflow-safe dimensions and resource limits, raw-word payload preservation, integrity coverage and a complete 52-byte demonstration. A native scalar writer is not automatically cross-endian stable.
Prerequisites

ListItem.Content: Interpretation contract — Representation, type, and lifetime must identify what object exists.
Fixed-width integer types — The representation width fixes byte count and valid shift range.
Endianness — Byte order tells how digit significance maps to sequence positions.

Appendix.Content: Used by

Checksums CRCs and hashes — uses this mechanism to define its representation, error or validation contract.
Floating-point canonicalization — uses serialization to establish this mechanism’s representation or policy.
Atomic publication and durability — uses this mechanism as stated in its prerequisites.

Appendix.title: Shader buffer ABI
Appendix.Content: Shader buffer ABI

A shader buffer is a binary interface between independently compiled code. CPU and shader code must agree on member offsets, element widths, alignment, array stride, matrix layout, and total record stride. “These structs have the same fields” is not enough.

Suppose a record logically contains a 3-vector followed by a scalar. The mathematical payload is four floats, but the ABI may impose an alignment boundary for the vector or the containing record. The only safe statement is the one established by the layout rules and, ideally, reflection/compiled shader metadata.
Layout is a function of context

Different interfaces can have different rules: vertex attributes, constant/uniform buffers, storage buffers, argument buffers and push/root constants are not interchangeable contracts. Matrix row/column-major convention is another independent dimension.

On the CPU side, standard C++ object layout also has rules about padding and alignment. Copying bytes from a native struct into a shader buffer is valid only when the native representation is deliberately made compatible or explicit serialization writes the expected offsets.
Verify rather than guess
A robust pipeline should generate or reflect a machine-readable layout description and compare it with CPU declarations:

ListItem.Content: expected offset for every member;
expected array stride;
matrix stride and orientation;
record size/alignment;
scalar widths and signedness.

Appendix.Content: Static assertions can catch CPU layout changes. Shader reflection or compiler metadata catches shader-side changes. A golden byte dump can test the complete bridge.
Failure modes

Common failures include using a 12-byte mental model for a vector type whose ABI slot is 16 bytes, mixing bool widths, assuming packed enums, copying pointer-containing structs, row/column-major disagreement, and updating one side of the interface without rebuilding the other.
Teach and reconstruct: Continuous Notes/Computing Foundations - From Bits to C++ and Systems APIs#Make a shader record an explicit binary contract.
Related: Alignment and padding, GPU vertex specification, Tensor runtime layout and views.

Appendix.title: Shamir secret sharing
Appendix.Content: Shamir secret sharing

Shamir secret sharing splits a secret into shares so that any threshold number can reconstruct it while fewer shares reveal no information in the ideal finite-field construction when coefficients are chosen uniformly at random.

Choose a prime field <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mi mathvariant="double-struck">F</mi> </mrow> <mi>p</mi> </msub> </math> containing the secret value and a threshold <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>t</mi> </math>. Construct a random polynomial
Appendix.RawBlock: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"> <mi>f</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>x</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>=</mo> <mi>s</mi> <mo>+</mo> <msub> <mi>a</mi> <mn>1</mn> </msub> <mi>x</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mo>⋯</mo> <mo>+</mo> <msub> <mi>a</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mi>t</mi> <mo>−</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msub> <msup> <mi>x</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mi>t</mi> <mo>−</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msup> </math>
Appendix.Content: with secret <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>s</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mi>f</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math>. Give participant <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>i</mi> </math> the share <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>,</mo> <mi>f</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math> for distinct nonzero <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> </math>.

Any <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>t</mi> </math> shares recover <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>f</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math> through Lagrange interpolation:
Appendix.RawBlock: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"> <mi>s</mi> <mo>=</mo> <munder> <mo data-mjx-texclass="OP">∑</mo> <mi>i</mi> </munder> <msub> <mi>y</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <munder> <mo data-mjx-texclass="OP">∏</mo> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mi>j</mi> <mo>≠</mo> <mi>i</mi> </mrow> </munder> <mfrac> <mrow> <mo>−</mo> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mi>j</mi> </msub> </mrow> <mrow> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>−</mo> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mi>j</mi> </msub> </mrow> </mfrac> <mspace width="1em" /> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>mod</mi> <mspace width="0.333em" /> <mi>p</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>.</mo> </math>
Appendix.Content: Every division is multiplication by a finite-field inverse. Ordinary integer division is wrong.
Security condition

The coefficients must be generated with a cryptographically secure random generator. Deterministic or predictable coefficients destroy the information-theoretic secrecy claim even though interpolation still reconstructs correctly.
Share identifiers also matter: using duplicate x coordinates makes interpolation invalid.
Evidence boundary
tools/labs/crypto_primitives_lab.cpp demonstrates a three-share reconstruction over prime field 257 and reconstructs the same secret from two different three-share subsets.
Its polynomial coefficients are deliberately deterministic so the test is reproducible. Therefore the laboratory proves interpolation arithmetic, not production secrecy.
A production system additionally needs CSPRNG coefficients, authenticated share transport/storage, versioning, participant identity, compromise/recovery policy and secure erasure.
Related: Integrity and authenticity, HMAC and HKDF.

Appendix.title: Shift operations
Appendix.Content: Shift operations
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: C001 · Latest development: C002
Definition and mechanism
Relocate bit significance; unsigned shifts can correspond to multiply or floor-divide by powers of two within their validity range.

Logical right shift fills high positions with zero; arithmetic right shift replicates the sign bit. In C++23, signed right shift rounds toward negative infinity; signed integer division rounds toward zero. Thus −5>>1 gives −3 while −5/2 gives −2. A built-in shift count must be nonnegative and smaller than the promoted left operand’s width.
Prerequisites

ListItem.Content: Bit significance — LSB means least significant bit, normally position 0 with weight 1.
Machine word — A processor’s natural integer processing width is often called its word width, but the term is architecture dependent.

Binary long division — uses shift operations as part of its representation or reasoning.

Pages and page offsets — depends on this concept; see its prerequisite explanation.
