Appendix.title: Shift-and-add multiplication
Appendix.Content: Shift-and-add multiplication
Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C002 · Latest development: C002
Definition and mechanism

Each set multiplier bit selects a shifted multiplicand partial product; an exact product of two <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>N</mi> </math>-bit values may need <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mn>2</mn> <mi>N</mi> </math> bits.

Multiplier bit i selects multiplicand shifted i positions. 13×11 uses 11=1011₂, hence 13+26+104=143. Keep the shifting multiplicand in the widened type; shifting a uint16_t variable repeatedly discards high partial-product bits even if the accumulator is uint32_t.
Prerequisites

ListItem.Content: Shift operations — Logical right shift fills high positions with zero; arithmetic right shift replicates the sign bit.
Full adder — A full adder adds A, B, and carry-in.

Appendix.title: Short-circuit evaluation
Appendix.Content: Short-circuit evaluation
Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C001 · Latest development: C001
Definition and mechanism
&& may skip its right operand after false; || may skip it after true, so evaluation safety is part of semantics.

Built-in logical AND skips its right operand after false; logical OR skips it after true. ptr && ptr->ready() guards the dereference. A bitwise & evaluates both operands. Operator spelling therefore determines both result meaning and whether a dangerous expression is evaluated.

Appendix.title: Signed integer overflow
Appendix.Content: Signed integer overflow
Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C002 · Latest development: C002
Definition and mechanism
A signed arithmetic result outside its type’s range is undefined in C++; hardware low bits do not create a language-level wrap guarantee.

Overflow concerns the operation’s signed type after promotions. int maximum + 1 is undefined. For checked addition, reject b>0 and a>max−b, or b<0 and a<min−b, before evaluating a+b. Hardware status flags do not change the C++ contract.
Prerequisites

ListItem.Content: Minimum signed value — N-bit two’s complement spans −2ᴺ⁻¹ through 2ᴺ⁻¹−1.
Undefined behavior — The C++ language imposes no requirements on an execution that invokes undefined behavior.

Appendix.title: Signed magnitude
Appendix.Content: Signed magnitude
Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C002 · Latest development: C002
Definition and mechanism
The high bit selects sign while remaining bits encode magnitude; this is intuitive but has positive and negative zero and needs sign-aware arithmetic.

The high bit holds sign and the remaining bits hold magnitude. Eight-bit +5 is 00000101, −5 is 10000101, and 00000000 and 10000000 both denote zero. Mixed signs require magnitude comparison and subtraction rather than ordinary raw-bit addition.

Appendix.title: Signed zero
Appendix.Content: Signed zero
Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C004 · Latest development: C004
Definition and mechanism
Exponent and fraction zero permit either sign. 00000000 and 80000000 compare numerically equal, but signbit and reciprocal distinguish them. Ordinary x<0 does not detect negative zero.

Reconstruction depth

IEEE-754 has both <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo>+</mo> <mn>0</mn> </math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo>−</mo> <mn>0</mn> </math>. They compare equal numerically in ordinary equality, but the sign remains observable through operations such as reciprocal, sign-bit inspection and some branch-cut-sensitive functions:
Appendix.RawBlock: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"> <mfrac> <mn>1</mn> <mrow> <mo>+</mo> <mn>0</mn> </mrow> </mfrac> <mo>=</mo> <mo>+</mo> <mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mstyle scriptlevel="0"> <mspace width="2em" /> </mstyle> <mfrac> <mn>1</mn> <mrow> <mo>−</mo> <mn>0</mn> </mrow> </mfrac> <mo>=</mo> <mo>−</mo> <mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi> <mo>.</mo> </math>
Appendix.Content: Signed zero preserves directional information after underflow or exact cancellation. That can matter in complex functions, interval boundaries and geometric code that interprets the sign of a quantity near a separating surface.

It can also surprise serialization, hashing and deterministic comparison. If the application’s semantic model says both zeros are identical, canonicalization may deliberately map negative zero to positive zero before hashing or bytewise equality. If directional zero is meaningful, that canonicalization destroys information.

Tests should distinguish numeric equality from bit representation and include operations that expose the sign. This is one reason floating-point equality policy must start from domain semantics rather than from a universal epsilon.

Appendix.title: Stable reformulation
Appendix.Content: Stable reformulation
Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C005 · Latest development: C005
Definition and mechanism

A mathematically equivalent expression can avoid unnecessary numerical loss. sqrt(x+1)−sqrt(x)=1/(sqrt(x+1)+sqrt(x)) for x≥0; at double x=1e16 the direct result is zero while the reciprocal form remains near 5e-9.
Prerequisites

ListItem.Content: Cancellation and loss of significance — Near-equal operand errors motivate exact-subtraction distinctions and reformulation.

Appendix.Content: Used by
Connect later dependent concepts here when their lessons arrive.

ListItem.Content: Stable quadratic root evaluation ## Recall and next depth

Pending: Every reformulation still needs domain, range, conditioning and accuracy checks.

Algebraic equivalence is not numerical equivalence

Two formulas can be identical over real arithmetic and behave very differently in finite precision. Stable reformulation changes the computational path while preserving the intended mathematical quantity.
For the quadratic equation, the textbook root expression can subtract nearly equal numbers and lose most significant digits. Computing one root with a sign-aware expression such as
Appendix.RawBlock: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"> <mi>q</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mo>−</mo> <mstyle displaystyle="false" scriptlevel="0"> <mfrac> <mn>1</mn> <mn>2</mn> </mfrac> </mstyle> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="INNER"> <mo data-mjx-texclass="OPEN">(</mo> <mi>b</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mi>sign</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>b</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <msqrt> <msup> <mi>b</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msup> <mo>−</mo> <mn>4</mn> <mi>a</mi> <mi>c</mi> </msqrt> <mo data-mjx-texclass="CLOSE">)</mo> </mrow> </math>
Appendix.Content: and obtaining the other as <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>c</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>/</mo> </mrow> <mi>q</mi> </math> avoids that cancellation in many cases.

The same idea appears in log-sum-exp, hypot-style norms, rationalizing expressions, compensated sums, and solving least squares with QR rather than normal equations. A reformulation is not automatically stable: its overflow/underflow regions and exceptional inputs still need analysis.

Tests should compare against a higher-precision reference across adversarial inputs, not only ordinary random values. The goal is to show that the reformulated algorithm reduces forward/backward error where the naive expression is fragile.

Appendix.title: Standard-layout and trivial copyability
Appendix.Content: Standard-layout and trivial copyability
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: C007 · Latest development: C009
Definition and mechanism

Rule-Zero composition is not itself a trivially-copyable, standard-layout or serialization promise. Hand-written/defaulted special functions can change triviality, and relocation is not generic permission to memmove a nontrivial owner.

Standard-layout is a structural language property supporting useful low-level layout reasoning; it does not promise no padding or a portable ABI. Trivial copyability permits particular byte-copy operations on valid objects/representations, not arbitrary byte validity or serialization. Aggregate, trivial and trivially-copyable are separate traits.
Prerequisites

ListItem.Content: ABI and object layout — ABI offsets and padding must be separated from standard-layout and byte-copy language eligibility.

Appendix.title: Static storage and initialization
Appendix.Content: Static storage and initialization
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: C003 · Latest development: C007
Definition and mechanism

constinit requires static initialization without making an object const. Dynamic initialization across translation units requires ordering care; explicit owners or function-local statics can provide a clear dependency path. Local-static first initialization is synchronized since C++11, but later calls/mutations still require normal concurrency rules. Initialization and shutdown dependencies are distinct.

Namespace-scope/static objects have program-duration storage. Initialized writable objects commonly use data-like regions; zero-initialized objects use BSS-like zero-fill, avoiding literal zeros in the executable. Some objects require runtime dynamic initialization; cross-unit order is a distinct problem from storage allocation.
Prerequisites

ListItem.Content: Storage duration and object lifetime — Access requires an object and backing storage that are still valid.

Appendix.title: Sterbenz lemma
Appendix.Content: Sterbenz lemma
Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C005 · Latest development: C005
Definition and mechanism

For nonnegative stored radix-format floats x,y with x/2≤y≤2x, the difference is representable exactly under appropriate gradual-underflow assumptions. This does not recover errors already present in the operands.
Prerequisites

ListItem.Content: Cancellation and loss of significance — Near-equal operand errors motivate exact-subtraction distinctions and reformulation.
Subnormals and gradual underflow — An exact tiny difference may need gradual-underflow representability.

Appendix.Content: Used by
Connect later dependent concepts here when their lessons arrive.
Recall and next depth

Pending: Prove range/significand details for a chosen format; FTZ changes assumptions.
Source and navigation
M005 teaching chapter · Part definitions · Dependency Map
Exact subtraction in a bounded ratio

Sterbenz’s lemma gives a rare exactness guarantee for floating subtraction. Under the usual floating-point assumptions, if two finite floating values <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>x</mi> </math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>y</mi> </math> satisfy
Appendix.RawBlock: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"> <mfrac> <mi>y</mi> <mn>2</mn> </mfrac> <mo>≤</mo> <mi>x</mi> <mo>≤</mo> <mn>2</mn> <mi>y</mi> <mo>,</mo> </math>
Appendix.Content: then <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>x</mi> <mo>−</mo> <mi>y</mi> </math> is exactly representable in the same floating format, provided the result remains in the supported range conditions.

This explains why cancellation is not synonymous with rounding error. Subtracting two nearby floating numbers can lose relative information about the original quantities, yet the subtraction operation itself may be exact. The conditioning of the problem and the rounding of an operation are different questions.

The lemma is useful when proving error bounds for compensated algorithms and geometric predicates. A reconstruction test should generate representable pairs inside and outside the ratio interval, compare the subtraction against a higher-precision exact reference, and distinguish an exactly rounded zero/small difference from a well-conditioned final answer.

Appendix.title: Subnormals and gradual underflow
Appendix.Content: Subnormals and gradual underflow
Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C004 · Latest development: C004
Definition and mechanism

Exponent zero and nonzero fraction remove the hidden one and hold the effective exponent at the normal minimum. Binary32 values are F×2^-149, connecting smoothly to 2^-126. Absolute spacing stays fixed while relative precision degrades.
Prerequisites

ListItem.Content: Exponent bias — Stored exponents must be translated to effective powers before reconstructing value or spacing.
Significand and hidden bit — Fraction weights and effective precision determine value and the smallest retained position.

Appendix.title: Subtraction through addition
Appendix.Content: Subtraction through addition
Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C002 · Latest development: C002
Definition and mechanism

<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>A</mi> <mo>−</mo> <mi>B</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mi>A</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mo>∼</mo> <mi>B</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mn>1</mn> </math>, allowing the same adder to implement both operations; some ISAs fold borrow state into carry-in.
At N-bit residue width, A−B equals A+NOTₙ(B)+1. Binary 6502-style SBC computes A−B−(1−C), equivalently A+NOT₈(B)+C. C=1 means no incoming borrow; output carry=1 means no outgoing borrow.
Prerequisites

ListItem.Content: Two's complement — For raw unsigned value u in N bits, signed decoding is u when u<2ᴺ⁻¹, otherwise u−2ᴺ.
Full adder — A full adder adds A, B, and carry-in.

Appendix.title: TLB
Appendix.Content: TLB
Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C003 · Latest development: C003
Definition and mechanism

The translation lookaside buffer caches recent address translations and relevant access metadata, not the bytes being loaded. A miss may trigger a valid page-table walk without OS fault handling. A TLB hit can coexist with a data-cache miss. Context and permissions matter; it is not just a global VPN-only dictionary.
Prerequisites

ListItem.Content: Page tables and MMU — Cached or faulting translation starts from the mapping/protection mechanism.

Appendix.Content: Used by

ListItem.Content: Huge pages and TLB reach — uses this mechanism as stated in its prerequisites.

Appendix.Content: Recall and next depth
Distinguish a translation miss, cache miss, and page fault.
Pending: ASIDs/PCIDs, shootdowns, hierarchy, associativity, and measured reach.
Source and navigation
C003 teaching chapter · Part definitions · Dependency Map
Reconstruction depth

The Translation Lookaside Buffer caches recent virtual-page to physical-frame translations. Without a cached translation, the processor performs a page-table walk, which itself requires memory accesses and can stall an otherwise cache-friendly loop.

TLB locality differs from data-cache locality. A traversal can touch one cache line from thousands of separate pages: each useful access is small, but the page working set can exceed TLB capacity. Huge pages increase TLB reach because one translation covers more bytes, although they introduce allocation and fragmentation trade-offs.

When profiling, do not diagnose every unexplained memory stall as a TLB problem. Hardware performance counters can separate cache misses, page walks and TLB misses on supported CPUs. Synthetic experiments should vary stride and working-set pages while keeping useful work controlled.

For engine data, dense arrays often help both cache and TLB locality; pointer-heavy structures can hurt both. NUMA adds another axis: a translation may be cached while the physical page still resides on a remote node.

Appendix.title: Temporary lifetime extension
Appendix.Content: Temporary lifetime extension
Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C008 · Latest development: C008
Definition and mechanism

Ordinary temporary destruction occurs at the full-expression’s end unless specified extension applies. Direct local binding can extend lifetime, but a returned parameter reference cannot transitively extend it. Aggregate braces and parentheses differ for reference members; new-initializer extension does not last as long as the allocated holder.
Prerequisites

ListItem.Content: Reference binding and converted temporaries — The chosen original or converted referent determines the destruction deadline.
Storage duration and object lifetime — The referent and its backing storage must survive each alias use.

Appendix.title: Tensor runtime layout and views
Appendix.Content: Tensor runtime layout and views

A tensor runtime does not begin with neural-network vocabulary. It begins with a byte-addressing contract. A tensor value needs an element type, a rank, a shape, a mapping from logical indices to storage offsets, and an ownership/lifetime rule for the backing storage. If any of those are implicit, later operations such as broadcasting, transposition, slicing, matrix multiplication, device transfer, or quantized kernels can silently disagree about what the same bytes mean.
For a contiguous row-major tensor with shape
Appendix.RawBlock: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msub> <mi>d</mi> <mn>0</mn> </msub> <mo>,</mo> <msub> <mi>d</mi> <mn>1</mn> </msub> <mo>,</mo> <mo>…</mo> <mo>,</mo> <msub> <mi>d</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mi>r</mi> <mo>−</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>,</mo> </math>
Appendix.Content: the canonical stride of axis <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>i</mi> </math> is
Appendix.RawBlock: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"> <msub> <mi>s</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <munderover> <mo data-mjx-texclass="OP">∏</mo> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mi>j</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mi>i</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mi>r</mi> <mo>−</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </munderover> <msub> <mi>d</mi> <mi>j</mi> </msub> <mo>,</mo> </math>
Appendix.Content: so an index <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msub> <mi>i</mi> <mn>0</mn> </msub> <mo>,</mo> <mo>…</mo> <mo>,</mo> <msub> <mi>i</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mi>r</mi> <mo>−</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math> addresses
Appendix.RawBlock: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"> <mi>offset</mi> <mo>=</mo> <munderover> <mo data-mjx-texclass="OP">∑</mo> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mi>k</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>0</mn> </mrow> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mi>r</mi> <mo>−</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </munderover> <msub> <mi>i</mi> <mi>k</mi> </msub> <msub> <mi>s</mi> <mi>k</mi> </msub> <mo>.</mo> </math>
Appendix.Content: Shape describes the logical domain while strides describe the storage map. A transposed or sliced view may have the same elements without being contiguous. A runtime that assumes offset = row × width + column for every two-dimensional tensor will eventually misread a view.

A rank-zero tensor is a scalar and has shape []; it is not the same object shape as a rank-one tensor of shape [1]. A zero-sized dimension is also meaningful: shape [4,0,8] has zero elements but still has rank three. These distinctions matter when importing external graph formats because shape information is part of the interface contract rather than decoration.
Broadcasting is an index transformation

Broadcasting does not physically duplicate the smaller tensor. Align the input and output shapes at the trailing axes. For every aligned axis, the input size must either equal the output size or equal one. If the input size is one, every output index on that axis maps to input index zero.

For a bias of shape [3] applied to a matrix [2,3], output coordinates across both rows map back to bias indices 0,1,2 repeatedly. This is why some runtimes can represent a broadcast axis with a zero stride: advancing the logical output coordinate does not advance the input address.
Views, aliases, and mutation

A view is cheap because it shares storage. That also means it shares lifetime and mutation hazards. A runtime must decide whether an operation accepts arbitrary strided inputs, requests a contiguous materialization, or dispatches to separate kernels. Reshape is metadata-only only when the requested logical order can be represented by the existing storage arrangement; otherwise it requires a copy.

The same question appears on the GPU. A kernel receiving shape and stride metadata can support arbitrary views, but the extra integer arithmetic and irregular memory access can cost more than making a compact copy. The correct choice is workload-dependent and should be measured.
Executable reconstruction

tools/labs/phase29_ml_runtime_lab.cpp contains a standalone C++20 tensor representation with checked element counts, contiguous strides, multi-index addressing, and trailing-axis broadcasting. Its negative test rejects incompatible shapes rather than allowing an accidental indexing interpretation.

The witness is intentionally small enough to rebuild from memory. It does not claim to implement a production tensor allocator, autograd engine, sparse tensor representation, or GPU device-memory manager.
External contract

The ONNX IR specification defines tensors by values plus shape, distinguishes scalar shape [] from a one-element vector, and requires top-level graph inputs and outputs to carry rank information even when individual dimensions are symbolic. When an ONNX model is imported, the internal tensor representation must preserve those distinctions instead of flattening everything into an untyped byte blob.
Primary reference: https://onnx.ai/onnx/repo-docs/IR.html
Failure probes

A tensor-runtime implementation should deliberately test integer overflow while multiplying dimensions, out-of-range indexing, zero-sized dimensions, rank-zero scalars, incompatible broadcasting, views whose strides are not contiguous, aliased mutation, negative or unsupported strides if the API exposes them, and CPU/GPU disagreement over element size or alignment.
The central reconstruction question is: given only shape, strides, element size and an index tuple, can you prove which byte is being accessed and whether that byte remains alive?
Related: Shader buffer ABI, Quantization and compressed weights, ONNX graph import and lowering, Transformer attention and KV cache runtime.

Appendix.title: Terminating fractions and dyadic rationals
Appendix.Content: Terminating fractions and dyadic rationals
Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C005 · Latest development: C005
Definition and mechanism
A reduced rational p/q terminates in base B iff q divides a power of B. In binary q must be a power of two. Binary32 0.1 is exactly 13421773/2^27, chosen as an approximation of non-dyadic 1/10.
Prerequisites

ListItem.Content: Positional notation — Finite fractional digits correspond to an integer over a power of the base.
Binary32 — Its finite significand/exponent makes each stored finite value a dyadic rational.

Appendix.Content: Used by
Connect later dependent concepts here when their lessons arrive.
Recall and next depth
Reconstruct the definition’s example and name the assumptions that make it valid.
Pending: Other bases, decimal conversion algorithms and exact rational arithmetic.
Source and navigation
M005 teaching chapter · Part definitions · Dependency Map
Why decimal-friendly numbers can be binary-hostile

A reduced rational number <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>p</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>/</mo> </mrow> <mi>q</mi> </math> has a terminating representation in base <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>b</mi> </math> exactly when every prime factor of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>q</mi> </math> also divides <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>b</mi> </math>. Base 10 has prime factors 2 and 5, so fractions such as <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mn>1</mn> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>/</mo> </mrow> <mn>10</mn> </math> terminate. Base 2 has only prime factor 2, so only dyadic rationals with denominator <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msup> <mn>2</mn> <mi>k</mi> </msup> </math> terminate.

That is why <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mn>0.5</mn> </math>, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mn>0.25</mn> </math>, and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mn>0.125</mn> </math> are exact in ordinary binary floating point while <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mn>0.1</mn> </math> repeats forever and must be rounded. The issue is not that floating point is “bad at decimals”; it is a consequence of positional representation.

This perspective helps debugging: multiplying a binary approximation to 0.1 by ten need not recreate the exact path one imagines from decimal arithmetic. For currency or protocol fields whose semantics are decimal-exact, scaled integers or decimal floating formats may be better contracts.

A reconstruction exercise should reduce several fractions, classify their denominator prime factors, and predict whether they terminate in bases 2, 10, and 16 before checking actual floating encodings.

Appendix.title: Thread-local storage
Appendix.Content: Thread-local storage
Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C007 · Latest development: C007
Definition and mechanism

thread_local gives a separate object/storage instance per thread; block scope does not make it automatic. Initialization, access costs and destruction follow implementation/language rules. Thread-local state does not make shared pointees thread-safe, and escaped addresses need a valid thread/object lifetime.
Prerequisites

Appendix.title: Transform hierarchies TRS and shear
Appendix.Content: Transform hierarchies TRS and shear
Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: Phase7 · Latest development: Phase7
Definition and mechanism

A TRS transform stores translation, rotation and diagonal scale, with an explicit application order. General affine matrices are closed under composition; TRS without shear is not. Parent nonuniform scale and rotated children can create shear, so exact world composition may require an affine matrix. Dirty caches must invalidate all dependent results.
Reconstruction cue: Nonorthogonal columns in a composed linear map rule out a pure rotation-times-diagonal-scale representation.

Appendix.title: Transformer attention and KV cache runtime
Appendix.source: Concepts/Transformer attention and KV cache runtime.md
Appendix.Content: Transformer attention and KV cache runtime
A transformer runtime becomes understandable when tensor shapes remain visible. For one attention head, let a token representation produce query, key and value vectors
Appendix.RawBlock: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"> <mi>q</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>k</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>v</mi> <mo>∈</mo> <msup> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi> </mrow> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mi>d</mi> </mrow> </msup> <mo>.</mo> </math>
Appendix.Content: For a query attending to keys <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>k</mi> <mi>j</mi> </msub> </math>, the scaled score is
Appendix.RawBlock: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"> <msub> <mi>ℓ</mi> <mi>j</mi> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <mfrac> <mrow> <msup> <mi>q</mi> <mi>T</mi> </msup> <msub> <mi>k</mi> <mi>j</mi> </msub> </mrow> <msqrt> <mi>d</mi> </msqrt> </mfrac> <mo>,</mo> </math>
Appendix.Content: followed by a stable softmax
Appendix.RawBlock: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"> <msub> <mi>p</mi> <mi>j</mi> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <mfrac> <msup> <mi>e</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <msub> <mi>ℓ</mi> <mi>j</mi> </msub> <mo>−</mo> <mi>m</mi> </mrow> </msup> <mrow> <munder> <mo data-mjx-texclass="OP">∑</mo> <mi>t</mi> </munder> <msup> <mi>e</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <msub> <mi>ℓ</mi> <mi>t</mi> </msub> <mo>−</mo> <mi>m</mi> </mrow> </msup> </mrow> </mfrac> <mo>,</mo> <mstyle scriptlevel="0"> <mspace width="2em" /> </mstyle> <mi>m</mi> <mo>=</mo> <munder> <mo data-mjx-texclass="OP" movablelimits="true">max</mo> <mi>t</mi> </munder> <msub> <mi>ℓ</mi> <mi>t</mi> </msub> <mo>,</mo> </math>
Appendix.Content: and the output is
Appendix.RawBlock: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"> <mi>o</mi> <mo>=</mo> <munder> <mo data-mjx-texclass="OP">∑</mo> <mi>j</mi> </munder> <msub> <mi>p</mi> <mi>j</mi> </msub> <msub> <mi>v</mi> <mi>j</mi> </msub> <mo>.</mo> </math>
Appendix.Content: Subtracting <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>m</mi> </math> does not change the distribution because the same factor appears in numerator and denominator, but it prevents overflow when logits are large.
Causal masking

For autoregressive decoding at token position <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>t</mi> </math>, a query must not observe keys and values from future positions. In a batch attention matrix this is represented by a causal mask before softmax. During incremental decoding, a correctly managed KV cache gives the same structural guarantee: only keys and values through the current token have been appended.

The cache exists because recomputing all earlier K/V projections every token is wasteful. If each layer has key/value vectors of head width <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>d</mi> <mi>h</mi> </msub> </math>, number of KV heads <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>h</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mi>k</mi> <mi>v</mi> </mrow> </msub> </math>, sequence length <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>L</mi> </math>, and element size <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>b</mi> </math>, the rough storage per layer is
Appendix.RawBlock: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"> <mn>2</mn> <mi>L</mi> <msub> <mi>h</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mi>k</mi> <mi>v</mi> </mrow> </msub> <msub> <mi>d</mi> <mi>h</mi> </msub> <mi>b</mi> </math>
Appendix.Content: bytes before allocator and alignment overhead. Cache datatype, paging strategy and maximum context length are therefore memory-system decisions.
Multi-head and grouped-query attention

Multiple heads perform the same mechanism with separate projected subspaces. Grouped-query attention may use fewer key/value heads than query heads; the mapping from query head to KV head must be explicit. GGUF metadata commonly carries head-count and key/value dimension information, so model loading and runtime shape validation meet at this boundary.
Residual, normalization, and feed-forward structure

Attention is only one sublayer. A complete transformer block also needs residual paths, normalization, and a feed-forward network or architecture-specific alternative. The order—pre-norm versus post-norm, RMSNorm versus LayerNorm, activation and gating choice—is part of the model architecture and must come from the model contract rather than a generic “transformer” assumption.
Executable witness

tools/labs/phase29_ml_runtime_lab.cpp implements stable softmax and a small incremental KV cache. Two keys with distinct values make the weighting observable; a single-token case proves that incremental causal attention cannot see a future token that has not been appended.

It intentionally does not claim multi-head batching, rotary position embeddings, grouped-query attention, tokenizer behavior, paged KV caches, fused kernels or production-model parity. Those are separate implementation milestones.
Related: Tensor runtime layout and views, GGUF binary model loading, ONNX graph import and lowering, Quantized matvec and dequantization.

Appendix.title: Two's complement
Appendix.Content: Two’s complement
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: C001 · Latest development: C002
Definition and mechanism

An <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>N</mi> </math>-bit negative <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo>−</mo> <mi>x</mi> </math> is residue <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msup> <mn>2</mn> <mi>N</mi> </msup> <mo>−</mo> <mi>x</mi> <mo>=∼</mo> <mi>x</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mn>1</mn> </math>; the signed high-bit weight is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo>−</mo> <msup> <mn>2</mn> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mi>N</mi> <mo>−</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msup> </math>, giving one zero and an asymmetric range.

For raw unsigned value u in N bits, signed decoding is u when u<2ᴺ⁻¹, otherwise u−2ᴺ. Thus 0xAD means 173−256=−83. Negation uses width-limited complement plus one modulo 2ᴺ. Signed interpretation and unsigned residue share bits but have different language arithmetic contracts.
Prerequisites

ListItem.Content: Unsigned modular arithmetic — Modulo m retains the remainder class after division by m.
Bitwise NOT — Complement must specify width: eight-bit complement of 0x0F is 0xF0, while sixteen-bit complement is 0xFFF0.

A unit in the last place describes local spacing. Inside normal binade [2e,2(e+1)), p-bit precision gives spacing 2^(e-(p-1)). Immediately above 1 the binary32 gap is twice the gap below it.

An <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>n</mi> </math>-bit UNORM integer <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>q</mi> <mo>∈</mo> <mo stretchy="false">[</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo>,</mo> <msup> <mn>2</mn> <mi>n</mi> </msup> <mo>−</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo stretchy="false">]</mo> </math> represents a real value approximately in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">[</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo stretchy="false">]</mo> </math> through
Appendix.RawBlock: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"> <mi>x</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mfrac> <mi>q</mi> <mrow> <msup> <mn>2</mn> <mi>n</mi> </msup> <mo>−</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </mfrac> <mo>.</mo> </math>
Appendix.Content: Quantization reverses that map with a declared rounding rule and saturation. The endpoint denominator matters: dividing by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msup> <mn>2</mn> <mi>n</mi> </msup> </math> would make the largest code fail to represent exactly <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mn>1</mn> </math>. This is why a normalized color channel can round-trip its endpoints even though most interior values incur quantization error.

SNORM maps a signed integer code to approximately <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">[</mo> <mo>−</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo stretchy="false">]</mo> </math>. APIs differ in how the most-negative integer is treated, so the format specification—not intuition—owns the exact decode rule. This matters for normals and tangent vectors: decoding produces components, not a guaranteed unit vector. A sampled normal map usually requires later reconstruction or normalization and a coordinate-space convention.

A useful test suite checks endpoint codes, monotonicity, round-trip error bounds, saturation outside the nominal domain, and the API’s exact most-negative SNORM behavior. Treating UNORM/SNORM as small floats hides where nonlinear color encoding, signed-vector normalization, and integer filtering contracts actually enter.

Appendix.title: Undefined behavior
Appendix.Content: Undefined behavior
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: C001 · Latest development: C002
Definition and mechanism
Invalid shifts, out-of-bounds access, signed overflow, division by zero, and INT_MIN / -1 provide no valid C++ execution result; optimizers may assume they never occur.

The C++ language imposes no requirements on an execution that invokes undefined behavior. It is not an error value or a guaranteed trap. Signed overflow, division by zero, invalid shift counts, and out-of-bounds accesses are examples. Check preconditions before performing the operation.
Prerequisites

ListItem.Content: Interpretation contract — For 0xAD, unsigned interpretation gives 173; eight-bit two’s complement gives −83.

Appendix.Content: Used by

Packed structures and misaligned access — depends on this concept; see its prerequisite explanation.

Appendix.title: Unit roundoff
Appendix.Content: Unit roundoff
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: C004 · Latest development: C005
Definition and mechanism
Under nearest binary rounding the conventional relative bound for normal-range results is u=2^-p, half upward epsilon. For binary32 this is 2^-24. The bound has range/rounding assumptions.

Repeated-rounding bounds use <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>γ</mi> <mi>n</mi> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mi>u</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>/</mo> </mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>−</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mi>u</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math> when <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>n</mi> <mi>u</mi> <mo><</mo> <mn>1</mn> </math>, under the stated rounding and range assumptions. Summation error also depends on operand magnitudes; this is not a universal relative-error guarantee.
Prerequisites

ListItem.Content: ULP and representable spacing — Adjacent representable points define rounding candidates, errors and step distances.
Rounding to nearest ties to even — Midpoint parity determines discarded-tail decisions and the normal relative-error bound.

Appendix.Content: Used by

ListItem.Content: Absolute and relative error — The local normal-rounding bound supplies the error-analysis scale.
Accumulated rounding error — The local normal-rounding bound supplies the error-analysis scale.

Appendix.title: Unsigned modular arithmetic
Appendix.Content: Unsigned modular arithmetic
Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: C001 · Latest development: C002
Definition and mechanism

Conversion and arithmetic in an unsigned <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>N</mi> </math>-bit domain produce residues modulo <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msup> <mn>2</mn> <mi>N</mi> </msup> </math>; intentional wrap is valid, but wrapped bounds expressions can become security bugs.

Modulo m retains the remainder class after division by m. An unsigned N-bit domain uses m=2ᴺ: 250+10 becomes 4 when stored in eight bits, and 0−1 becomes 255. Narrow operands may promote first, so identify the operation type separately from the destination type.
Prerequisites

ListItem.Content: Positional notation — A base is the number of available digits.
Machine word — A processor’s natural integer processing width is often called its word width, but the term is architecture dependent.

Appendix.title: Usual arithmetic conversions
Appendix.Content: Usual arithmetic conversions
Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C002 · Latest development: C002
Definition and mechanism
After promotions, binary operators choose a common type according to rank, signedness, and representability; the operands may change value before comparison or arithmetic.

After promotions, equal-signedness operands use the higher-ranked type. For signed S and unsigned U: if U rank≥S rank, convert S to U; otherwise use S if it represents all U values; otherwise use S’s unsigned counterpart. Rank and width are related but distinct.
Prerequisites

ListItem.Content: Integral promotion — Narrow integer types become int if int represents every original value; otherwise they become unsigned int.

Appendix.title: Virtual and physical contiguity
Appendix.Content: Virtual and physical contiguity
Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C003 · Latest development: C003
Definition and mechanism

Consecutive virtual addresses can map nonadjacent physical frames. Vector’s contiguous elements guarantee adjacent object storage in the process model, not one contiguous physical allocation. File offsets and storage-device placement are separate adjacency notions. Contiguity must always name the space being discussed.
Prerequisites

ListItem.Content: Pages and page offsets — Page identity is translated while within-page position is preserved.

Appendix.Content: Used by
Update downstream uses when later chunks build on this concept.
Recall and next depth
Map three adjacent virtual pages to frames 912/17/404.
Pending: DMA, physical allocation, IOMMU and scatter/gather.
Source and navigation
C003 teaching chapter · Part definitions · Dependency Map
Reconstruction depth

A virtually contiguous array occupies one uninterrupted range of virtual addresses. The page table may map those virtual pages to physical frames scattered through RAM. Most user-space code only requires virtual contiguity because ordinary loads and stores are translated by the MMU before reaching memory.

Physical contiguity matters at different boundaries: some DMA devices, huge-page mappings, kernels or fixed hardware buffers may impose stronger requirements. Modern IOMMUs can themselves provide device-visible address translation, reducing the need for physically contiguous host memory in some designs.

This explains why a large dynamic allocation can succeed even when free physical RAM is fragmented into many regions: the operating system can assemble the virtual range from separate frames and may not commit all of them until faults occur.

For performance, virtual contiguity still does not guarantee identical locality. Page placement can span NUMA nodes, and TLB reach depends on page size and access footprint. Therefore contiguous storage is a statement about address iteration and element layout, not a complete claim about physical placement.

Appendix.title: Weak observation and ownership cycles
Appendix.Content: Weak observation and ownership cycles
Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C010 · Latest development: C010
Definition and mechanism

std::weak_ptr<T> observes a shared_ptr ownership group without increasing its strong count. lock() atomically attempts to create a temporary strong owner; the result is empty if the managed object is no longer alive. Replacing one edge of an otherwise all-strong ownership cycle with a weak observation can allow the strong count to reach zero. A check with expired() followed later by access is not equivalent to a successful lock().
enable_shared_from_this joins the already-established shared ownership group; it must not create a second shared_ptr control block from this.
Prerequisites

ListItem.Content: Exclusive and shared smart-pointer ownership — Weak observation belongs to a real shared ownership group.

M001 - Width-safe fields and LSB-first bit packing
Kind: Canonical Introduced by: C001 / M001 Language: C++23
Contract

ListItem.Content: Field width is 1-32; shift + width must fit a 32-bit carrier.
Field insertion rejects values that do not fit instead of silently truncating them.
Bit arrays contain only 0 or 1 and are packed LSB-first within each byte.
Unpacking rejects a requested count larger than the source capacity.

Appendix.Content: Snippet
Cost and failure behavior

Field access over a fixed carrier is constant work. Packing and unpacking are <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>O</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math>, with <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo fence="false" stretchy="false">⌈</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>/</mo> </mrow> <mn>8</mn> <mo fence="false" stretchy="false">⌉</mo> </math> packed bytes. The guards make width, value range, and source-capacity failures explicit rather than allowing invalid shifts, silent field truncation, or out-of-bounds access.
Verification

Compiled with Homebrew Clang in C++23 mode using warnings as errors. Assertions covered 0xAD, field replacement, LSB-first packing, round-trip unpacking, full-width masks, and rejected oversized unpack counts. See the current task verification record; no repository implementation was claimed by this canonical snippet.
M002 - Exhaustive 8-bit addition oracle and saturation
Kind: Canonical Introduced by: C002 / M002 Language: C++23
Contract

ListItem.Content: Inputs model two eight-bit operands plus a carry-in of 0 or 1.
The calculation widens before retaining the architectural low byte.
carry and overflow report unsigned and signed representability separately.
Saturating addition clamps after widened calculation rather than allowing byte wrap.

Appendix.Content: Snippet
Cost and failure behavior

For a fixed eight-bit architecture this is constant work. Widening preserves the ninth carry bit; the overflow expression independently compares operand and result signs. Invalid carry input fails explicitly. Saturation prevents wrap but intentionally changes algebraic behavior.
Verification

Compiled with Homebrew Clang in C++23 mode and warnings as errors. An exhaustive driver checked all 131,072 (a,b,carry_in) states against independent widened unsigned and signed-range calculations, plus saturation boundaries and invalid carry rejection.
Arithmetic reconstruction helpers

These are canonical teaching implementations. The multiplication helper widens the shifting partial product before any shift; widening only the final accumulator would lose information. Division widens the partial remainder so shifting it cannot discard the extra bit. Checked signed addition proves representability before executing the operation. Mixed-sign comparison checks the lower bound as well as the upper bound.

For subtraction, reusing add8 on the complemented operand also produces the correct binary subtraction overflow predicate. Decimal arithmetic and complete instruction timing are outside this helper’s contract. The helper tests below cover its complete arithmetic input domain.
M003 - Explicit byte codecs and checked alignment
Kind: Canonical · Language: C++23 · Source: C003 / M003.

Contract: octets are eight bits; exact uint32/uint64 types must exist. Encode an unsigned 32-bit value in declared order; decode four bytes at a checked offset without typed unaligned dereferences. The input span is borrowed for the call only. Insufficient input or invalid power-of-two alignment/page shift throws invalid_argument; numeric rounding/translation overflow throws overflow_error. These functions manipulate bytes and numeric offsets; they neither allocate aligned objects nor query real page tables. Complexity is O(4) per codec and O(1) per numeric helper.

Why no reinterpret_cast load: a span may start at any byte offset; bytewise decoding avoids assuming a live aligned uint32 object and imposes the external order explicitly. memcpy into an existing aligned object can copy representation safely for appropriate types, but does not convert host byte order. std::endian and std::byteswap are optional implementation tools, not substitutes for a format contract.
Layout probe, not a wire format

Use sizeof, alignof, and offsetof on these standard-layout types to observe your compiler. Expected 12/24/16-byte results are conditional on the stated member alignments, not portable compile-time mandates. Neither object is serialized by copying its native bytes.
M003 regression driver

Compile the canonical M001/M002/M003 snippets above together with this driver; it deliberately does not execute invalid pointer accesses. Tests cover golden bytes, both codec round trips, odd byte offset, truncation/huge-offset rejection, alignment minimality and maximum-boundary behavior, page decomposition/reconstruction, and measured ABI layout.
Limits: numeric page functions are a model, not a live MMU test. This host’s layout does not establish cross-platform ABI, SIMD performance, filesystem durability, or Kairo repository behavior.
M004 - Binary interchange inspection and strict rounding laboratory

This cumulative section extends the existing driver, not a new per-chunk source file. The raw-word classifier never evaluates signaling NaNs as floats. Finite reconstruction requires the checked binary32/binary64 host. NaN numeric reconstruction is intentionally omitted because it would not preserve payload/signaling information.

Compile all cpp fences in this file in order with Clang C++23, warnings-as-errors, sanitizers, and -ffp-model=strict. The M003 main calls run_m004_lab(), defined below. Strict floating settings and a supported runtime environment are prerequisites; this is not a fast-math demonstration. See Clang floating-point controls.

Limits: no exhaustive binary32 test, live repository calls, signaling-NaN arithmetic, performance benchmarks, FTZ/DAZ mode changes, complete FPU implementation, or cross-platform payload-preservation claim. The laboratory restores rounding direction; it deliberately exercises operations that may set floating status flags and does not promise to restore those flags.
M005 - Strict arithmetic and state-update laboratory

Reuse M004’s field inspection, validated float comparison and strict assumptions. This section adds arithmetic/order demonstrations and a simplified source-shaped weighted recurrence. It calls no Kairo or Maveb API. Compile all cpp fences in order with -ffp-model=strict -ffp-contract=off; run the shared driver, which calls this section after M004.
Representation codecs and bounded file laboratory

Contract: this is a standalone teaching implementation, not a NanoQuant patch or a promised compatible production format. It requires eight-bit octets and the binary32 host checks already used by the cumulative lab. Fixed storage is int32; binary fraction count is 0–16, with int64 intermediates proved large enough. Fixed conversion uses half-away; fixed multiply/divide use nearest-even, checked narrowing and explicit zero rejection. Quantization accepts finite samples and a positive finite scale, uses nearest-even and clips to the declared small code domain before integer conversion. NaNs canonicalize in the half/BF16 converters, while tensor serialization preserves raw uint32 words.

The source-shaped tensor image fixes 28 header bytes, little-endian fields and words, nonzero dimensions, exact file length, and at most 4096 elements. It returns raw words rather than manufacturing typed objects in mapped bytes. CRC is calculated separately over specified complete bytes; no integrity field is claimed in a source repository format. These routines are bounded examples, not a complete application library.
Compile all cpp fences in order with warnings-as-errors, strict floating semantics, implicit contraction disabled, and sanitizers. The existing main calls run_m006_lab().

Navigation and first-use risks found by the live link inventory

The three books contained approximately 23 links into the old archival volumes at the inspected head: 1 from Mathematics, 11 from Graphics and 11 from Game Engine. The source targets still exist, so these are mostly legacy detours, not missing files. Nevertheless they violate the spirit of one reader-facing continuous destination per subject. Their replacement requires determining which in-book heading now owns each prerequisite; a blanket text substitution would break provenance and risk moving a reader to the wrong derivation. Until reconciled, the old link is supporting provenance rather than an instruction to start a fourth book.

A first-pass wiki-link regex reported spurious missing targets such as nodiscard, no_unique_address, GPU attributes and media paths. Those are often C++/shader syntax, escaped expressions, or images, not Obsidian page links. An audit tool must ignore fenced/inline source and distinguish image attachments from Markdown notes before treating these as missing content. Heading existence itself also proves only the presence of a title, not a coherent implementation.

The Engine source insertion is particularly large and now occupies roughly forty thousand lines before the original mid-engine renderer material. Graphics also contains an early full XR source block. These are high-priority reading-flow issues even though the mechanical content-preservation checks are green. Preserve original words, but use linking, carefully justified section placement and substantive bridge explanations to make the story follow a recurring engine problem rather than a pasted source queue.
Implementation-depth contract for every developed concept

A reader should be able to close the book and build the mechanism. Therefore a concept is not “done” until its first meaningful use provides: the forcing engineering problem; definitions of every symbol, convention and unit; the derivation and its assumptions; the concrete memory/state representation and ownership; the full algorithm and decision branches; a complete documented implementation or a clearly labeled API-specific implementation; a numerical trace with inspectable intermediate state; failure/degeneracy and alternatives; proof of invariants and bounded behavior; and reproducible positive, negative and metamorphic tests. The note itself must contain these, not just a heading, a pointer to a video, or a code file that the reader must discover elsewhere.

Witness categories must remain distinct. A CPU-only pedagogical model can prove logic, arithmetic and expected rejection cases. It cannot prove production GPU memory visibility or Apple/NVIDIA driver behavior. A reference engine test cannot establish the current Kairo integration unless the exact Kairo commit and reproducible build are inspected. A mathematically derived assumption is not an observed result; a video transcript’s claim is not verified code; the 3,000-part route map is an ownership assignment rather than 3,000 completed reconstructions.
Current development increment: logical render-graph compiler

The Game Engine volume now carries a full C++20 pass-graph compiler inline at the point where renderer intent becomes backend work. The independent laboratory is tools/labs/render_graph_contract_lab.cpp, source-synchronized through tools/check_continuous_code_sync.py. It builds a DAG from per-resource last-writer and reader-cohort state, records RAW/WAR/WAW hazards, handles imported history, topologically sorts with deterministic tie-breaking, and rejects duplicate resources, uninitialized transient reads, feedback and explicit cycles. The six-pass G-buffer/shadow/lighting/temporal/tone-map/present trace and negative cases make those semantics inspectable. GCC and Clang compiled/reran the reference locally with -O1 and -O2 -DNDEBUG, warnings-as-errors.

Boundary: This is a single-queue logical whole-resource compiler, not an implemented Vulkan or Metal render graph. It does not emit stage/access masks, image layout transitions, queue-family ownership, timeline waits, transient aliasing or device-loss recovery. Those remain first-class milestones, not implicit features of this passing laboratory. See the Vulkan synchronization specification for the separate memory-model obligations.

Cell.Content: Supplied topic, expanded mechanism and narrative node
SCALARS AS ELEMENTS OF A NUMBER FIELD — Field laws make nonzero division and vector scaling meaningful; a floating type is only an approximation. Scalars fields and real-number models

REAL NUMBERS AND THE PROPERTIES GRAPHICS RELIES ON — Order, intervals and completeness justify real geometry; bounded machine values are not the complete number line. Scalars fields and real-number models

COMPLEX NUMBERS AND TWO-DIMENSIONAL ROTATION INTUITION — Unit complex multiplication rotates a plane; conjugation reverses it, and magnitude drift adds unwanted scale. Complex numbers and planar rotations
VECTORS AS GEOMETRIC DISPLACEMENTS — Free displacement survives translation of its starting point; location and movement are different roles. Vectors coordinates and affine points
VECTORS AS COORDINATE TUPLES — An ordered tuple gives components, but neither its basis nor physical role follows from storage shape. Vectors coordinates and affine points

THE DISTINCTION BETWEEN A VECTOR AND ITS COORDINATES — One physical vector has different coordinates in different bases; distinguish passive description from active motion. Vectors coordinates and affine points
VECTOR SPACES AND THEIR AXIOMS — Closure and vector-space laws enable consistent combinations; unit directions are a constrained non-example. Vector spaces subspaces and span
SUBSPACES — A nonempty subset closed under arbitrary two-vector combinations is a subspace; shifted planes need affine language. Vector spaces subspaces and span
LINEAR COMBINATIONS — Arbitrary coefficients generate movements, not necessarily averages; negative weights are valid. Vector spaces subspaces and span
SPAN — The span is the smallest subspace containing generators; redundant inputs do not enlarge it. Vector spaces subspaces and span
LINEAR INDEPENDENCE — A zero combination must have only zero coefficients for independence; near dependence is a numerical question. Basis coordinates and dimension
BASIS VECTORS — Spanning ensures reachability and independence ensures uniqueness; both are necessary for a basis. Basis coordinates and dimension
DIMENSION OF A VECTOR SPACE — Dimension counts basis elements over the selected field; a plane stored in three components still has dimension two. Basis coordinates and dimension
COORDINATE REPRESENTATION RELATIVE TO A BASIS — Coordinates weight an ordered basis; reconstruct the physical arrow before interpreting the tuple. Basis coordinates and dimension
CHANGING BASIS CONCEPTUALLY — Changing coordinates solves the new basis relation; near-parallel basis axes amplify coefficient uncertainty. Basis coordinates and dimension

STANDARD BASIS IN <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msup> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi> </mrow> <mn>2</mn> </msup> </math> — The two standard unit axes reconstruct every planar coordinate; visual up/right conventions remain separate. Basis coordinates and dimension

STANDARD BASIS IN <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msup> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi> </mrow> <mn>3</mn> </msup> </math> — Three standard unit axes reconstruct spatial coordinates; no universal camera forward direction follows. Basis coordinates and dimension
VECTOR ADDITION FROM THE PARALLELOGRAM RULE — Head-to-tail and parallelogram movement yield componentwise addition in a common basis. Vectors coordinates and affine points
SCALAR MULTIPLICATION OF VECTORS — Scalar scaling stretches and may reverse direction; velocity times elapsed time yields displacement with correct units. Vectors coordinates and affine points

VECTOR SUBTRACTION AS DISPLACEMENT DIFFERENCE — Subtraction adds the opposite vector; ordered point difference produces the displacement from one location to another. Vectors coordinates and affine points
AFFINE POINTS VERSUS FREE VECTORS — Affine points have no intrinsic zero; point differences and translations are valid without choosing an origin. Vectors coordinates and affine points

POSITION VECTORS AND WHY POINTS ARE NOT MATHEMATICALLY VECTORS — A position vector is point minus chosen origin; changing the origin cancels only in appropriate differences. Vectors coordinates and affine points
DIRECTION VECTORS — Direction answers which way and must be nonzero; translation does not affect it. Vectors coordinates and affine points
DISPLACEMENT VECTORS — Displacement records change in position and may validly be zero; units and frame must match. Vectors coordinates and affine points
UNIT VECTORS — Unit vectors retain direction but remove magnitude; the zero vector cannot satisfy this promise. Vectors coordinates and affine points
EUCLIDEAN VECTOR MAGNITUDE — Pythagoras yields Euclidean length only in orthonormal coordinates; a slanted basis needs its metric. Norms lengths and induced distances
SQUARED MAGNITUDE AND WHY GRAPHICS OFTEN AVOIDS SQUARE ROOTS — Squared length avoids some square roots in comparisons but is neither a norm nor a metric. Norms lengths and induced distances
NORMALIZING A VECTOR — Divide a nonzero vector by its length to normalize; this operation is nonlinear. Unit directions and safe normalization
ZERO-VECTOR NORMALIZATION AND ROBUST HANDLING — Reject zero/non-finite inputs and scale before squaring; application noise thresholds are a separate policy. Unit directions and safe normalization
L1 NORM — The first norm sums absolute coordinates; its unit ball is a coordinate-dependent diamond. Norms lengths and induced distances
L2 NORM — The second norm is Euclidean; Cauchy–Schwarz proves its triangle inequality. Norms lengths and induced distances
L-INFINITY NORM — The infinity norm is the maximum absolute component; its unit ball is a coordinate-dependent box. Norms lengths and induced distances
DISTANCE INDUCED BY A NORM — A norm induces a metric by measuring point difference; different norms can choose different nearest points. Norms lengths and induced distances
DOT PRODUCT ALGEBRAIC DEFINITION — The real-coordinate dot sums component products under an orthonormal metric assumption. Dot products and orthogonality
DOT PRODUCT GEOMETRIC INTERPRETATION — Dot measures magnitude-weighted alignment; it equals cosine only for unit inputs. Dot products and orthogonality
DERIVING THE COSINE-ANGLE RELATION FOR THE DOT PRODUCT — Compare an expanded squared difference with the cosine rule to derive the angle relation. Dot products and orthogonality
ORTHOGONAL VECTORS — Orthogonality is zero inner product; zero has no angle, and numerical tests need scale-aware criteria. Dot products and orthogonality
VECTOR PROJECTION ONTO ANOTHER VECTOR — Require the along-axis remainder to be orthogonal to derive the target squared-length denominator. Projection rejection and scalar components
VECTOR REJECTION FROM ANOTHER VECTOR — Rejection removes the projected component and enables tangent-plane movement. Projection rejection and scalar components
SCALAR PROJECTION — Signed scalar projection is length along a target direction, not the coefficient multiplying the target vector. Projection rejection and scalar components
GRAM MATRIX CONCEPT — Pairwise basis dots form a Gram metric; coordinates measure physical lengths through this matrix. Gram matrices and coordinate metrics

Cross product definition in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msup> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi> </mrow> <mn>3</mn> </msup> </math> — Reconstructed enrichment: perpendicular oriented-area vector definition precedes the supplied determinant derivation. Cross products and oriented area
CROSS PRODUCT DETERMINANT DERIVATION — Signed coordinate-plane minors yield the cross formula; direct expansion verifies perpendicularity. Cross products and oriented area
CROSS PRODUCT GEOMETRIC MEANING — Cross produces an area normal, not merely an arbitrary perpendicular direction. Cross products and oriented area
CROSS-PRODUCT MAGNITUDE AND PARALLELOGRAM AREA — Cross magnitude equals base times height; triangle area is half the parallelogram area. Cross products and oriented area
CROSS-PRODUCT ORIENTATION AND THE RIGHT-HAND RULE — Input order and a chosen positive orientation fix the cross sign; mirrored transforms add a determinant sign. Coordinate handedness and orientation

WHY THE CROSS PRODUCT IS SPECIAL TO THREE DIMENSIONS — Ordinary graphics cross identifies bivectors with vectors in three dimensions; higher dimensions need qualifications. Coordinate handedness and orientation
SCALAR TRIPLE PRODUCT — Dotting an oriented area with a third movement produces a signed scalar volume. Triple products and signed volume
TRIPLE PRODUCT AS SIGNED VOLUME — Triple product is parallelepiped volume; a four-point tetrahedron has one sixth of its absolute value. Triple products and signed volume
VECTOR TRIPLE-PRODUCT IDENTITY — Expand a nested cross into dot-weighted vectors; cross grouping is not associative. Triple products and signed volume
ANGLES BETWEEN VECTORS — Nonzero finite directions define an unsigned angle in the interval from zero to pi. Robust vector angles
ROBUST ANGLE COMPUTATION WITH atan2 — Scale first and use atan2 of cross length and dot; a signed angle additionally needs an oriented plane. Robust vector angles
REFLECTION OF A DIRECTION ACROSS A NORMAL — Reverse the normal component to reflect across a plane; unit-normal and general-normal formulas differ. Reflection refraction and shading directions
REFRACTION GEOMETRY FROM SNELL’S LAW — Snell scales the tangent component; a negative transmitted squared cosine indicates total internal reflection. Reflection refraction and shading directions
HALF-VECTOR CONSTRUCTION IN SHADING — Normalize the sum of unit outward light/view directions; opposite inputs have no unique half-vector. Reflection refraction and shading directions
TANGENT VECTORS ON A SURFACE — Surface derivatives or triangle edges span tangent movement; texture tangents may retain physical stretch. Surface tangents normals and bitangents
NORMAL VECTORS ON A SURFACE — Geometric normals measure perpendicularity; shading normals can differ and need their own contract. Surface tangents normals and bitangents
BITANGENT VECTORS — Solve edge/UV equations for a second tangent; degenerate UVs and mirrored-island signs need explicit handling. Surface tangents normals and bitangents
ORTHONORMAL BASES — Unit perpendicular axes give an identity Gram matrix and simple dot-based reconstruction. Orthonormal frames and Gram-Schmidt
CONSTRUCTING AN ORTHONORMAL BASIS FROM ONE DIRECTION — A least-aligned helper yields a nondegenerate frame from one direction, but does not ensure continuity. Orthonormal frames and Gram-Schmidt
GRAM-SCHMIDT ORTHOGONALIZATION — Repeated projection removal preserves span while producing perpendicular axes for independent generators. Orthonormal frames and Gram-Schmidt
MODIFIED GRAM-SCHMIDT AND NUMERICAL STABILITY — Measuring updated residuals changes rounding behavior; reorthogonalization cannot repair uncertain input rank. Orthonormal frames and Gram-Schmidt
HANDEDNESS OF COORDINATE BASES — Triple-product sign classifies an ordered basis relative to chosen orientation, not memory layout. Coordinate handedness and orientation
RIGHT-HANDED COORDINATE SYSTEMS — Positive frame orientation is preserved by proper rotations and cyclic axis permutations. Coordinate handedness and orientation
LEFT-HANDED COORDINATE SYSTEMS — A reflected frame has opposite orientation while preserving Euclidean distances; API conventions need separate statements. Coordinate handedness and orientation
ORIENTATION TESTS IN 2D USING SIGNED AREA — Signed doubled triangle area supplies a two-dimensional orientation predicate with a documented axis convention. Coordinate handedness and orientation
ORIENTATION TESTS IN 3D USING TRIPLE PRODUCTS — Four-point triple products decide plane side and coplanarity under an explicit ordering convention. Coordinate handedness and orientation
BARYCENTRIC COORDINATES AS AFFINE WEIGHTS — Triangle weights sum to one for affine meaning; nonnegative weights identify the convex interior. Barycentric coordinates and interpolation

DERIVING BARYCENTRIC COORDINATES FOR A TRIANGLE — Edge Gram solves or signed area ratios recover weights; degeneracy and off-plane residuals remain separate checks. Barycentric coordinates and interpolation

INTERPOLATING ATTRIBUTES WITH BARYCENTRIC COORDINATES — The same affine weights interpolate attributes; nonlinear encoding and unit length require additional policies. Barycentric coordinates and interpolation
AFFINE COMBINATIONS VERSUS LINEAR COMBINATIONS — Only sum-one weights preserve point translation; sum-zero weights describe a displacement. Convex combinations and convex hulls
CONVEX COMBINATIONS — Nonnegative affine weights produce convex mixtures; extrapolation is affine but not convex. Convex combinations and convex hulls
CONVEX SETS — A convex set contains every line segment between its members; a boundary need not be convex. Convex combinations and convex hulls
CONVEX HULL INTUITION — A convex hull is all finite convex mixtures and may fill source concavities or holes. Convex combinations and convex hulls
MINKOWSKI SUM INTUITION — Pairwise set-coordinate addition represents sweeps and expansions; symmetric robot dilation is a special case. Minkowski sums and support mappings
MINKOWSKI DIFFERENCE INTUITION — Collision difference means A plus reflected B here, not set subtraction; overlap is origin membership. Minkowski sums and support mappings
SUPPORT FUNCTIONS OF CONVEX SHAPES — Support scalar and support point differ; opposite-direction support queries construct difference extrema on demand. Minkowski sums and support mappings

HOMOGENEOUS COORDINATES AS PROJECTIVE REPRESENTATIVES — Nonzero common scale defines projective equivalence; finite representatives divide by their final coordinate. Homogeneous coordinates and perspective division

POINTS AND DIRECTIONS THROUGH HOMOGENEOUS <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>w</mi> </math> — Homogeneous one distinguishes points from zero-tagged directions under affine translation; zero tuple is invalid projectively. Homogeneous coordinates and perspective division

NORMALIZED DEVICE-COORDINATE INTUITION AS A VECTOR-SPACE MAPPING — NDC standardizes device-coordinate ranges, not length; perspective division is nonlinear and follows clipping. Homogeneous coordinates and perspective division
DUAL VECTORS AND COVECTORS — Covectors are linear scalar measurement rules; a metric hides their distinction from ordinary vectors. Covectors linear functionals and normal transforms

WHY SURFACE NORMALS TRANSFORM DIFFERENTLY FROM POSITIONS — Preserve the normal’s pairing with transformed tangents to derive inverse transpose; singular cases need policy. Covectors linear functionals and normal transforms
LINEAR FUNCTIONALS — A linear functional distributes across weighted vector sums; its kernel contains movements it measures as zero. Covectors linear functionals and normal transforms
EXTERIOR-PRODUCT INTUITION — Exterior algebra retains areas and volumes without requiring a vector-valued cross in every dimension. Exterior products and geometric algebra
WEDGE PRODUCT AS ORIENTED AREA CONCEPT — Antisymmetric bilinear wedges encode oriented area; dependent generators have zero wedge. Exterior products and geometric algebra
GEOMETRIC-ALGEBRA MOTIVATION FOR GRAPHICS — The geometric product combines dot and wedge; plane elements connect to complex-like rotation structure. Exterior products and geometric algebra
FLOATING-POINT VECTOR STORAGE IN C++ — Floating storage has bounded precision and target layout; trivial copying does not certify external representation. Vector storage SIMD and boundary layouts
VEC2 DATA STRUCTURE DESIGN — A two-component value type needs initialization, safe access and explicit semantic roles. Vector value types and component access
VEC3 DATA STRUCTURE DESIGN — Three-component storage supports spatial operations but is not automatically a point, normal or unit direction. Vector value types and component access
VEC4 DATA STRUCTURE DESIGN — Four-component storage can serve distinct roles; homogeneous coordinates and quaternions require separate contracts. Vector value types and component access
OPERATOR OVERLOADS FOR VECTOR ARITHMETIC — Overloads should express unambiguous vector arithmetic; name dot, cross and componentwise multiplication. Vector value types and component access
SWIZZLES AND COMPONENT ACCESS — Read swizzles reorder components; writable swizzles need temporary-copy and duplicate-destination policies. Vector value types and component access
ALIGNMENT OF VECTOR TYPES — Measure alignment, size and stride; greater alignment may add padding and is not a performance guarantee. Vector storage SIMD and boundary layouts
PACKED VERSUS ALIGNED VEC3 REPRESENTATIONS — Compact storage and aligned compute types can coexist with explicit conversion at boundaries. Vector storage SIMD and boundary layouts
SIMD IMPLEMENTATION OF VECTOR ARITHMETIC — SIMD within one vector differs from SIMD across objects; layouts, reductions and FMA affect throughput and results. Vector storage SIMD and boundary layouts
APPROXIMATE VECTOR EQUALITY — Exact, componentwise, distance, angular and ULP comparisons answer different questions; closeness is not transitive. Vector tolerances and finite-state diagnostics
DEBUGGING NaN VECTORS — Catch the first invalid input or operation using finite checks; NaN propagation can silently skip decisions. Vector tolerances and finite-state diagnostics
VECTOR INVARIANTS IN ENGINE APIs — Validated wrappers establish finite/unit promises and operations must preserve or explicitly drop them. Coordinate-space types and validated invariants

DISTINGUISHING WORLD-SPACE AND LOCAL-SPACE VECTOR TYPES — Space-tagged points, vectors and transforms reject broad frame mistakes; dynamic local-frame identity remains a separate issue. Coordinate-space types and validated invariants

Reconstructing a Production-Ready Vec3 Library from First Principles — Reconstruct the scalar library from the mathematics, then verify contracts with edge cases and seeded properties. Inline capstone and tests

Cell.Content: Definition, mechanism, and concrete reconstruction cue

Translation units and linking — Source → preprocessing → semantic compilation → object/BMI → link. A declaration can permit compilation while an absent implementation fails linking; BMI is not object code.
Declarations and definitions — Every definition is a declaration, not conversely. extern int x declares; int x=0 defines. Forward class is incomplete; fixed-underlying opaque enum is complete.
One Definition Rule — Multiple translation units must describe coherent entities. Header guards are per-TU; ordinary external definitions and inline/template exceptions have different constraints.
Scopes and name lookup — Scope belongs to a name; qualified lookup selects a context; hiding changes lookup without deleting the hidden object. ADL adds associated candidates.
Storage duration and object lifetime — Automatic/static/thread/dynamic classify storage. A block-scope static outlives the block; a local pointer and its dynamic pointee have distinct durations.

Object construction and storage reuse — Sufficient aligned storage and completed initialization establish an ordinary object lifetime. destroy_at can end the object while the byte buffer remains; casts do not construct arbitrary objects.

Object identity and generation handles — Equal values need not be one object, and reused addresses host different occupants. A slot/generation needs live-registry validation, not merely a non-sentinel index.
Fixed-width integer types — sizeof(char)=1 C++ byte; CHAR_BIT≥8. int has minimum capacity, not a universal32-bit width. Exact/least/fast and size_t express different requirements.

Scoped enums and validated domains — Scoped enumerators and no implicit integer conversion reduce accidents. Explicit underlying width does not validate received codes; states and combinable flags need separate designs.

Aggregate initialization — C++20/23 aggregate criteria are not the older user-provided-constructor rule. Designators follow member declaration order. Braces may select initializer-list or ordinary constructors instead.
Class access and invariants — struct defaults members and bases public; class defaults them private. Both are class types. Record/invariant intent is convention, not a syntactic capability limit.

Standard-layout and trivial copyability — Alignment creates internal/tail padding. Traits do not imply array traversal, packing, serialization or GPU compatibility. Named x/y/z require explicit indexing or actual array storage.

Appendix.Content: Read the C++ narrative from buildable text through entities, storage, occupants, domains and layout. Source numbers belong in this ledger, not in teaching chapters. Independent code and essential traces remain inline in that volume.

This cumulative supplement retains the per-part definition and coverage ledger. The connected teaching volumes now explain the essential foundations, unfamiliar terms and worked steps directly; readers should not need this ledger to reconstruct a lesson. Concept links provide optional navigation. Examples and clarifications are explanatory material; repository claims retain their evidence status in Supplementary/Sources and Code Anchors.
All fourteen supplied parts are accepted. Source numbering audits coverage; it does not divide the teaching story. M009 now develops parameter passing and value transfer in Parts127–147.

Cell.Content: Definition, mechanism, and concrete reconstruction cue
References and aliases — Binding establishes an alias; assignment acts on the referent. A reference-to-pointer can reseat that pointer, unlike a reference to its pointee.

Reference binding and converted temporaries — Type/category select the referent. const int& can track the original; const double& can bind a converted snapshot. Arrays keep extent through array references; bit-fields require special handling.

Temporary lifetime extension and Move casts and forwarding references — Direct local binding can extend a temporary, not transitive function-return aliases. Braces/parentheses/new exceptions matter; move is a cast, and deduced T&& forwarding collapses references.

Value categories and materialization — lvalue/xvalue identify, prvalue produces; glvalue and rvalue overlap at xvalue. A named T&& is an lvalue in ordinary use. decltype(name) differs from decltype((name)).
Pointer arithmetic and provenance — A pointer is an access path, not ownership. Null/object/one-past/invalid states differ; dereference requires live, aligned, type-accessible in-range storage.
Null pointers and optional access — nullptr distinguishes pointer absence from integer zero. Typed null deletion is valid; bare delete nullptr is ill-formed. Non-null does not prove lifetime.

Named members versus array elements — Array-relative positions zero through N may be formed; only zero through N-1 dereferenced. Same-array subtraction must fit ptrdiff_t. Adjacent members do not authorize array indexing.

Pointer arithmetic and provenance — A pointer’s storage relationship is not manufactured by a plausible integer. Specified round trips do not resurrect occupants or authorize arbitrary arithmetic; P3407 is discussion, not C++23 law.

Borrow invalidation and logical identity — Vector reallocation can dangle a borrow; swap assignment can leave a live slot with a different logical owner. Valid handles do not certify previous component references.

Deferred captures and borrowed views — Reference members, spans, string views and captured this pointers require referent lifetime. Copying a view does not own its buffer; an owning capture supplies a different contract.

Const qualification and shallow constness and Auto decltype and reference collapsing — Read-only access is not global immutability. Top-level const is often dropped by value deduction; actual const objects cannot be made writable by casts.

Multilevel pointer qualification — Separate pointer and pointee qualification. int** to const int** would enable unsafe injection; intermediate const blocks it. Const span descriptors do not imply const elements.

Ref-qualified accessors — const member functions restrict the object path; &/&& constrain caller category. Persistent getters can borrow; both mutable and const temporary getters need value/deleted policies.

Logical constness and mutable caches — Eligible mutable members permit representation changes under const access. Cache/source invariants require invalidation and synchronization; return protected snapshots. Mutable closures are not automatically thread-safe.
