Appendix.Content: The supplied source contains exactly twenty-one parts. At acceptance, it extended Volume02 to Parts101–147; M010 subsequently added Parts148–160. Teaching headings remain concept-led; exact coverage is recorded in the current ledger.

Cell.Content: Parameter passing and sink contracts — Argument expressions initialize separate value-parameter objects. Lvalue/xvalue/prvalue routes differ; a sink retains/transforms a value, and copied pointer members still alias.

References and aliases — Mutable/const/rvalue reference parameters borrow with different access and consumption contracts. Aliased source/destination references can change a sequential update’s result.

Parameter passing and sink contracts — Pointer parameters copy pointer values; T*& or pointer-output protocols can reseat caller state. Null optionality must be documented; array parameters adjust to pointers without extent enforcement.

Return values and copy elision — Result objects can be constructed directly; NRVO is optional while appropriate same-type prvalue initialization requires no intermediate transfer. Eligible local/parameter return expressions implicitly move in C++23.

Ref-qualified accessors and Temporary lifetime extension — Reference/view results retain owner lifetime/invalidation obligations. Temporary getters require policies for const rvalues too; decltype(auto) can return a reference through parentheses.

Constructors and invariant establishment — Members/bases initialize before the body. Initializers establish state; body assignments replace it. Constructor failure and factory error results are different protocols.

Default and value initialization — Default, zero, aggregate and value initialization differ. First-declaration defaulting is not an empty user-provided body; braces do not universally initialize every scalar.
Member order and delegating constructors — Declaration order governs members regardless of colon-list spelling. Provider-before-dependent order establishes correct construction/reverse cleanup.
Member order and delegating constructors — Delegation centralizes a target initialization path, then runs its own body. The target is the sole initializer; cycles are ill-formed.

Destruction and partial construction — Destructor body precedes reverse subobject cleanup; failed ordinary construction destroys completed subobjects. Delegating-target completion changes the whole-object cleanup case.

Copy semantics and resource identity — New-object copying follows members’ semantic operations; equal-sign initialization is not assignment. Pointer/reference copies preserve associations rather than clone referents.
Assignment and exception guarantees — Existing-object replacement must handle old ownership, self-aliasing and failure. Prepare before commit; reference/const members can delete generated assignment.

Copy semantics and resource identity — Deep/shallow are contract choices, not good/bad labels. Pixel values may duplicate, handles identify, graph clones remap; copy-on-write adds mutation/lifetime/synchronization costs.

Move operations and moved-from states — New-object moves can take resources and repair source state; scalar/inline members need not become cheaper. Ordinary constructors alone do not suppress implicit move generation.
Move operations and moved-from states — Move assignment also handles the destination’s former resource and self-move. Allocator policy can prevent constant-time adoption.
Move casts and forwarding references — move changes category, not ownership itself; const remains const. Explicit local-return moves can inhibit NRVO; move_if_noexcept selects a transfer access path.

Move operations and moved-from states — Source lifetime continues after moving. Valid-but-unspecified is not destroyed or undefined; operation preconditions still apply. A custom empty source needs an explicit maintained invariant.
Return values and copy elision — Immovable types can use guaranteed direct result construction; a named-local fallback still needs usable operations. Accessible destruction remains required.
Rules of Three Five and Zero — Destructor/copy constructor/copy assignment are coordinated raw-owner decisions; copying may instead be deleted. It is a design heuristic, not a compiler mandate.

Special member generation and traits — Five adds both moves. User-declared versus user-provided matters; a defaulted destructor suppresses dedicated implicit moves, while move-constructible traits can still classify copying as viable.

Rules of Three Five and Zero — Compose tested member owners rather than repeat transfer/release logic. Zero does not forbid ordinary constructors or prove cross-member invariants; Relocation versus move remains a versioned research bridge.

Appendix.Content: M010 continues the same Volume 02 story from Rule-of-Zero composition into the concrete ownership and lifetime protocols underneath it. The source specifies Parts 148–160. Repository paths named in the pasted lesson are source-provided examples and remain To verify until their repositories/revisions are inspected. These entries identify coverage; the expanded teaching narrative is in Volume 02.

Cell.Content: Definition, mechanism, and concrete reconstruction cue
RAII and resource handles — Bind matched acquisition/release responsibility to a live owner; scope exit handles early return and unwinding. External asynchronous use can require deferred reclamation.
RAII and resource handles — Each fully acquired resource must immediately enter an owner; completed subobjects clean up if construction fails. CPU ownership does not alone establish GPU completion.
Ownership and non-owning views — Ownership means responsibility for ending use/lifetime; a borrow provides access without extending lifetime.
Exclusive and shared smart-pointer ownership — unique_ptr is a move-only exclusive owner; get() borrows while release() transfers responsibility.
Exclusive and shared smart-pointer ownership — A custom deleter pairs a native handle with its actual release protocol; deleter state/type can affect representation and conversion safety.
Exclusive and shared smart-pointer ownership — shared_ptr copies join a control block’s strong ownership group; object and control-block lifetimes may differ.
Exclusive and shared smart-pointer ownership — Reference-count operations have costs; control-block coordination does not synchronize arbitrary pointee operations.
Weak observation and ownership cycles — A weak edge avoids extending object lifetime; lock() safely attempts to obtain a temporary strong owner and can break cycles.
Weak observation and ownership cycles — enable_shared_from_this joins an existing owner group; never build an independent shared_ptr control block from this.

Placement construction and explicit lifetime management — Allocation functions acquire raw storage; new-expressions combine allocation and initialization. Size, alignment, construction, failure cleanup and deallocation must match.
Placement construction and explicit lifetime management — Arrays require correct count-aware construction/destruction and matching new[]/delete[]; containers usually own this protocol more safely.
Placement construction and explicit lifetime management — Placement construction/construct_at begins an object lifetime in adequate pre-existing storage; it does not allocate that storage.

Placement construction and explicit lifetime management — Explicit destruction ends an occupant’s lifetime, not necessarily storage. Reuse, transparent replacement and laundering have distinct conditions.

M011 — Parts 161–180: a request changes shape and a backend changes implementation

Source status: authored reconstruction from the canonical integrated 180-chunk / original 3,000-part curriculum contract, not a received M011 teaching transcript. Teaching placement: the continuous C++ narrative, immediately after the M010 ownership chapter and before the API-publication chapter. The concrete example follows a typed renderer request through a polymorphic backend; it does not substitute a dictionary entry for each numbered part.

Cell.Content: Reason the concept appears in the request-to-backend narrative
A command record can hold overlapping alternatives but not several simultaneously active objects.
Raw union active-member and lifetime rules; trivial union assignment in tested C++20 lab.
A request must carry its active alternative rather than guess an interpretation from bytes.
std::variant, get_if, holds_alternative and visit, replacement and exceptional empty state; executable request-state checks.
An editor should depend on the backend’s promised operations, not the native implementation.
Base/derived interface contract contrasted with composition and closed alternatives.
A derived object contains a base subobject with its own identity and layout constraints.
Static versus dynamic object view; no invented vptr byte layout.
A base reference must call the selected backend’s implementation.
Virtual dispatch with observable CountingBackend result in the lab.
Indirection has implementation and performance consequences, but no mandated vtable layout.
Implementation-model explanation, devirtualization caveat and proposed measurement controls.
A backend contract needs operations without constructing the incomplete base.
Pure virtual operation and abstract interface; concrete derived override.
An owner typed as base must destroy the concrete derived object correctly.
Virtual destructor through std::unique_ptr<Backend>; derived-destruction assertion.
Copying a derived object into a base value can erase its specialized identity.
MeshObject / NamedObject slicing contrasted with a base reference; tested.
A backend can implement multiple independent interfaces, creating distinct base views.
Multiple inheritance, ambiguity and subobject-adjustment explanation.
A diamond may duplicate a common base unless virtual inheritance shares it.
Diamond with two paths through a virtual Root; identical subobject address test.
Upcasting to a public base is different from a downcast that assumes an actual derived object.
static_cast guarantees and the conditions it does not dynamically test.
A diagnostic needs to ask whether the runtime backend really has a concrete type.
dynamic_cast success and failed pointer cast tested; RTTI and design cautions.
Byte reinterpretation must not masquerade as object construction or safe aliasing.
reinterpret_cast limitations; byte views and bit_cast alternatives.
Removing const qualification is not the same as making a const object writable.
Operators should communicate a domain operation and preserve invariants.
Resource handles versus durations and inappropriate hidden side effects.
A handle’s equality includes its generation, not merely a reused slot.
Defaulted operator== derived from <=> and two identity assertions.
Identifiers need meaningful ordering; NaN can make floating comparison unordered.
Strong integer ordering, partial floating ordering and strict-weak-order concerns.
Overload selection is a compile-time decision based on arguments and conversions.
Integer/double overload calls tested; ambiguity and conversion cautions.
Virtual implementation selection and default-argument binding happen at different times.
Base default 2 with derived body produces 20; derived default 7 produces 70; tested.

Appendix.Content: Executed reference, scope and limits. tools/labs/backend_choice_lab.cpp was compiled with GCC 14.2.0 on Linux as C++20 using -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -Werror -fsanitize=address,undefined -fno-omit-frame-pointer and executed with all assertions passing. The committed source was independently compared byte-for-byte to that locally executed source by FNV-1a checksum (both 0x22332ec3, length 6,431 bytes). This checksum comparison establishes identical bytes for the compared artifact; the compiler run remains a single compiler/platform witness, not every possible C++ implementation. The example intentionally simulates renderer behavior and contains no native graphics API execution. Current Kairo and AI-provider repositories were not re-inspected here; the listed original code-lab paths are curriculum targets, not verified implementation claims.

M012 — Parts 181–200: typed asset requests, deferred callbacks and transactional publication

Provenance and status: authored reconstruction using the original 3,000-part contract’s exact M012 titles (not a received M012 lesson transcript). The material belongs directly in the continuing computing-foundations narrative. It follows the existing M011 backend selection chapter and precedes the pre-existing general API-contract chapter. The 20 original identifiers remain a coverage map, not a substitute for the connected explanation.

Cell.Content: Why the renderer story requires it and where the evidence sits
A raw integer is not automatically a meaningful byte count; the chapter contrasts implicit construction with deliberate unit conversion.
explicit ByteCount(std::size_t) prevents mistaken copy-initialization; compile-time checks verify the conversion restriction, not range validity.
explicit operator std::size_t() requires deliberate extraction; contextual conversions and overload effects are explained.
A synchronous C-style progress callback receives a function pointer plus borrowed context; the lab checks the invocation.
A Reporter member pointer requires a particular live instance; the lab calls the member through an object.
The copyable callable wrapper hides target type, not allocation/copy/lifetime cost; the lab checks an owning target and empty invocation.
AddBytes::operator() carries state for a progress update; pointer-member lifetime remains a borrow.
The closure object combines an operation with stored or referenced captured state; no concrete closure byte layout is claimed.
Snapshot and shared-owner captures show the difference between copied scalar state and an owned lifetime.
190 · Lambda capture by reference and lifetime hazards
A reference capture reads later mutations only while its referent lives; invalid async scene callback is explained but not executed.
The deliberately injected failure after resource creation unwinds a private local owner; typed result conversion occurs at the public boundary.
Resource destructor and move operations express non-escaping exception promises; compile-time traits connect to vector insertion guarantees.
193 · Strong, basic, and no-throw exception guarantees
Prepare privately, publish once, compare stored state and native-handle counts after failure; guarantee is limited to stated observable state.
194 · Error codes versus exceptions in engine code
Empty input and operational failure map to typed UploadError; exception categories remain an implementation detail within the bounded example.
The lab’s verify is active under NDEBUG; external input checks and internal invariant failures use distinct policies.
Invalid lifetime, out-of-bounds, aliasing and data-race examples are explained, never deliberately run as undefined behavior.
A raw file cannot be safely interpreted as a typed struct merely by pointer cast; object type-access and lifetime conditions are explicit.
IEEE binary32 bit_cast is tested under platform assertions; a separate little-endian serializer establishes portable file bytes.
199 · Trivial, trivially copyable, and standard-layout properties
WireHeader traits are checked without falsely asserting its raw storage is a six-byte file layout; differing type categories are explained.
200 · Designing a resource-owning C++ type from blank memory to safe API
Resource develops empty/owning/moved-from states, matching release, deleted copy, noexcept move and a device-outlives-owner contract; AssetStore adds a failure-atomic publication boundary.

Exact committed Git blob bc811fb2c659b635af290d2f3abb58a6c38a06fc matches the locally executed lab’s Git hash. Local SHA-256: 32e93bc026677e074aaa77711c7b3fea721e0f582e64eb5d86c2d740425df92c. Ran successfully with GCC 14.2.0, -std=c++20 -O1 -g -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -Werror -fsanitize=address,undefined -fno-omit-frame-pointer; also compiled and ran under Clang 17.0.0 with warning flags and GCC release-style -DNDEBUG -O2. Their existence does not claim exhaustive normative clause analysis.

M013 — Parts 201–216: generic asset preparation with constrained APIs

Provenance: authored reconstruction of the exact original M013 part titles from the integrated 180-chunk / 3,000-part contract, not a received M013 source transcript. The actual lesson is the continuous asset-pipeline narrative, placed directly after M012 rather than scattered into 16 separate disconnected definitions.

Cell.Content: Why it becomes necessary, with directly inspectable witness
One asset_bytes operation handles multiple supported asset types; T is deduced from actual mesh and texture calls.
AssetDepot<T, Capacity> represents independent statically typed storage for mesh and shader records.
Capacity and texture Channels are compile-time values affecting type identity, storage and byte-size policy.
A complete AssetTraits<Mesh> specialization supplies mesh-specific byte-size behavior.
AssetTraits<Texture<Channels>> supplies one rule for the family of supported channel counts.
const T& and Args&& follow distinct deduction rules; callers need not manually name every deduced type.
All four &/&& combinations are derived, with lvalue and rvalue assertions in the lab.
The function-template Args&&... preserves incoming lvalues and rvalues across a generic API boundary.
std::forward<Args>(args)... selects the intended copy or move constructor for Mesh; both paths are tested.
total_bytes(const T&... assets) accepts a heterogeneous, compile-time-checked group, including an empty pack.
A built-in comma fold performs checked left-to-right byte accumulation; 12+48+15=75 and zero-argument cases tested.
HasByteSize uses std::void_t, decltype and declval to detect a valid trait expression without a hard error in its substitution context.
Named Uploadable accepts mesh and supported textures but not an unknown asset; tested with static_assert.
Compound requirements check the label’s conversion and exact byte-size result type, but do not execute runtime validation.
AssetDepot::emplace requires std::constructible_from<T, Args&&...>; invalid integer-to-mesh construction rejected at compile time.
route has a generic fallback and a Uploadable-constrained overload; correct static routing tested for supported and unknown types.

Appendix.Content: Actual compiled witness: C++20 reference laboratory, 249 lines / 10,302 bytes (ASCII), SHA-256 a5db53514d74ae247b4ac42fafb8504ae701bd0746141ab4861ce874f496e30f, Git blob e673da4c89e50114b3e49c5b1b32dda7bf019ec8, verified byte-identical with the executed source. It passed three actual builds: GCC 14.2.0 -std=c++20 -O1 -g -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -Werror -fsanitize=address,undefined -fno-omit-frame-pointer; Clang 17.0.0 -std=c++20 -O1 -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -Werror; GCC 14.2.0 -std=c++20 -O2 -DNDEBUG -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -Werror. Each executable printed generic_asset_pipeline_lab: all checks passed. An initial compiler warning from the empty pack under GCC -Werror was corrected by explicitly marking the sometimes-unused fold helper [[maybe_unused]]; the final committed blob is the passing version.

What was checked: compile-time admission/rejection; lvalue copying versus rvalue transfer; capacity rejection without state change; failed shader construction without publication; unused slot reuse; traits for 3/4 channels; numerical overflow rejection; batch sum and empty-pack behavior; and preferred constrained overload selection. What was not checked: KairoMath/Matrix.cppm, KairoECS/SparseSet.cppm or other live external repository code; C++ module build; GPU execution; multithreaded asset lifetime, cancellation, driver synchronization, full exception fault injection, or comparative performance.

Language references and research direction: cppreference function-template argument deduction, cppreference constraints and concepts, cppreference fold expressions, cppreference partial class-template specialization, cppreference std::forward. Next, benchmark the bounded generic depot against a concrete store and a generational/page-backed alternative using identical payload sizes and publication/failure workloads; do not assume generic dispatch is faster without data.

Completion classification: all 16 original titles mapped to continuous authored teaching and one representative, executable, standards-conscious laboratory. This does not certify 16 independent programs, learner recall, received-source equivalence, cross-platform ABI equivalence, or a current Kairo implementation audit. M014 — Parts 217–230: one tile planner and its compile-time policy decisions

Status and provenance: authored reconstruction grounded in the original integrated curriculum and confirmed language references. Not a received M014 lesson transcript. The complete narrative continues the same generic asset-pipeline problem from M011–M013: a pixel format and policy may be fixed during compilation while tile dimensions, payload length, failure state, and budget limits still demand runtime validation. Original numbered parts are retained only as coverage traceability, not as a string of disconnected teaching sections.

Cell.Content: An internal pixel format and empty validation policy need compile-time properties; std::is_empty_v and std::is_base_of_v are checked in the lab and semantic limitations are explained.
PixelTraits<Format> inherits std::integral_constant<std::size_t,Channels>, giving static channel counts for supported formats.
Known RGBA versus RGB format selects whether a prepared plan has alpha; both variants are tested.
checked_product performs safe size multiplication both in static_assert and using runtime inputs; overflow is rejected before multiplication.
inline constexpr tile definition and precomputed Morton table are constant-expression objects, distinct from mutable diagnostics.
make_tile_definition requires a valid compile-time tile configuration, and make_morton_table builds the lookup table during constant evaluation.
constinit std::uint32_t g_plans_recorded=0 guarantees suitable static initialization but remains mutable and not thread-safe; the single-threaded count is checked.
A sixteen-entry table spreads four coordinate bits; morton4(3,5)=39 is derived and compile-time/runtime tested.
A concrete CRTP recorder and a std::function<void(const TilePlan&)> target each receive the same plan under different static/runtime contracts; neither is benchmarked.
RecorderBase<CountingRecorder>::record calls record_impl via a derived cast; the derived-object precondition and nonvirtual semantics are explained and tested.
TilePlanner<Format,BudgetPolicy,Recorder> composes budget validation and recording; both 64-byte bounded and stateless no-budget variants are exercised.
VerifyPayloadTag and MetadataOnlyTag select overloads that verify real bytes or deliberately produce only a manifest; invalid length is rejected in verified mode.
A holder deriving from an empty policy is measured beside an ordinary empty-policy member; observed sizes are toolchain-specific, not promised.
A policy member eligible for overlap is used in TilePlanner and an isolated holder; local sizeof results and MSVC portability differences are documented.

Appendix.Content: Executable witness: C++20 reference laboratory, 258 lines and 10,788 bytes, SHA-256 f5eb017280bb6b2ae6b1475dfb014694235f805a6948df36548b17145d889951, Git blob f4379dbce70c261f2832f8311a628e346f7471f7, byte-identical to the locally executed source. Compiled and executed successfully with GCC 14.2.0 using -std=c++20 -O1 -g -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -Werror -fsanitize=address,undefined -fno-omit-frame-pointer; Clang 17.0.0 with -std=c++20 -O1 -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -Werror; and GCC 14.2.0 release-style -std=c++20 -O2 -DNDEBUG -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -Werror. Each execution printed compile_time_asset_policy_lab: all checks passed; local layout observations were PlainPolicyHolder=16, EboPolicyHolder=8 and CompactPolicyHolder=8 bytes on that Linux target.

Evidence limits: the code plans tiles and checks an optional CPU byte span. It does not allocate native graphics memory, enqueue a GPU transfer, validate a device format, establish a real asynchronous transaction, measure speed, or certify a portable ABI layout. Its MetadataOnlyTag deliberately does not check that a payload exists, so the result cannot be represented as a verified upload. constinit supplies no synchronization, CRTP supplies no runtime plugin selection, and local object-size observations cannot be treated as standard-required sizes. No live Kairo/Maveb repository sources were re-inspected. Research and project-code gates remain open.

Language-source anchors: cppreference if constexpr, constexpr, consteval, constinit, empty base optimization, [[no_unique_address]], including implementation notes, and class-template type traits. These clarify specific language rules; they do not stand in for a real cross-compiler benchmark.

Completion classification: fourteen original titles mapped to one connected, implementable authored chapter and a representative three-toolchain test. It is not fourteen separately certified mastery gates or a received-source integration. Next canonical M015, Parts 231–250, should arise as the in-memory asset store moves beyond its fixed-capacity demonstration into standard container growth, invalidation, storage and lookup choices.
M015 — Parts 231–250: growing the asset registry without losing identities

Source status: authored reconstruction from the original integrated 180-chunk / 3,000-part curriculum contract. No received M015 teaching transcript is claimed. The single coherent explanation is the growing asset registry narrative, directly after M014 and before the existing general API-contract chapter. The numbered rows below preserve exact titles and indicate what mechanism required each concept; they are not the main teaching body.

Cell.Content: Where the problem forces its use; evidence
A bounded asset depot begins growing; the lab distinguishes live elements from reserved storage and checks contiguous values.
Derive the geometric relocation sum and amortized append cost; the lab observes capacity 2→4 on its local implementation, not a standard-prescribed factor.
Growth invalidates old element pointers/iterators; the lab checks the growth event without accessing stale addresses.
reserve(2) does not create elements; resize(5) constructs new ones with the tested default int values.
Compile-time fixed channel/counter sequences keep their own element storage and do not use vector growth semantics; array indexing tested.
Editor arrival/consumption needs front/back operations without pretending an entire deque is a single contiguous allocation; front/back/index test.
Editing work transfers nodes while retaining iterators to unaffected nodes; splice tested.
A singly linked worklist removes a successor using erase_after, needing the predecessor iterator; tested.
Ordered asset names with logarithmic comparison-based operations and ordered iteration; tree shape remains an implementation detail.
A set of IDs removes duplicates and preserves comparison order; 8,3,8,5 yields three unique values.
Persistent name-to-generation-handle index uses owned std::string keys; its hash lookup and rehash rules are explained.
Pending-name membership without mapped values; duplicate insertion and contains tested.
243 · Hash function quality and collision behavior
A deliberately constant hash places all 24 distinct names in one bucket without corrupting key equality; lookup correctness is tested.
load_factor=n/b, max_load_factor(0.5) and reserve(96) illustrate the bucket policy; old rehash-invalidated iterators are never dereferenced.
Uploads require priority selection, plus explicit sequence-number tie-breaking because the adapter alone does not guarantee stability.
Editor undo/traversal needs LIFO; push 7,8 then pop yields 8 before 7.
Incoming jobs need FIFO; push 7,8 then pop yields 7 before 8.
248 · std::span as a non-owning contiguous view
A checksum consumes byte data synchronously without copying it, with owner lifetime and reallocation constraints explicit.
249 · std::string storage and small-string optimization concept
Asset names own characters; locally observed short/long capacities 15/1000 are not portable SSO or allocation guarantees.
Borrowed path substring "stone" is copied into an owning string before the source is changed; substring may lack a terminating NUL.

Appendix.Content: Tested implementation: C++20 reference laboratory, 292 lines / 13,525 bytes; Git blob c9a323bcf4a3f2e41df13db9d10d381bdd71468f, SHA-256 e829cf731b17419e282775cf0b8224c210819ed3d81da36fce45014a04e4afae. The committed bytes are identical to the local file compiled and executed with GCC 14.2.0 using -std=c++20 -O1 -g -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -Werror -fsanitize=address,undefined -fno-omit-frame-pointer, Clang 17.0.0 using -std=c++20 -O1 -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -Werror, and GCC 14.2.0 using -std=c++20 -O2 -DNDEBUG -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -Werror. All three executions reported asset_container_lab: all checks passed. The implementation tests two distinct rollback injections (before preparation, after candidate slot creation), stale-handle rejection after slot recycling, list/deque/forward_list behaviors, pathological hash collisions, load-factor checks, scheduling semantics and safe ownership boundaries.

Precisely bounded claims: AssetRegistry is a single-threaded teaching model. It does not prove correct concurrent deletion, GPU fence retirement, persistent identity across sessions, byte-for-byte stable ABI, all custom allocator/hash exception behaviors, uniformly fast worst-case hashing, or measured performance of competing containers. The example is stronger than an append-only depot—it supports removal and generational reuse—but intentionally lacks the full production allocator/threading/hot-reload model. Project-specific KairoECS/SparseSet.cppm and KairoRenderer/RenderGraph.cppm remain targets to verify from current independent repository source; nothing here is attributed to those implementations.

Conceptual references consulted: cppreference vector, vector reserve, vector resize, deque, unordered_map, span, string_view. These are supporting language-library sources; the original supplied curriculum remains the title/coverage authority.

Completion classification: all 20 titles connected to one engineered narrative and one compile-tested illustrative registry, not 20 individually completed mastery gates or a newly received source batch. The next canonical M016 / Parts 251–270 introduces optional/variant/any/expected-like results, algorithms and iterator categories only when the registry’s queries, transforms and failure return paths actually need them.
M016 — Parts 251–270: the asset registry becomes a query and transformation pipeline

Provenance: authored reconstruction from the canonical integrated 180-chunk / original 3,000-part contract, not a received M016 lesson transcript. The continuous M016 narrative begins when the Phase 5 generation-checked registry needs an isolated, owned report, typed lookup failures, sorting, searching, aggregation and removal. Its twenty source identifiers remain an audit contract, not twenty separate main chapters.

Cell.Content: find_optional returns a value-copied logical handle for rock.mesh and nullopt for an absent name; it cannot explain an invalid input.
Inspect, Upload and Evict are closed, distinct request shapes; std::visit and an overload set count each command.
Open-ended diagnostics hold a copied string, reject any_cast<int> with bad_any_cast and release the value at reset.
A deliberately limited C++20 ExpectedLike<T,E> distinguishes valid handle, empty name and nonexistent name; it is not a complete C++23 std::expected substitute.
Pair carries count/error fields together; tuple carries report name/count/version; both are product types, not variant alternatives.
auto [..] copies the pair; auto& [..] aliases the original and updates its error count.
C++20 static assertions distinguish input, forward, bidirectional and random-access capabilities across stream, forward_list, list and deque.
Vector iterators are contiguous; deque iterators are random-access but not contiguous; both facts statically checked.
259 · Iterator invalidation as an API contract
Owned snapshots avoid live-registry relocation; sort changes positional meanings, erase invalidates affected vector iterators, and no invalidated pointer is deliberately accessed.
A byte/name comparator gives a deterministic sorted snapshot; common introsort-like implementations are explained without claiming the standard mandates one.
A descending-priority sort preserves sky.tex before ui.tex and brick.mesh before rock.mesh within equal-priority groups.
Partition mesh vs nonmesh, validate both sides and recover the boundary with partition_point; no false sorting/stability claim.
Sort by the byte key and find first non-less-than-48 position, index one; note forward-iterator increment cost.
Upper bound for 48 gives index three, equal_range returns the matching [1,3) interval; a bidirectional heterogeneous comparator is supplied.
One-off name lookup scans an owned name vector without rebuilding an index; compare with the live registry’s maintained hash index.
Convert owned asset records into byte counts with a back_inserter to a separate destination; no automatic SIMD/threading claim.
Ordered left fold with std::size_t{0} yields the exact small payload total 304; explain why accumulator type matters.
Integer test also yields 304; a binary64 regrouping demonstration produces 3 vs 4, without pretending this library must select one grouping.
remove_if produces a retained logical prefix but leaves vector size six until erase destroys the removed suffix; final IDs are 1,3,5.
C++20 erase_if removes two texture rows from the report copy and separately removes one matching unordered diagnostic entry, without evicting the live registry.

M001 - Parts 1-20

RowCard.Content: Definition, mechanism, and concrete reconstruction cue

RowValue.Content: Definition, mechanism, and concrete reconstruction cue

Physical and logical binary states: a device maps ranges of a physical measurement to 0/1; thresholds and noise margins let imperfect signals represent stable logical values. Storage retains state, while combinational logic calculates from present inputs.
Definition, mechanism, and concrete reconstruction cue

Positional notation: bit <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>b</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> </math> at position <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>i</mi> </math> contributes <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>b</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <msup> <mn>2</mn> <mi>i</mi> </msup> </math>. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>N</mi> </math> independent bits provide <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msup> <mn>2</mn> <mi>N</mi> </msup> </math> patterns, whose unsigned values run from 0 through <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msup> <mn>2</mn> <mi>N</mi> </msup> <mo>−</mo> <mn>1</mn> </math>.
Definition, mechanism, and concrete reconstruction cue

Binary conversion by Euclidean division: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>n</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>2</mn> <mi>q</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mi>r</mi> </math>, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>r</mi> <mo>∈</mo> <mo fence="false" stretchy="false">{</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo fence="false" stretchy="false">}</mo> </math>. Save <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>r</mi> </math>, repeat on <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>q</mi> </math>, and reverse the saved sequence. For 13, remainders 1,0,1,1 give 1101. Handle zero explicitly.
Definition, mechanism, and concrete reconstruction cue

Weighted decoding sums set-bit weights. Horner decoding repeatedly uses <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>v</mi> <mo stretchy="false">←</mo> <mn>2</mn> <mi>v</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mi>b</mi> </math> from left to right. Reading 1101 yields 1,3,6,13, confirming the same value.
Definition, mechanism, and concrete reconstruction cue
Hexadecimal has 16 digits; four bits make one nibble and one hex digit. 1010 is A, 1101 is D, so 10101101 is AD.
Definition, mechanism, and concrete reconstruction cue
Octal has eight digits and groups three bits. Left-pad 10101101 to 010 101 101, giving octal 255. Leading zero in a C++ integer literal requests octal.
Definition, mechanism, and concrete reconstruction cue
Byte and octet: octet means eight bits; C++ byte width is CHAR_BIT. Machine word describes a processing convention, not a fixed unit. Exact format widths need explicit types.
Definition, mechanism, and concrete reconstruction cue

Bit mask: a pattern selects owned positions. A low-width mask is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msup> <mn>2</mn> <mi>w</mi> </msup> <mo>−</mo> <mn>1</mn> </math> because subtracting one from a power of two fills all lower positions with ones.
Definition, mechanism, and concrete reconstruction cue

Bitwise AND filters: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>x</mi> <mo>∧</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo>=</mo> <mn>0</mn> </math>, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>x</mi> <mo>∧</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>=</mo> <mi>x</mi> </math>. AD & 07 = 05. Compare the result with zero for any selected flag, or with the full mask for all selected flags.
Definition, mechanism, and concrete reconstruction cue

Bitwise OR sets: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>x</mi> <mo>∨</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> </math>, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>x</mi> <mo>∨</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo>=</mo> <mi>x</mi> </math>. AD \| 40 = ED. Repeating the same set operation has no further effect.
Definition, mechanism, and concrete reconstruction cue

Bitwise XOR toggles: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>x</mi> <mo>⊕</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>=</mo> <mi mathvariant="normal">¬</mi> <mi>x</mi> </math>, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>x</mi> <mo>⊕</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo>=</mo> <mi>x</mi> </math>. AD ^ 08 = A5; toggling again restores AD. XOR of two states marks differing positions.
Definition, mechanism, and concrete reconstruction cue
Bitwise NOT inverts all positions at a stated width. Eight-bit NOT(0F)=F0; promoted int-width NOT has more positions. State width before interpreting its value.
Definition, mechanism, and concrete reconstruction cue

Shift operations relocate bits. Logical right shift zero-fills; arithmetic right shift sign-fills. Left shift zero-fills low positions; discard behavior and numeric meaning depend on width and language rules.
Definition, mechanism, and concrete reconstruction cue

For nonnegative unsigned arithmetic, left shift by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>k</mi> </math> resembles multiplication by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msup> <mn>2</mn> <mi>k</mi> </msup> </math> and right shift floor division. Truncation changes the exact answer; signed division toward zero differs from arithmetic right shift for negative odd values.
Definition, mechanism, and concrete reconstruction cue
Bit field extraction normalizes with right shift and isolates with a low mask: (AD >> 4) & 03 = 2. Mask-only gives 0x20, still at its original significance.
Definition, mechanism, and concrete reconstruction cue
Insertion clears the destination mask, shifts the valid new value, then ORs it into the cleared word. Preserve outside-mask bits. Replacing quality 2 with 1 in AD produces 9D.
Definition, mechanism, and concrete reconstruction cue
Bit packing combines disjoint, range-checked fields. OR contributions 05,08,20,00,80 to obtain AD. Packing saves payload bytes but introduces extraction and update work.
Definition, mechanism, and concrete reconstruction cue

Unpacking reverses the declared schema. For LSB-first bits use byte <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo fence="false" stretchy="false">⌊</mo> <mi>i</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>/</mo> </mrow> <mn>8</mn> <mo fence="false" stretchy="false">⌋</mo> </math> and offset <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>i</mi> <mo lspace="thickmathspace" rspace="thickmathspace">mod</mo> <mn>8</mn> </math>. Check the requested count, source capacity, and unused padding before indexing.
Definition, mechanism, and concrete reconstruction cue
Boolean algebra defines false/true operations by truth tables. Logical versus bitwise operators differ in result domain; built-in logical AND/OR also skip unnecessary operands.
Definition, mechanism, and concrete reconstruction cue
De Morgan's laws swap AND and OR when negation crosses the operator. Enumerate four inputs to prove both identities; keep a fixed width for the bitwise versions.

Appendix.Content: M002 - Parts 21-40

RowCard.Content: Definition, mechanism, and concrete reconstruction cue

RowValue.Content: Definition, mechanism, and concrete reconstruction cue

Unsigned <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>N</mi> </math>-bit range is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">[</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo>,</mo> <msup> <mn>2</mn> <mi>N</mi> </msup> <mo>−</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo stretchy="false">]</mo> </math>. Distinguish state count 256 from maximum eight-bit value 255.
Definition, mechanism, and concrete reconstruction cue

Signed magnitude uses one sign bit and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>N</mi> <mo>−</mo> <mn>1</mn> </math> magnitude bits. It has two zeros and requires sign-aware magnitude arithmetic. Eight-bit −5 is 10000101.
Definition, mechanism, and concrete reconstruction cue
One's complement encodes negatives by bit inversion. −5 is 11111010. All ones is negative zero; addition returns a final carry to the low end as end-around carry.
Definition, mechanism, and concrete reconstruction cue

Two's complement uses the negative residue <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msup> <mn>2</mn> <mi>N</mi> </msup> <mo>−</mo> <mi>x</mi> </math> and signed top-bit weight <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo>−</mo> <msup> <mn>2</mn> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mi>N</mi> <mo>−</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msup> </math>. Decode AD as 173−256=−83. The same adder supports positive and negative residues.
Definition, mechanism, and concrete reconstruction cue

Negation follows <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msup> <mn>2</mn> <mi>N</mi> </msup> <mo>−</mo> <mi>x</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msup> <mn>2</mn> <mi>N</mi> </msup> <mo>−</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>−</mo> <mi>x</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>+</mo> <mn>1</mn> </math>. The first term is the width-limited complement, so −13 is NOT(00001101)+1=11110011.
Definition, mechanism, and concrete reconstruction cue
Negating zero gives all ones plus one, leaving low bits zero. Two’s complement has exactly one zero and assigns every pattern a distinct signed integer.
Definition, mechanism, and concrete reconstruction cue

Minimum signed value follows the asymmetric range <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">[</mo> <mo>−</mo> <msup> <mn>2</mn> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mi>N</mi> <mo>−</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msup> <mo>,</mo> <msup> <mn>2</mn> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mi>N</mi> <mo>−</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msup> <mo>−</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo stretchy="false">]</mo> </math>. For int minimum, same-type negation, abs, or division by −1 cannot represent the positive result. Narrow storage may promote first.
Definition, mechanism, and concrete reconstruction cue

Unsigned modular arithmetic retains residues modulo <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msup> <mn>2</mn> <mi>N</mi> </msup> </math>. 250+10 becomes 4 when narrowed to eight bits; on the usual host the original byte addition expression is int 260.
Definition, mechanism, and concrete reconstruction cue
Signed integer overflow is Undefined behavior at the operation type’s width. Check bounds before evaluating, or use a type proved large enough. Evaluating overflow and checking afterward is too late.
Definition, mechanism, and concrete reconstruction cue

Unsigned 0−1 wraps to maximum; going below signed minimum is signed overflow. A size_t loop condition i>=0 never becomes false. Prefer reverse iteration or a decrement-before-index pattern with a correct termination guard.
Definition, mechanism, and concrete reconstruction cue

Carry and borrow move arithmetic information between digit positions. Four-bit 13+7 gives low 4 with carry 1. Unsigned carry differs from signed range failure. Borrow conventions depend on architecture.
Definition, mechanism, and concrete reconstruction cue
Half adder: sum=A XOR B, carry=A AND B. Full adder adds carry-in; sum is three-way parity and carry is the majority of three inputs. A majority function is true when at least two inputs are true.
Definition, mechanism, and concrete reconstruction cue
Ripple-carry addition chains full adders. Worst-case circuit delay grows with width; fixed-width software addition remains constant work. Generate/propagate terms permit parallel carry networks.
Definition, mechanism, and concrete reconstruction cue

Subtraction through addition uses <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>A</mi> <mo>+</mo> <msub> <mi>NOT</mi> <mi>N</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>B</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>+</mo> <mn>1</mn> </math>. Binary 6502-style SBC instead includes C: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>A</mi> <mo>−</mo> <mi>B</mi> <mo>−</mo> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>−</mo> <mi>C</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math>, so C=1 means no borrow.
Definition, mechanism, and concrete reconstruction cue
Shift-and-add multiplication sums one shifted multiplicand for every set multiplier bit. 13×11=13+26+104=143. Both the shifting partial value and accumulator must hold the required wider range.
Definition, mechanism, and concrete reconstruction cue

Binary long division shifts dividend bits into a partial remainder, then compares and conditionally subtracts the divisor. Check <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>D</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mi>Q</mi> <mi>d</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mi>R</mi> </math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mn>0</mn> <mo>≤</mo> <mi>R</mi> <mo><</mo> <mi>d</mi> </math>. For 13/3, Q=4,R=1. Zero division and int-min/−1 are invalid.
Definition, mechanism, and concrete reconstruction cue
Saturating arithmetic clamps a widened answer to endpoints: 250+20 becomes 255. Signed saturation is not associative, so evaluation order matters. Do not prematurely clamp an HDR intermediate.
Definition, mechanism, and concrete reconstruction cue

Fixed-width integer types define exact widths when available. Least and fast families promise at least the width, with different goals. size_t is for sizes, ptrdiff_t for differences; plain char signedness varies.
Definition, mechanism, and concrete reconstruction cue

Integral promotion occurs first; Usual arithmetic conversions then select a common type. Track stored type, promoted type, operation type, and destination conversion separately. ~uint8_t{0} is usually int −1.
Definition, mechanism, and concrete reconstruction cue

Mixed signedness can convert negative operands to large unsigned values. Use consistent semantic types or std::cmp_* helpers; valid indexing still requires nonnegative and less-than-size conditions. std::in_range checks conversion representability.

Appendix.Content: Notation and validity

<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>N</mi> </math> is carrier width, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>i</mi> </math> a bit position, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>w</mi> </math> field width, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>s</mi> </math> offset, and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>b</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> </math> a 0/1 digit. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo>∧</mo> </math>, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo>∨</mo> </math>, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo>⊕</mo> </math>, and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi mathvariant="normal">¬</mi> </math> mean AND, OR, XOR, and NOT; integer vectors require a stated width. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo>≪</mo> </math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo>≫</mo> </math> denote shifts. Modulo records a residue; floor rounds downward. A bijection pairs every element of one set with exactly one element of the other. An invariant is a property that must remain true across steps. An ALU is an arithmetic and logic unit.

Keep number semantics separate from executable C++ operators. A word-level formula assumes a fixed unsigned carrier; C++ built-in operators act after promotion. For C++23, signed right shift rounds toward negative infinity. Claims about signed overflowing addition remain subject to undefined behavior.
Why these dependencies matter

Representation supplies the weights needed for masks. Boolean operators supply the gates needed for adders. Masks and shifts supply the field operations needed for compact data. Finite width supplies the modular model needed for two’s complement. Promotions and conversions determine the domain in which C++ actually performs each operation. See Dependency Map and each concept’s prerequisites before reconstructing a later mechanism.
M003 - Parts 41-60

Cell.Content: Definition, mechanism, and concrete reconstruction cue

Endianness orders significance bytes at increasing addresses. It does not change the integer value or reverse bits inside each octet. Separate significance, address traversal, and intra-byte packing order.

Little endian puts the least-significant byte first: 0x12345678 produces 78 56 34 12. Extract byte i by unsigned right shift by 8i, then narrow to eight bits; reconstruct by shifting each byte into its significance position.
Big endian puts the most-significant byte first: 12 34 56 78. Read left-to-right with value←256×value+byte: M001 Horner decoding in base 256.

Byte swapping and network order: swapping reverses octet significance; host/network conversion is a no-op when orders already match. Classic Internet fields often use big endian, but each protocol defines its own contract. Serialization fixes widths/order and validates lengths without native padding.

Alignment and padding: alignment A restricts starting addresses to multiples of A. C++ alignof reports the requirement; alignas requests a supported stronger alignment. Align-up needs nonzero A and overflow checks; an aligned numeric offset is not automatically a live pointer.

Internal and tail padding: internal padding precedes a member to meet its alignment. Under 1/4/1 member alignments, byte–uint32–byte uses offsets 0/4/8, with three internal padding bytes. ABI and object layout determines actual offsets.

Tail padding rounds complete-object size for aligned array stride. The same example ends at byte nine and rounds to size 12; the next object’s four-aligned member remains aligned. Never infer sizeof solely by summing payload sizes.

Field reordering and AoS versus SoA: order by decreasing alignment can reduce holes. A 1/8/1/4 example commonly shrinks 24→16 bytes. Measure sizeof/alignof/offsetof; ABI compatibility and hot/cold access patterns can outweigh smaller size. AoS stores complete records; SoA has one array per field.

Packed structures and misaligned access: packing extensions can remove holes but weaken member alignment. They do not define endianness, versions, or lifetime. A packed native object differs from a specified wire format.

Misalignment can cross cache-line/page boundaries, slow access, or fault depending on instruction/platform. C++ access still needs a suitably aligned live object. Reconstruct bytes or copy representation into an existing aligned trivially copyable object; copying alone does not normalize endianness.

Pointer arithmetic and provenance: address is a location identifier; a C++ pointer is a constrained typed access path. Within an array, p+i advances i×sizeof(T) bytes; one-past can be formed but not dereferenced. Numeric addresses alone do not establish access rights.

Addresses and virtual memory translates process-visible addresses to physical addresses. A contiguous vector buffer can span scattered frames. Virtual and physical contiguity distinguishes address-space adjacency from backing placement.

Process isolation and page permissions: each address space has its own mapping context. VA 0x400000 can map to frame 27 in A and frame 913 in B. Shared mappings may select the same frame; read/write/execute/user permissions constrain access.

Pages and page offsets: a virtual page is an address block; a frame is corresponding physical storage. For P=2^k, VPN=floor(VA/P), offset=VA mod P. The 4-KiB example uses k=12; actual page size depends on platform/configuration, not universally 4096.

Page tables and MMU: entries supply frame identity, permissions, and state; MMU is the translation/protection mechanism. The TLB caches translations, not data. A miss may resolve through page-table walking without a page fault.

Page faults and demand paging: OS intervention is needed under current mapping state. Valid demand loading/zero-fill may install a frame and retry; Copy-on-write may copy on first write. Unmapped/forbidden access may fail. A fault does not necessarily imply disk I/O.

Call stack and stack frames: calls conventionally use LIFO frames for return state, registers, spills, and some locals. Downward growth is a convention; not every local has a stack slot. Returning a dead-local pointer violates Storage duration and object lifetime, even if bytes remain.

Dynamic allocation and heap subdivides OS regions into variable-lifetime blocks. Allocator fragmentation distinguishes slack within allocated blocks (37 requested in a 48-byte class leaves 11) from separated free holes unable to satisfy one request. Allocation cost differs from access latency.

Static storage and initialization: namespace/static objects have program-duration storage. Initialized writable data commonly uses data-like regions; zero-initialized storage uses BSS-like zero-fill without literal executable zero payload. Dynamic initialization and cross-unit ordering need later treatment.

Read-only data and code: text commonly contains instructions, read-only regions constants. Writable-or-executable policy limits writable executable mappings. Modifying a string literal is undefined behavior; const automatic objects are not forced into read-only segments. Segment names/layout are implementation choices.

Appendix.Content: Bridges and distinctions that must not be omitted

ListItem.Content: ASLR randomizes mapping locations; a textbook process diagram is not a layout guarantee.

Thread storage duration exists alongside automatic, static, and dynamic duration; thread-local storage is not simply the call stack. Storage duration governs available storage; lifetime governs the live object within it.

Appendix.Content: Clarifications: the layout examples assume stated ABI rules; reordering may break a published ABI. Bounds and lifetime remain necessary even with valid mappings/alignment. Wording cross-checked against the C++ draft alignment, storage duration, and endianness sections.
M004 - Parts 61-76

Cell.Content: Definition, mechanism, and concrete reconstruction cue
IEEE-754 floating point: finite nonuniform representation plus explicitly specified rounding/special-value behavior; formats do not make every C++ float binary32.
Binary32: 1/8/23 stored fields, 24-bit normal precision and bias 127; 1.0 has word 3F800000.
Binary64: 1/11/52 stored fields, 53-bit normal precision and bias 1023; more precision is distinct from more exponent range.
Signed zero: floating sign is separate from magnitude; signbit sees negative zero whereas x<0 does not.
Exponent bias: normal stored exponent E=e+B; E=130 decodes to e=3 for binary32; classify reserved fields first.
Significand and hidden bit: normal leading binary 1 is implicit; 23 fraction bits plus it give 24 significant bits.
Floating-point encoding and decoding: 10.625=1.010101₂×2³ gives S=0,E=130,F=2A0000, word 412A0000.
Floating-point encoding and decoding: C1540000 has S=1,E=130,F=540000; reconstruct −1.65625×8=−13.25.
Signed zero: 00000000 and 80000000 compare numerically equal but have distinct representations/reciprocals.
Floating-point infinities: all-one exponent with zero fraction; distinct from maximum finite and dependent on sign/rounding in overflow.
NaNs and payloads: all-one exponent with nonzero fraction; unordered comparisons, quiet/signaling distinction, payload preservation caveats.
Subnormals and gradual underflow: E=0 uses no hidden one; binary32 x=(-1)^S F×2^-149, filling the normal-to-zero gap.
Machine epsilon: spacing above 1, 2^-23 for binary32, not min(), denorm_min(), or a universal tolerance.
ULP and representable spacing: normal binade spacing is 2^(e-23) for binary32; 1 has different immediate lower/upper gaps.
Rounding to nearest ties to even: choose nearest neighbor; exact halfway picks even retained significand; guard/round/sticky summarize discarded bits.
Directed rounding modes: upward, downward and toward-zero are signed directions; runtime environment changes must be checked and restored.

Cell.Content: Definition, mechanism, and concrete reconstruction cue
Fixed-point representation: a signed raw integer I at scale S represents I/S; F=16 gives step 2^-16 and raw 212992 for 3.25.
Fixed-point range and resolution: require 2^-F≤requested step and M·2F≤2(N-1)-1. A 32-bit domain ±1e6 with step≤0.001 permits F=10 or 11.
Fixed-point rescaling: multiply at scale S², then round/divide by S; division uses A·S/B. Prove intermediate width, handle negative ties and zero divisors, and check destination range.

Arithmetic policies remain necessary for fixed point. Nearest unclipped absolute error≤1/(2S); near-zero relative error can be large. Controlled integer arithmetic can improve repeatability, not make every operation associative.

Affine quantization and zero point maps finite values to codes and reconstructs s(q-z). Groupwise scales cost metadata; source-shaped offset INT4 codes [1,5,8,11,15] pack to 51 B8 0F. One-bit row centroids are not automatically ±1.
UNORM and SNORM: UNORM8 reconstructs q/255; SNORM8 clamps q/127 at −1. Quantized normal components can require safe renormalization; sRGB is a separate interpretation.
Binary16 uses 1/5/10 fields, bias15, 11 normal precision bits, maximum65504, normal minimum2^-14, subnormal minimum2^-24. Word3E00 encodes1.5.

Bfloat16 uses1/8/7 fields, bias127, 8 normal precision bits; it trades detail for wide exponent range. Nearest-even conversion must classify NaNs instead of discarding their low payload into infinity.

Bit casting and representation transfers suitable initialized object representation; numeric cast converts a value. Eligibility does not solve byte order, arbitrary valid representations, alignment or mapped-object lifetime.

Binary format contracts declare widths/order/representation/version; Checked binary parsing validates products, subtracted bounds, exact lengths and resource limits. Magic/version are not integrity or authenticity.

Checksums CRCs and hashes summarize specified content. Additive sums miss byte reordering; CRC requires named parameters; a cryptographic digest needs a trusted reference, MAC or signature for an adversarial trust claim.

Memory dump interpretation decodes by offset/schema/byte order. The 2×3 demonstration has a28-byte header and24-byte binary32 payload; identical bytes have different meanings under integer, float or character interpretations.

RowValue.Content: 1. Functions are mappings, not merely equations — Part 801
Suppose Kairo’s renderer is given a 3D point. It must compute where that point appears on the screen.
2. Function composition: building complex systems from smaller ones — Part 802
A graphics system rarely performs one isolated transformation.
3. Limits: understanding behavior without necessarily evaluating a point — Part 803
A limit describes what a function approaches as its input approaches some value.
4. Continuity: when small input changes cannot cause finite output jumps — Part 804
A function \(f\) is continuous at \(a\) when:

Inverse trigonometric functions reconstruct angles from ratios and geometric relationships.

People often memorize that the gradient points uphill. We should prove it and understand its assumptions.
Partial derivatives examine one input while other independent coordinates remain fixed.

We now reach one of the central ideas of the entire graphics curriculum.

We will now derive the result used throughout camera geometry, 3D Gaussian splatting, visual reconstruction, and many inverse-rendering systems.

First derivatives describe local slope. Second derivatives describe how that slope changes.
First derivatives describe local slope. Second derivatives describe how that slope changes.
22. Taylor series in one variable — Part 828
Linearization means replacing a nonlinear system near an operating point with its first-order affine approximation.
25. Error terms and the limits of local approximations — Part 831
The usefulness of a local approximation depends on whether we can control its error.
1. Integration means accumulating infinitesimal contributions — Part 832
Suppose an object moves in one dimension with velocity:
2. Riemann sums: constructing an integral from finite computations — Part 833
A computer cannot literally sum an infinite number of infinitesimal contributions. It can only perform a finite sequence of operations.
3. The fundamental theorem of calculus — Part 834
The relationship between integration and differentiation is much deeper than saying that one is the reverse of the other.
4. Rectangle rules: the first numerical quadrature methods — Part 835
Quadrature is the numerical approximation of definite integrals.
A rectangle approximates the integrand as constant over each interval. The trapezoidal rule approximates it using the straight line connecting the endpoint values.
6. Simpson’s rule: integrating a local quadratic approximation — Part 837
The trapezoidal rule uses a degree-one polynomial. Simpson’s rule uses a degree-two interpolating polynomial over two adjacent subintervals.
7. Ordinary differential equations: representing laws of continuous evolution — Part 838
We now move from integrating a known function to a more difficult problem: the rate of change may itself depend on the state whose evolution we want to calculate.
8. Initial-value problems: why a law does not determine a unique history — Part 839
A differential equation tells us the permitted evolution of a system. We also need a starting state.
9. Explicit Euler: deriving a simulator from a differential equation — Part 840
11. Semi-implicit Euler: why update order changes the dynamics — Part 841
Semi-implicit Euler is often called symplectic Euler or Euler–Cromer integration when applied in the appropriate canonical position-momentum formulation.
12. Midpoint integration: sampling a slope where it matters — Part 842
Explicit Euler assumes the derivative throughout a timestep equals the derivative at the beginning.
13. Runge–Kutta second order: a family, not one formula — Part 843
There is an important distinction between the explicit midpoint method and the broader RK2 family.
The classical RK4 method estimates the state derivative four times within a timestep.
Accuracy and stability are not the same property.
Stiffness is one of the most misunderstood numerical simulation concepts.
19. Finite differences: approximating derivatives from samples — Part 847
In M049, we defined the derivative as a limit:
Suppose an objective depends on \(n\) parameters:

Automatic differentiation is neither symbolic algebra in the usual sense nor numerical finite differentiation.
Forward mode propagates input perturbations toward the outputs.
30. Computational graphs and reverse traversal — Part 855
A computational graph represents intermediate values as nodes and data dependencies as directed edges.
1. Objective functions: translating a problem into mathematics — Part 856
Optimization starts before we choose an algorithm. We first need to decide precisely what we are trying to minimize.

Gradient descent uses local slope but does not directly account for curvature.

BFGS is named after Broyden, Fletcher, Goldfarb, and Shanno.

Backtracking is an implementable way to satisfy Armijo sufficient decrease without performing a complete one-dimensional optimization.

Lagrange multipliers handle equality constraints. KKT conditions extend first-order optimality to inequality constraints.
Least squares is one of the most important optimization structures in geometry, inverse problems, sensor calibration, and physical parameter estimation.
In a nonlinear least-squares problem, residuals depend nonlinearly on parameters.
Newton’s method for least squares would solve:
Gauss–Newton can produce excellent steps near a good solution. It can also fail far from the solution when residual linearization is inaccurate, or when \(J^TJ\) is singular or nearly singular.
23. Regularization: modifying the objective to encode preferences — Part 881
Suppose measurements do not uniquely determine all the unknown parameters.
25. L2 regularization and ridge-type stabilization — Part 883
We covered finite differences and automatic differentiation in M052, so here the focus is on how gradient verification becomes an engineering gate for an optimizer.
Conditioning describes how sensitive a mathematical solution is to changes in the problem’s data or parameters.

Suppose one parameter is camera translation measured in metres and another is rotation measured in radians.
Suppose physical parameters are represented by:

A numerical optimizer performs a long sequence of floating-point calculations.
A numerical optimizer must eventually stop, but reaching a small numerical quantity does not automatically mean it has found a useful solution.
Absolute tolerances compare values against fixed units or magnitudes.
Stagnation means the optimizer is making little or no progress, but it has not necessarily satisfied the desired optimality conditions.

RowValue.Content: 1. Experiments, outcomes, and sample spaces — Part 901
Imagine a graphics engine running a stochastic visibility test.
An event is a set of outcomes.
A probability measure is a function:
Suppose we are interested in an event \(A\), but we have learned that another event \(B\) occurred.
5. Independence: when information does not change probability — Part 905
Bayes’ theorem is not an additional axiom. It follows from the definition of conditional probability.
7. Random variables: turning outcomes into mathematical quantities — Part 907

A probability space describes possible outcomes and assigns probabilities to events. But numerical algorithms usually do not operate directly on abstract outcomes. They operate on numbers and vectors derived from outcomes.
A discrete random variable takes values in a finite or countable set.
A continuous random variable with a probability density assigns probability to intervals through integration.
For a discrete random variable, define the probability mass function, or PMF:
For a continuous random variable whose distribution is absolutely continuous with respect to Lebesgue measure, a probability density function, or PDF, is a nonnegative function \(p_X\) satisfying:
The cumulative distribution function, or CDF, is defined for every real-valued random variable:
13. Expected value: what a random quantity averages to — Part 913
The expected value describes a probability-weighted average.
14. Variance: measuring spread around the mean — Part 914
Expected value gives the distribution’s centre in an average sense.
Variance uses squared deviations, so its units are the square of the underlying variable’s units.
Variance describes the spread of one variable.
Covariance depends on the units of its variables.
So far, we have often treated random variables one at a time.
A marginal distribution describes one variable without retaining the detailed value of the other variables.
A conditional distribution describes one variable after accounting for information about another.
A Bernoulli random variable represents one binary trial.
A binomial random variable counts the number of successes in \(n\) independent, identically distributed Bernoulli trials.
The continuous uniform distribution assigns equal probability density across an interval.
The Gaussian distribution is one of the most important continuous probability families.
The standard normal distribution is the special case:
The exponential distribution models a nonnegative waiting time in a memoryless event process.
The Poisson distribution models counts of events under an idealized Poisson process or other situations satisfying the appropriate count law.
We now extend the Gaussian distribution from one uncertain scalar to an entire uncertain vector.
We have already introduced covariance matrices, but now we will study their full structure.
30. Why covariance must be positive semidefinite — Part 930
This is one of the most important results of M056 because it connects probability directly to symmetric matrices, eigenvalues, Cholesky factorization, and numerical robustness.
1. Sampling a uniform random variable — Part 931
The starting point of many randomized algorithms is a random variable:
A pseudorandom-number generator, or PRNG, is a deterministic algorithm designed to produce sequences with useful statistical properties.
A linear congruential generator, or LCG, uses:
The Mersenne Twister family was designed to produce long-period pseudorandom sequences with strong equidistribution properties for its intended applications.
PCG stands for Permuted Congruential Generator.
A seed determines the initial state or initial parameters of a pseudorandom generator.
A stateful PRNG consumes its sequence in order.
This is where probability theory meets actual image quality.

We now have a source of approximately uniform random values. But a ray tracer needs directions on hemispheres, positions on surfaces, microfacet-normal distributions, lens samples, and many other nonuniform quantities.
Inverse-transform sampling requires access to an inverse CDF or a convenient sampling transformation.
Importance sampling is among the most consequential concepts in Monte Carlo rendering.
14. Probability density under variable transformation — Part 944
Importance sampling is valid only when the estimator uses the PDF corresponding to the actual sampled variable and measure.
Monte Carlo estimation uses randomized sampling to approximate an expectation or integral.
An estimator \(\widehat\theta\) is a random quantity constructed from observed samples.
The bias of an estimator is:
Bias measures systematic average displacement from the target.
The law of large numbers explains why sample averages can approach expected values as more observations are collected.
The law of large numbers tells us where the sample mean tends to go.
Sample variance measures the spread of observed values around their sample mean.
Why do we divide by \(N-1\) rather than \(N\) when estimating population variance?
Suppose samples arrive one at a time.
25. Welford’s numerically stable variance algorithm — Part 955
This is one of the most practically valuable statistical algorithms in the phase.
A histogram groups observations into intervals called bins.
A quantile describes a threshold below which a specified fraction of a distribution lies.
Robust statistics concerns procedures that remain informative when data contain outliers, heavy tails, deviations from modeling assumptions, or contamination.
Suppose our goal is to estimate a population mean:
Hypothesis testing evaluates how compatible observed data are with a specified statistical hypothesis.
The term mean squared error, or MSE, has two closely related but distinct uses.
Mean absolute error, or MAE, is:
