Appendix.title: Rigid Contact - Persistent Manifolds and Solver Reconstruction
Appendix.source: Supplementary/Rigid Contact - Persistent Manifolds and Solver Reconstruction.md
Appendix.Content: Rigid contacts: from point velocity to a persistent contact manifold

BlockQuote.Content: Scope: original, independently reconstructed teaching for the existing engine collision-response narrative. The executable witnesses are rigid_contact_lab.cpp and persistent_contact_lab.cpp. These are 2D velocity-level CPU witnesses; they do not claim to be Kairo’s engine implementation, 3D production manifold generation, or continuous collision detection. Symbols and sign conventions below follow those two witnesses.

Appendix.Content: Why a contact is a constraint rather than a force chosen by eye

Imagine a box descending onto a static floor. The collision detector reports that the geometry is touching or overlapping, but it does not say which velocities are physically admissible. With body A as the floor and body B as the box, define the contact normal n to point from A toward B. At contact position p, the lever arms measured from each body’s centre of mass are r_A = p − x_A and r_B = p − x_B. For a planar rigid body, its point velocity is v(p) = v_com + ω × r, where planar scalar angular speed ω produces ω × (r_x,r_y) = (−ω r_y, ω r_x). This matters because an object rotating toward the floor can be closing at a corner even when the centre of mass is moving away.

The relative velocity of the two material points is u = (v_B + ω_B × r_B) − (v_A + ω_A × r_A). The normal component u_n = u · n tells us whether those two points are closing (u_n < 0) or separating (u_n > 0). For a non-penetrating unilateral contact without restitution, the desired post-solve condition is u_n ≥ 0, with a nonnegative accumulated contact impulse λ_n ≥ 0. Their complementarity condition is λ_n u_n = 0 at an exact solution: either the contact carries a positive separating-prevention impulse and reaches zero normal speed, or the bodies separate freely and the contact carries no impulse. Finite-iteration solvers only approximate this coupled condition.
Deriving effective inverse mass, rather than memorizing its denominator

The impulse on B is +λ n and the reaction on A is −λ n. Newton’s linear momentum law gives Δv_B = +λ m_B⁻¹ n and Δv_A = −λ m_A⁻¹ n. Angular impulse about the centre of mass gives Δω_B = +λ I_B⁻¹ (r_B × n) and Δω_A = −λ I_A⁻¹ (r_A × n), where the planar cross product of vectors is the scalar r_x n_y − r_y n_x. A rotation changes point velocity through Δω × r, and its projection onto n adds an angular term proportional to the squared lever arm.
Consequently the normal relative velocity changes by Δu_n = k_n λ, where
Appendix.RawBlock: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"> <msub> <mi>k</mi> <mi>n</mi> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <msubsup> <mi>m</mi> <mi>A</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>−</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msubsup> <mo>+</mo> <msubsup> <mi>m</mi> <mi>B</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>−</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msubsup> <mo>+</mo> <msubsup> <mi>I</mi> <mi>A</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>−</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msubsup> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msub> <mi>r</mi> <mi>A</mi> </msub> <mo>×</mo> <mi>n</mi> <msup> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mn>2</mn> </msup> <mo>+</mo> <msubsup> <mi>I</mi> <mi>B</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>−</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msubsup> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msub> <mi>r</mi> <mi>B</mi> </msub> <mo>×</mo> <mi>n</mi> <msup> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mn>2</mn> </msup> <mo>.</mo> </math>
Appendix.Content: Here k_n is inverse effective mass in the contact direction, not mass itself. The same physical impulse changes normal speed less when the effective mass is large. The equation follows from the full point-velocity update; it is not valid to omit rotational terms whenever the contact is off-centre. A static body uses zero inverse mass and inertia, but two completely unresponsive bodies yield k_n = 0 and must not be divided by. The corresponding tangential value k_t is obtained by substituting the perpendicular unit tangent t = (−n_y, n_x) for n.
For a desired post-impact normal speed b, one unconstrained correction is Δλ = (b − u_n)/k_n. A real contact cannot pull the bodies together, so the accumulated normal multiplier is projected:
Appendix.RawBlock: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"> <msubsup> <mi>λ</mi> <mi>n</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mi>n</mi> <mi>e</mi> <mi>w</mi> </mrow> </msubsup> <mo>=</mo> <mo data-mjx-texclass="OP" movablelimits="true">max</mo> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="INNER"> <mo data-mjx-texclass="OPEN">(</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo>,</mo> <msubsup> <mi>λ</mi> <mi>n</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mi>o</mi> <mi>l</mi> <mi>d</mi> </mrow> </msubsup> <mo>+</mo> <mfrac> <mrow> <mi>b</mi> <mo>−</mo> <msub> <mi>u</mi> <mi>n</mi> </msub> </mrow> <msub> <mi>k</mi> <mi>n</mi> </msub> </mfrac> <mo data-mjx-texclass="CLOSE">)</mo> </mrow> <mo>.</mo> </math>
Appendix.Content: Apply only the difference, Δλ_n = λ_n^{new} − λ_n^{old}, to body velocities. Applying the whole accumulated value every iteration would add the same historical impulse repeatedly, making motion energy grow artificially. Conversely, resetting the accumulator on every sweep defeats the projected Gauss–Seidel interpretation and prevents reliable friction bounds.
Restitution is a contact-creation decision, not a new bounce each iteration

For an impact with pre-solve normal speed u_n^before < −v_threshold, the outgoing speed target in this simplified solver is b = −e u_n^before, with restitution coefficient e ∈ [0,1]. This target must be sampled before contact impulses change the velocity and then held fixed during the iteration. If a solver recomputes b from the current velocity at every visit, a persistent resting point can acquire artificial new bounce energy. The witness distinguishes a new impact from a persistent contact through an explicit newImpact argument; a production engine requires an actual contact-state machine and impact detection so the decision is not left to a careless caller.

For the central collision test, both bodies have mass 1 kg, A starts at 2 m/s, B at 0 m/s, and the normal is +x. Their relative closing speed is −2 m/s; with e=1 and k_n=2 kg⁻¹, we need Δλ_n = (2 − (−2))/2 = 2 kg·m/s. The resulting velocities are 0 m/s and 2 m/s. Linear momentum remains 2 kg·m/s, and the kinetic energy remains 2 joules. This equality is specific to the elastic, frictionless, central, idealized two-body case—not a conservation promise for frictional or inelastic impacts.
Why friction depends on the normal impulse

For the upward normal n=(0,1) the laboratory chooses the tangent t=(−1,0). The sliding box initially moves at +3 m/s in x, so its tangent-coordinate velocity is u_t = −3 m/s. The unconstrained tangent impulse is −u_t/k_t; here k_t=1 kg⁻¹, giving +3 kg·m/s. The normal collision supplies λ_n=2 kg·m/s. With coefficient μ=0.5, the Coulomb limit is μλ_n=1 kg·m/s, so the stored tangent impulse is +1, not −1. Multiplying +1 × (−1,0) produces an x-directed impulse of (−1,0), reducing the box’s x velocity from +3 to +2 m/s. The sign of the stored scalar is relative to the chosen tangent direction; it cannot be interpreted without that basis.

The projected update is λ_t^{new} = clamp(λ_t^{old} − u_t/k_t, −μλ_n, +μλ_n). This is a scalar tangent model for 2D; real 3D contact has a two-dimensional tangent plane and requires a disk-cone constraint or a chosen approximation. The witness applies a single coefficient and does not model static-versus-dynamic friction transition, anisotropy, rolling friction, torsional friction or compliant materials.
Why a manifold needs persistent identity and sequential sweeps

A wide box can contact a floor at two corners. Both rows modify the same centre-of-mass velocity and angular velocity. Solving one row therefore changes the velocity seen by the next row. A one-pass independent pair of impulses is not equivalent to solving their coupled system. The reference witness stores two world-space contact points, evaluates each row in sequence, and repeats sweeps. The residual normal speeds and angular velocity are checked after twenty sweeps. Its iteration result is deterministic for its fixed row order but should not be advertised as an order-independent exact solution.

On the next frame, a geometry matcher must identify whether each physical contact feature persisted. If the same feature, body pair, contact orientation, and compatible basis survive, previously accumulated impulses are useful initial guesses. Warm-start once by applying the cached impulses to the newly constructed pre-solve velocities before iteration. Never warm-start twice, and never reuse a tangential scalar after rotating the tangent basis without transforming it. A changed feature ID, reversed A/B order, altered normal, teleport, or discontinuous mass/inertia change may invalidate the cache. The witness includes a feature ID as data but does not implement feature matching; that is a separate production requirement.

Caches may also require dt-aware scaling when timestep changes, and a true contact solver must decide how speculative contacts and missed or sleeping frames are handled. Warm-starting can improve convergence, but it is not a substitute for manifold quality.
Contact identity: why matching by memory address or contact index is insufficient

The physical reaction at a point can be reused between frames only if the cache still refers to the same interacting surface features. When two faces touch, clipping may produce two manifold points whose array order changes as the bodies rotate. If we cache impulse #0 against array position #0, a later reordering can accidentally apply the left-corner impulse at the right corner, creating a torque that was never physically demanded. A robust narrow phase should assign each contact a stable feature pair, for example an incident vertex/edge identifier and reference face identifier, with deterministic canonicalization of body ordering. These identifiers are geometric facts maintained by collision generation, not sequential indices assigned by a container.

The executable contact-cache witness concentrates on the subsequent policy rather than inventing a complete polygon clipper. The Key holds canonical body IDs plus two feature identifiers. The map stores the previously accepted normal and tangent impulse, its local normal direction, the previous friction coefficient, timestep, and last-seen frame. The cache is valid only if the same key was seen on the immediately preceding frame, the normal has changed by no more than 15 degrees, and the new timestep is between half and twice the cached timestep. These are documented laboratory thresholds, not universally optimal thresholds or engine-wide facts. The code rejects reversed body order because reversing A and B changes the sign of the normal and impulse convention.

A tangent impulse is a vector in world space, although this 2D solver stores it as one scalar relative to a perpendicular tangent. When the normal rotates from n_old to n_new, the tangent axes t_old=(-n_old.y,n_old.x) and t_new=(-n_new.y,n_new.x) also rotate. The old physical friction impulse is P_t_old=λ_t_old t_old. The scalar along the new tangent is its dot projection:
$ \lambda{t,new}^{seed} = \frac{\Delta t_{new}}{\Delta t_{old}} \left(\lambda{t,old},\mathbf t_{old}\cdot\mathbf t_{new}\right). $

The normal cache receives the same heuristic timestep ratio, and the tangent is clamped to ± μ_new λ_n_new. With an old upward normal (0,1), the old tangent is (-1,0). If the normal turns 10 degrees, the tangent projection of a previous scalar impulse 0.5 is 0.5 cos(10°) ≈ 0.492404, while the world impulse direction has changed consistently. Reusing 0.5 unchanged would preserve the scalar but not the intended projection onto the new contact tangent. This linear projection is a warm-start heuristic, not an exact solution of the new contact constraint; the subsequent iterative solver must still correct its residual.

An edit to the friction coefficient clears only the tangential cached impulse in this experiment, retaining the normal impulse if all other validity rules pass. A material change in restitution, velocity discontinuity, teleport, substantial mass/inertia change, sleeping transition, or topology discontinuity may also require cache rejection in a production system and is not automatically detected by this small input type. Impulse scaling by timestep ratio is similarly a common starting heuristic, not an unconditional physical identity; the test exercises ratios 0.5, 1, and 4 and rejects the last. A caller must invoke begin_frame, use lookup to seed each new manifold row, warm-start those rows once, run velocity iterations, store each final impulse exactly once, and prune stale entries. Pruning at the wrong moment can erase still-needed contacts; storing duplicate feature keys silently makes iteration results depend on array ordering, so the witness rejects duplicates.

The implementation has a testable boundary: it assumes a reliable feature matcher has already produced identifiers, that contact validity has been established by the geometry system, and that stable body IDs are never prematurely recycled. A generation-counted body handle would be safer than an integer object index alone. The cache does not detect 3D tangent-frame rotation, it does not calculate a physically accurate contact point, and its ordered map is a reference implementation rather than a measured real-time allocation strategy. A production engine should benchmark a preallocated flat hash map or per-pair cache with explicit frame ownership and deterministic iteration requirements.
Velocity correction is not penetration correction

The equations above change velocities. They do not, by themselves, repair existing overlaps in positions. A production pipeline generally needs a distinct and carefully scoped policy: geometry generation and signed separation, speculative contact margins, split impulses or position-level stabilization, and consistent timestep handling. Naively adding a large position-error velocity bias can inject energy, make stacks jitter, or break restitution. This CPU witness intentionally has no position integrator, no Baumgarte term, no split impulse and no continuous collision detection. Therefore its passing tests cannot establish the correctness of CCD tunneling prevention or deep-overlap recovery.
From end-of-frame overlap to continuous time of impact

The contact solver described above only acts on contacts it has been given. A fast-moving disk can start to the left of a thin obstacle and finish to the right of it without overlapping at the end of a fixed simulation step. If collision detection samples positions only at the step boundary, it sees no collision, so even a mathematically perfect impulse solver cannot prevent tunneling. This is the reason continuous collision detection (CCD) is a separate geometric question: what is the first time, within the proposed integration interval, when the moving shapes touch?

For two disks with initial centres x_A and x_B, constant velocities v_A and v_B, and radii r_A, r_B, define the relative centre separation p = x_B - x_A, relative velocity v = v_B - v_A, and sum of radii R = r_A + r_B. Their separation at time t is p(t) = p + tv. They first touch when the squared centre distance equals the squared radius sum:
$ \lVert \mathbf p+t\mathbf v\rVert2=R2. $
Expanding the dot product gives the quadratic
$ at^2+bt+c=0,\qquad a=\mathbf v\cdot\mathbf v,\quad b=2\mathbf p\cdot\mathbf v,\quad c=\mathbf p\cdot\mathbf p-R^2. $

The meaning of the coefficients is crucial. c is the initial squared-distance gap: c<0 means the disks are already overlapping and this witness returns t=0, assigning overlap correction to a separate solver; c=0 means initial touching. If a=0, the relative geometry never moves during the interval. For initially separated disks, b≥0 means squared distance is not initially decreasing, so a collision cannot occur under these constant velocities. A discriminant D=b²−4ac<0 means the motion line misses the expanded-radius disk. D=0 gives a tangent or grazing touch, which counts as a contact in this laboratory.

The familiar quadratic expression (-b−sqrt(D))/(2a) can lose precision when nearly equal quantities are subtracted. The swept-disk CPU witness instead computes a stable intermediate q = -0.5(b − sqrt(D)) in its restricted b<0 branch, then evaluates the roots as t_near = c/q and t_far = q/a. Their product remains c/a, and the smaller root is tested against 0≤t≤Δt. The code uses std::fma in the discriminant to avoid one rounding step, but this is still finite-precision arithmetic; reliable collision detection across extreme dynamic ranges needs scale-aware error analysis or a more robust predicate policy.

Consider a disk of radius 1 m stationary at the origin and another radius-1 disk initially at x=10 m moving left at 100 m/s. Its centre must move 8 m before touching, so the time of impact is 0.08 s. At Δt=0.1 s, the moving disk would end at the origin and overlap if sampled; for an even faster moving disk it could end past the obstacle and be missed entirely. An analytical time-of-impact query reports the 0.08 s encounter regardless of the end position. During a simulation step, a practical engine can advance up to this impact, generate a contact normal, solve or schedule the event, and then advance the remaining time, with a bounded substep count and an explicit policy for simultaneous events and resting contacts.

The event’s collision normal is the normalized relative separation n(t) = (p+tv)/|p+tv|, pointing A to B. When initial centres coincide, there is no unique geometric normal; the witness uses a deterministic velocity-based fallback or +x if relative velocity is zero. This fallback is a test policy rather than a geometrically determined surface normal. The tests explicitly examine grazing touch, no-hit trajectories, hits outside the requested frame, existing overlap, coincident centres, invalid parameters, a high-dynamic-range trajectory, and Galilean invariance under equal velocity added to both bodies. The latter should not change relative motion or time of impact.

What this does not solve: disk CCD assumes translational linear motion throughout the interval and fixed radii. It does not include forces or acceleration changing the trajectory, rotation of polygons, concave meshes, vertex-edge events, general convex support functions, conservative advancement, broadphase swept bounds, contact island rescheduling, stable substep integration, or CCD after multiple impulses. It also does not prove the absence of false misses at all floating-point scales. These exclusions must be explicit when moving from a CPU analytic oracle to the engine’s full collision pipeline.
A complete impact event: geometry, first time, impulse and remaining interval

The earlier swept-disk query identifies an impact but does not evolve a scene. The independent disk event pipeline laboratory connects geometry, state integration, simultaneous constraints and the remainder of the frame. It does not claim to be Kairo’s actual world step. The model assumes fixed-radius, non-spinning disks, piecewise constant velocities, instantaneous frictionless impulses, and linear motion between impacts. There are no forces, torque, resting-contact stabilization, soft contacts or arbitrary polygons.

The entire algorithm follows from keeping one variable: remaining time. At each iteration, query all unordered disk pairs for their first collision in that remaining interval. If no pair collides, advance every position by its current velocity times the entire remaining interval. If collisions exist, find the earliest time, move all disks to that instant, collect other impacts at approximately the same time, freeze each event’s incoming normal velocity and restitution target, solve their normal impulses, then repeat the time-of-impact scan because the impulses have changed the future motion.

The numerical trace is visible in the first laboratory test. A radius-1 stationary disk is at x=0. Another radius-1 disk starts at x=10 with velocity −100 m/s, and the requested frame duration is 0.10 s. The moving disk must travel 8 m before the two surfaces meet, giving TOI=0.08 s. The world advances both disks through 0.08 s, then an elastic impulse against the infinite-mass disk reverses its incoming velocity to +100 m/s. The remaining time is 0.02 s, so its centre ends at x=4 m. An end-of-frame overlap test cannot reconstruct this physically meaningful trajectory by merely reversing the velocity at t=0.10 s.

For non-spinning disk collisions along the line of centres, the inverse effective mass is the sum of inverse masses, k = m_A⁻¹ + m_B⁻¹. With unit collision normal n pointing from A to B, relative normal speed u_n=(v_B−v_A)·n, and fixed impact target b=−e u_n_before, the solver’s unilateral accumulated impulse is
$ \lambda{next}=\max\left(0,\lambda{previous} +\frac{b-(\mathbf v_B-\mathbf v_A)\cdot\mathbf n} {m_A{-1}+m_B{-1}}\right). $

Only the difference Δλ = λ_next − λ_previous changes velocities. In a simultaneous batch, multiple contact rows may share a disk, so each row modifies the velocities seen by subsequent rows. The laboratory runs 32 sequential sweeps, freezing the original bounce target rather than repeatedly inventing a new restitution event. A symmetric three-disk scene tests two simultaneous impacts; another three-disk scene tests two impacts at different times in one frame.

The discovery procedure is O(n²) for each rescan because it checks every unordered pair, with no spatial acceleration. The same-time grouping threshold and near-touch geometry threshold are explicit finite-precision policies, not robust computational-geometry predicates. Grazing trajectories with zero closing normal speed are skipped. Deep initial overlaps are rejected rather than repaired. An event budget throws when exhausted, preventing an infinite event loop from masquerading as successful advancement. Importantly, a thrown exception can leave the input scene partly advanced: a production caller needs a rollback snapshot or transactional step if partial state mutation is unacceptable.

The nine deterministic tests exercise fast impacts, isolated elastic momentum and energy conservation, simultaneous row coupling, separating pairs, initial overlap rejection, event-budget exhaustion, chained events, ideal inelastic energy loss, and zero-duration/duplicate-ID validation. These tests establish a small analytic oracle, not a general proof of energy or convergence for arbitrary many-body simultaneous collisions, a guarantee against floating-point tunneling, support for rotating convex objects, or a persistent resting-contact engine. For an impact against an externally fixed body, momentum conservation of the two displayed disks alone is not the correct closed-system invariant; the stationary environment receives the reaction.
Reducing collision search without losing collisions: conservative swept bounds

The event-step laboratory above asks every pair of disks whether they will collide during the remaining time interval. With n bodies, this examines n(n−1)/2 unordered pairs after each event. For 1,000 disks, that is 499,500 expensive exact pair-time queries per scan—even if almost every disk is far away from the others. A broad phase exists to reject pairs that cannot possibly interact using a cheaper geometric test; it is not allowed to reject a true collision merely to be fast. This is why the central proof obligation is conservative coverage, not an attractive benchmark on one scene.

For a disk of radius r, initial centre p=(p_x,p_y), velocity v=(v_x,v_y) and remaining interval Δt, its centre under constant velocity travels along the segment from p to p+vΔt. Every possible disk position lies inside its swept axis-aligned rectangle. Its x bounds are min(p_x,p_x+v_xΔt)−r and max(p_x,p_x+v_xΔt)+r; y is analogous. The swept-broadphase reference lab conservatively rounds each boundary one representable floating-point value outward with std::nextafter. The exact continuous disk shape is a capsule around the segment, while its swept AABB is a larger rectangle: the rectangle admits extra pairs but must not discard any collision, provided the endpoints and bounds are correctly represented.

The algorithm sorts these rectangles by their minimum x coordinate, breaking ties by stable disk ID. As it visits each new rectangle, it removes from an active set any earlier rectangle whose maximum x lies strictly before the current minimum x. Every remaining active rectangle overlaps along x; the algorithm then compares their y intervals. Pairs that pass both checks are returned in deterministic lexicographically sorted index order, with a duplicate assertion. A true disk impact at time t∈[0,Δt] means the two disk regions intersect at that time; their swept AABBs must both contain the intersection point. Therefore their AABBs overlap in x and y and the pair must survive the broad-phase filtering. The reverse implication is false: AABBs may overlap even when the disks pass at different times or miss geometrically. The exact TOI narrow phase must therefore test every candidate before scheduling an event.

The laboratory compares its candidate set with an independent analytic disk TOI predicate, rather than comparing the broad phase against itself. Each true TOI pair must appear in the returned set. It tests a high-speed crossing, 100 stationary well-spaced disks with zero candidates, 200 seeded randomized scenes containing 35 disks each, and malformed identity/time inputs. The random scenes therefore examine up to 119,000 unordered pairs for conservative coverage, because each 35-disk scene contains 595 pairs. These are useful regression witnesses, not a proof against all finite-precision failures.

Sorting has O(n log n) comparison cost. Maintaining the simple active vector has potentially O(n²) scanning and removal cost when many broad AABBs overlap; the output itself can contain O(n²) candidate pairs in a dense scene. A scalable production version may use a better interval structure, broadphase BVH, grid, or incremental pair cache, and should benchmark temporally coherent motion rather than assuming this sample has production throughput. The original broadphase witness remains independently testable; the event stepper now has an optional swept-candidate mode alongside its exhaustive reference mode. Both generate candidate pairs for the current remaining interval, and the event stepper rebuilds candidates after each velocity-changing impact. A differential test source is committed to compare complete outcomes, but its successful GitHub-hosted execution remains unverified. This code-level integration is not yet native Kairo runtime integration or evidence of speedup.
How to reconstruct and verify the witness

Read the Row fields as a prepared contact Jacobian in compressed form: ra/rb are the lever arms, n/t are the constraint axes, kn/kt are scalar rows of the matrix J M⁻¹ Jᵀ. The method relative_velocity computes Jv, inverse_effective_mass computes a row’s inverse effective mass, solve_one projects impulse increments, and warm_start applies an already-owned cache once. make_row validates data and freezes the impact target. The six tests cover central momentum/energy, friction orientation, angular impulse, separating and static degeneracies, coupled two-contact iteration/next-frame cache, and nonfinite-input rejection.

Run strict compilation and execution, then run a sanitizer build. Expected output is persistent-contact witness: 6 suites PASS. This verifies only the tested cases on the compiling environment; the repository GitHub Actions workflow repeats strict and undefined-behavior checks, with remote status to be verified separately.

A reconstruction exercise is to add two bodies with unequal masses and an off-centre contact, compute kn by hand and compare every intermediate u_n, Δλ_n, Δv and Δω. A stronger follow-up exercise is to implement real feature matching, deliberately reverse normals between frames, and demonstrate that incorrectly reused cached tangential impulses generate artificial energy. Neither extension is presently claimed as implemented.
Verified boundary and research questions

The lab does not verify Kairo’s current renderer or physics engine, broadphase pair generation, narrowphase contact topology, 3D Jacobians, static/dynamic island management, precise multi-contact complementarity, numerical convergence across arbitrary scenes, determinism across compilers, robust CCD, or real-time performance. Before a research claim about stability or speed, define independent scene families, error metrics (maximum penetration, residual closing speed, drift, energy increase), iteration budgets, timestep families and order-randomization trials. Compare warm versus cold starts without changing geometry, feature matching or tolerances at the same time.

The user identified the first volume as overcompressed. The restored material includes constraint/hyperplane geometry; a constructive rank-nullity proof and both orthogonal-complement relationships; complete REF/RREF and elimination traces; permutation and packed-LU invariants; Cholesky and scalar/block LDLT; Gram–Schmidt, Householder, Givens and full least-squares residual derivation; multiplicity, spectral-theorem reasoning, power/inverse/Rayleigh/QR/Jacobi iterations and sensitivity; full/thin/compact SVD dimensions and both null spaces; Moore–Penrose identities and least-squares/minimum-norm proofs; spectral/Frobenius low-rank error bounds; PCA scores, reconstruction and plane fitting; polar and nearest proper rotation; bidiagonal/Jacobi SVD computation and stopping; checked matrix ownership/views/workspace; norms, matrix functions and branches; CSR/CG/preconditioning; and an SVD API design with explicit shapes and statuses.

ListItem.Content: Reduced QR retains the fixed perpendicular residual term. Dropping it preserves the minimizer but changes the reported objective value.

The REF/RREF example’s number of coefficient columns now matches its four-variable solution family.

Real QR eigenvalue iteration targets Schur blocks, and eigenvalue sensitivity formulas state simple-eigenvalue assumptions.
A row-sample point cloud uses a right singular vector for its geometric normal. Sample covariance requires at least two samples.
Wide SVD output shapes and zero-singular-value orthonormal completion are stated explicitly. A rectangular matrix cannot contain more orthonormal columns than its row dimension.
A view rejects a null pointer with a nonzero claimed extent. Preconditioned CG preserves the required symmetry/positive-definite structure and stops before zero-residual divisions.

Corrections and conventions made explicit

ListItem.Content: Use active right-handed rotations, column vectors, radians in code and Hamilton scalar-first quaternions. Storage order remains independent. A file/library boundary can use a different component order without changing the algebra.

The determinant comparison in the supplied conditioning text does not have equal determinants. The revised equal-determinant pair has determinants <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msup> <mn>10</mn> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>−</mo> <mn>20</mn> </mrow> </msup> </math> and conditions one versus <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msup> <mn>10</mn> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mn>20</mn> </mrow> </msup> </math>.
Diagonal matrices can represent half turns. General unit-diagonal mixing is not necessarily an elementary shear or volume preserving.
Pointer arithmetic starting at a separate named Mat2 member does not establish an array. The chapter uses actual arrays and logical bounds checks.

The source’s camera walk reaches view depth zero under the common <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>w</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mo>−</mo> <mi>z</mi> </math> perspective convention. The replacement uses a valid view depth <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo>−</mo> <mn>5</mn> </math>, explicit projection/depth endpoints, clip coordinates and a checked divide.

The supplied TBN example is orthonormal with determinant <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo>−</mo> <mn>1</mn> </math>. The chapter retains it with the required handedness sign rather than calling it implicitly right-handed.

A nonunit quaternion using its true inverse still rotates without scale. Conjugate substitution and the unit-only optimized expression have different off-unit behavior; the chapter gives explicit counterexamples.

Corrections and modeling contracts

The planar display’s average PPD must not be labeled its central local density. The expanded notes derive the projection derivative: FOV47.658899degrees, average40.286285PPD, center37.936213PPD for W0.53m/D0.60m/N1920. Spectral amplitude reporting distinguishes interior one-sided amplitudes from normalized complex magnitudes; DC/Nyquist are not doubled. Balanced difference-of-Gaussian constant cancellation requires gain/normalization conditions.

Exact-Nyquist phase is a boundary hazard; post-filtering cannot generally undo alias ambiguity. A fixed display refresh rate is not a universal perceptual cutoff. Motion-vector units/direction and jitter need contracts; TAA is not exposure integration. Temporal variance benefits require stationarity, independent noise and valid alignment. Psychometric correctness differs from generic detection, curve parameters differ from a selected threshold, and nonsignificance is not equivalence. A simulated foveation filter that computes a full reference first does not prove saved shading work or human invisibility.

The selected passages reinforce three teaching distinctions: deduction can discard top-level const/reference information; move/forward are category casts rather than resource transfers; const cache methods still need concurrency discipline. “Universal reference” in older material is identified with the narrower current forwarding-reference mechanism, not every T&& spelling.

Appendix.Content: Corrections and explicit implementation contracts

ListItem.Content: Fixed conversion rejects non-finite input before rounding/casting. The supplied range checks alone do not reject NaN.

Fixed multiplication/division use proved int64 intermediates and checked destination narrowing. Negative nearest-even rescaling uses unsigned magnitudes and quotient/remainder; it never negates INT64_MIN or adds a potentially overflowing positive half-scale.

C++23 signed shifting is not described as universally undefined. Instead the lab uses scaled multiplication and an explicit rounding algorithm to avoid confusing modular shift behavior, floor, truncation and desired rescaling.

The source’s lrint quantizer follows the active rounding direction. The teaching quantizer declares nearest-even, validates finite samples/scales, and bounds the ratio before integer conversion. It is not represented as identical production behavior.
Offset code q+8 is distinguished from two’s-complement INT4. Half-step quantization bounds exclude clipping and finite-parameter/evaluation error.

Smaller groups trade adaptation for metadata, without a universal monotonic quality guarantee. Full-group asymptotic bits/sample are distinguished from exact ceiling-based storage for small/partial groups.
Binary16 loss scaling is not presented as a cure for already-large values; BF16 keeps exponent width but not every FP32 endpoint or precision property.
BF16/half NaNs are explicitly canonicalized in the toy converters; raw tensor words preserve bits without signaling-NaN arithmetic.
Parser bounds use subtraction after offset validation; shape products are checked before multiplication; exact length and a 4096-element resource cap precede allocation.
Zero-copy mapping requires representation, bounds, alignment, lifetime and permitted typed-access rules—not merely an offset divisible by four.
The dump helper rejects zero/excessive row width, advances by remaining bounded length and uses a local formatting stream.
Error metrics promote float operands before subtracting when evaluated in double. Scalar reconstruction error is not task-level accuracy.
CRC detection, cryptographic integrity, authenticity, schema validity, publication and durability remain separate contracts. No security primitive or production format migration was implemented.

Appendix.Content: Corrections and teaching decisions

ListItem.Content: The binary subtraction operands are 1753/1024 and 1751/1024, giving 2^-9; the supplied difference/exponent was incorrect.
Numeric equality is not byte identity: signed zeros compare equal, while NaNs are unordered.
The cross-product example loses the +1 during binary32 input conversion near 1e8, before product rounding. Later promotion cannot recover it.
Distinct binary32 neighbors near 1e9 differ by 64; the source’s +32 example can round to the same input.
The existing validated, widened float comparator is reused. An unchecked generic tolerance formula is not labeled production-safe.
Gamma bounds retain algorithm, range, magnitude and conditioning assumptions. Exact nearby subtraction does not imply accurate original inputs.
Capped weighted recurrence is history-dependent even with exact representable arithmetic; this is separate from persistent-state narrowing.

The mixed-state laboratory fixture uses 0.5 and its next binary32 neighbor, staying within its normalized [-1,1] sample contract. An initial out-of-contract fixture threw during development; it was corrected before both final builds.

The local materialization example uses const rather than requiring reference-bearing automatic-local objects to be constant expressions. The intrusive stack explicitly forbids copy and move, unlinks surviving nodes on destruction, and requires linked caller-owned tasks to remain alive at stable addresses. Tests cover both permitted operations and rejected expressions, plus destruction/unlink/reuse.

bash tools/m018/build_m018_lab.sh completed successfully under the available Homebrew Clang 18.1.8 and Apple Clang 21.0.0. On this machine g++ names Apple Clang; this local result is not independent GNU GCC evidence. The script now also runs python3 tools/m018/check_note_examples.py --compiler clang++, which extracts three selected displayed note blocks and compiles/evaluates them. A private temporary-fixture check confirmed that it rejects both the former constexpr error and a deliberately incorrect arithmetic result. It does not compile every fragment in the book. The C++ workflow now triggers on changes to this continuous note as well as its existing code paths; no new hosted CI result is claimed for the uncommitted refinement.

The engine book gains inline teaching on closest-point sphere/box contact, corner misses and containment, SAT projection/near-parallel limits, feature-keyed contact retention versus active constraints, warm-start validity, and reconnect seat ownership. The graphics book gains coordinate/stride/overflow-aware pixel animation, specified Java/C++ cast behavior, and controlled depth/order/blending experiments. Source material includes directly checked supplied physics/design pages and selected retained caption units; the numeric traces and engineering policies are identified as original development. Existing engine and graphics teaching lines were verified to remain in order. Recall companions link directly to the expanded passages; new horizontal diagrams were rendered and visually inspected.

A bounded Python witness passed the corner-distance and containment examples, 1,000 projection-radius comparisons against eight-corner enumeration, pixel row-spill and quantization examples, distinct cache/activation decisions, reconnect deadline/owner/generation/sequence cases, and depth-versus-blending order examples. These prove the stated model examples, not a native collision solver, renderer or network service. Java cast behavior was checked against JLS narrowing conversion; C++ conversion against the language draft, with C++20 compilation for the saved examples. Vulkan fragment operations supplies the depth-state distinction; tutorial captions do not establish a captured GPU pipeline state.

The current retention audit found byte-identical saved originals for Passes 10–17, all 762 normalized source code bodies in the live continuous volumes, and no absent normalized source lines. This is retention evidence, not independent semantic review of every source claim. The full-vault target/fence audit checked 423 Markdown notes and resolved 8,568 wiki links without an error; eight earlier heading links were repaired. MathJax accepted 33,927 expressions without an error. These syntax/target checks do not prove all mathematics, diagrams or native Obsidian layout correct.

Detailed receipts, backups, extracted programs, negative tests, source decisions and rendered figures are retained in the local November 12 refinement checkpoint. Full earlier-source integration and whole-book reading remain unfinished. No commit, push, PR merge or acquisition restart was performed in this refinement.
November 12 continuation — clipping, conservative bounds and editor state

The shader explanation now distinguishes homogeneous clip coordinates from NDC with a negative-w counterexample and an edge-plane trace whose homogeneous parameter is 1/5 rather than the divided-coordinate parameter 1/3. OpenGL conventions and object/storage behavior were checked against the official 4.6 and 4.5 Core specifications. Computing Foundations separately explains buffer names, initialized objects, storage capacity and undefined initial contents; its OpenGL fragment requires an appropriate context and was not executed natively.

The graphics book develops the point-to-infinite-line formula, the enclosure argument required for conservative directional-shadow rejection, transformed object bounds and a shear counterexample. The two-panel D3 geometry figure is generated from the stated coordinates and transform; both panels have equal aspect ratio within their own axes. The original numerical model passed the worked examples and 2,000 property iterations. The exact saved Python reference was extracted from the book and executed successfully. This does not prove any inspected engine implements the reference or the episode’s timing claims.

The engine also gains directory-cache invalidation and stale-request publication traces, plus world-space editor gizmo depth/clipping/picking policies. Source proposals remain identified as proposals. The new sections are connected to compact recall cards and existing concept nodes. No old teaching lines were removed from the three continuous volumes; preserved baselines and final hashes are in the local continuation receipt.

Executed checks include the saved-note C++ checker (exit 0), the numerical witness (pass), the saved Python reference (exit 0), MathJax (33,995 expressions, zero errors), local wiki/fence validation and git diff –check. A damaged LaTeX delimiter in a staged formula was corrected and the MathJax check rerun successfully. The clipping flowchart and the geometry illustration were rendered and visually inspected. Source-receipt validation also caught a truncated unit ID; the corrected standardized receipt passed before its reading count advanced. No native OpenGL execution, commit, push or PR merge is claimed.
November 12 pulled consolidation — supervised spring, contact and design additions

Main was fast-forwarded from e334232 to 635dec4 (40 commits). The current README’s canonical destinations are Mathematics, Graphics and Game Engine. Former Foundations, XR, rigid-body and Systems files remain source/provenance copies. No original file was retired in this pass. A preexisting Systems formatting edit was backed up; its equations and hexadecimal prefixes were normalized and the corrected full source synchronized into Engine. HKDF’s counter is now identified as one octet, following RFC 5869 section 2.3. The retained original and pre-pull dirty version remain recoverable.

Three small agents screened staged work against the newly pulled canonical chapters. Already-covered contact-cache, manifold, editor-panel and best-first solver material was not duplicated. The genuinely missing additions are now inline in Engine: spring/bungee sign behavior and potential-energy derivation; the printed fake-spring dimensional/integration-order discrepancy; all three linear damping regimes; incremental contact-depth refresh after translation/small rotation; and formal/experiential/cultural analysis with four interaction modes and a shared-kit trace. The signed force plot is generated from the stated laws and was visually inspected.

Original physics PDF physical pages 110, 112 and 119 were visually checked by the supervisor, confirming the two printed force-sign patterns and Eq. 6.5. The smaller-agent review also checked physical pages 93–94 for the actual position-first integrator and 117–120 for the oscillator/damping context. The spring witness uses the intended force laws and scalar reductions of the printed patterns; it does not compile Cyclone. The contact witness uses frozen normals and planar small rotations; it is not a full detector or solver. Damping-model numerical witnesses verify initial conditions, near-critical continuity and the differential-equation residual in underdamped, critical and overdamped examples.

Executed checks: the three-volume preservation audit passed (all source bodies and 3/3 historical canonical books retained); the nine-program source-to-book sync audit passed; the canonical M018 saved-note example compiled/evaluated; spring strict and release/NDEBUG builds ran successfully; spring Apple Clang 21 ASan/UBSan build ran successfully; contact strict release/NDEBUG and Apple Clang UBSan builds ran successfully; and the pulled basis-measurement reference compiled/ran. A duplicate test variable caught on the first spring compile was corrected in both copies before successful reruns. Homebrew Clang 18’s combined sanitizer runtime stalled during initialization before main; a process sample captured the reentrant initializer and the process was terminated. That attempt is not counted as a passing sanitizer run. The successful sanitizer result belongs to the explicitly built Apple Clang executable.

Local link/fence and MathJax checks are separate from semantic and native Obsidian review. Exact pull receipts, source corrections, intermediate failures, compiled witnesses and the current checkpoint are in the local resume checkpoint. Hosted main checks passed for 635dec4 before these uncommitted additions; no hosted CI, commit, push or PR merge is claimed for this local pass.

The same supervised continuation adds the force-level material-pair interpretation of Coulomb friction, the 45/60/65 N static-limit trace and 40 N kinetic example, and a projectile comparison that distinguishes equal energy from equal momentum. Its drag-free horizontal-launch derivation also explains why reducing speed twentyfold requires gravity four hundredfold lower to preserve drop at fixed range. The source’s smaller gravity adjustment is explicitly a tuning recipe. The Kohi integer DLL smoke-test receipt is retained privately as corroborating evidence for already-developed binary-boundary teaching; it was not counted as a new mechanism.

Appendix.title: Vault Repair and Source Retention - 2026-11-14
Appendix.Content: Vault repair and source retention — 14 November 2026

This is the supervised local repair of the active iCloud/Obsidian Master vault, beginning at commit c142869a391c32d55068ddfbf4d4ac11ce52762c. The vault’s existing hidden .obsidian configuration and unrelated Finder/workspace edits are left in place. The three continuous books remain the teaching surface; this record tracks changes and evidence, not a fourth lesson book.
Integrated teaching and code comments

Computing Foundations now embeds its temporary-lifetime, SE(3) exp/log and paired-inference witnesses at their teaching seams. The misplaced closing fence after the reverse-mode Tape includes is removed, keeping the class inside its C++ block. The statistical witness validates finite inputs, normalizes its sign-flip comparison and checks measurement-unit rescaling; the pose witness exercises its documented near-pi rejection.

Graphics now embeds the planar eight-state EKF, 3-D zero-order-hold IMU preintegration and discrete NeRF volume-rendering witnesses. The planar camera is explicitly co-located and aligned with the body. The original 1,842-line perceptual/XR packet is relocated intact after rendering so the mathematical prerequisites precede it. The relocation itself preserves 240,779 characters exactly; earlier wiki-route corrections are recorded separately.

Game Engine now embeds the block contact, symbolic subresource-state, rollback, audio and AI witnesses. The new bounded scene-persistence example teaches explicit versioned fields, strict decimal input, stable IDs, forward references, iterative cycle rejection, migration and candidate-then-swap publication. Negative fixtures prove failed loads keep the live scene unchanged. This is an in-memory schema/transaction witness, not filesystem durability or a production scene format.

For these added and revised programs, implementation reasoning, state meanings, units, branch choices and limits are explained in comments beside the relevant operations. Conceptual prerequisites remain before code. Existing teaching elsewhere was preserved; this pass does not claim to have re-commented every historical snippet.
Navigation, formatting and supervision

Retired Mathematics, XR and Systems wiki targets now lead to the actual canonical books, retaining labels and anchors. Four dangling concept links point to existing developed explanations rather than new glossary stubs. The retired rigid-body route resolves to the preserved Foundations section.

Independent small-agent reviews exposed the missing camera/body extrinsic assumption, scale-dependent statistical tie tolerance, nonfinite-data handling and an untested near-pi branch; those findings were repaired before final verification. Five existing concept cards also had control-byte/missing-command corruption in TeX. Their GGX/Fresnel, homology, spherical harmonics, impulse/friction and Beer–Lambert formulas were repaired with units and domain assumptions.

The source guard compares complete parsed code blocks, including comments, instead of relying on a common first include line or counting only one fence style. The preservation guard pins the actual pre-repair books and permits only the documented route, Tape-fence, closure-statement and intact-XR-relocation changes. It still rejects removal or reordering of other prior teaching.
Verification and its limits

Appendix.Content: The eight revised/new C++ labs were compiled and executed with Apple Clang under strict warnings-as-errors, optimized -DNDEBUG, and AddressSanitizer/UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer profiles. The four Python witnesses were executed normally and with -O; their validation survives optimization. Recorded receipts include initial failures and subsequent successful reruns. Final counts and equation/diagram checks are recorded in the private verification checkpoint linked below.

The final-pass workflows now have read-only repository permissions and verify the checked-in books. They no longer apply or push repairs. They run on the checked-out revision rather than silently targeting an authoring branch. Native Vulkan/Metal, production-engine integration and human-subject XR evidence are separate; this pass does not re-certify them or every existing code fragment.
Caption and acquisition-tool cleanup decision

The deletion condition is not met. The retained source ledger has 590 extracted records and 29,715 claim texts: 28,485 reviewed and 1,230 pending. The newer 693-job queue contains 590 extracted jobs, 96 queued jobs, four failed book jobs, two paused book jobs and one visual-review job. Its 103 open jobs and lack of complete per-source merge proof prevent certifying that all captions are accounted for.

All original captions, ASR text, book extracts, source-unit receipts and acquisition scripts remain available. No acquisition run was started. The current work does not claim full reading of the seven mathematics PDFs’ 4,205 pages. Only untracked, reproducible Python bytecode caches were removed; ignore rules keep future interpreter/Finder clutter out of new commits without altering existing tracked workspace metadata.

Source retirement can proceed later under the user’s existing conditional authorization once exact source contributions and destinations are closed. A read claim or a similar topic heading alone does not satisfy that condition.

Appendix.title: Worked Traces
Appendix.Content: Worked Traces
Phase 9-10 worked-trace navigation
The full numerical traces remain in the continuous volumes; this page does not duplicate their calculations:

Phase 9 Jacobian trace · Phase 9 integral and quadrature traces · Phase 9 oscillator and stability traces · Phase 9 optimization traces · Phase 10 outcomes and Bayes trace · Phase 10 Monte Carlo trace · Phase 10 online statistics · Phase 10 uncertainty and error metrics
Phase 8 - From constraints to a stable SVD contract
Follow one small rank-deficient fit through its geometry, answer, and checks. This supplements the Phase 8 story.
Let
Appendix.RawBlock: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"> <mi>A</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="INNER"> <mo data-mjx-texclass="OPEN">[</mo> <mtable columnspacing="1em" rowspacing="4pt"> <mtr> <mtd> <mn>3</mn> </mtd> <mtd> <mn>0</mn> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd> <mn>0</mn> </mtd> <mtd> <mn>0</mn> </mtd> </mtr> </mtable> <mo data-mjx-texclass="CLOSE">]</mo> </mrow> <mo>,</mo> <mstyle scriptlevel="0"> <mspace width="2em" /> </mstyle> <mi>b</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="INNER"> <mo data-mjx-texclass="OPEN">[</mo> <mtable columnspacing="1em" rowspacing="4pt"> <mtr> <mtd> <mn>6</mn> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd> <mn>5</mn> </mtd> </mtr> </mtable> <mo data-mjx-texclass="CLOSE">]</mo> </mrow> <mo>.</mo> </math>
Appendix.Content: The first row observes <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mn>1</mn> </msub> </math> with gain three. The second row has zero coefficients, so it cannot produce the requested measurement five. The rank is one, the column space is the horizontal axis, and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>b</mi> </math> lies outside it. The null space is the vertical axis: changing <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msub> </math> is invisible to the map.

The SVD is already diagonal: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>U</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mi>V</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mi>I</mi> </math>, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mi>A</mi> </math>. The pseudoinverse is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msup> <mi>A</mi> <mo>+</mo> </msup> <mo>=</mo> <mi>diag</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>/</mo> </mrow> <mn>3</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math>. Therefore <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msup> <mi>A</mi> <mo>+</mo> </msup> <mi>b</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>2</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math>. Every <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>2</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mi>t</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math> has the same residual <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mo>−</mo> <mn>5</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math>; <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>t</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>0</mn> </math> is its minimum-norm choice. This trace separately answers consistency, rank, nullity, residual, and the pseudoinverse policy.

For <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>k</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> </math> truncation, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>A</mi> <mn>1</mn> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <mi>diag</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>3</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math>. Here the input already has rank one, so the approximation is exact. If instead <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>A</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mi>diag</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>3</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>2</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math>, then keeping only the first singular direction gives <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>A</mi> <mn>1</mn> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <mi>diag</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>3</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math>, spectral error <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mn>2</mn> </math>, and Frobenius error <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mn>2</mn> </math>. The norm names state which reconstruction discrepancy is being reported.

Now use centered planar samples <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mo>−</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>,</mo> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>,</mo> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math>. Their sample covariance with divisor <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>N</mi> <mo>−</mo> <mn>1</mn> </math> is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>diag</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math>. The first component follows the horizontal line; the zero second eigenvalue says the observed samples have no vertical spread. Add small measurement noise and that zero becomes small, making the rank or PCA cutoff a scale-aware modeling decision.

An SVD routine should return dimensions and status, not just three arrays. Check <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo data-mjx-texclass="ORD" fence="false" stretchy="false">‖</mo> <mi>A</mi> <mo>−</mo> <mi>U</mi> <mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi> <msup> <mi>V</mi> <mi>T</mi> </msup> <mo data-mjx-texclass="ORD" fence="false" stretchy="false">‖</mo> </math> relative to a declared input scale; check <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msup> <mi>U</mi> <mi>T</mi> </msup> <mi>U</mi> </math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msup> <mi>V</mi> <mi>T</mi> </msup> <mi>V</mi> </math> separately, with identity sizes matching full/thin conventions; verify descending nonnegative singular values; enforce a maximum iteration count and surface nonconvergence. Passing these checks establishes those measured properties at the tested scale; it does not certify every singular value or guarantee an accurate solution for an ill-conditioned application.
Phase 7 - The moving-panel tracebook

Use active right-handed rotations, column vectors, radians in code, and the declared illustrative minus-Z projection with near 1, far 10 and NDC depth <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">[</mo> <mo>−</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo stretchy="false">]</mo> </math>.
One local point reaches a screen-relative description

Let local scale be <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>2</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math>, orientation a positive-Z quarter turn, translation <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>10</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math>, and point <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>p</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math>. The camera sits at world <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>10</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>5</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math> with identity orientation.

Cell.Content: Scaling occurs in the declared local axes.
Right-hand positive Z maps X toward Y.
Camera is five units above the world plane and looks along <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo>−</mo> <mi>Z</mi> </math>.
Finite nonzero divisor; this point is within the selected clip volume.

Appendix.Content: Reconstructing local coordinates undoes translation, then rotation, then scale. Applying the inverse orientation with a guessed untranslated offset would mix frames. The same row-major scalar array could implement every operation if logical access and upload conventions remain correct.
The tangent and normal take different paths

Take local tangent <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>u</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math> and local normal <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>n</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mo>−</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math>. Scale then rotate gives <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msup> <mi>u</mi> <mo data-mjx-alternate="1">′</mo> </msup> <mo>=</mo> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mo>−</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>2</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math>. Reciprocal-scale then rotate gives <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msup> <mi>n</mi> <mo data-mjx-alternate="1">′</mo> </msup> <mo>=</mo> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>/</mo> </mrow> <mn>2</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math>. Their dot is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo>−</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>+</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>=</mo> <mn>0</mn> </math>. Normalizing <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msup> <mi>n</mi> <mo data-mjx-alternate="1">′</mo> </msup> </math> for shading changes its length, not the perpendicularity. Neither vector receives translation. A mirrored model additionally needs an explicit winding/orientation policy.
Diagnose interpolation using a quarter point

Interpolate identity to a positive-Z <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msup> <mn>120</mn> <mo>∘</mo> </msup> </math> orientation. At <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>t</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>/</mo> </mrow> <mn>4</mn> </math>, ideal SLERP gives a <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msup> <mn>30</mn> <mo>∘</mo> </msup> </math> turn. NLERP normalizes coefficients <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>7</mn> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>/</mo> </mrow> <mn>8</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo>,</mo> <msqrt> <mn>3</mn> </msqrt> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>/</mo> </mrow> <mn>8</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math>, yielding about <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msup> <mn>27.795772496</mn> <mo>∘</mo> </msup> </math>. The midpoint alone would not expose this speed difference. With endpoints <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>q</mi> </math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo>−</mo> <mi>q</mi> </math>, sign-aligning first avoids a zero midpoint and preserves the common orientation.
A parent edit invalidates only actual dependencies

For car → door → mirror, editing the door’s local transform makes door-local and door-world caches stale, along with mirror-world and derived inverse/normal caches. Mirror-local and car caches remain valid. Reparenting the mirror changes its world dependency even if its local coefficients remain identical. Preserving world pose during reparenting instead requires solving the new local map and checking whether the result still fits the allowed TRS representation.
Phase 6 - The robot panel tracebook
This cumulative trace extends the self-contained Phase 6 volume. The numbers are illustrative laboratory inputs, not observations from a real robot or renderer.
One physical object through six representations

Start with metre-valued workcell points <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>A</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math>, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>B</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>4</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math>, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>C</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>3</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math> and sensor point <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>P</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math>.

RowValue.Content: Point differences, not new point locations.
Oriented area vector in square metres.
Finite unit front normal; triangle area is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mn>6</mn> </math>.
Sum is one and all weights are positive.

Content.RawInline: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>5</mn> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>/</mo> </mrow> <mn>12</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mn>20</mn> <mo>+</mo> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>/</mo> </mrow> <mn>4</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mn>40</mn> <mo>+</mo> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>/</mo> </mrow> <mn>3</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mn>50</mn> <mo>=</mo> <mn>35</mn> </math>

RowValue.Content: Affine temperature model, not an asserted physical heat solution.

Appendix.Content: Move a point <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>D</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>2</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math> above the panel. The area normal dotted with <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>D</mi> <mo>−</mo> <mi>A</mi> </math> is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mn>24</mn> </math>, yielding tetrahedron volume <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mn>4</mn> </math>. Swap <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>B</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>C</mi> </math> and both signs reverse; ordinary area and volume do not.
A mirror changes orientation, not all measurements

Mirror horizontal coordinates with <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>R</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mi>diag</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mo>−</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math>. New first edge is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mo>−</mo> <mn>4</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math> and second edge remains <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>3</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math>. Their cross becomes <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mo>−</mo> <mn>12</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math>. All edge lengths and all original pairwise dot products remain unchanged. The Gram matrix cannot tell us that the orientation flipped.

The ordinary transformed normal direction <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>R</mi> <mi>n</mi> </math> is still <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math>. The cross-derived oriented normal gains the additional factor <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo data-mjx-texclass="OP" movablelimits="true">det</mo> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>R</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>=</mo> <mo>−</mo> <mn>1</mn> </math>. This is why a mesh pipeline needs a consistent front-face and mirror policy rather than one generic “transform vector” call.
Nonuniform scaling exposes a hidden normal bug

For tangent <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math> and normal <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mo>−</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math>, double only the horizontal scale. Tangent becomes <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>2</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math>. A naively transformed normal <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>2</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mo>−</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math> gives dot <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mn>3</mn> </math>, not zero. The inverse-transpose normal <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>/</mo> </mrow> <mn>2</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mo>−</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math> gives dot zero. Normalize the latter only after deriving its correct direction.
A frame can be valid without being continuous

With normal <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math>, a least-aligned horizontal helper produces tangent <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mo>−</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math> and bitangent <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math>. All axes are unit and perpendicular, and the frame is positive. Perturb the normal through a helper-selection tie: a different helper can become preferred abruptly. Correct axes do not establish smooth frame evolution. Animated systems must decide whether continuity or a texture reference is required.
Perspective-correct attribute trace

For two projected endpoints with <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>w</mi> <mn>0</mn> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>,</mo> <msub> <mi>w</mi> <mn>1</mn> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <mn>2</mn> </math>, equal screen weights <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mn>1</mn> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>/</mo> </mrow> <mn>2</mn> </math> produce reciprocal-weight denominator <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mn>1</mn> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>/</mo> </mrow> <mn>2</mn> <mo>+</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>/</mo> </mrow> <mn>4</mn> <mo>=</mo> <mn>3</mn> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>/</mo> </mrow> <mn>4</mn> </math>. Surface weights become <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mn>2</mn> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>/</mo> </mrow> <mn>3</mn> </math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mn>1</mn> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>/</mo> </mrow> <mn>3</mn> </math>. If endpoint attributes are <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mn>0</mn> </math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mn>1</mn> </math>, affine surface interpolation at that screen location gives <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mn>1</mn> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>/</mo> </mrow> <mn>3</mn> </math>, not the naive <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mn>1</mn> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>/</mo> </mrow> <mn>2</mn> </math>.
The first lost quantity can precede every formula

Store intended horizontal coordinates <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msup> <mn>10</mn> <mn>8</mn> </msup> </math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msup> <mn>10</mn> <mn>8</mn> </msup> <mo>+</mo> <mn>1</mn> </math> in binary32. Near that scale, one unit is below the local representable spacing, so both can round to the same value. Subtraction then yields zero. Promoting those already-rounded values to binary64 does not recover their difference. Retain a wider global representation or subtract in an appropriately local frame before narrowing.
Collision difference without an explicit shape

Take intervals <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>A</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mo stretchy="false">[</mo> <mn>2</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>4</mn> <mo stretchy="false">]</mo> </math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>B</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mo stretchy="false">[</mo> <mn>3</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>5</mn> <mo stretchy="false">]</mo> </math>. In positive direction, the difference support is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mn>4</mn> <mo>−</mo> <mn>3</mn> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> </math>. In negative direction, choose <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mn>2</mn> <mo>−</mo> <mn>5</mn> <mo>=</mo> <mo>−</mo> <mn>3</mn> </math>. The origin lies between them, consistent with overlap. For <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>A</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mo stretchy="false">[</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo stretchy="false">]</mo> </math>, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>B</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mo stretchy="false">[</mo> <mn>3</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>4</mn> <mo stretchy="false">]</mo> </math>, the extrema are <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo>−</mo> <mn>4</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mo>−</mo> <mn>2</mn> </math>, both negative; the intervals do not overlap. A full higher-dimensional collision algorithm must manage its simplex and stopping policies separately.
What the executed lab actually demonstrates

The inline scalar program checks the panel weights, area, frame, projection, rejection, reflection, finite-state rejection, huge/tiny scaled normalization, angles, transmission and total internal reflection. It also runs 2,000 deterministic moderate-range cases for decomposition, orthogonality, projection idempotence, reflected length and cross antisymmetry/perpendicularity. None of these tests certify all floating-point inputs, performance, a robust orientation implementation, or human understanding.

C++ - Value-transfer and cleanup board traces
Essential code and traces remain inline in the payload journey and the event laboratory.

Cell.Content: Both members completed; complete Whole did not. No destructor-body -3 event.
Destructor body precedes reverse member cleanup.
Delegating target completes, delegating body throws
Complete target established object; cleanup invokes its destructor then member destruction.

Appendix.Content: Positive IDs mean construction/body entry, negatives mean destruction. The fixed recorder does not allocate from destructors. Exception traces establish the tested lifetime rules, not a policy for every subsystem’s error handling.
Assignment failure versus successful ownership transfer

Start A with byte7 and B with byte9 in separate buffers. Prepare B=A with an injected allocation failure: B still holds byte9 at the same live buffer, A still byte7, and allocation count is unchanged. Move-construct C from A: C owns byte7, A is documented empty. Copy-construct from empty A: new owner is empty without traversing a null range. Move-assign C into B: B’s byte9 allocation is released, B takes byte7, C becomes empty. Self-move B through its alias preserves its value under this particular owner’s contract. Reset B to empty and end scope: live allocation count0.
The aliased update does not behave like two copies

For destination+=source; source*=0.5, starting with distinct source4/destination4 gives destination8/source2. If both parameters designate one float, its state is4→8→4. The second statement sees the first statement’s write. Passing scalar values instead creates independent parameter values; no caller mutation is implied.
Observation is not a mandatory NRVO count

On the recorded Clang C++23 build, the named Probe return observed zero moves ordinarily and one with optional elision disabled. The immovable same-type prvalue result remained valid in both. This differentiates language-required direct construction from a compiler-selected named-local elision. Do not substitute these observed counts for a timing or allocation benchmark.
C++ - Borrow deadlines and dense-pool identity

The essential explanation remains inline in the borrow story. This deeper board exercise separates the targets of three paths. Assume a vector with three live Slot objects, enough capacity, and assignments that do not end the destination Slot lifetime.

Cell.Content: Still live until pop; moved-from state
Must be invalidated for removal under registry policy
Can still identify other live entities if registry validates them
New valid path to current owner33
Lookup binds identity to current location

Appendix.Content: Do not read a moved-from value without its type’s specified contract; this example’s integer members and Slot assignment make the first-slot result explicit. Not every pool implementation uses this algorithm. The source-reported Kairo anchors remain To verify.
Direct alias versus converted snapshot

Start count=10, bind const int& live=count and const double& snapshot=count. The first referent is count; the second is a new converted double containing10.0. After count=50, live observes50 and snapshot observes10.0. At the end of their enclosing scope the extended double temporary dies; no separate double was owned by count.
A function call does not renew the deadline

Construct temporary string → bind call parameter → return that same path → bind caller’s receiving reference → complete full-expression → destroy temporary. The receiver’s longer lifetime is irrelevant. Contrast direct local binding, which specifies extension, with returning std::string by value, which establishes an owning result. The complete rule is in Temporary lifetime extension, not “references make temporaries live longer.”
Cache invalidation without exposed storage

Source3/cache-empty → Get holds mutex, computes9, copies9, unlocks → Set holds mutex, replaces source with4, clears cache, unlocks → Get computes16 and copies it under mutex. The earlier returned9 remains a valid independent snapshot. If Get had exposed a reference, clearing the optional could end that referenced integer’s lifetime. Locking only while obtaining the reference does not protect its later use.
