Essential traces stay inside the build story and the escaped-address story. The complete inline laboratory supplies observable constructions/destructions without executing stale access.

Cell.Content: Byte storage; no explicit Tracked occupant yet
Old handle no longer names live occupant

Appendix.Content: This deliberate reuse is not the same as dereferencing a pointer to an automatic object after its storage duration ended. Transparent replacement has specific rules; std::launder is not a universal cure for stale pointers.
Longer hand traces live here. Organize by mechanism so later chunks can extend the same trace with deeper representation, math, implementation, or hardware behavior.
A trace should include a concrete input, every state transition that matters, the final output, one invariant check, and one deliberately failing or boundary input when useful.
M001 - The 0xAD control byte
Input and conventions
Schema, from least to most significant position:
Appendix.Code: bits 0-2 mode | bit 3 visible | bits 4-5 quality | bit 6 locked | bit 7 dirty
Appendix.Content: Input: {mode=5, visible=1, quality=2, locked=0, dirty=1}. Field zero occupies the least-significant available bits.
State-by-state trace
Base interpretations:
Quality extraction:
LSB-first bit-array packing of [1,0,1,1,0,1,0,1] accumulates 01, 05, 0D, 2D, then AD; unpacking index 5 computes (0xAD >> 5) & 1 = 1.
Result and invariant checks

ListItem.Content: Every field round-trips to its input value.
The five fields occupy eight non-overlapping bits exactly.
Changing quality to 3 clears 0x30, writes 0x30, and yields 0xBD; all non-quality bits remain unchanged.

Appendix.Content: Boundary or failure trace

OR-only replacement fails when a new value needs to clear an old 1. For example, replacing quality 3 with 1 via word | (1 << 4) leaves the old high field bit set and still decodes as 3. Clear-before-OR produces the intended 1.
M002 - Carry and overflow are different questions
Input and conventions
Use eight-bit result storage. C is the ninth unsigned bit, V reports signed two’s-complement range failure, N copies result bit 7, and Z tests whether the low result byte is zero.
State-by-state trace
Case 1 - signed overflow without carry:
Appendix.Code:
01111111 unsigned 127, signed 127 + 00000001 unsigned 1, signed 1 ---------- 10000000 unsigned 128, signed -128
C=0: no ninth bit; unsigned 128 fits V=1: signed mathematical 128 does not fit [-128,127] N=1: result high bit is set Z=0: result is nonzero
Appendix.Content: Case 2 - carry without signed overflow:
Appendix.Code:
11111111 unsigned 255, signed -1 + 00000001 unsigned 1, signed 1 ---------- 1 00000000
C=1: unsigned mathematical 256 needs a ninth bit V=0: signed mathematical result is valid zero N=0: low result high bit is clear Z=1: low result byte is zero
Appendix.Content: Subtraction example:
Result and invariant checks

ListItem.Content: C and V are independent; neither can replace the other.
N reports the stored sign bit, not whether a signed overflow occurred.
An eight-bit emulator must retain a wider temporary long enough to compute C, then mask the architectural result.

Appendix.Content: Boundary or failure trace

10000000 represents -128. Complement-plus-one returns 10000000 because mathematical +128 cannot fit. At the fixed-bit residue level the pattern is stable; evaluating same-type signed negation in C++ overflows and is undefined.
Reconstructing each state change
Decimal to binary and back

For 173, successive quotient/remainder pairs are (86,1), (43,0), (21,1), (10,1), (5,0), (2,1), (1,0), (0,1). The remainders are low bits first, so reverse them to get 10101101. Horner accumulators while reading this result are 1,2,5,10,21,43,86,173. This checks both directions without assuming that the displayed order equals array order.
Replacing a field while preserving neighbors
Replace quality 2 with 1 in AD:
Appendix.Code: field width w=2, offset s=4 low mask L=03; positioned mask M=30 eight-bit NOT(M)=CF clear: AD & CF = 8D encode new value: (01 & 03) << 4 = 10 write: 8D | 10 = 9D read back: (9D >> 4) & 03 = 01 outside field: AD & CF = 9D & CF = 8D
Appendix.Content: The last equality proves preservation rather than only checking the new field value.
Multiplication by selected partial products
Multiply 13 by 11. Start result=0, partial=13, multiplier=11. A low multiplier bit of 1 includes the partial product; shift the multiplier right and the widened partial left between stages.
Check 13×11=143. The widened partial is essential: if it were retained in a narrow original operand, shifts could lose bits before the accumulator sees them.
Division by shifting the remainder

Divide binary 1101 (13) by 3, reading dividend bits from most to least significant. At each stage append the next bit to the partial remainder, compare with 3, subtract if possible, and append the quotient decision.
Quotient 4 and remainder 1 satisfy 13=4×3+1, with 0≤1<3.
C++ expression types and a safe index
For uint8_t a=250,b=10 on the host used here:

ListItem.Content: Stored operands are eight-bit unsigned values.
Integral promotion converts each to int because int represents 0–255.
Addition executes as int arithmetic, producing int 260.
auto keeps int 260; explicit conversion to uint8_t stores residue 4.

Appendix.Content: For int index=−1 and unsigned size=10, an ordinary mixed-sign comparison may convert −1 to a large unsigned value. std::cmp_less(-1,10u) correctly returns true mathematically, but that alone does not authorize indexing. The valid condition is index>=0 && std::cmp_less(index,size).
Binary subtraction and incoming borrow

Take A=5, B=3. With carry C=1, compute 5+NOT₈(3)+1=5+252+1=258: result=2, carry-out=1 (no borrow). With C=0, compute 257: result=1, since an incoming borrow subtracts one extra. For A=3,B=5,C=1, exact unsigned difference is −2: low result=254, carry-out=0 (borrow). This is the binary SBC convention, independent of any repository implementation claim.
M003 - Bytes to physical memory
A matching and mismatching endian decode
Bytes are hexadecimal. Reading LE bytes as BE produces 78563412; no intra-octet bit reversal occurs. A schema version=1, count=0x12345678, payloadSize=9, written U8/U32-LE/U64-LE, yields:
Field offsets are 0/1/5, length 13. A typical native record places fields at 0/4/8, size 16. Packing may resemble the schema length but does not define its byte order or version contract.
Struct layout and an aligned array
Assume member size/alignment pairs 1/1, 8/8, 2/2, 4/4.
Holes are seven plus two bytes; payload 15, size 24. Reordering id/color/layer/flags gives 0-7/8-11/12-13/14 plus one tail byte: size 16. Verify on the target ABI.
A 1/4/1 record ends at nine but has size 12. At base 0x1000, next object starts 0x100C and its integer at 0x1010. A fictitious stride nine would put that integer at 0x100D, breaking alignment.
Page translation with an unchanged offset
Assume 4-KiB pages and an allowed resident mapping.
Appendix.Code: VA 0x12345ABC P 0x1000 = 4096 VPN = VA / P 0x12345 offset = VA % P 0xABC mapping VPN 0x12345 -> PFN 0x987 frame start 0x987000 PA = start + offset 0x987ABC
Appendix.Content: Process B may map the same VPN to another PFN; adjacent virtual pages may map distant frames. These are address-space mappings, not endian conversions.

Four bytes starting at offset FFE occupy FFE/FFF in page one and 000/001 in page two. A valid first mapping does not prove the second readable. Four bytes at cache-line offset 62 similarly span two 64-byte lines.

With stated little-endian float representation, 00 00 80 3F corresponds to bits 3F800000 and float 1.0; IEEE-754 floating point develops why later.

Appendix.Content: A TLB miss can walk valid tables without OS faulting. A nonresident valid page can fault, acquire backing, and resume. A forbidden access may fail. Real processors overlap this conceptual sequence.
Ownership and lifetime, not geography

A local vector object commonly occupies a frame; elements occupy its separate dynamic buffer. A copied span points to elements, not vector metadata. Returning that span after destroying the vector dangles it; reallocation can also invalidate views. Keeping an owner alive is necessary but not always sufficient.

Static locals retain storage across calls; automatic const locals need not use read-only mappings; string literals have static storage and must not be modified. Old numeric addresses or remaining bytes do not extend lifetime.
Fault recovery and copy-on-write

Two mappings share frame F read-only. For a permitted private COW write, OS allocates F2, copies F, changes the writer’s mapping to F2 with write permission, and restarts. Not every protection violation is repairable.

Diagnosis: absurd decoded value→byte order; second array element misaligned→stride/tail padding; released vector span→lifetime; first-touch latency→fault/commitment; allocation fails amid holes→fragmentation; published file lost after crash→publication versus durability.

Kahan trace at binary32 precision

Naive loses both ones in this order. Kahan preserves this particular aggregate; it is not a universal order-independent sum. Pairwise on [2^24,1,1] splits one item from two, adds the ones first, and also reaches 2^24+2.
Precision lost on input cannot be recovered later

Intended component 100000001 becomes binary32 100000000. Promoting that stored float gives exact binary64 100000000, not the intended integer. Directly converting the original integer to double preserves it. The cross-product example must distinguish input loss from later multiplication/subtraction error.

Two values <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mn>0.5</mn> </math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mn>0.5</mn> <mo>+</mo> <msup> <mn>2</mn> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>−</mo> <mn>24</mn> </mrow> </msup> </math> average to exact midpoint <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mn>0.5</mn> <mo>+</mo> <msup> <mn>2</mn> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>−</mo> <mn>25</mn> </mrow> </msup> </math>. nextafter(2.5,−infinity) rounds to pixel 2 via llround; nextafter(2.5,+infinity) rounds to 3. The exact midpoint rounds to 3 by the halfway-away-from-zero rule. A small perturbation crossing this boundary changes which observation is sampled.

A scalar field value changing sign near zero can change a surface-extraction case. Scalar RMS error, sign-change count, vertex displacement and topology measure different consequences; none was measured on real reconstruction data in this merge.

Appendix.title: 01 - Bits, Numbers and Memory - Visual Recall
Appendix.source: Visual Recall/01 - Bits, Numbers and Memory - Visual Recall.md
Appendix.Content: Bits, Numbers and Memory - Visual Recall
Scope: Parts 1–100 only, M001–M006. Companion to From Signals to Meaning. No C++ Volume 02 material is included. This is a retrieval desk, not another textbook.
How to use this desk

Cover the visual, sketch it from memory, answer the numbered prompts, then expand the answer key. Score each prompt 0 (missing/wrong), 1 (correct label but weak explanation), or 2 (can reconstruct an example and its limits). Revisit weak prompts in the linked teaching section. Do not turn recognition of a diagram into a mastery claim.

Mermaid shows relationships; byte strips show placement; tables show exact distinctions; state/sequence diagrams show what changes over time. Diagrams are conceptual models, not fixed CPU/OS layouts. Answer keys use collapsible Obsidian callouts.
Short-form recall — the whole route

Pattern is not meaning. A representation contract assigns weights and interpretation. → Bits become decisions. Masks select fields; packing needs widths, ranges, and a policy. → Arithmetic is finite. Choose wrap, saturation, rejection, or widening before calculation. → Real values use a ruler. Floating point trades spacing against range; fixed point chooses a scale. → Operations expose error. Rounding, cancellation, conditioning, and reproducibility matter. → Keep the needed information. Quantization/codebooks spend precision deliberately. → Bytes occupy places. Alignment, lifetime, ownership, and virtual mapping are distinct. → Files are agreements. Define schema, validate lengths, then decode and check integrity.

Caption: Follow one value from physical signal to stored bytes and back. At every transition ask: Which bits? What meaning? What range/error policy? Where and during which lifetime? What format contract? For the end-to-end laboratory, see the complete journey.

BlockQuote.Content: [!abstract] Compact teaching notes Represent: bits are patterns; interpretation supplies meaning. Bit-pattern example · Two's-complement derivation

Select and compute: mask = select; shift = reposition; pack = preserve neighbors plus insert validated fields. Arithmetic needs an explicit overflow policy. Field figure/formulas · Packing lab · Overflow choices

Approximate: floating point has nonuniform spacing; fixed point has a chosen scale. Rounding is part of each operation; tolerance is a domain rule, not a universal epsilon. Worked encoding · Cancellation figure · Fixed-point example

Store and exchange: address alone does not prove valid access; alignment, lifetime, ownership, and permissions are separate. A file needs an explicit schema and checked lengths. Address translation · Memory model · Parser safety lab · Hex-dump lab

Appendix.Content: Figure-linked pocket notes

Read one row, reconstruct its example, then follow the figure for the diagram and caption or explanation for the full teaching account. These four figures also live inside the continuous chapter, so the teaching text and recall desk share one reference. Each figure is a separate compact horizontal panel; the complete volume covers more than one printable page.

Cell.Content: Same bits, different weights: AD is unsigned 173 or signed −83. State width and encoding first.
Validate → clear → position → OR. AD→9D changes quality 2→1; outside-mask bits remain 8D.

Exact <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mn>250</mn> <mo>+</mo> <mn>20</mn> <mo>=</mo> <mn>270</mn> </math>: eight-bit wrap gives 14, saturation 255, rejection no value. Widen before evaluating.
Classify exponent/fraction first; normal binary32 has 24 precision bits, including its implicit leading one.

FMA rounds once; separate multiply/add rounds twice. For the stated example: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msup> <mn>2</mn> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>−</mo> <mn>46</mn> </mrow> </msup> </math> versus zero.
Cancellation can expose previous input errors even when subtraction of stored operands is exact. Tolerance needs units and a policy.
Fixed point chooses a constant step; floats choose a changing step; quantization chooses a finite codebook. Packing valid codes loses no further information.
Mapping changes page identity and preserves offset: 12345ABC→987ABC under the example 4-KiB mapping.
Bounds, alignment, lifetime, permitted access and mapping are separate obligations; old bytes prove none alone.
Specify schema → validate arithmetic/limits → decode. Integrity, authenticity and durability require their own contracts.

A bit has two logical states; octet means exactly eight bits; C++ byte has CHAR_BIT bits and sizeof(char)=1. A word is architecture-specific; a character can need multiple bytes. Historical byte sizes varied.
13→6 remainder1→3 remainder0→1 remainder1→0 remainder1; reverse gives1101. Horner states1→3→6→13. Bases16 and8 are powers2^4 and2^3.

Zero negates back to zero after the carry is discarded. The positive counterpart of −128 is128, outside the signed eight-bit range. BlockQuote.Content: [!answer]- Reveal 7–10 Half-adder sum=A XOR B, carry=A AND B. Full-adder carry is true when at least two of its three inputs are true. Ripple chains carry dependencies; prefix designs combine generate/propagate information. Carry answers an unsigned question; overflow a signed-range question; N observes a result sign bit; Z observes all-zero result. Borrow conventions vary: binary6502 SBC uses A−B−(1−C), with C=1 meaning no borrow.

Set multiplier bits select shifted partial products. Division shifts bits into a remainder, conditionally subtracts, and satisfies D=Qd+R with0≤R<d. Prove partial/intermediate ranges. Reject division by0 and same-type signed-min/−1.

Policies follow meaning: bounded samples may clamp, modular counters may wrap, sizes usually need checked arithmetic. Signed overflow remains undefined behavior; widening after the overflowing expression is too late. Saturation and capped updates are order-dependent.

An unsigned i≥0 never terminates a reverse loop. char signedness varies; exact-width aliases are optional, least/fast may be wider. Promotions/common-type conversions can turn a negative operand into a large unsigned value. Track all five stages, not only storage width.

Draw factored/distributed and FMA/unfused evaluation graphs. What do pairwise/compensated sums, wider accumulation and fixed order solve—and not solve?

BlockQuote.Content: [!answer]- Reveal 14–17 A reduced rational terminates iff its denominator is a power of two. Sterbenz’s nearby-float condition x/2≤y≤2x for nonnegative stored values can give exact subtraction under the stated gradual-underflow conditions. A small difference can still expose earlier input uncertainty; sensitivity scales with (|x|+|y|)/|x−y|.
Tiny and underflow are not synonyms. Flags also include inexact, overflow, divide-by-zero and invalid; classify the actual operation/environment.

Absolute error has units; relative error needs a nonzero reference. Forward error measures output discrepancy; backward error asks how perturbed inputs explain the output. Conditioning belongs to the problem, stability to the algorithm. Validate tolerances and non-finite inputs first; pairwise closeness need not be transitive.

FMA rounds ab+c once; unfused arithmetic rounds the product too. Reassociation/distribution move rounding points. Pairwise and compensated algorithms can reduce error but do not reconstruct lost input bits or guarantee identical cross-platform execution. Wider transient arithmetic does not preserve a repeatedly narrowed state. Determinism needs order, precision, compiler/environment and algorithm contracts; capped TSDF-style weighted updates can remain history-dependent mathematically.

Appendix.Content: 6 - Choose what information to keep
Repair representation choices · Fixed-point representation · Affine quantization and zero point
Appendix.Code:
fixed F=8: 1.5 → raw384 2.25 → raw576 multiply: 384×576 =221184 (scale256²) rescale: 221184/256=864 (scale256) decode: 864/256=3.375
offset INT4 codes: [1,5,8,11,15] low nibble first: [5|1] [11|8] [padding0|15] → 51 B8 0F quantization loses information; packing valid codes does not.

ListItem.Content: Choose F for a signed32-bit fixed domain ±10^6 with step≤0.001. Derive multiply/divide rescaling and nearest unclipped error.
Encode1.5 in FP16; compare FP16/BF16 near1 and at large magnitude. Why can truncating a NaN payload accidentally produce infinity?
Explain affine q/z/scale, outlier effects, group metadata, learned one-bit centroids, RMSE/MAE and normalized graphics/color-space distinctions.

BlockQuote.Content: [!answer]- Reveal 18–20 Require <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msup> <mn>2</mn> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>−</mo> <mi>F</mi> </mrow> </msup> <mo>≤</mo> <mn>0.001</mn> </math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msup> <mn>10</mn> <mn>6</mn> </msup> <msup> <mn>2</mn> <mi>F</mi> </msup> <mo>≤</mo> <msup> <mn>2</mn> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mn>31</mn> </mrow> </msup> <mo>−</mo> <mn>1</mn> </math>: F=10 or11. Multiply raw operands at scale S² then round AB/S; quotient rounds AS/B for B≠0. Prove intermediate capacity before calculating, check destination range, and define negative ties. Nearest unclipped error≤1/(2S); relative error can explode nearzero.

FP16 1.5→3E00; bias15, normal min2^-14, subnormal min2^-24. BF16 bias127, normal spacing above1 is2^-7 versus FP16’s2^-10. Dropping a nonzero discarded NaN fraction can leave all-one exponent and zero fraction: infinity. Classify first; canonicalization is a policy.

Affine reconstruction is scale×(q−z), with positive valid scale; nearest unclipped ideal error≤scale/2. A max-absolute outlier can erase small values. INT4 payload costs ceil(N/2)+4ceil(N/G) bytes with float32 scales, not four bits/value universally. At N=5,G=32 it costs7 bytes. One-bit labels can select learned means rather than±1. RMSE squares errors; MAE takes magnitudes; neither proves application quality. UNORM is not sRGB; quantized normals may need safe renormalization and still lose direction.

Appendix.Content: 7 - Placement, translation and lifetime are separate
Repair memory reasoning · Endianness · Alignment and padding · Page tables and MMU
Appendix.Code:
value 12345678 hex increasing byte addresses → little endian 78 56 34 12 big endian 12 34 56 78
ordinary ABI example: char / uint32 / char, alignments1/4/1 offset 0: [a][pad][pad][pad][b b b b][c][tail][tail][tail] member offsets0,4,8; size12; alignment4; array stride12
Appendix.Content: Example4-KiB pages: VA12345ABC → VPN12345, offsetABC → PFN987 → PA987ABC. A TLB miss is not automatically a fault; a fault is not automatically disk I/O or a crash.

ListItem.Content: Why does swapping bytes not reverse bits? Derive aligned offsets and tail padding; compare packing, reordering, AoS/SoA and CPU/GPU layouts.
Reconstruct the address translation. Distinguish process isolation, shared mappings, TLB/data-cache misses, faults, COW, virtual/physical contiguity and huge-page tradeoffs.
Separate stack/heap/static regions from storage duration and object lifetime. Explain fragmentation, dangling views, mapped files, const, W^X and ASLR.

BlockQuote.Content: [!answer]- Reveal 21–23 Endianness orders significance bytes, not bits within an octet. Align each member under stated ABI requirements; round total extent for aligned array stride. Reordering can reduce holes but change ABI. Packing may misalign; smaller is not automatically faster. AoS groups records, SoA fields; hot access patterns and backend layout contracts decide.

For page size P, VPN=floor(VA/P), offset=VA mod P; PA=PFN×P+offset. Context/permissions matter. TLB caches translations; data cache caches contents. COW copies a shared backing page when a permitted write needs a private copy. Consecutive virtual pages may use scattered frames. Larger pages increase simplified TLB reach entries×pageSize but reduce granularity/flexibility.

Automatic objects often use stack frames, but optimization/ABI can differ; heap allocation manages variable-lifetime blocks. Static duration can still need runtime initialization. Internal fragmentation is allocated slack; external fragmentation is separated holes. A span does not own/extend backing life. A mapped file needs bounds, permissions and access/lifetime validity. const does not force a read-only segment; W^X concerns mapping permissions; ASLR varies locations. Old bytes do not prove a live object.

Appendix.Content: 8 - External bytes need a complete agreement
Repair external bytes · Checked binary parsing · Integrity and authenticity

Cell.Content: Trust if attacker replaces digest too

ListItem.Content: State bit-cast preconditions; distinguish native ABI from external schema. Give safe multiplication and range checks before parsing.
Explain checksum blind spots, specified CRC parameters, hash collisions, authenticity and durability. Decode the mini-dump below.

BlockQuote.Content: [!answer]- Reveal 24–25 Bit-cast needs same size, trivially copyable types and valid initialized representations under the applicable rules. It is not numeric conversion, endian conversion or permission for arbitrary typed access.

Before unsigned a×b check a=0 or b≤MAX/a. Before reading n bytes at o in length L, check o≤L then n≤L−o. Check header≤length, exact payload length, size_t representability and practical resource limits before allocation.

Additive byte sums miss reorderings. A CRC needs polynomial, initial/final operations, reflection/order and covered range. CRC-32/ISO-HDLC check string123456789 gives CBF43926. Finite digests necessarily have collisions over unrestricted messages. A hostile replacement requires trusted digest/key policy; valid decoding, integrity, authenticity, publication and durability are different claims.

Appendix.Content: Mini-dump - Reconstruct before revealing
Assume explicit little-endian uint32 version, uint64 dimensions and IEEE binary32 payload. What are shape, header size, payload size and total size? What changes if payload byte80 becomes00?

BlockQuote.Content: [!answer]- Reveal the dump Shape2×3; header28 bytes; payload24 bytes; total52 bytes. First word3F800000 decodes1. Flipping80→00 gives3F000000, value0.5. Magic, dimensions and file length can remain plausible; structural validation alone misses this substitution. This is a teaching schema, not a freshly verified production format.

Appendix.Content: Final blank-board test

Without looking above, draw: interpretation fork → mask/extract/replace → adder with two flag questions → floating classifier → rounding graph → precision-choice table → byte/alignment strip → virtual translation → live-object state → safe reader.

For every diagram supply one numeric example, one invariant, one failure case and one assumption. Then explain the same stored bytes under two interpretations. A round trip is only one test: demand independent golden bytes and invalid-input checks too.

This map is navigation, not partwise lesson segmentation. Overlapping examples may revisit a concept; the listed coverage ranges assign each of1–100 exactly once.

Appendix.title: 02 - C++ - Objects, Ownership and Lifetime - Visual Recall
Appendix.source: Visual Recall/02 - C++ - Objects, Ownership and Lifetime - Visual Recall.md
Appendix.Content: C++: Objects, Ownership and Lifetime — Visual Recall

Scope: Companion to Continuous Notes/Computing Foundations - From Bits to C++ and Systems APIs. A compact teaching board, not a substitute for the worked chapter. Draw each model from memory; explain every arrow and state its preconditions.
One-page short notes

Cell.Content: Translation makes declarations visible, definitions executable, and linking joins program pieces.
Storage is the place; lifetime is the interval; identity is the occupant. Same address does not promise same object.
A pointer/reference/view grants access, not ownership. Validity depends on the referent, lifetime, mutation, and invalidation contract.
Construction creates; assignment replaces; move may transfer responsibility while source remains alive. Rule of Zero composes tested owners.
RAII binds cleanup to an owner lifetime; external users may require deferred release.
unique_ptr = one duty; shared_ptr = shared lifetime; weak_ptr = observe, then lock() to try. Shared ownership does not synchronize the pointee.
Exclusive ownership · Shared ownership · Weak observation
Allocation obtains bytes; construction starts an object; destruction ends its life; deallocation returns bytes. Placement construction does not allocate.

Appendix.Content: Board in one breath: source → object → borrow/owner → value transfer → RAII cleanup → safe external reclamation. At every arrow ask: who owns it, how long is it valid, and what ends use?
The notes above target a single landscape page when rendered at ordinary study-note scale. The diagrams and answer keys below remain the linked detail, not required reading for every review pass.
One story: from source text to responsibly released resource
Caption: Resource safety starts with the object model but ends only when the external-use contract permits release. A C++ destructor is not a GPU completion fence.
Four figure briefs
Use one row as a small revision card. Open its figure to see the caption and the surrounding worked example. The four cards supplement the existing notes and ownership boards.

Cell.Content: Declare to compile a call; supply the definition to link it. Header guards act inside one translation unit.
Why can a call compile yet fail at link time?
Reallocation can dangle a path; slot assignment can keep it live while changing the entity. Validate, then reacquire.
Can the same address still reach the wrong entity?
Construction creates a destination; a move operation may transfer duty. The source remains alive under its type’s contract.

Content.Link: CPP-03 · two live objects, one duty

Cell.Content: Why does std::move(x) alone release nothing?
RAII triggers the selected cleanup protocol; GPU completion governs when native release is safe.
Which owner keeps the device and pending release queue alive?

Appendix.Content: Answers: translation sees a usable declaration but linking still needs the definition; yes, semantic invalidation can preserve a live slot; std::move changes expression category and requires a consuming operation; the renderer must explicitly own the queue/device until all pending duties complete.
Ownership decision board
Caption: Pick semantics first, syntax second. A raw pointer usually borrows; it does not extend lifetime. Shared ownership is a relationship, not a generic safety upgrade.

Cell.Content: Caller must preserve lifetime and validity.
get() borrows; release() transfers the duty.
Control-block safety does not synchronize T.
Check the returned owner; expired() then use is a race.
Match the API, device/context, and allocator.

Appendix.Content: RAII: move cleanup from branches into scope
Caption: Partial construction is safe only for responsibilities already held by fully constructed members/guards. A naked raw handle between acquire and adoption is a leak window.
Storage, object and occupant are different states

Caption: Destroying an occupant does not necessarily free its storage. Same address does not mean same object. Correct alignment, size, construction, destruction and replacement rules still apply; std::launder does not construct or revive anything.
The four questions to ask at a resource boundary

Cell.Content: Arena slot large and aligned enough for Widget.
Who ends its lifetime/releases the handle?

Appendix.Content: Retrieval prompts

ListItem.Content: Why can a stack object own heap or GPU resources?
What does RAII automate, and what release timing must a GPU wrapper still know?
Why is shared_ptr copying not a synchronization policy for the pointed-to object?
Why does weak_ptr::lock() give a stronger test than checking expired() first?
How can a weak_ptr keep control-block storage allocated after object destruction?
What is the difference among new T, ::operator new, construct_at, destroy_at, and deallocation?
Why does unique_ptr<Derived> converting to unique_ptr<Base> require a correct base destruction contract?
What exactly does std::launder not do?

BlockQuote.Content: [!answer]- Compact key Scope-based owners run cleanup on normal exit and unwinding. External completion is a separate condition. Shared-pointer thread safety concerns ownership bookkeeping, not arbitrary pointee mutation. lock() atomically attempts to obtain a strong owner. Weak observers can keep the control block, but not the managed object’s lifetime, alive. A new-expression combines storage allocation and initialization; allocation functions alone only acquire storage; construction starts an object lifetime; destruction ends it; deallocation returns storage. Base deletion needs a valid virtual destructor or a deleter retaining the concrete type. launder can obtain a pointer to an already-live object only under its rules; it is no general repair tool.

Appendix.Content: Teach the full ownership story · Part coverage · Dependency Map
Added retrieval prompt

Borrow: T& or const T&. Consume: unique_ptr<T> by value. Retain shared lifetime: shared_ptr<T> by value. Borrow an existing shared handle: const shared_ptr<T>& only for that call. Use a matching deleter for non-memory resources. Rebuild the API lab.
Requests and replaceable backends — M011 retrieval experiment

A renderer’s command is one of several known shapes; the runtime backend is one implementation of a common contract. These are two different decisions, so redraw the story without looking: command value → active alternative → borrowed submit call → virtual override → checked visitor → logical result → correctly destroyed owner. Then explain what remains separate from the story: the GPU’s completion and native-resource release rules.

Cell.Content: What the answer must account for
Why can a union’s storage not be treated as several simultaneously live objects?
One active member and the correct lifetime transitions; a byte pattern is not a type tag.
How does a request prove its form?
variant discriminant, checked get_if / visit, and possible exceptional valueless state.
Why does a base reference call the derived implementation but a copied base value not preserve it?
Static type, dynamic type, subobjects, virtual dispatch and slicing.
Why is the interface destructor virtual?
Destruction through an owning base pointer must reach the derived destructor; external GPU use has its own completion rule.
What does a diamond with a virtual common base mean?
Two inheritance paths reach one most-derived common-base subobject, not a mandated memory offset.

static_cast follows a statically permitted conversion; dynamic_cast can runtime-check polymorphic relationships; reinterpret_cast does not create objects; const_cast does not legalize writing to genuinely const storage.
Why must two handles with the same slot but different generations compare unequal?
Identity includes the occupant generation; equality still does not prove current liveness.
Why does the overridden reserve body see 2 through a base view but 7 through a derived view?
Default argument from static type; virtual body from dynamic type.
Can <=> always produce a total order?
Integer ID fields can support strong ordering; NaN yields unordered floating comparisons and demands an explicit container key policy.
Can we claim this is the fastest dispatch architecture?
No: compare allocation, memory layout, branch behavior and optimizer effects on the same workload.

Appendix.Content: Blank-file reconstruction: Recreate Clear, DrawMesh, Upload, Request, Backend and CountingBackend with a single exclusive owner; verify command counts, derived destructor execution, failed runtime cast, slicing, shared virtual base, generation-aware equality, NaN’s unordered comparison, overload selection and static default-argument binding. Full code and the checked build command are in the M011 C++20 laboratory; complete derivations and failure explanations are in the continuous narrative. Do not infer Kairo or GPU execution from this standalone test.
One request, one transaction, callbacks that may outlive their caller — M012 reconstruction

Read the complete M012 narrative only after attempting this recall route. The important picture begins with an editor requesting a resource and ends with either a fully published asset or the original published store unchanged.

The first thing to reconstruct is why each arrow is necessary. The request’s count must be distinct from an asset index, because identical raw integer types do not carry the same domain meaning. The file must be decoded as checked bytes, not by assuming any pointer cast creates a live WireHeader. Preparation must be private because callbacks or render systems must never observe half-constructed state. Every acquired handle must have one owner before a throwing operation can intervene. Publication needs a precise boundary: an exception before the commit must not modify existing records under the stated guarantee; a callback that throws afterward is a different event requiring its own policy.

Cell.Content: Minimum evidence the reader must produce
Why is a raw std::size_t a dangerous API for bytes?
Show accidental unit mixing; write explicit ByteCount with explicit conversion back.
Can a function pointer close over a local variable?
No: a plain pointer carries a callable identity; extra state needs a context, whose lifetime is separately guaranteed.
Why is a member-function pointer not an ordinary callback address?
Explain the required instance and demonstrate object.*member invocation.
What does a functor or lambda actually store?
Draw state fields or references; contrast capture of an integer, pointer, view and this.
How do value and reference captures differ after mutation?
Predict snapshot 10 and live view 20; explain why a deferred reference may dangle.
What changes when a lambda is stored in std::function?
Type erasure, copyable target, possible storage cost, empty-call error; no guaranteed inline capacity.
Which exceptions cause cleanup, and what cannot be rolled back?
Distinguish stack unwinding/local RAII from preexisting external side effects.
What are the basic, strong and no-throw guarantees?
State valid-but-changed, unchanged observable state, and non-escaping exceptions; give each an example.
Why must the native resource move be non-throwing?
Trace vector growth, element relocation, and the relevant strong-guarantee conditions.
Why can’t input validation live only in assert?
NDEBUG can remove it; show typed invalid-input errors separately from programmer invariant failures.
What do bit_cast and trivially copyable prove?
A constrained representation-value operation, not a portable six-byte disk schema.
Why is a typed pointer into an arbitrary file unsafe?
Length, alignment, lifetime, alias rules, endian and padding are independent checks.
Reproduce counts: (0,0,0), (1,1,0), (1,2,1), (2,3,1), then 0 live at destruction.

Appendix.Content: Blank-file laboratory: Rebuild ByteCount; the fake device; the move-only Resource; the private AssetRecord; AssetStore::upload returning a typed result; function/member/functor callbacks; value/reference and owning-lifetime lambda captures; and a six-byte little-endian serializer. Compile under C++20 and warnings as errors, execute the deliberate failure after handle acquisition, then repeat under -DNDEBUG. The tested reference and exact commands are in the M012 lab and the source/evidence record. Do not classify this exercise as complete learner mastery until it can be reconstructed and explained independently.
One asset pipeline, many types — M013 retrieval

The preceding recall exercise ended with a safe, published asset. Now the editor wants the same preparation and publication guarantees for meshes, textures with different channel counts, and shader records. We must avoid duplicating stores without erasing type safety. Redraw this path from memory, then justify every boundary rather than reciting template vocabulary:

Imagine one Mesh containing three unsigned indices, one Texture<4> containing twelve texels, and one Texture<3> containing five texels. Explain why a trait gives 12, 48 and 15 source bytes, then derive why the checked batch accumulator returns 75. Show why a bound such as texel_count > max/Channels must be checked before multiplication. Finally explain why none of these counts establishes the actual GPU allocation size.

Now reconstruct the implementation without opening the reference. Start with template<class T> function-template deduction. Build template<class T, size_t Capacity> with fixed optional slots and explain why the non-type capacity changes the class specialization. Provide the full AssetTraits<Mesh> specialization and the partial AssetTraits<Texture<Channels>> specialization, then contrast class-template specialization with function overloading. Derive U& & → U&, U& && → U&, U&& & → U&, and U&& && → U&&. Use those results to show why meshes.emplace(input) makes a copy while meshes.emplace(std::move(input)) selects a move path; do not assume the moved-from vector must be empty.

The next reconstruction must connect a heterogeneous parameter pack to a checked fold. Show what happens for zero arguments and why a fold’s grouping is not itself a universal left-to-right side-effect guarantee. Then implement the earlier std::void_t SFINAE detection pattern and a clearer Uploadable concept with compound requirements. State exactly what a requires expression checks and what it does not execute. Constrain emplace with std::constructible_from and show why the overload route(const T&) selects the constrained path for supported assets and the generic fallback for UnknownAsset.

Finally prove publication. If the published count is c, slots [0,c) are live and slots [c,Capacity) are empty. When the constructor throws in slot c, the count is not incremented. Reconstruct the deliberately failed CheckedShader(-1) attempt and show why the previously published version 3 remains valid and version 4 can use the next slot. Explain what would break if we supported deletion, stored raw references after the depot’s lifetime, invoked the API concurrently or replaced the CPU-only record with an asynchronously used GPU buffer without retirement bookkeeping.

Evidence and full explanation: the M013 narrative, the tested C++20 laboratory and the 16-part coverage map. The test checks representative semantics, not the learner’s independent ability to reconstruct these decisions or current Kairo implementation details.
The tile planner makes a choice — M014 reconstruction
This recall path belongs after the full M014 narrative and the C++20 lab. Its purpose is to rebuild the decision chain from memory, not to duplicate an encyclopedia of template keywords.

Picture one 8×2 RGBA texture tile, a budget of 64 bytes, a 64-byte CPU buffer, and a counting recorder. Before the renderer tries to use it, the planning layer must establish what is known from the type and what still depends on the incoming data. Draw this path, then explain each transition and its failure condition:

A correct reconstruction should derive (8\times2\times4=64) bytes from the uncompressed source representation, then explain why (8\times3\times4=96) fails the budget. It should show why a 4×4 RGBA request with no buffer fails only when the verification tag demands a real payload. The metadata-only 4×4 RGB path may report 48 planned bytes, but it has not proved any upload complete. Show how overflow is rejected by checking (x > \mathrm{max}/y) before multiplication, not by multiplying and inspecting the wrapped result.

Rebuild PixelTraits<Format> using std::integral_constant and distinguish the fact that a type is empty from an assertion that it costs zero bytes in every containing object. Demonstrate an if constexpr RGBA branch and contrast it with a normal runtime if. Write a constexpr function that accepts either compile-time or runtime arguments; then change the problem so that a consteval function demands a valid compile-time tile definition. Explain why constinit permits a mutable, single-threaded diagnostic counter but does not make it const or atomic.

Derive the four-bit Morton lookup without memorizing its answer. Spread (x=3) to binary 00000101 and (y=5) to 00010001. Shift the second pattern and OR the results to recover decimal 39. Construct the sixteen-entry table during constant evaluation. Then explain when a small lookup table might lose to shift/mask arithmetic because memory traffic and locality matter.

From that setup, implement a stateless policy and a stateful budget policy with the same validate operation. Use TilePlanner<Format,Policy,Recorder> to compose the behavior without a runtime backend switch. Show why RecorderBase<Derived> may call Derived::record_impl only when it is genuinely part of an appropriately derived object; compare this static dispatch with a runtime-selected std::function target. Construct VerifyPayloadTag and MetadataOnlyTag and explain exactly how overload resolution chooses a validation path from the caller’s tag type. Finally compare normal empty-policy membership, private empty-base inheritance, and [[no_unique_address]] membership. On the tested Linux compilers their respective sizes were 16, 8 and 8 bytes; the rule is a permitted optimization, not a universal numeric contract, and compilers can treat the attribute differently.

A complete blank-screen test recreates the accepted 64-byte RGBA plan, rejected 96-byte budget attempt, rejected empty verified payload, accepted 48-byte metadata-only RGB plan, and rejected overflowing extent. The recorder receives exactly two plans in the demonstrated sequence; failed requests do not reach it. Then state why this is not a real GPU resource, performance benchmark, atomic transaction for arbitrary throwing recorders, or proof of thread safety. The evidence ledger preserves the exact compiled commands and original fourteen-part mapping: M014 traceability · verification record.
A growing asset store must preserve its promises — M015 retrieval

A previously working fixed-capacity asset depot now grows, removes assets, accepts work in different scheduling orders, and lets the editor find items by name. Do not use the following as a replacement for the derivations in the complete M015 chapter. Start with this diagram and explain why its arrows and lifetime boundaries exist:

First distinguish size from capacity, and prove why reserve(2) creates zero live elements whereas resize(5) creates five. With a geometric capacity sequence 1,g,g²,..., derive the sum of relocation work and explain why an individual append can still have linear latency while amortized append cost remains constant. State the operations that invalidate vector pointers and the difference between an append with spare capacity, one requiring reallocation, a middle erase and reserve that does or does not change capacity. A pointer does not move itself when the vector relocates.

Then reconstruct the identity protocol. Slot zero holds generation one; a handle {0,1} reaches it. After erase, that occupant is destroyed, its generation advances, and a new asset occupies slot zero at generation two. Draw why {0,1} no longer resolves. Explain what happens if generation wraps, if a raw Asset* or span was retained across reallocation, or if the renderer still has an asynchronous GPU read in flight. Distinguish a CPU identity check from the device-completion requirement.

Show the two injected publication failures: one before any slot change, another after a new slot has been populated but before the name index becomes discoverable. Prove why the rollback resets the candidate and removes a newly appended unpublished slot; explain why the test’s successful outcome is not an unrestricted claim about arbitrary throwing user callbacks or all allocator behaviors.

Now change the workload. A fixed-size channel array needs std::array, not vector growth. A front/back event stream makes deque attractive, but its iterator stability differs from that of its existing element references. A list can transfer a node with splice while keeping an iterator to an unaffected node; a forward_list needs the predecessor for erase_after. Explain what those guarantees cost in nodes, pointer chasing and cache locality compared with a contiguous vector scan.

Next give two lookup problems. For ordered traversal and range queries, consider std::map / std::set, with logarithmic comparison-based behavior. For name-to-handle lookup or membership, use std::unordered_map / std::unordered_set and explain expected versus worst-case complexity. Write a hash that returns zero for every string; twenty-four distinct names now collide in the same bucket without becoming equal. Derive load_factor = size/bucket_count, explain what max_load_factor(0.5) and reserve(96) request, and state why rehash invalidates unordered iterators but does not generally invalidate references to surviving elements.

Finally build the scheduling choices from user needs: a FIFO queue, LIFO stack, and a priority_queue whose comparator orders priority 3 before priority 1 and earlier sequence numbers before later ones within equal priority. Explain why priority_queue does not promise tie stability unless the comparator defines it.

Finish by distinguishing borrow from ownership. A span<const uint8_t> carries a range while its byte vector remains alive and stable; it does not own the bytes. A string_view may point into only the middle of a stored string and need not be NUL-terminated at its end. Copy "stone" into std::string before destroying or modifying the source. Describe why the local observed short-string capacity of 15 cannot be advertised as a portable SSO specification.

Actual reconstruction witness: M015 C++20 lab, compiled and run with GCC sanitizers, Clang, and a GCC release-style build. A learner should be able to recreate the sequence of checks without the reference and explain every failure. Original 20-part mapping · Exact test and provenance ledger. Do not claim personal mastery or real Kairo/GPU verification merely because this standalone model passes.
Query the registry without confusing identity and a snapshot — M016 reconstruction

The previous M015 exercise produced a generation-checked asset registry. The new problem is to report on assets without changing their live ownership and without assuming that a handle stays current forever. Read the full M016 narrative before testing recall; the questions below should be reconstructed as one processing story, not as twenty memorized API names.

Starting with the five records brick.mesh (48 bytes, priority 2), sky.tex (64, priority 3), ui.tex (16, priority 3), terrain.mesh (128, priority 1) and rock.mesh (48, priority 2), answer each part in coherent explanations:

ListItem.Content: Describe each result’s meaning. Why does optional<AssetHandle> mean “possibly absent” but fail to distinguish an empty query from a missing name? Build ExpectedLike<AssetHandle,LookupError> as a C++20 model. Explain exactly what its has_value() contract requires before value() is accessed and why it is not a full replacement for C++23 std::expected. Then distinguish that result from an Inspect/Upload/Evict variant and from a diagnostic any. Predict a wrong any_cast.

Rebuild the report shape. Group count and error count in a pair and three report fields in a tuple. Show that auto [a,b] = pair copies this pair, while auto& [a,b] = pair aliases it. Explain why a named struct can be clearer at a long-lived public API boundary and why a borrowed structured binding needs an owner that outlives it.

Prove the traversal capabilities before selecting the algorithm. Classify istream_iterator<int>, forward_list<int>::iterator, list<int>::iterator, deque<int>::iterator and vector<int>::iterator according to input, forward, bidirectional, random-access and contiguous iterator concepts. Why can std::sort operate on the vector’s random-access iterators but not directly on list iterators? Why may binary search over forward iterators have logarithmic comparison count but linear iterator advances?

Choose ordering by what the editor needs. Write a comparator that first orders byte counts, then asset names so equal byte counts have deterministic tie breaking. Explain why std::sort need not preserve the order of comparator-equivalent records and why common introsort-like implementations are not mandated by the C++ standard. For descending priorities, write stable_sort and predict the relative order of sky.tex vs ui.tex and brick.mesh vs rock.mesh. State the strict-weak-ordering requirements the comparator must satisfy.

Partition only when the task is binary membership. Use std::partition to put mesh records before non-mesh records; verify both halves and use partition_point on the resulting already-partitioned range. Explain why the two groups are not automatically sorted and why partitioning does not promise to retain original relative order. Say when stable_partition would be appropriate.

Derive the binary-search boundaries. Once the byte-count ordering is [16,48,48,64,128], prove that lower_bound(48) returns index 1 and upper_bound(48) returns index 3. Explain why equal_range gives [1,3) and why lower_bound(50) points to index 3 despite having no match. Supply comparator overloads in both element/value and value/element orders. Describe why using a priority-sorted sequence here would violate the precondition.

Compare one-off scanning with a maintained index. Use std::find to look for sky.tex in an unsorted name snapshot. Explain when this simple linear scan is preferable to building a fresh hash index, and when repeated lookups should instead use the registry’s already maintained name index.

Transform and reduce with the correct numeric meaning. Derive [48,64,16,128,48] using std::transform and an output back inserter, then calculate 304 using an explicit std::size_t{0} initial accumulator. Write the ordered std::accumulate fold and explain why std::reduce may regroup operations, even if a particular run happens to use one thread. Use (10{20},1,-10{20},3) to derive both 3 and 4 from different floating-point groupings. State separate overflow, accuracy and deterministic-reproducibility policies.

Erase at the correct ownership boundary. Starting with {1,2,3,4,5,6}, use remove_if to keep odd IDs but demonstrate that the vector still reports size six until erase destroys the suffix. Then use C++20 std::erase_if to remove the two texture records from an owned report snapshot, leaving three rows. Explain why the live asset registry has not evicted those assets and what additional generation validation, index cleanup and GPU retirement a real eviction would require.

Appendix.Content: Blank-file witness: reconstruct the program in asset_query_algorithm_lab.cpp with active failure checks, compile under C++20 with warnings as errors, then rerun with -DNDEBUG and sanitizers. The reference was actually run with GCC 14.2 ASan/UBSan, Clang 17 and GCC release flags. Reconstruct the expected values before running it; a passing executable is not a substitute for understanding the data/iterator/lifetime contracts.

Audit: the original 20-part mapping and the source and verification ledger. The registry’s live concurrency, the separately named Kairo implementations and the learner’s independent reconstruction remain unverified here.
From borrowed reports to module boundaries — M017 reconstruction

The Phase 6 report used an owned snapshot so that sorting and erasing metadata did not mutate live engine state. The next problem is making that report composable without accidentally copying intermediates, choosing where its scratch allocations live, and sharing its API with separately compiled consumers. The full explanation is the M017 continuous chapter. Reconstruct the mechanism below from the problem, not by reciting the names of its twenty C++ features.

First reconstruct what the loop means. Draw the hidden range variable, begin iterator, end sentinel and increment/compare/dereference sequence behind a range-for. Define a cursor that holds a borrowed pointer to the snapshot vector and a numeric index, and makes operator++ skip retired slots. State the invariants for normal, end and default-created iterators; do not dereference the end. Explain why your cursor models std::forward_iterator and why it does not model random access or contiguity. With one 512-byte retired texture and live byte counts 48,64,16,128,48, predict exactly five visits and total 304.

Next reconstruct laziness and lifetime. Compose views::all(rows) | views::filter(...) | views::transform(...) to obtain four names from those live rows with at least 48 bytes. Explain why merely forming the pipeline does not copy all four names into a vector and why iterating it later can call the predicate again. Predict why it is wrong to rely on a precise predicate invocation count for arbitrary repeat traversals. Compare views::all(lvalue_vector) with views::all(rvalue_vector) and explain how a ref_view can satisfy borrowed_range without keeping the vector itself alive. Conversely, explain why an owning view storing the vector need not qualify as a borrowed range when the view’s own destruction destroys the data.

Use a projection only when the search needs one property. Without constructing a separate names vector, use std::ranges::find(rows, "sky.tex", &Row::name) and predict the record’s byte count. Sort an owned copy by &Row::bytes and state why the 512-byte retired row will still appear at the end unless you filtered it first. Discuss why the source vector’s contiguity does not make a filter view a writable random-access container. Compare AtLeastBytes{48} against an equivalent threshold-capturing lambda, giving a plan for benchmarking actual instruction and allocation costs instead of asserting one form is always faster.

Now choose who owns allocation. Build a typed TrackingAllocator<T> that shares statistics across copies and rebindings, uses proper alignment and pairs successful storage acquisitions with deallocation. Explain why allocation is not the same as constructing a T object, and why allocator equality/propagation matter when a container moves or swaps. Then replace the compile-time allocator type with a std::pmr::vector and a std::pmr::unordered_map, both pointing to a counting memory_resource. Explain how unordered buckets/nodes and nested PMR strings may require allocator propagation, and why the resource must outlive both containers.

Derive the arena lifetime, not just its common-case speed. Give a 128-byte aligned scratch buffer to a monotonic resource, then allocate 2,048 64-bit values. Explain why the initial buffer cannot contain the entire request; the resource must obtain upstream blocks. Predict why destroying the vector does not immediately free those blocks and why destroying/releasing the arena later can. Repeat with a 64-byte buffer and null_memory_resource upstream and predict std::bad_alloc. State the difference between a frame scratch lifetime and staging memory still held by an asynchronous GPU operation; neither the presence of PMR nor a move-only vector resolves the missing completion fence.

Finally build an actual module graph. In separate files, put a :rules partition containing an exported 1,024-byte preview budget, a primary export module allmight.asset_query interface that re-exports that partition, and a module allmight.asset_query; implementation unit defining make_preview. Compile in dependency order. Write two separate importing translation units that use an exported inline function, link them with the implementation, and explain which declarations are exported and why that is distinct from C++ namespace naming or C language linkage. Build asset_query_interop.hpp as a header unit before using import "asset_query_interop.hpp";; compare this with an ordinary #include and explain macro/toolchain implications. Then expose a small versioned C header declaring int allmight_asset_approved_v1(uint64_t); build a C11 consumer using gcc and link it with the C++ wrapper and module objects. Explain exactly what this test establishes about the chosen GCC14 toolchain, and why it does not certify ABI stability across unrelated compilers or plugin versions.

The real sources are the tested C++20 CPU lab and the executable module graph script. The local runtime lab passed GCC14 ASan/UBSan, Clang17 and GCC14 release; the module graph passed GCC14’s ordered module/header-unit build with three linked consumers. The original twenty-title coverage map and verification ledger distinguish that evidence from external Kairo audits and unmeasured performance. Personal mastery is earned only after independent explanation, tests and failure-case reconstruction; the authored lesson and one passing lab cannot grant it automatically.
Preserve an asset while the engine changes — M018 reconstruction

The editor selected a teapot before the asset service started deleting, reallocating and reusing storage. The renderer has independently compiled clients, several classes of resource handles and mathematical values from different coordinate frames. Reconstruct the API by starting with the event, not with a memorized list of PIMPL, concepts and expression templates. The complete reasoning lives in the M018 continuous chapter. The actually compiled service and its test program are in the test laboratory and the multi-TU build.

Reconstruction 1 — identity, storage, and ABI. A mesh occupies slot zero in catalog A at generation one, and the client retains a handle. The vector reallocates, the mesh is erased, and a second mesh occupies the same slot. Explain precisely why a pointer might become invalid on reallocation, why a stale index could identify the wrong mesh, why a generation alone does not distinguish two separate catalogs, and why a MeshTag prevents a texture handle being silently passed to a mesh operation. The correct handle is a value containing a type-level kind and catalog/slot/generation runtime identity. A valid lookup compares all required fields and checks that the slot still holds a live value. After erase, the old generation must fail even when the slot is reused. The returned optional MeshInfo is a copy, so keeping it after erase cannot dangle, although its description is now stale. Confirm with the executable’s delete/reuse and cross-catalog tests.

Reconstruction 2 — the public header is not the implementation. Write a declaration of an asset service that contains only an incomplete Impl and a unique pointer to that implementation. Explain why the destructor and move assignment must be defined where Impl is complete. Identify which client recompilations PIMPL can avoid and which ABI questions remain. Then identify the actual costs: one implementation allocation in the constructed design, pointer indirection and possible out-of-line call overhead. PIMPL is appropriate for a relatively cold service boundary, not automatically for every inner-loop vector, task or splat. Name the deep-const hazard: an owning pointer stored in a const public object does not in itself make the pointee immutable.

Reconstruction 3 — three floats are not automatically the same mathematical value. Demonstrate why a world-space displacement and a camera-space displacement must be different C++ types, while also explaining the actual linear or affine transform that converts between them. Show why a point requires translation but a direction does not, why a normal may require inverse-transpose transformation, and why a quantity in meters cannot simply be added to a quantity in seconds. The phantom marker constrains type checking without adding a stored tag field; the underlying numeric representation does not perform a coordinate transform. Compare a fixed-size Vector<float,3,WorldSpace> with a runtime span requiring an explicit extent check. Explain why the supplied RealScalar concept intentionally rejects integers and user-defined autodiff scalars.

Reconstruction 4 — materialization is both a performance and a lifetime decision. Trace eager a+b+c. Then trace a SumExpr storing references and evaluating operator[](i) on demand. Construct the dangerous saved outer expression that refers to a destroyed temporary inner node, and explain why its later evaluation is undefined behavior. Rewrite the example so the inner expression outlives evaluation. Explain how aliasing, SIMD, floating-point reassociation and compiler optimization affect the claim that lazy evaluation must be faster. The tested vectors produce (12,15,18); matching output is necessary but cannot alone establish absence of hidden allocations or the safety of every expression tree.

Reconstruction 5 — own storage or embed links? Compare an intrusive task stack, where the task contains its next pointer and must outlive its membership, against a forward_list owning its elements. Show what breaks when a linked Task is destroyed, moved or inserted twice. The tested stack rejects duplicate membership and unlinks on pop. That is not a safe general-purpose ownership scheme for arbitrary user destruction. Predict how allocation, locality and mutation patterns could make either representation preferable.

Reconstruction 6 — interrogate the machine rather than assuming zero cost. Compile the assembly probe with optimized GCC and Clang. Find the named externally visible function. Decide whether the templated addition was inlined and whether there are calls or unnecessary transfers on that compiler/target. Explain why a different ISA, link-time optimization, compiler flags or fast-math setting can produce different machine code and numerical results. State a fair baseline and define actual comparable workloads before declaring one catalog representation faster. A successful presence check for an assembly symbol is a build witness, not a timing benchmark.

Final synthesis. Draw the lifetime sequence from editor selection to catalog erase and eventual GPU retirement. Distinguish three independently necessary guarantees: the CPU logical handle remains validated, the public C++ representation remains insulated as promised, and a GPU resource stays alive while submitted work may still read it. The M018 sample tests the first two in a limited CPU setting and does not implement the third. Compile under release -DNDEBUG and explain why the test program uses throwing checks instead of ordinary asserts. Then independently implement an asset handle with one additional version or session policy, state its invariants and design negative tests that could falsify those invariants.

Mastery criterion: without looking up the code, reconstruct the public header, its out-of-line implementation, the validation predicate, an exception-safe reuse transition, a typed fixed/dynamic math interface, a lifetime-safe lazy expression evaluation, and a falsifiable compiler-cost experiment. Reading the answers is not evidence of independent reconstruction.
Make the rejected operation part of the lesson

Read the figure: type checks decide whether the operation has the right meaning; lifetime checks decide whether its borrowed objects still exist. Both must hold. A successful type check does not extend an operand’s lifetime.

Cell.Content: Two vector types differ; is mixing prevented?
Test the actual eager, lazy and materialization operations. Every path needs the same scalar/space/extent restrictions.
[[Continuous Notes/Computing Foundations - From Bits to C++ and Systems APIs#The delayed path must preserve the same mathematical contract
Does a named inner expression become constexpr?
Naming extends this node’s usable lifetime; it does not make references to automatic locals valid in that constexpr initializer. The saved lab uses const.
[[Continuous Notes/Computing Foundations - From Bits to C++ and Systems APIs#Expression templates: delaying evaluation can remove an intermediate and create a lifetime bug
Why forbid copying this intrusive stack?
Two head pointers can share hooks; popping one clears membership while the other still points at that node.
[[Continuous Notes/Computing Foundations - From Bits to C++ and Systems APIs#Intrusive storage exposes a different ownership contract
Caller-owned linked tasks must survive at stable addresses; the destructor clears hooks without deleting tasks.

Appendix.Content: Reconstruct: predict the sequence A.push(task), copy A to B, B.pop(), A.push(task). Explain the duplicate-pop failure in the unchecked design and why the current stack rejects copying before execution. Then draw task/stack destruction order and show a valid unlink-and-reuse sequence.

No. Keep its referenced generation and allocation alive through pending uses.
[[Continuous Notes/Game Engine - From First Frame to Living Worlds#Let a renderer evolve without losing resource ownership
Workgroups cooperate with shared storage and barriers; subgroups expose a smaller execution collective. Width is not universally 32.

Appendix.Content: Explain the two barriers in tiled matrix multiplication: one protects complete tile loading; one protects reuse after every consumer finishes. Explain why a later dispatch still needs the API’s execution and memory dependency, rather than assuming a dispatch boundary flushes everything.
API resource stages

A name, initialized API object, allocated storage, initialized bytes and completed use are different states. glCreateBuffers establishes the object; a storage command establishes capacity; null initial data does not mean zero-filled bytes. Open the worked API distinction. A nonzero integer alone proves neither a safe draw range nor safe retirement.
Temporary objects — retrieve the lifetime boundary

Cell.Content: Does every reference extend a temporary’s lifetime?
No. The binding context matters; a borrowed view never owns its source.

Topic route
Six figures

F09-1. Tangent prediction and local residual. At h=0.2, the exact residual for the shown exponential is about 0.03529 and the quadratic leading term about 0.03297; this illustrates local-order behavior.
F09-2. Accumulated area and the derivative that recovers the integrand. For A(x)=x cubed/3 at x=1.8, A=1.944 and A prime=3.24=x squared.

F09-3. Quadrature error as sample intervals increase. For exp(x) on [0,1] at N=16, left-rule error is about 0.053137, trapezoid error 5.593e-4, and Simpson error 1.456e-7; Simpson uses an even interval count.

F09-4. Energy behavior for the stated harmonic-oscillator step size. At h=0.1 for 80 periods, explicit Euler energy reaches about 2.62e21, semi-implicit Euler stays in [0.47619,0.526316], and RK4 ends near 0.499965. This is the plotted setup, not a universal ranking.
F09-5. Full Newton step versus Armijo backtracking for the plotted log-cosh example. At x=3, the full step is about -100.8566; backtracking first accepts alpha=0.03125 in this setup.

F09-6. Central-difference truncation and roundoff for sin(x) at x=0.7. The analytic derivative is cos(0.7), about 0.7648422; the best sampled step has error about 8.94e-13. Guide curves are qualitative.

Appendix.title: 10 - Probability and Monte Carlo - Visual Recall
Appendix.source: Visual Recall/10 - Probability and Monte Carlo - Visual Recall.md
Appendix.Content: Probability and uncertainty — visual recall
Shortest route: start with a model of outcomes, then ask what distribution the computer actually sampled, how it weighted each sample, and what evidence supports the estimate.
Reconstruct the chain

(Ω, F, P) describes outcomes, measurable events, and their probabilities. A random variable maps outcomes into numbers; a random vector preserves their joint behavior. A PMF assigns point mass to discrete values; a PDF gives density relative to a stated measure; a CDF accumulates probability and exists even when no PDF does.

Conditioning changes the information available. Independence means joint probability factors, not merely that events are disjoint. Bayes reverses the conditioning direction by multiplying likelihood by prior and normalizing over alternatives.

Expectation is a probability-weighted center. Variance is mean squared spread. Covariance records coupled variation; correlation divides it by both standard deviations but only captures linear association. For a vector, covariance is symmetric PSD because aᵀΣa = Var(aᵀX) ≥ 0.

Bernoulli describes one binary outcome; binomial counts IID Bernoulli successes. Uniform has constant density in its declared measure. Gaussian describes a quadratic-distance bell shape. Exponential waiting times are memoryless; Poisson counts belong to the corresponding constant-rate process. A multivariate Gaussian’s covariance sets ellipse/ellipsoid orientation and scale.
The computational chain is:
Appendix.Code: seed/state or keyed input → finite random bits → sample transform → actual PDF and measure → weighted contribution f(X)/p(X) → average → uncertainty/error report
Appendix.Content: Every arrow carries assumptions. A wrong PDF or measure can bias the result. A low-variance estimator can still be biased. Correlated observations change the standard error. Confidence intervals do not repair a wrong expectation.
Formula prompts

Cell.Content: P(A|B)=P(A∩B)/P(B); chain rule multiplies successive conditional probabilities.
E[AX+b]=Aμ+b; Cov(AX+b)=AΣAᵀ; local nonlinear approximation uses JΣJᵀ.
I=∫f dx=Eₚ[f(X)/p(X)]; average contributions and divide by the actual sampling density.
IID finite-variance mean has Var(Ȳ)=σ²/N, SE=σ/√N; four times samples halves SE.
Unbiased sample variance uses M₂/(n−1); update with δ=x−μ, μ←μ+δ/n, M₂←M₂+δ(x−μ).
MSE squares; RMSE returns original units; MAE uses absolute error; relative metrics fail or need policy near zero.

Supplied concise recall summary

The mathematical core is the probability space <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi mathvariant="normal">Ω</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mi data-mjx-variant="-tex-calligraphic" mathvariant="script">F</mi> </mrow> <mo>,</mo> <mi>P</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math>, random variables defined on that space, and probability laws for their values.

Conditional probability changes the reference information. Independence is a factorization property. PMFs assign masses to discrete values, while PDFs assign density relative to a measure. CDFs accumulate probability and exist for every real-valued random variable.

Expected value describes the weighted centre. Variance describes squared spread. Covariance describes coupled spread. Correlation standardizes covariance but does not measure every form of dependence.

Bernoulli models one binary trial. Binomial models the count of successes in independent identically distributed Bernoulli trials. Uniform models constant density over a region. Gaussian models a particular smooth bell-shaped distribution. Exponential models memoryless waiting times. Poisson models event counts under its defining assumptions.

A multivariate Gaussian combines mean, covariance, and correlations into a joint distribution. Positive-definite covariance permits a full-dimensional nonsingular Gaussian density. Singular PSD covariance describes a distribution confined to a lower-dimensional affine subspace.

Key engineering invariants: all probabilities are valid and normalized; PDF units match the integration measure; covariance is symmetric PSD; Gaussian density evaluation avoids unnecessary inversion; nonfinite inputs and singular cases are explicit; sampling tests use statistical tolerances rather than exact equality.

Appendix.Content: Cholesky whitening
From Sigma=LL transpose and x=mu+Lz, solve z=inverse(L)(x-mu); then Mahalanobis squared distance is z transpose z. A singular covariance is supported on a lower-dimensional affine subspace.
Rebuild the numerical witness.
Six figures

F10-1. Ordered outcomes and the exact two-dice sum PMF. The supplied lesson already derives this example; the figure is a visual check of the 36 ordered pairs. PMF numerators sum to 36 and P(S=7)=1/6.
F10-2. Zero covariance need not mean independence. For standard normal X, Cov(X,X squared)=0 by symmetry although X and X squared are dependent. Sample covariance is a finite-run witness.

F10-3. Uniform area sampling requires a square-root radial transform. The theoretical mean radius is 2/3 for uniform area in the unit disk and 1/2 for uniform radius; plotted sample means are finite-run illustrations.
F10-4. Monte Carlo random error and a fixed bias floor. For the stated integral, unbiased RMSE falls with sample count while the biased estimator retains its offset.

F10-5. A matched importance proposal can make contributions constant. For the stated nonnegative integrand and support, the matched proposal gives constant contributions; uniform-proposal variance is 4/45. This does not generalize to arbitrary signed integrands.

F10-6. A full-period toy LCG can still have a simple low-bit pattern. For m=16, a=5, c=1, all 16 states are visited but the least-significant bit alternates. Full period does not imply good multidimensional quality. The keyed-input sketch indicates deterministic indexing only: a different key does not establish statistical independence or collision freedom.

Appendix.Content: Checks before trusting a result

ListItem.Content: State arithmetic assumptions (normal/subnormal, overflow, rounding mode) and data scale.
Check both residual/backward error and conditioning before interpreting forward accuracy.
Verify interpolation range, boundary policy, and parameter units.
Separate discretization, truncation, roundoff, and sampling error.
Fix a reproducible reduction tree or record seed, sample design, and uncertainty.
Test exact identities, invariants, edge cases, convergence order, and randomized strata.

Appendix.Content: Continue in the volume
Numerical reliability figures and their explanations

ListItem.Content: N10-7 · Summation is an algorithm, not just a plus sign — Exact real sum is 10000. The three-term counterexample shows why Kahan is not an exact-arithmetic guarantee. Strict IEEE-style evaluation is assumed; reassociation can invalidate compensation.

N10-8 · More polynomial degree does not guarantee a better picture — Both interpolants match every node. Their behaviour between nodes differs. Chebyshev extrema reduce this example’s endpoint oscillation; this comparison is not a universal interpolation error bound.

N10-9 · Bézier and Hermite can tell the same curve story — Use Hermite tangents 3(P1−P0) and 3(P3−P2) for this cubic Bézier curve. The control polygon bounds the curve through nonnegative weights summing to one; inner control points need not lie on the curve.

N10-10 · A root solver needs both progress and a safety argument — The error comparison uses cos(x)−x with specified starting values. Bisection has a shrinking bracket; Newton and secant need additional hypotheses. The plotting floor is explicitly shown rather than interpreted as continuing convergence.

N10-11 · Arbitrary sample counts need full-domain support — Left: choosing the first five of nine equal cells and averaging equally gives E[y] = 0.3, while the uniform-square value is 0.5. Right: one point per marginal bin is a midpoint illustration; randomized LHS jitters and permutes appropriately, and is not full multidimensional stratification.

N10-12 · Algebraically equal formulas can have unequal numerical error — The reference uses 90-digit Decimal arithmetic and compares binary64 formulas for b from 100 to 10¹⁶. This bounded example illustrates cancellation, not a complete robust quadratic solver.

The scene/run pairing; finite observations; and a test statistic whose result does not change with measurement units.
