Appendix.Content:
This companion appears in Volume 2, The Visual Computing Bible — Volume II: Computational Geometry, Vision, Reconstruction and XR: Light spectra and radiometry — Light spectra and radiometry Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: XR01 · Latest development: University courses Definition and mechanism Light models distinguish wave propagation, photon energy and geometrical rays. Radiometry describes physical flux/radiance/irradiance; photometry adds standardized visual weighting. RGB requires an interpretation and cannot identify a unique spectrum. Prerequisites No formal graph prerequisite. Begin with the stated units and model; this is an independent-series foundation. Used by
Reflectance and rendering equation Retinal encoding and receptive fields Optical focus and binocular conflict Color encoding and linear-light operations Probability density and change of measure Surface orientation from image brightness
Recall and next depth Explain W, W/m², W/(m²·sr), lux and nits. Pending: spectral/colorimetric calibration. Written coverage is not a claim of learner mastery or accepted numbered-curriculum progress. Source and navigation Expanded teaching explanation · Independent coverage · Dependency Map University course development Radiometry distinguishes total radiant flux <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi> </math> in watts, irradiance <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>E</mi> </math> in watts per square metre, radiant intensity <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>I</mi> </math> in watts per steradian, and radiance <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>L</mi> </math> in watts per square metre per steradian measured with projected source area. A spectrum distributes the energy over wavelength; a three-channel RGB value is a measurement in a chosen color system and does not uniquely identify that spectrum. Solid angle measures directional extent rather than physical area. Consequently an area-light sample requires the projected-area and inverse-square Jacobian when expressed as a directional sample. Free-space radiance remains constant along an unobstructed ray, while irradiance from a point-like source changes with geometry. Photometry instead applies standardized visual weighting: luminous flux uses lumens, illuminance lux, and luminous intensity candela. These distinctions prevent treating brightness, exposure, flux and radiance as interchangeable scalar labels. Light measurement and radiometry. Open Light spectra and radiometry in Volume 2

Appendix.Content: This companion appears in Volume 2, The Foundations Bible — Volume II: Numerical Methods, Probability, Geometry and Camera Systems: Matrix factorization choices — Matrix factorization choices Choose a solver from the matrix promises and task: pivoted LU for general square systems, Cholesky for SPD systems, QR for full-rank least squares, SVD or rank-revealing methods when weak directions matter, and iterative methods for suitable large sparse workloads. Appendix.Content:
This companion appears in Volume 2, The Foundations Bible — Volume II: Numerical Methods, Probability, Geometry and Camera Systems: Cross products and oriented area — Cross products and oriented area Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: Phase6 · Latest development: Phase6 Definition and mechanism In oriented Euclidean three-dimensional space, the cross product is a perpendicular area vector. Its magnitude is parallelogram area; swapping inputs reverses its orientation. Ordinary component formulas assume an oriented orthonormal basis. Panel edges <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>4</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>3</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math> give <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>12</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math>, so triangle area is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mn>6</mn> </math>. This is also the reconstructed Part 542 definition missing as a standalone supplied lesson. Prerequisites
Dot products and orthogonality — Inner-product measurements supply the perpendicularity and alignment constraints.

This companion appears in Volume 2, The Foundations Bible — Volume II: Numerical Methods, Probability, Geometry and Camera Systems: Vector storage SIMD and boundary layouts — Vector storage SIMD and boundary layouts Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: Phase6 · Latest development: Phase6 Definition and mechanism Storage layout, compute lanes and external buffer layout are separate contracts. SIMD may operate within one vector or across objects. AoS, SoA and AoSoA change access patterns. Alignment and padding must be measured; a spare lane is not implicitly valid homogeneous data. One million twelve-byte vectors occupy four million fewer payload bytes than sixteen-byte vectors. A sixteen-byte load still needs sixteen accessible bytes even if one lane is discarded. Appendix.title: Cross-volume companion reference
Appendix.Content:
This companion appears in Volume 2, The Foundations Bible — Volume II: Numerical Methods, Probability, Geometry and Camera Systems: Nonlinear least squares: Gauss-Newton and Levenberg-Marquardt — Nonlinear least squares: Gauss-Newton and Levenberg-Marquardt Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 9 · Latest development: Phase 9 Definition and mechanism Nonlinear least squares minimizes one half the squared norm of a residual vector. Its gradient and Hessian involve the residual Jacobian; the exact Hessian also contains second derivatives of each residual. Gauss–Newton drops those latter terms, producing a positive-semidefinite normal matrix and an efficient local step when residuals are small or the model is close to linear. Levenberg–Marquardt adds damping to control ill-conditioned or overly aggressive steps, blending Gauss–Newton with gradient descent. These algorithms are useful for camera calibration, bundle adjustment, and geometric fitting. Residual scaling, parameter units, rank deficiency, and gauge freedoms influence the solution. Normal equations can square the condition number, so QR or other structured solves may be safer. A small residual does not prove parameters are identifiable or physically correct. Prerequisites
Jacobians, pushforwards, and pullbacks Hessians and local curvature Symmetric positive-definite matrices and Cholesky Constrained optimization and inverse kinematics

This companion appears in Volume 2, The Foundations Bible — Volume II: Numerical Methods, Probability, Geometry and Camera Systems: Position reconstruction from depth — Position reconstruction from depth Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 11 · Latest development: Phase 11 Definition and mechanism Given a pixel and an axial depth value, reconstruct a view-space point by converting the pixel to NDC, forming its camera ray, and scaling that ray so its forward-axis component equals the measured depth. Alternatively, transform the corresponding homogeneous clip point through an inverse projection matrix and divide by its resulting homogeneous coordinate. To obtain world position, apply the inverse view transform. These routes must share the actual viewport, pixel-centre, NDC-depth, and projection conventions used to render the image. In large worlds, subtract camera-relative origins before reducing precision; converting an already-rounded coordinate cannot restore lost detail. In a camera-relative renderer, reconstruct near the camera origin before adding a large global offset. Prerequisites
Axial depth and Euclidean range Hardware depth-buffer linearization Camera calibration and bundle adjustment Homogeneous coordinates and perspective division

This companion appears in Volume 2, The Foundations Bible — Volume II: Numerical Methods, Probability, Geometry and Camera Systems: Taylor models and approximation error — Taylor models and approximation error Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 9 · Latest development: Phase 9 Definition and mechanism A Taylor model approximates a smooth function near a reference point using its value, derivatives, and higher-order terms. The first-order model is the derivative’s linear map; the second-order model adds curvature through the Hessian. A remainder term describes what the finite truncation omits, so local accuracy depends on step size and higher derivatives over the region. Big-O notation gives an asymptotic scale, while a concrete error bound needs assumptions such as bounded derivatives. Taylor models power local optimization, camera Jacobian updates, uncertainty propagation, and numerical error analysis. They are not reliable far from the expansion point merely because the polynomial is easy to evaluate. When the input distribution is broad or crosses a singularity, first-order covariance propagation can miss bias and tail behavior; validate or replace the local model. Prerequisites
Derivative as a local linear map Hessians and local curvature

This companion appears in Volume 2, The Foundations Bible — Volume II: Numerical Methods, Probability, Geometry and Camera Systems: Online moments and Welford accumulation — Online moments and Welford accumulation Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 10 · Latest development: Phase 10 Definition and mechanism Online statistics update a mean and centered sum of squares as observations arrive, using constant storage. Welford’s recurrence computes a new mean from the old mean and one sample, then adds the product of deviations measured before and after that update. The centered form avoids severe cancellation in E[X²]−E[X]² for data with a large offset and small spread. Divide accumulated scatter by n for descriptive population-normalized variance or by n−1 for unbiased sample variance under IID finite-variance assumptions. The recurrence is numerically better behaved, not immune to overflow, count exhaustion, or all rounding error. Parallel workers can merge count, mean, and scatter summaries with a correction term for different means; merge order can change floating-point results. Prerequisites
Expectation, covariance, and dependence Accumulated rounding error

This companion appears in Volume 2, The Foundations Bible — Volume II: Numerical Methods, Probability, Geometry and Camera Systems: Robust geometric predicates — Robust geometric predicates Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: Phase6 · Latest development: Phase6 Definition and mechanism A geometric predicate decides a category from a sign, such as orientation. Near cancellation, ordinary floating arithmetic may not certify that sign. Adaptive arithmetic adds work only when justified error bounds leave uncertainty. Exact stored-input decisions cannot restore rounded-away physical information. A triangle can have an accurately small area estimate yet an uncertified orientation sign. Declaring every small value zero changes topology instead of proving a decision. Prerequisites
Cross products and oriented area — Oriented area supplies face normals, frame signs and geometric determinants. Dot and cross-product rounding — Cancellation and rounded inputs explain when a determinant sign or finite measurement is uncertain.

Source and navigation Teaching narrative · Coverage and source gap · Evidence and limits · Dependency Map Phase 11 camera development Adaptive orientation and incircle predicates protect discrete sign decisions from floating-point error by refining arithmetic when an error bound cannot certify the result. Camera estimation has a different uncertainty: noisy pixels and weak observability can leave pose uncertain even when every sign is exact. Predicate robustness does not improve measurement accuracy, and a low reprojection residual does not guarantee every combinatorial decision was reliable. Keep layers distinct: use robust predicates for topology, uncertainty weights for image residuals, and Jacobian spectra for weak directions. Named members are not an array. Named dot, cross and Hadamard operations avoid ambiguous vector multiplication; writable swizzles need explicit alias policies. A checked component accessor selects one of three real members and rejects out-of-range indices. It does not traverse from the address of the first member. Prerequisites

A valid impact had advanced two centres to a near-tangent configuration whose squared distance was a tiny amount below the squared combined radius; the original squared-distance tolerance rejected it as a deep overlap. Coordinate vectors measure physical dot products through <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msup> <mi>c</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mi mathvariant="sans-serif">T</mi> </mrow> </msup> <mi>G</mi> <mi>d</mi> </math>. It is positive semidefinite, and positive definite for independent generators. It records metric geometry but not orientation. The basis <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>,</mo> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math> has <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>G</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="INNER"> <mo data-mjx-texclass="OPEN">(</mo> <mtable columnspacing="1em" rowspacing="4pt"> <mtr> <mtd> <mn>1</mn> </mtd> <mtd> <mn>1</mn> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd> <mn>1</mn> </mtd> <mtd> <mn>2</mn> </mtd> </mtr> </mtable> <mo data-mjx-texclass="CLOSE">)</mo> </mrow> </math>. This companion appears in Volume 2, The Visual Computing Bible — Volume II: Computational Geometry, Vision, Reconstruction and XR: Exceptional projections and dimension — Exceptional projections and dimension Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses Definition and mechanism Projection usually lowers dimension, but a finite or fractal set may collapse unusually many points in special directions. For a finite planar set <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>X</mi> </math>, count pairs whose orthogonal projections coincide in direction <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>θ</mi> </math>; such pairs lie on lines parallel to the projection fibers. Averaging over directions gives a baseline, while exceptional directions produce larger fibers and encode geometric structure. For a density, the related transform integrates along each fiber, as in tomography; the Fourier-slice identity connects the transform of a projection to a slice of the original Fourier transform. Dimension and separation assumptions matter: finite point sets, thickened sets, measures, and finite-field analogues have different statements. A highly structured set can defeat naive random-grid intuition, and subfield examples in finite fields create strong obstructions. Results are estimates with hypotheses, not universal formulas for every dimension or projection family. This node connects geometric projection to incidence counting and harmonic analysis. Prerequisites
Basis coordinates and dimension Projection rejection and scalar components Fourier analysis and spectral phase Vector spaces subspaces and span
Used by
Finite-field projections turn image size into collision counts Real projections add scale, spacing, and incidence geometry Additive energy and approximate structure

SIMD applies an operation across multiple data lanes; GPU buffers and formats specify how values are arranged for parallel access. Packing can reduce traffic but adds decoding and alignment constraints. Lane layout, alignment, and access grouping require later treatment. Prerequisites
Machine word — A processor’s natural integer processing width is often called its word width, but the term is architecture dependent. Alignment and padding — Alignment is a required address multiple for an object.
Used by

Connect later chunks here when they use this concept. M003 development Alignment of vector loads and buffer offsets is a separate requirement from endian order. Packed structures and misaligned access may save space but introduce boundary crossings; Field reordering and AoS versus SoA can improve fieldwise access. CPU ABI layout is not automatically a GPU buffer schema. Appendix.title: Cross-volume companion reference

This companion appears in Volume 1, The Visual Computing Bible — Volume I: Image Formation, Rendering, GPU Systems and Geometry Queries: Automatic differentiation and backpropagation — Automatic differentiation and backpropagation Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: Phase 9 Definition and mechanism Automatic differentiation evaluates derivatives by applying the chain rule to the operations in a program. Each operation has a local derivative rule; composing the rules gives the derivative of the complete computation without symbolically expanding it or approximating it by finite differences. Forward mode propagates a tangent perturbation and computes a Jacobian-vector product (JVP), useful when there are few inputs. Reverse mode propagates sensitivities from outputs back to inputs and computes a vector-Jacobian product (VJP), making gradients of one scalar loss with respect to millions of parameters practical. Backpropagation is reverse-mode differentiation through a neural network’s computation graph. It does not remove numerical problems: nondifferentiable operations require conventions, saturated activations can yield tiny gradients, and an incorrect graph or reduction yields an incorrect gradient. Gradients are local sensitivity information, not proof of a global optimum. Finite differences remain a useful small-scale check, but cancellation and step-size tradeoffs make them a poor training method. Phase 9–10 development Forward mode propagates an input tangent through local derivatives and computes a Jacobian-vector product. Reverse mode propagates an output sensitivity backward and computes a vector-Jacobian product. These are chain-rule evaluations on the operation graph, distinct from finite differences, which perturb inputs and can suffer cancellation. The reverse pass requires a valid reverse-topological order and storage that remains alive until propagation finishes. Differentiating a converged solution uses an implicit equation and its local Jacobian; it is not automatically the same as differentiating every solver iteration. Prerequisites
Constrained optimization and inverse kinematics Matrix multiplication and composition order Floating-point reassociation Derivative as a local linear map Jacobians, pushforwards, and pullbacks
Used by

This companion appears in Volume 2, The Visual Computing Bible — Volume II: Computational Geometry, Vision, Reconstruction and XR: Antialiasing and sample allocation — Antialiasing and sample allocation Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: XR01 · Latest development: Phase 10 Definition and mechanism SSAA increases spatial observations; MSAA principally adds coverage-related sampling under its shading conventions. TAA reuses aligned temporal observations. Nonlinear shading makes pre-/post-filtering noncommutative, so coarse rates need appropriate input/output policies. Phase 9–10 development Antialiasing combines a sampling pattern with a reconstruction or integration footprint so unresolved variation contributes with controlled error. More samples can reduce Monte Carlo variance, while better placement can reduce structured error; these are different effects. Adaptive allocation based on observed samples changes the sampling procedure and can affect uncertainty estimates. Spatial sample allocation should remain distinct from importance sampling over path or event space. Prerequisites
Sampling aliasing and reconstruction — Allocation/filtering must respect what reduced samples can distinguish. Multiscale texture filtering — Coarse samples need appropriate prefilter/footprint representations. Appendix.title: Cross-volume companion reference
Appendix.Content:
This companion appears in Volume 2, The Foundations Bible — Volume II: Numerical Methods, Probability, Geometry and Camera Systems: Reflection refraction and shading directions — Reflection refraction and shading directions Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase6 · Latest development: University courses Definition and mechanism Plane reflection reverses a direction’s normal component. Refraction scales its tangent component by the incident/transmitted index ratio and solves for a unit normal component. A negative computed discriminant indicates total internal reflection under the stated model. Half-vectors require normalized outward light/view directions. Incident <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>0.6</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mo>−</mo> <mn>0.8</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math> reflects to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>0.6</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>0.8</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math> across normal <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math>. Antiparallel light/view directions have no unique half-vector. Prerequisites
Projection rejection and scalar components — Removing an unwanted component creates residuals, tangent axes and mirror decompositions. Unit directions and safe normalization — Validated finite unit directions establish the preconditions for simplified geometry formulas.
Used by Later curriculum sources can deepen this same node; no future coverage is marked complete. - Lens optics and depth of field Recall and next depth Declare arrow and medium conventions before deriving formulas; distinguish direction geometry from optical energy. Full production proofs, target-specific integration and learner mastery require further evidence. Source and navigation Teaching narrative · Coverage and source gap · Evidence and limits · Dependency Map University course development Extend the existing direction note by separating geometric surface orientation from optical ray behavior. The normal vector is perpendicular to a local tangent plane; it determines the cosine term in diffuse shading and the directions of ideal reflection and refraction. For unit incident direction <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>ω</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> </math> and unit normal <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>n</mi> </math>, specular reflection mirrors the direction about the normal, while refraction changes direction according to the ratio of refractive indices and may undergo total internal reflection. Direction conventions matter: some texts define incoming vectors toward the surface, others point away from it, so signs must be checked before applying formulas. A shading normal may differ from the true geometric normal, as in normal mapping, but it cannot change silhouette or visibility. Distinguish shading perturbations from geometry displacement, and use consistent normals when evaluating BRDFs, ray offsets, and medium transitions. Appendix.Content:
This companion appears in Volume 1, The Visual Computing Bible — Volume I: Image Formation, Rendering, GPU Systems and Geometry Queries: Probability density and change of measure — Probability density and change of measure Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: Phase 10 Definition and mechanism A probability density describes probability per unit of a chosen measure, not probability at a point. A density <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>p</mi> <mi>A</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>a</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math> over area differs from a density <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>p</mi> <mi>ω</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>ω</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math> over solid angle. When a mapping changes variables, its Jacobian converts density so total probability remains one: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>p</mi> <mi>B</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>b</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>=</mo> <msub> <mi>p</mi> <mi>A</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>a</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo stretchy="false">|</mo> </mrow> <mi>d</mi> <mi>a</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>/</mo> </mrow> <mi>d</mi> <mi>b</mi> <mo stretchy="false">|</mo> </math> in one dimension, with the determinant of the inverse Jacobian in multiple dimensions. In rendering, choosing a point on a light and using its direction from a shading point requires an area-to-solid-angle conversion involving distance squared and the light’s projected cosine. Estimator formulas are only correct when the sampling density and integral use the same measure. This concept prevents missing factors in importance sampling, environment-map sampling, and camera-lens integration. Phase 9–10 development A density is meaningful relative to a measure and its support; its value at a point is not itself an event probability. For a continuous scalar variable, an interval probability is the integral of the density over that interval. Under a differentiable one-to-one change of variables, the transformed density includes the absolute determinant of the inverse Jacobian. Values outside the transformed support have zero probability. A mixed law can contain both point masses and a continuous part, so one PDF alone cannot describe every distribution. When a renderer changes a surface-area density into a solid-angle density, the geometric Jacobian must preserve the same probability. Prerequisites

Appendix.title: Cross-volume companion reference
Appendix.Content:
This companion appears in Volume 2, The Foundations Bible — Volume II: Numerical Methods, Probability, Geometry and Camera Systems: Norms lengths and induced distances — Norms lengths and induced distances Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: Phase6 · Latest development: Phase6 Definition and mechanism A norm is nonnegative, definite, absolutely homogeneous and satisfies the triangle inequality. It induces distance by taking the norm of a point difference. Coordinate-defined first, second and infinity norms answer different geometric questions. For <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>3</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mo>−</mo> <mn>4</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math>, the three norms are <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mn>7</mn> </math>, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mn>5</mn> </math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mn>4</mn> </math>. Squared length scales quadratically and is not itself a norm or induced metric. Prerequisites
Basis coordinates and dimension — An ordered basis fixes coordinate meaning and the space whose geometry is measured.
Used by
Unit directions and safe normalization — Builds on this mechanism in the connected geometry story. Dot products and orthogonality — Builds on this mechanism in the connected geometry story. Matrix norms and numerical error — Extends this foundation into linear-systems and decomposition analysis. Collision barriers and continuous detection ## Recall and next depth
Draw the three unit balls; explain which comparisons can safely use squared length. Full production proofs, target-specific integration and learner mastery require further evidence. M004 - Representation and rounding learning spine Prerequisites Dependent Why these steps are needed IEEE-754 floating point, Bit field Binary32 A 32-bit binary interchange format with one sign bit, eight exponent bits and 23 fraction bits. Normal precision is 24 bits; exponent bias is 127. Word 3F800000 has E=127,F=0 and means 1. Binary32 Binary64 A 64-bit binary interchange format with 1/11/52 fields, 53 significant normal bits and bias 1023. Normal exponent range is −1022 through 1023. Word 3FF0000000000000 means 1. Binary32 Exponent bias Normal exponents are encoded as unsigned E=e+B. Binary32 B=127, so exponent 3 stores 130. Field zero and all-ones are reserved; classify before subtracting bias. Binary32, Positional notation Significand and hidden bit The significand supplies significant digits; the exponent supplies scale. A normal binary value begins 1.f, so its leading one is implied, not stored. Binary32 fraction F contributes F/2^23; subnormals instead begin 0.f. Exponent bias, Significand and hidden bit, Hexadecimal Floating-point encoding and decoding Encoding chooses fields for a value; decoding classifies fields and reconstructs their meaning. 10.625 normalizes to 1.010101₂×2³, giving 412A0000. C1540000 decodes to −13.25. Binary32 Signed zero Exponent and fraction zero permit either sign. 00000000 and 80000000 compare numerically equal, but signbit and reciprocal distinguish them. Ordinary x<0 does not detect negative zero. Binary32 Floating-point infinities All-one exponent and zero fraction encode signed infinity. This is not maximum finite. Infinity minus itself is NaN; overflow’s result also depends on rounding direction. Binary32 NaNs and payloads All-one exponent with nonzero fraction encodes a non-numerical, unordered NaN. Quiet and signaling classes differ; fraction bits can carry payload information. Ordinary NaN equality is false; use isnan. Raw words can be classified without consuming signaling NaNs as floating values. Exponent bias, Significand and hidden bit Subnormals and gradual underflow Exponent zero and nonzero fraction remove the hidden one and hold the effective exponent at the normal minimum. Binary32 values are F×2^-149, connecting smoothly to 2^-126. Absolute spacing stays fixed while relative precision degrades. Significand and hidden bit Machine epsilon For these binary types epsilon is upward spacing at 1: 2^-23 for binary32 and 2^-52 for binary64. It is neither minimum positive value nor a physical threshold. Machine epsilon, Exponent bias, Subnormals and gradual underflow ULP and representable spacing A unit in the last place describes local spacing. Inside normal binade [2e,2(e+1)), p-bit precision gives spacing 2^(e-(p-1)). Immediately above 1 the binary32 gap is twice the gap below it. ULP and representable spacing Rounding to nearest ties to even Choose the nearest representable value; exactly halfway choose the even retained significand integer. At toy precision three bits, 1.125→1 and 1.375→1.5. std::round uses halfway-away-from-zero instead. ULP and representable spacing, Rounding to nearest ties to even Unit roundoff Under nearest binary rounding the conventional relative bound for normal-range results is u=2^-p, half upward epsilon. For binary32 this is 2^-24. The bound has range/rounding assumptions. Boolean algebra, Rounding to nearest ties to even Guard round and sticky bits Guard is first discarded bit, round the next, sticky ORs all remaining bits. With retained low bit L, nearest-even increments when G AND (R OR sticky OR L). Sticky summarizes any nonzero tail. Rounding to nearest ties to even Directed rounding modes Upward means toward positive infinity, downward toward negative infinity, and toward-zero truncates magnitude. Upward rounding of −2.1 to an integer gives −2, not −3. Directed rounding modes, NaNs and payloads Floating-point environment and compiler modes The environment includes rounding direction and exception status. Runtime mode changes can fail and must restore prior state. Strict compiler settings are needed; fast-math may discard required special-value or environment assumptions. IEEE-754 floating point, Subnormals and gradual underflow Floating-point exception flags Invalid, divide-by-zero, overflow, underflow and inexact are status conditions, not C++ throw exceptions. Exact subnormal results need not signal underflow. Flag/trap behavior depends on the environment. Subnormals and gradual underflow, Floating-point environment and compiler modes Flush-to-zero and denormals-are-zero FTZ flushes certain tiny results to zero; DAZ treats subnormal inputs as zero in supporting environments. They change gradual-underflow behavior. Cost and support are target/mode-specific. Fixed-width integer types, Interpretation contract, IEEE-754 floating point Bit casting and representation A same-size eligible bit_cast transfers representation, not numeric value. On the checked binary32 host, bit_cast<uint32_t>(1.0f)=3F800000, whereas a numeric cast gives 1. Pointer punning is not an equivalent legal operation. ULP and representable spacing, Signed zero, NaNs and payloads ULP distance policies Distance counts representable steps under a declared ordering/equality policy. The finite-only laboratory collapses both zeros to one key and rejects NaNs/infinities. Across negative minimum subnormal to positive minimum subnormal distance is two. Machine epsilon, ULP and representable spacing, Floating-point infinities, NaNs and payloads Numerical tolerance policies Tolerance is a task-chosen allowed discrepancy: absolute in original units, relative to scale, or representable-step based. Machine epsilon is not automatically a norm cutoff. Handle non-finite values and validate tolerances before formulas. IEEE-754 floating point, Floating-point infinities Robust norm and intermediate range A final representable answer can be lost to overflowing intermediates. Squaring 1e20f overflows before a finite norm could be formed. Scale by maximum component or use hypot to avoid unnecessary squared overflow. Numerical tolerance policies Conditioning and singularity Conditioning measures sensitivity to input perturbation. A=1e-4 I has determinant 1e-8 but condition number one in the 2-norm. Uniform scaling changes determinant magnitude without changing this conditioning measure. Signed zero, NaNs and payloads, Serialization, Bit casting and representation Floating-point canonicalization Canonicalization deliberately merges encodings: both zeros to positive zero, all NaNs to one quiet pattern. Raw preservation instead keeps sign/payload distinctions. Neither is universally correct; this is a file/hash contract choice. Directed rounding modes, Floating-point environment and compiler modes Interval arithmetic An interval encloses a possible exact value between lower and upper bounds. Correct outward rounding can preserve containment when the whole algorithm honors necessary assumptions. The first volume covers all Parts 1–100. Prerequisites explain the story’s dependencies; they do not require leaving the continuous volume to learn an essential definition. Representation choices and external contracts Prerequisites Dependent Why these steps are needed Two's complement, Interpretation contract Fixed-point representation A raw integer I represents I/S for an agreed positive scale S and units. With S=2^16, raw 212992 means 3.25. The integer has no built-in fractional point. Fixed-point representation Fixed-point range and resolution For signed N-bit raw storage and F fraction bits, step is 2^-F and the positive endpoint is (2(N-1)-1)/2F. Required step 0.001 and magnitude 1e6 in 32 bits allow F=10 or 11. Fixed-point representation, Minimum signed value, Arithmetic policies Fixed-point rescaling Raw multiplication changes scale S to S²; divide the wide product by S with a declared rounding rule. Raw division uses A*S/B. Check the destination after widening, and handle divisor zero and signed minima. Fixed-point representation, Absolute and relative error Affine quantization and zero point A positive step s, integer zero point z and bounded code q reconstruct x̂=s(q-z). Nearest encode uses clamp(round(x/s)+z). Half-step error assumes no clipping and ideal parameters. Affine quantization and zero point, Bit packing Groupwise quantization and metadata Local groups share a scale, improving adaptation at a metadata cost. Symmetric INT4 calibration maxAbs/7 reconstructs codes around [-7,7]; float scales add about 32/G bits per value for full groups. Quantization and compressed weights One-bit centroid quantization One sign label selects one of two row means. Row [-1,-3,2,4] reconstructs [-2,-2,3,3], with RMSE one. Two float32 centroids cost 64 additional bits per row. Affine quantization and zero point UNORM and SNORM UNORM decodes q/(2^n-1); UNORM8 code128 gives128/255. SNORM commonly clamps q/(2^(n-1)-1) at -1, so -128 and -127 both map to -1 for eight bits. IEEE-754 floating point, Rounding to nearest ties to even Binary16 IEEE binary16 has 1/5/10 fields, bias15 and11 normal precision bits. Word3E00 is1.5; maximum finite65504; normal minimum2^-14 and subnormal minimum2^-24. IEEE-754 floating point, Rounding to nearest ties to even Bfloat16 BF16 has1/8/7 fields, bias127 and8 normal precision bits. It keeps broad exponent range at coarse spacing2^-7 above1. A nearest-even conversion must handle NaNs separately from finite rounding. Unsigned modular arithmetic, Interpretation contract Offset-binary coding A bias turns signed levels into unsigned codes. For the source-shaped INT4 convention c=q+8, -3 becomes nibble0101, not the two’s-complement nibble1101. Absolute and relative error, Quantization and compressed weights Quantization error metrics For N>0, RMSE is sqrt(sum squared discrepancies/N), MAE is mean absolute discrepancy, and max error is the largest observed magnitude. Promote float operands before subtraction when measuring in double. Serialization, Bit casting and representation Binary format contracts A schema declares field widths/order, byte order, numeric representation, valid values, lengths, version, padding and identity policy. Magic identifies a candidate format; version chooses a schema, neither authenticates content. Binary format contracts, Unsigned modular arithmetic, Short-circuit evaluation Checked binary parsing Validate products before size calculation, ranges with offset≤size and length≤size-offset, and practical resource limits before allocation. Mapping/alignment does not itself establish valid typed object access. Bitwise XOR, Serialization Checksums CRCs and hashes Checksums/digests summarize specified bytes. Additive checksums miss reorderings; CRCs use GF(2) polynomial remainders and declared parameters. Cryptographic hashes need a trusted reference to support integrity claims against substitution. Checksums CRCs and hashes, Interpretation contract Integrity and authenticity Integrity compares content with a declared reference; authenticity requires a trust mechanism such as a MAC or signature. Replacing both file and untrusted digest defeats a simple hash comparison. Endianness, Bit casting and representation, Binary format contracts Memory dump interpretation Raw octets gain meaning from offsets, width, encoding and byte order. Bytes00 00 80 3F mean integer1065353216 or binary32 one under different little-endian contracts. A dump does not prove a typed object is live. This companion appears in Volume 2, The Foundations Bible — Volume II: Numerical Methods, Probability, Geometry and Camera Systems: Symmetric positive-definite matrices and Cholesky — Symmetric positive-definite matrices and Cholesky A real symmetric matrix <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>A</mi> </math> is positive definite if every nonzero <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>x</mi> </math> has positive quadratic energy <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msup> <mi>x</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mi mathvariant="sans-serif">T</mi> </mrow> </msup> <mi>A</mi> <mi>x</mi> </math>. Positive semidefinite permits zero energy directions and may be singular, so Cholesky’s assumptions and failure status must be respected. Use it when: covariance, Gram systems, energy minimization, or an SPD solve is established. This companion appears in Volume 2, The Foundations Bible — Volume II: Numerical Methods, Probability, Geometry and Camera Systems: Scalars fields and real-number models — Scalars fields and real-number models Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: Phase6 · Latest development: Phase6 Definition and mechanism A scalar is an element of the field used by a vector space. A field supports addition, multiplication and nonzero division under specified algebraic laws. The reals also supply order and completeness. Floating-point values approximate this model but do not form a mathematical field. An integer reciprocal need not be an integer; <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msup> <mn>2</mn> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>−</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msup> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>/</mo> </mrow> <mn>2</mn> </math>. A real scalar can carry metres or seconds. A finite representation cannot preserve every real-number operation. Prerequisites The chapter establishes this foundation directly; no earlier accepted phase is assumed complete. Used by

Appendix.Content:
This companion appears in Volume 2, The Foundations Bible — Volume II: Numerical Methods, Probability, Geometry and Camera Systems: Newton and quasi-Newton optimization — Newton and quasi-Newton optimization Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 9 · Latest development: Phase 9 Definition and mechanism Newton’s method builds a local quadratic model of an objective from its gradient and Hessian, then solves for the model’s stationary point. Near a well-conditioned solution with suitable smoothness and curvature, it can converge faster than gradient descent. Away from that regime, the Hessian may be indefinite, poorly scaled, or a poor model over the proposed step. Line searches and trust regions control step acceptance. Quasi-Newton methods such as BFGS estimate curvature from successive parameter and gradient changes, avoiding repeated exact Hessian construction. Their guarantees depend on assumptions and update safeguards. Optimization should monitor objective change, gradient norm, step size, constraints, and numerical failures; a small step alone can indicate stagnation rather than success. The method’s result is a local solution unless global structure proves more. Prerequisites
Hessians and local curvature Constrained optimization and inverse kinematics
Used by

This companion appears in Volume 1, The Engine Builder's Bible — Volume I: From First Frame to Core Runtime Systems: Field reordering and AoS versus SoA — Field reordering and AoS versus SoA Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: C003 · Latest development: C003 Definition and mechanism Reordering fields can reduce alignment holes: conventional 1/8/1/4 members shrink 24→16 bytes when arranged 8/4/1/1. AoS (array of structures) interleaves full records; SoA (structure of arrays) separates each field into its own array. Smaller records do not prove faster code; hot fields and access patterns matter, and layout changes may break ABI. Prerequisites
Internal and tail padding — The position and amount of unused layout space determine reordering/packing effects. Cache lines and memory bandwidth — Field adjacency and stride affect useful bytes fetched per access.

Appendix.Content: This companion appears in Volume 2, The Foundations Bible — Volume II: Numerical Methods, Probability, Geometry and Camera Systems: LU factorization and reusable solves — LU factorization and reusable solves LU stores elimination as triangular factors. With row pivoting in this vault’s convention, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>P</mi> <mi>A</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mi>L</mi> <mi>U</mi> </math>; apply the same permutation to each right-hand side, then solve one lower- and one upper-triangular system. Factorization cost is amortized across repeated solves. Use it when: solving square general systems, especially with multiple right-hand sides. Developed in Phase 8: The multipliers used to eliminate entries become the lower factor, while the remaining upper triangle records the reduced system; with row exchanges the convention is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>P</mi> <mi>A</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mi>L</mi> <mi>U</mi> </math>. Appendix.title: Cross-volume companion reference
Appendix.Content:
This companion appears in Volume 2, The Engine Builder's Bible — Volume II: Tools, Worlds and Living Systems: BVH build traversal and workload selection — BVH build, traversal, and workload selection A bounding-volume hierarchy is a tree whose nodes bound groups of primitives. Its purpose is not to make intersection magically faster; it is to let a query prove that large groups cannot matter. For an overlap query Q, traversal follows a simple implication: if Q does not overlap node.bounds, then Q cannot overlap any primitive below that node. That pruning claim is only correct when every child primitive is actually contained by every ancestor bound. Tree construction therefore owns an invariant: each internal bound is the union of its children, and each leaf bound contains the primitives assigned to the leaf. Build choices A median split sorts or partitions primitive centroids and divides them into similarly sized groups. It is simple and usually avoids catastrophically unbalanced trees, but equal primitive counts do not imply equal traversal cost. Surface-area heuristic construction estimates expected query/ray work. In the common ray-tracing interpretation, a split cost has the form <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block"> <mi>C</mi> <mo>=</mo> <msub> <mi>C</mi> <mi>T</mi> </msub> <mo>+</mo> <mfrac> <msub> <mi>A</mi> <mi>L</mi> </msub> <msub> <mi>A</mi> <mi>P</mi> </msub> </mfrac> <msub> <mi>N</mi> <mi>L</mi> </msub> <msub> <mi>C</mi> <mi>I</mi> </msub> <mo>+</mo> <mfrac> <msub> <mi>A</mi> <mi>R</mi> </msub> <msub> <mi>A</mi> <mi>P</mi> </msub> </mfrac> <msub> <mi>N</mi> <mi>R</mi> </msub> <msub> <mi>C</mi> <mi>I</mi> </msub> <mo>,</mo> </math> where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>A</mi> <mi>P</mi> </msub> </math> is parent surface area, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>A</mi> <mi>L</mi> </msub> <mo>,</mo> <msub> <mi>A</mi> <mi>R</mi> </msub> </math> are child areas, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>N</mi> <mi>L</mi> </msub> <mo>,</mo> <msub> <mi>N</mi> <mi>R</mi> </msub> </math> are primitive counts, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>C</mi> <mi>T</mi> </msub> </math> is traversal cost and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>C</mi> <mi>I</mi> </msub> </math> is primitive-intersection cost. Binned SAH approximates candidate split positions efficiently. LBVH chooses hierarchy structure from Morton ordering. It can build quickly and map well to parallel hardware, but tree quality can be worse than a careful SAH build for some scenes. Which strategy wins depends on how often the scene rebuilds and how expensive later queries are. Traversal representation A production BVH must choose node layout as deliberately as split policy. Questions include:
binary versus wider nodes; array indices versus pointers; parent links or stackless encodings; leaf primitive ranges; AoS versus SoA bounds; quantized bounds; traversal stack depth and overflow behavior; child ordering by query direction or distance.
For GPU traversal, divergence and memory coalescing can dominate the nominal tree complexity. Dynamic scenes Refitting recomputes ancestor bounds without changing topology. It is cheap when objects move modestly, but tree quality can decay. Rebuilding restores quality at higher cost. A useful dynamic policy measures a quality proxy and rebuilds when continued bad traversal is more expensive than reconstruction. Dynamic AABB trees instead maintain a mutable hierarchy and often enlarge leaf bounds by a motion margin. The margin trades fewer reinserts for more false candidates. Executable reference tools/labs/spatial_index_lab.cpp builds a median-split BVH over deterministic random AABBs and compares 250 overlap queries against a brute-force oracle. Any missed or extra primitive is a test failure. The same laboratory also contains A* graph search with relaxation, reinsertion and unreachable-goal handling. The witness does not claim SAH quality, LBVH construction, dynamic updates, SIMD traversal, ray packet behavior, navmesh construction, or KairoSpatial parity. Those remain separate evidence layers. Related: AABB overlap and containment, Prefix scan and stream compaction, Field reordering and AoS versus SoA. SAH, Morton and refit witness tools/labs/bvh_sah_refit_lab.cpp advances the construction side beyond the earlier median-split query oracle. It computes prefix/suffix bounds for candidate partitions and minimizes the surface-area-weighted primitive cost, verifies that two separated three-object clusters split between the clusters, tests 3D Morton bit interleaving on a controlled monotone coordinate sweep, and refits a parent bound after one child moves. This is enough to make the equations executable, but not enough to call the builder a production binned SAH or LBVH. A complete next layer needs fixed-bin accumulation, stable primitive partitioning, LBVH range/split construction from Morton prefixes, dynamic-tree rotations or reinsertion, and measured build-versus-query trade-offs on real workloads.. Open BVH build traversal and workload selection in Volume 2

This companion appears in Volume 2, The Foundations Bible — Volume II: Numerical Methods, Probability, Geometry and Camera Systems: Triple products and signed volume — Triple products and signed volume Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: Phase6 · Latest development: Phase6 Definition and mechanism A scalar triple product measures oriented parallelepiped volume. Four-point orientation uses edge differences; tetrahedral volume is one sixth of the absolute result. A vector triple product is a different, vector-valued identity, and cross products are not associative. The panel with <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>D</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>2</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math> has signed volume <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mn>24</mn> </math> and tetrahedron volume <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mn>4</mn> </math>. Parenthesis changes can turn a nested cross from a nonzero vector into zero. Prerequisites
Cross products and oriented area — Oriented area supplies face normals, frame signs and geometric determinants. Dot products and orthogonality — Inner-product measurements supply the perpendicularity and alignment constraints.
Used by

Appendix.Content: This companion appears in Volume 2, The Foundations Bible — Volume II: Numerical Methods, Probability, Geometry and Camera Systems: Sparse and iterative solvers — Sparse and iterative solvers Sparse storage avoids zeros when structure and scale justify its index overhead. Iterative methods replace a dense factorization with matrix-vector products and a convergence process. Conjugate gradient requires symmetric positive definiteness; preconditioning, residual criteria, and a maximum iteration count belong in the contract. Use it when: large structured systems make dense storage or factorization impractical. Developed in Phase 8: Sparse storage pays off when zeros and dimensions outweigh indexing overhead, while direct factorization can create fill that destroys sparsity. Iterative methods instead use matrix-vector products and stopping tests; conjugate gradient requires an SPD operator, and preconditioning, a maximum iteration count, and a true residual make convergence reviewable. storage and fill · direct versus iterative solving Prerequisites Linear systems and fundamental subspaces, Symmetric positive-definite matrices and Cholesky, Matrix norms and numerical error. Row-major storage does not choose any of those mathematical conventions. Column 1: Topic Column 2: Shortest useful rule Column 3: Figure or explanation Meaning Shortest useful rule A rectangular table becomes a map only after input/output bases and roles are fixed. Columns are input-basis images. Figure or explanation M1: weighted columns Shape Shortest useful rule <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>m</mi> <mo>×</mo> <mi>k</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>k</mi> <mo>×</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math> yields <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>m</mi> <mo>×</mo> <mi>n</mi> </math>; shared dimensions must match. Noncommutative order is separate from associative grouping; floating-point regrouping can change bits. For <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>R</mi> <mi>y</mi> </msub> </math>, rotate the oriented pair <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>z</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>x</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math>, then restore <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>x</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>y</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>z</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math> order. Trace is similarity-invariant, not a full map identifier. Figure or explanation Transpose, symmetry and trace Determinant Shortest useful rule Magnitude = volume scale; sign = orientation; zero = rank loss for square maps. It does not measure conditioning alone. Figure or explanation M3: determinant questions Inversion Shortest useful rule Cofactors explain a formula; pivoted elimination explains an algorithm. Solve directly when the inverse itself is unnecessary. Figure or explanation Full elimination trace Sensitivity Shortest useful rule <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>κ</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>A</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>=</mo> <mo data-mjx-texclass="ORD" fence="false" stretchy="false">‖</mo> <mi>A</mi> <mo data-mjx-texclass="ORD" fence="false" stretchy="false">‖</mo> <mo data-mjx-texclass="ORD" fence="false" stretchy="false">‖</mo> <msup> <mi>A</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>−</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msup> <mo data-mjx-texclass="ORD" fence="false" stretchy="false">‖</mo> </math> in a compatible norm. Stable code cannot restore information lost to input uncertainty. This companion appears in Volume 2, The Visual Computing Bible — Volume II: Computational Geometry, Vision, Reconstruction and XR: Sampling aliasing and reconstruction — Sampling aliasing and reconstruction Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: XR01 · Latest development: Phase 10 Definition and mechanism Uniform samples identify frequencies only modulo sample rate and corresponding real-signal equivalences. Strictly band-limited ideal reconstruction needs non-overlapping spectral replicas; exact-Nyquist phase is a boundary hazard. Prefilter before decimation. Phase 9–10 development Signal aliasing occurs when distinct signal frequencies produce the same sampled values; reconstruction then cannot recover which signal generated the samples without additional assumptions. Stratification, low-discrepancy sequences, and blue-noise point sets describe where samples are placed, not a guarantee that the signal is band-limited or that an estimator is unbiased. Each strategy still needs a valid support, probability weight, and reconstruction filter. Prerequisites
Fourier analysis and spectral phase — Frequency and phase reveal transfer, sampling ambiguity and structural loss.
Used by
Multiscale texture filtering Spatiotemporal sampling and retinal motion Antialiasing and sample allocation Triangle rasterization and coverage tests Edge localization and subpixel contours PDE fields and discrete Laplacians Learned image features and CNNs Radiance fields and Gaussian splatting Reservoir resampling and ReSTIR Sampling quality: stratification, quasi-Monte Carlo, and blue noise Tensor-product interpolation ## Recall and next depth
Prove 13Hz and 3Hz sample identity at 10Hz. Pending: anisotropic/nonuniform sampling and actual reconstruction errors. Written coverage is not a claim of learner mastery or accepted numbered-curriculum progress. Source and navigation Expanded teaching explanation · Independent coverage · Dependency Map University course development Sampling records measurements of a continuous signal on a discrete grid. Frequencies that differ by integer multiples of the sampling rate can produce the same samples, so the sampled values alone cannot identify which original signal was present. For ideal band-limited reconstruction, the signal must be restricted below half the sampling rate; equality at the limiting frequency needs additional phase and endpoint conditions. A real pixel also integrates light over area and exposure time, making its measurement a filtered sample. Prefiltering attenuates frequencies that would alias, while reconstruction estimates a continuous signal from the stored samples. Ideal sinc reconstruction has infinite support; practical filters trade computation, sharpness, ringing and residual aliasing. More samples reduce integration error only when their placement and weights match the intended pixel or path-space measure. Sampling continuous signals and image formation · Image sampling, filtering, and efficient reconstruction Full teaching explanation

This companion appears in Volume 2, The Foundations Bible — Volume II: Numerical Methods, Probability, Geometry and Camera Systems: Discretization, truncation, and roundoff — Discretization, truncation, and roundoff Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 10 · Latest development: Phase 10 Definition and mechanism Discretization replaces a continuous object or domain with a finite grid; truncation omits terms or limits an iterative expansion; roundoff comes from finite-precision arithmetic. They have different causes and respond to different changes. Refining a spatial grid may reduce discretization error while increasing computation. Adding more terms can reduce truncation error. Increasing precision or reformulating arithmetic can reduce roundoff, though a poor algorithm may still dominate. A signed-distance field sampled too coarsely can lose a thin feature entirely, while an ODE’s Euler step has a local truncation error even under exact arithmetic. An error budget should distinguish these mechanisms instead of calling every disagreement “numerical error.” Prerequisites
Accumulated rounding error Taylor models and approximation error Numerical quadrature and error
Used by
Convergence order and Richardson extrapolation Numerical error budgets
Full teaching explanation
Separate discretization, truncation, and roundoff; measure convergence

Use it when: separating local rigid-like motion from symmetric deformation. Developed in Phase 8: Polar decomposition factors a map into an orthogonal part and a positive-semidefinite stretch. This companion appears in Volume 2, The Visual Computing Bible — Volume II: Computational Geometry, Vision, Reconstruction and XR: GPU vertex specification — GPU vertex specification Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses Definition and mechanism A GPU vertex-input specification explains how bytes in one or more buffers become per-vertex shader inputs. A buffer object owns bytes; a vertex array object records their interpretation: enabled attributes, component count and type, normalization, stride, byte offset, and the buffer binding used for fetch. Stride is the number of bytes between successive vertices; offset is the first component’s byte position. For vertex i, the address is base + offset + i × stride. For interleaved records containing position (3 floats), normal (3), and UV (2), the stride is 8 × 4 = 32 bytes and the UV offset is 24 bytes. Modern binding APIs separate attribute format from the buffer binding; older pointer-style calls can capture the buffer bound at setup time. A wrong stride may still address valid memory, so the symptom is often plausible but scrambled geometry. The contract must agree with CPU packing, shader input types, and the API’s state-capture rules. Prerequisites
Vector storage SIMD and boundary layouts Matrix storage indexing and strides Camera view and clip-space pipeline Pointer arithmetic and provenance
Used by
Rasterization, coverage, and depth Homogeneous clipping and perspective interpolation
Full teaching explanation

This companion appears in Volume 2, The Foundations Bible — Volume II: Numerical Methods, Probability, Geometry and Camera Systems: Derivative as a local linear map — Derivative as a local linear map Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 9 · Latest development: Phase 9 Definition and mechanism The derivative measures first-order change. In one variable it is the limit of the difference quotient; in several variables it is the linear map that best predicts small output changes near a point. For a scalar function, this local model is the tangent line. For a vector-valued function, it is a matrix acting on an input perturbation. The derivative is local: its approximation error becomes small relative to the perturbation as the step shrinks, but the linear model need not remain accurate over a large region. This view unifies instantaneous velocity, gradients, Jacobians, and optimization directions. It also gives a practical check: compare a small finite perturbation with the derivative’s predicted change, while remembering that floating-point rounding and curvature limit how small or large the perturbation should be. Prerequisites
No earlier concept node is required in this planned path.

Visual angle measures directional separation, while ray differentials describe local change in generated rays and may include lens sampling. For fisheye or omnidirectional cameras, angular footprint varies across the image. Transform sampling densities with the correct Jacobian when changing from pixel area to solid angle. This companion appears in Volume 2, The Foundations Bible — Volume II: Numerical Methods, Probability, Geometry and Camera Systems: Numerical quadrature and error — Numerical quadrature and error Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 9 · Latest development: Phase 9 Definition and mechanism Quadrature approximates a definite integral from finitely many function evaluations. Left, right, and midpoint rectangle rules use constant local models; the trapezoid rule uses linear interpolation; Simpson’s rule integrates a local quadratic fit over paired intervals. Their errors depend on smoothness, interval size, and rule-specific derivative bounds. Refining the mesh usually improves accuracy for smooth functions, but increases computation and may expose floating-point accumulation error. Adaptive quadrature places more samples where the integrand changes rapidly, provided its error estimator is trustworthy. Quadrature differs from Monte Carlo: deterministic rules have dimension-dependent behavior, while random sampling is attractive in high dimensions but has statistical uncertainty. Report the interval, nodes, weights, stopping tolerance, and error-control method so numerical results can be reproduced. Prerequisites
Definite integrals and the fundamental theorem Absolute and relative error
Used by

It is consistent exactly when <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mi mathvariant="bold">b</mi> </mrow> </math> lies in the column space. The null space contains input changes invisible to every measurement; rank-nullity counts observable versus free directions. A reflection reverses it; a proper rotation preserves it. It does not specify up axis, camera direction or matrix storage order. The sign of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi> </mrow> <mo>×</mo> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi> </mrow> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>⋅</mo> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mi mathvariant="bold">z</mi> </mrow> </math> classifies a nondegenerate frame. Swapping two axes flips the sign. Prerequisites
Cross products and oriented area — Oriented area supplies face normals, frame signs and geometric determinants.

Gaussian transfer suppresses high-frequency contrast under a linear shift-invariant model. Real optics can vary by position, wavelength and focus. Prerequisites

Convolution and filter footprints — A weighting footprint establishes the filtered response, boundary effects and frequency transfer.

This companion appears in Volume 2, The Foundations Bible — Volume II: Numerical Methods, Probability, Geometry and Camera Systems: Dot products and orthogonality — Dot products and orthogonality Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: Phase6 · Latest development: Phase6 Definition and mechanism An inner product provides a scalar measurement of two vectors. In orthonormal real coordinates the dot is a sum of component products. Its geometric form is length product times angle cosine. Orthogonality means zero inner product; zero itself has no angle. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>3</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>4</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>⋅</mo> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>2</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>=</mo> <mn>6</mn> </math>, while the cosine is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mn>6</mn> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>/</mo> </mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>5</mn> <mo>⋅</mo> <mn>2</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>=</mo> <mn>0.6</mn> </math>. Coordinate dotting assumes the correct metric. Prerequisites
Norms lengths and induced distances — Lengths and their domains are needed before unit directions or angular measurements.

Appendix.title: Cross-volume companion reference
Appendix.Content:
This companion appears in Volume 2, The Foundations Bible — Volume II: Numerical Methods, Probability, Geometry and Camera Systems: Time integrators and symplectic updates — Time integrators and symplectic updates Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 9 · Latest development: Phase 9 Definition and mechanism A time integrator turns a differential equation into a discrete state update. Explicit Euler uses the current slope; midpoint and Runge–Kutta methods combine several slope evaluations to improve local accuracy; semi-implicit Euler updates velocity before position and can behave better for mechanical systems. Symplectic methods preserve the geometric structure of Hamiltonian dynamics, often keeping long-run energy error bounded rather than allowing systematic drift. No method is universally best: order, stability region, cost, conservation, and stiffness all matter. A higher formal order does not guarantee better behavior at an unsuitable step size or under discontinuous forces. Compare integrators on the same problem, step policy, and error target. Update order is part of the algorithm: changing it can change stability and physical behavior, not merely code style. Prerequisites
ODE initial-value problems and stiffness
Used by
ODE integration and stability

Appendix.title: Cross-volume companion reference
Appendix.Content:
This companion appears in Volume 2, The Engine Builder's Bible — Volume II: Tools, Worlds and Living Systems: Production manifests and transactional publication — Production manifests and transactional publication A production manifest is a durable description of what should be built and published. It prevents a pipeline from depending on hidden editor state or on “whatever files happen to be in this directory.” A useful manifest separates identity from location. A logical asset ID names the thing the project means. Source and output paths say where a particular revision is read and written. A cryptographic digest can identify exact content bytes. A schema version says how to interpret all fields. Path safety Normalize paths before planning any write. A production-safe policy normally rejects parent traversal, unexpected absolute paths, ambiguous separators, and paths that escape the declared project root after symlink resolution. Lexical normalization alone cannot prove symlink safety. The filesystem must be queried at the point where real paths are resolved, and the resolved target must still lie inside the approved root. Deterministic plans The same manifest and tool versions should produce the same ordered build plan. Determinism makes logs diffable, cache keys stable and failures reproducible. Planning should be side-effect free. A dry run should reveal every intended output, overwrite, deletion and dependency before publication begins. Staging and commit A safe publication sequence is:
validate the whole request; write derived outputs to staging names or directories; validate staged bytes and metadata; fsync or equivalent when durability is part of the promise; publish with the platform’s proven atomic replacement mechanism; update manifest/index state; retain enough evidence to diagnose rollback or partial failure.
Atomicity and durability are separate. A rename can make a new name appear atomically yet still not guarantee survival across power loss unless the required data and directory metadata were persisted. Idempotence Repeating the same publication should either be a no-op or produce the same visible state. A pipeline that appends duplicate records, increments versions accidentally or rewrites unrelated timestamps on every run is harder to cache and reason about. tools/labs/production_pipeline_contract_lab.cpp models deterministic plan generation and idempotent publication in memory. It intentionally labels real filesystem durability as unproved. Related: Atomic publication and durability, DCC adapters and engine publication.. Open Production manifests and transactional publication in Volume 2

Shortest reliable answer Reciprocate every positive <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>σ</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> </math>; it minimizes original residual, then chooses minimum norm. Deep read / figure Exact pseudoinverse · L7 What does <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msubsup> <mi>A</mi> <mi>τ</mi> <mo>+</mo> </msubsup> </math> change? Shortest reliable answer It discards positive values at or below <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>τ</mi> </math>; the original least-squares residual can increase. Deep read / figure PCA scores What does polar decomposition call a reflection? Shortest reliable answer <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>U</mi> <msup> <mi>V</mi> <mi>T</mi> </msup> </math> is orthogonal; if its determinant is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo>−</mo> <mn>1</mn> </math>, it is improper, and nearest <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>S</mi> <mi>O</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math> flips a least-singular direction. Deep read / figure Jacobi convention What bounds a strided matrix view? Shortest reliable answer Check <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>c</mi> <mo>≤</mo> <mi>s</mi> </math>, checked last offset <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>r</mi> <mo>−</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mi>s</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>c</mi> <mo>−</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo><</mo> <mi>e</mi> </math>, and null pointer only with zero extent. Deep read / figure View bounds · Workspace bounds When is the principal matrix log defined? Shortest reliable answer When the spectrum avoids the closed negative real axis, including zero; other real logs may still exist. Shortest reliable answer Use SPD PCG/symmetric preconditioning; vanilla CG on arbitrary <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msup> <mi>M</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>−</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msup> <mi>A</mi> </math> may lose symmetry. Stop before zero-residual divisions. Deep read / figure CG preconditioning and true residual · L10 What makes an SVD API result inspectable? Shortest reliable answer Shapes/mode, rank threshold, workspace, convergence status, and independent reconstruction/orthogonality checks. Rebuild the example.
M08-1. A covariance ellipse and its whitened coordinates. For Sigma=[[4,1.2],[1.2,1]], L=[[2,0],[0.6,0.8]], mu=(3,-1), z=(1,1), x=(5,0.4), Mahalanobis squared distance 2, Euclidean squared distance 5.96, and density exp(-1)/(3.2 pi), about 0.0366 for an SPD 2D Gaussian.. Appendix.title: Cross-volume companion reference
Appendix.Content:
This companion appears in Volume 2, The Visual Computing Bible — Volume II: Computational Geometry, Vision, Reconstruction and XR: Reflectance and rendering equation — Reflectance and rendering equation Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: XR01 · Latest development: University courses Definition and mechanism A BRDF relates incident irradiance to outgoing radiance with directional weighting. The surface rendering equation adds emission and cosine-weighted incoming contributions. Visibility and transport assumptions matter; blurring completed output does not avoid shading. Prerequisites
Light spectra and radiometry — The light quantity and units must be established before its interaction or visual effect is modeled.
Used by Later independent XR sources will extend this same node. - Monte Carlo rendering estimators and variance - Surface orientation from image brightness
Reservoir resampling and ReSTIR ## Recall and next depth
Explain Lambertian rho/pi and identify what sampled shading approximates. Pending: transport estimators and actual workload profiling. Written coverage is not a claim of learner mastery or accepted numbered-curriculum progress. Source and navigation Expanded teaching explanation · Independent coverage · Dependency Map University course development Extend the existing light-transport note with the distinction between a material’s directional response and the incident illumination it receives. At surface point <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>x</mi> </math>, outgoing radiance depends on emitted radiance plus an integral over incoming directions. The BRDF <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>f</mi> <mi>r</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>x</mi> <mo>,</mo> <msub> <mi>ω</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>,</mo> <msub> <mi>ω</mi> <mi>o</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math> is reflected outgoing radiance per incident irradiance, with units of inverse steradians; it depends on incoming direction <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>ω</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> </math> and viewing direction <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>ω</mi> <mi>o</mi> </msub> </math>. A physically plausible BRDF is nonnegative and conserves energy, but can still have narrow glossy lobes that are difficult to sample. The rendering equation combines this local material response with visibility, incoming radiance, and the cosine foreshortening factor. This form explains why shading, direct lighting, global illumination, and Monte Carlo integration are connected parts of one transport calculation rather than independent image effects. Reflectance, BRDFs, and shading · The rendering equation and light transport · Numerical integration and Monte Carlo estimation. Open Reflectance and rendering equation in Volume 2

Physical intensity filtering uses the appropriate linear quantity; black/white averaging then sRGB encoding gives about 0.735, not encoded 0.5. Tone/gamut mapping and absolute display luminance need separate contracts. Prerequisites

Source and navigation Expanded teaching explanation · Independent coverage · Dependency Map University course development Extend the existing color note with why image-processing arithmetic must distinguish encoded values from light. A display encoding such as sRGB uses a nonlinear transfer curve so code values allocate precision in a way that suits perception and storage. Averaging or adding those encoded numbers does not generally average or add emitted light. Decode to linear-light RGB before blending, filtering, estimating radiance, or compositing, then encode for display. If two equal-area samples contain linear intensities <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mn>0</mn> </math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mn>1</mn> </math>, their physical average is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mn>0.5</mn> </math>; averaging their encoded sRGB values and treating that result as light yields a different, brighter answer. Color primaries and a white point also define the coordinate system of RGB, so a numeric triplet is incomplete without its color space. Keep scene-referred radiance, display-referred color, and perceptual appearance separate. This companion appears in Volume 2, The Foundations Bible — Volume II: Numerical Methods, Probability, Geometry and Camera Systems: Algorithmic stability — Algorithmic stability Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 10 · Latest development: Phase 10 Definition and mechanism A numerical problem can be sensitive even when an algorithm handles it well. Stability describes whether the finite-precision algorithm introduces only the error expected from rounding, often by showing that its output exactly solves a nearby problem. Backward stability is one useful form; forward stability asks directly how close the computed answer is to the exact answer for the original input. The claim must name its assumptions, arithmetic model, and problem class. For example, a stable linear solver can still have a large forward error on an ill-conditioned matrix. Stability therefore belongs beside conditioning, not in its place. A dot product with a small residual can still conceal an ill-conditioned problem, so report which notion of stability is actually supported. Prerequisites
Forward and backward error Conditioning and singularity
Used by
Stable quadratic root evaluation Bracketed and open root solvers Numerical error budgets
