This companion appears in Volume 2, The Foundations Bible — Volume II: Numerical Methods, Probability, Geometry and Camera Systems: Convergence order and Richardson extrapolation — Convergence order and Richardson extrapolation Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 10 · Latest development: Phase 10 Definition and mechanism If an approximation has leading error <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>Q</mi> <mi>h</mi> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <msup> <mi>Q</mi> <mo>∗</mo> </msup> <mo>+</mo> <mi>C</mi> <msup> <mi>h</mi> <mi>p</mi> </msup> <mo>+</mo> <mi>O</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msup> <mi>h</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mi>p</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msup> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math>, halving the step reduces that term by about <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msup> <mn>2</mn> <mi>p</mi> </msup> </math>. Comparing results at <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>h</mi> </math>, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>h</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>/</mo> </mrow> <mn>2</mn> </math>, and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>h</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>/</mo> </mrow> <mn>4</mn> </math> estimates the observed order; Richardson extrapolation combines two resolutions to cancel the leading term when the assumed order is valid. The method is diagnostic, not magic: measurements must be in the asymptotic regime, the same mathematical quantity must be computed at each resolution, and roundoff or stochastic noise must not dominate. For Euler integration, first-order refinement predicts the leading error to halve. Record the sequence and residuals rather than reporting an order from one pair alone. Ratios near an expected power provide evidence, but one noisy ratio is not a convergence study. Prerequisites
Discretization, truncation, and roundoff Finite differences and step-size balance Numerical quadrature and error
Used by
Numerical error budgets Reproducible numerical benchmarking
Full teaching explanation
Separate discretization, truncation, and roundoff; measure convergence

Appendix.title: Cross-volume companion reference
Appendix.Content:
This companion appears in Volume 2, The Foundations Bible — Volume II: Numerical Methods, Probability, Geometry and Camera Systems: PCA and covariance eigensystems — PCA and covariance eigensystems Center sample rows, then find the orthogonal directions of greatest variance. For centered <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>X</mi> </math>, SVD gives directions in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>V</mi> </math>, scores in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>U</mi> <mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi> </math>, and covariance eigenvalues <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msubsup> <mi>σ</mi> <mi>i</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msubsup> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>/</mo> </mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>N</mi> <mo>−</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math>. Units and feature scaling change the question; near-equal eigenvalues make individual axes unstable. Use it when: describing point clouds, reducing dimensions, or estimating a best-fit plane. Developed in Phase 8: PCA first centers observations so the covariance measures variation around the sample mean. The right singular vectors of centered data give principal directions, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>U</mi> <mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi> </math> gives scores, and squared singular values scaled by sample count give covariance eigenvalues; feature units and small eigengaps affect interpretation. centering and principal axes · plane fits and eigengaps Phase 9–10 development: For a random vector <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>X</mi> </math> with finite second moments, covariance is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mi> </mrow> <mo stretchy="false">[</mo> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>X</mi> <mo>−</mo> <mi>μ</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>X</mi> <mo>−</mo> <mi>μ</mi> <msup> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mi>T</mi> </msup> <mo stretchy="false">]</mo> </math>. For every vector <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>v</mi> </math>, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msup> <mi>v</mi> <mi>T</mi> </msup> <mi mathvariant="normal">Σ</mi> <mi>v</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mi> </mrow> <mo stretchy="false">[</mo> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msup> <mi>v</mi> <mi>T</mi> </msup> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>X</mi> <mo>−</mo> <mi>μ</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <msup> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mn>2</mn> </msup> <mo stretchy="false">]</mo> <mo>≥</mo> <mn>0</mn> </math>, so covariance is positive semidefinite. Its eigenvectors give uncorrelated principal directions and the eigenvalues give variance along them. Whitening rescales nonzero-variance directions and needs a stated policy for zero or tiny eigenvalues. A Gaussian kernel used to model rendering footprints is a spatial distribution model, not automatically a statement about epistemic uncertainty. Prerequisites Eigenvalues and eigenspaces, Singular value decomposition, Symmetric positive-definite matrices and Cholesky. - Expectation, covariance, and dependence - Multivariate Gaussian distributions and whitening - Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse - QR factorization and least squares Used by Polar decomposition, Matrix factorization choices. Teaching path: PCA from data. Full teaching explanation

Appendix.title: Cross-volume companion reference
Appendix.Content:
This companion appears in Volume 2, The Visual Computing Bible — Volume II: Computational Geometry, Vision, Reconstruction and XR: Additive energy and approximate structure — Additive energy and approximate structure Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses Definition and mechanism Additive energy measures how often two pairs from a set have the same sum: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>E</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>A</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>=</mo> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo stretchy="false">|</mo> </mrow> <mo fence="false" stretchy="false">{</mo> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>a</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>b</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>c</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>d</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>∈</mo> <msup> <mi>A</mi> <mn>4</mn> </msup> <mo>:</mo> <mi>a</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mi>b</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mi>c</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mi>d</mi> <mo fence="false" stretchy="false">}</mo> <mo stretchy="false">|</mo> </math>. A random-like set has relatively few repeated sums; a set with many additive coincidences often contains a structured subset. The Balog–Szemerédi–Gowers principle turns high energy into a large subset with small doubling, while Ruzsa-style inequalities and Freiman-type theorems describe how small doubling constrains approximate additive structure. In finite fields, sum-product results show that a set cannot remain simultaneously additively and multiplicatively concentrated unless it has special algebraic structure, such as subfield behavior. These implications are quantitative and depend on group or field hypotheses, subset size, and constants. High energy does not mean the entire set is a subgroup, and a small-doubling conclusion may apply only after discarding many elements. Energy is a counting diagnostic that guides structure theorems, not a complete classification by itself. Prerequisites
Vector spaces subspaces and span Basis coordinates and dimension Scalars fields and real-number models Exceptional projections and dimension
Used by
Additive structure explains repeated coincidences Dynamics connect projection growth to rich tubes
Full teaching explanation
Additive structure explains repeated coincidences Dynamics connect projection growth to rich tubes
Recall and next depth

This companion appears in Volume 2, The Visual Computing Bible — Volume II: Computational Geometry, Vision, Reconstruction and XR: Fourier analysis and spectral phase — Fourier analysis and spectral phase Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: XR01 · Latest development: University courses Definition and mechanism Fourier coordinates encode frequency magnitude and phase; phase places structure. DFT analyzes a finite periodic block, FFT computes that transform efficiently, and finite-window leakage differs from bin spacing. Interior one-sided amplitude bins need conjugate-pair normalization. Prerequisites
Continuous signals and discrete samples — Filtering/frequency analysis operates on a declared domain and its samples.
Used by
Sampling aliasing and reconstruction Convolution and filter footprints PSF OTF and MTF Perceptual metrics and display calibration Exceptional projections and dimension ## Recall and next depth
Recover the two tested sinusoid amplitudes and explain leakage. Pending: FFT implementations, windows and finite-boundary estimates. Written coverage is not a claim of learner mastery or accepted numbered-curriculum progress. Source and navigation Expanded teaching explanation · Independent coverage · Dependency Map University course development Extend the existing frequency-domain treatment with visual interpretation and filtering consequences. A Fourier coefficient records how strongly a sinusoidal basis function occurs at a given frequency and phase. In images, the origin of a two-dimensional spectrum represents slow spatial variation; moving farther from it corresponds to finer variation. A broad bright center indicates low-frequency structure, while energy far from the center often represents edges and texture. Filtering multiplies each frequency by the filter response: a low-pass response suppresses fine detail, and a high-pass response emphasizes it. Aliasing folds unresolved high frequencies into lower ones because sampled sinusoids can share identical sample values. This explains moiré patterns and animated shimmer, and shows why a spectrum is useful for diagnosing sampling problems rather than only for theoretical signal processing. Sampling continuous signals and image formation · Image sampling, filtering, and efficient reconstruction · Edges, contours, and subpixel localization. This companion appears in Volume 2, The Foundations Bible — Volume II: Numerical Methods, Probability, Geometry and Camera Systems: Stable quadratic root evaluation — Stable quadratic root evaluation Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 10 · Latest development: Phase 10 Definition and mechanism The direct quadratic formula can lose nearly all significant digits in one root when it subtracts nearly equal values. For real coefficients with nonzero leading coefficient and a valid nonnegative discriminant, compute a signed large-magnitude numerator first: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>q</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mo>−</mo> <mfrac> <mn>1</mn> <mn>2</mn> </mfrac> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>b</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mi>copysign</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msqrt> <msup> <mi>b</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msup> <mo>−</mo> <mn>4</mn> <mi>a</mi> <mi>c</mi> </msqrt> <mo>,</mo> <mi>b</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math>, then obtain roots as <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>q</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>/</mo> </mrow> <mi>a</mi> </math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>c</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>/</mo> </mrow> <mi>q</mi> </math>. The second root follows from the product relation <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mn>1</mn> </msub> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <mi>c</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>/</mo> </mrow> <mi>a</mi> </math>. This avoids cancellation in the small root, but it does not prevent overflow in the discriminant or cover degenerate coefficients, nonfinite inputs, or <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>q</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>0</mn> </math>; a robust solver also scales inputs and handles those cases explicitly. For example, the small root of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msup> <mi>x</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msup> <mo>+</mo> <msup> <mn>10</mn> <mn>8</mn> </msup> <mi>x</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>=</mo> <mn>0</mn> </math> is near <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo>−</mo> <msup> <mn>10</mn> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>−</mo> <mn>8</mn> </mrow> </msup> </math>, exactly the root most endangered by direct subtraction. This companion appears in Volume 2, The Foundations Bible — Volume II: Numerical Methods, Probability, Geometry and Camera Systems: Reproducible numerical benchmarking — Reproducible numerical benchmarking Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 10 · Latest development: Phase 10 Definition and mechanism A useful numerical benchmark separates sample-level variability from run-level variability and pairs competing methods on the same inputs or seeds. Record the algorithm, precision, compiler/runtime settings, sample count, seed or keyed input, warm-up policy, timing method, and error metric. Compare distributions or paired differences rather than a single favorable run. A speed improvement is meaningful only if accuracy and failure rates remain acceptable for the target workload. For Monte Carlo methods, repeat independent runs and report uncertainty; for deterministic solvers, use analytical or manufactured solutions and measure convergence. Reproducibility is an experimental contract, not merely a fixed random seed. If the workload is stochastic, compare paired seeds and report both runtime and error distributions. Prerequisites
Numerical reproducibility Confidence intervals and sequential evidence Robust summaries and error metrics Numerical error budgets Convergence order and Richardson extrapolation Latin-hypercube sampling

Appendix.title: Cross-volume companion reference
Appendix.Content:
This companion appears in Volume 2, The Foundations Bible — Volume II: Numerical Methods, Probability, Geometry and Camera Systems: Robust summaries and error metrics — Robust summaries and error metrics Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 10 · Latest development: Phase 10 Definition and mechanism Histograms, quantiles, medians, and robust scales summarize different features of a finite dataset. Histogram bar area represents probability only when heights are divided by sample count and bin width. Quantile conventions differ across software, so report the interpolation rule. The median minimizes absolute deviation and resists some extreme observations; the mean minimizes squared deviation and is more sensitive to outliers. MAD and trimmed means provide other robustness choices with efficiency tradeoffs. MSE and RMSE emphasize large errors, MAE is less sensitive to them, and relative metrics can become unstable near zero. Aggregating per-scene scores differs from pooling every observation. Choose the metric from the scientific question, units, and failure cost, and report tail behavior when rare large errors matter. Prerequisites
Expectation, covariance, and dependence Absolute and relative error

Appendix.Content: This companion appears in Volume 2, The Foundations Bible — Volume II: Numerical Methods, Probability, Geometry and Camera Systems: QR factorization and least squares — QR factorization and least squares QR writes <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>A</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mi>Q</mi> <mi>R</mi> </math> with orthonormal columns in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>Q</mi> </math> and triangular <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>R</mi> </math>. Orthogonal coordinates preserve Euclidean lengths, so least squares reduces to a triangular solve and a perpendicular residual. Householder QR is a stable dense method; Gram–Schmidt explains the geometry but can lose orthogonality. Use it when: fitting overdetermined data with known full column rank. Developed in Phase 8: Orthogonal transformations change coordinates without changing Euclidean lengths. QR therefore separates the fitted component, solved through triangular <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>R</mi> </math>, from the constant perpendicular residual; the Householder construction is the stable dense route, with Gram–Schmidt retained to make the geometry visible. Householder and Givens construction · least squares and its residual Prerequisites Linear systems and fundamental subspaces, Dot products and orthogonality, Conditioning and singularity. Used by Matrix factorization choices, Singular value decomposition, PCA and covariance eigensystems. Teaching path: QR and fitting.. Open QR factorization and least squares in Volume 2

This companion appears in Volume 2, The Foundations Bible — Volume II: Numerical Methods, Probability, Geometry and Camera Systems: Orthonormal frames and Gram-Schmidt — Orthonormal frames and Gram-Schmidt Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: Phase6 · Latest development: Phase6 Definition and mechanism An orthonormal frame has unit perpendicular axes, so its Gram matrix is identity. Gram–Schmidt constructs axes by repeated rejection. Modified order uses the updated residual and changes rounding behavior. Frame existence, numerical reliability and output continuity are distinct questions. For <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math>, rejection produces <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>/</mo> </mrow> <mn>2</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mo>−</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>/</mo> </mrow> <mn>2</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math>. A least-aligned helper axis avoids a near-parallel cross but can switch discontinuously. Prerequisites
Surface tangents normals and bitangents — The surface tangent plane gives the axes that orthogonalization must preserve. Gram matrices and coordinate metrics — Pairwise basis measurements define the systems and metric used in reconstruction.

Appendix.Content:
This companion appears in Volume 2, The Foundations Bible — Volume II: Numerical Methods, Probability, Geometry and Camera Systems: Homogeneous coordinates and perspective division — Homogeneous coordinates and perspective division Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase6 · Latest development: University courses Definition and mechanism Phase 7 derives the affine block matrix, distinguishes a singular affine map from an invertible frame, and traces model → view → homogeneous clip → NDC using a declared projection. The worked figure keeps the divisor visible and checks the chosen near/far depth endpoints. An affine homogeneous point has last coordinate one; a direction has zero. Nonzero common scale defines projective equivalence, while dehomogenization divides by a nonzero final component. Clip representatives and projective classes have related but distinct semantics. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>2</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>4</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>6</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>2</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>2</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>3</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math> describe one finite projective point. NDC normalization standardizes ranges, not vector length. Prerequisites
Vectors coordinates and affine points — Point, displacement and coordinate roles determine which geometric operations are meaningful.
Used by
Linear affine and projective transformations
Later curriculum sources can deepen this same node; no future coverage is marked complete. - Ray-triangle intersection - Camera calibration and bundle adjustment
Homogeneous clipping and perspective interpolation Position reconstruction from depth Camera gauge freedoms and observability
Recall and next depth Explain why perspective division is nonlinear and why clipping must precede casual division. Full production proofs, target-specific integration and learner mastery require further evidence. Source and navigation Teaching narrative · Coverage and source gap · Evidence and limits · Dependency Map University course development Extend the existing account with the geometric reason for the final divide. A 3D point is stored as <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>x</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>y</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>z</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math>; after multiplying by a projective matrix it becomes <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>X</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>Y</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>Z</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>W</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math>. Dividing the first three components by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>W</mi> </math> maps the homogeneous representative to ordinary coordinates. Any nonzero scalar multiple of a homogeneous vector represents the same point, which is why this division is meaningful. For a perspective camera, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>W</mi> </math> is chosen to depend on depth, so apparent size shrinks with distance. A direction has homogeneous coordinate zero and is not translated like a point. Projection matrices encode the camera frustum before division; afterward, a viewport transform scales and shifts normalized coordinates to pixels and commonly flips the vertical axis because image rows increase downward. Keep clipping before division to avoid unstable behavior around <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>W</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>0</mn> </math>. Coordinate frames, transformations, and pose · Cameras, projection, and calibration Phase 11 camera development Homogeneous image coordinates represent a ray up to nonzero scale; perspective division produces normalized image coordinates. Monocular reconstruction has a separate physical scale gauge: multiplying all scene points and camera translations by the same positive factor preserves projections. Do not confuse representational scale with unknown metric scale. A known object dimension, baseline, or depth measurement can anchor metres; normalizing a homogeneous vector cannot. This assumes calibrated perspective projection without an external scale prior. The distinction explains why a numerically precise reconstruction can still lack physical units. Link: A camera model must close the loop; research: Four deeper links from the TUM lecture review.. Open Homogeneous coordinates and perspective division in Volume 2

Appendix.title: Cross-volume companion reference
Appendix.Content:
This companion appears in Volume 1, The Engine Builder's Bible — Volume I: From First Frame to Core Runtime Systems: Ownership and non-owning views — Ownership and non-owning views Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: C003 · Latest development: C010 Definition and mechanism By-value copies use member semantics, not recursive deep cloning. Rule-Zero composition delegates ownership to members; raw owners must coordinate transfer and release. Copying a pointer/view/handle is not acquiring ownership. Copying span/string_view or capturing a view by value copies only a descriptor. An owning string capture supplies independent storage; a view or handle does not automatically pin a deferred resource. The inline C++ laboratory distinguishes NamedVector::to_array, which copies values into a new array, from ArrayVector::view, which aliases actual array elements without owning them. Neither span nor pointer extends backing lifetime. Ownership and RAII are introduced as next-depth connections, not yet a full exception-safety treatment. M010 makes the distinction operational: an owner is responsible for release; a borrow only accesses. std::unique_ptr expresses exclusive ownership, std::shared_ptr retains a shared lifetime, and std::weak_ptr observes without extending that lifetime. Smart pointers do not remove the borrow/invalidation rules of raw pointers obtained from them. See RAII and resource handles and Exclusive and shared smart-pointer ownership. An owner controls a resource’s validity and release; a view merely refers to it. Vector owns its element buffer; span does not copy or prolong that buffer’s life. Owner destruction or invalidating reallocation can dangle the span. A reader retaining a span needs stable live backing for every read, not only at construction. Prerequisites
Storage duration and object lifetime — Access requires an object and backing storage that are still valid. Dynamic allocation and heap — Allocated buffers/blocks supply the storage whose ownership and fragmentation matter.
Used by

Appendix.Content:
This companion appears in Volume 2, The Foundations Bible — Volume II: Numerical Methods, Probability, Geometry and Camera Systems: Stable probability normalization and log-sum-exp — Stable probability normalization and log-sum-exp Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 10 · Latest development: Phase 10 Definition and mechanism To normalize nonnegative weights, divide each by their sum; direct summation can overflow even when the normalized probabilities are representable. Scale by the largest weight before summing. For log weights <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>a</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> </math>, compute <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>m</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mi>log</mi> <mo data-mjx-texclass="NONE">⁡</mo> <munder> <mo data-mjx-texclass="OP">∑</mo> <mi>i</mi> </munder> <msup> <mi>e</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <msub> <mi>a</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>−</mo> <mi>m</mi> </mrow> </msup> </math>, where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>m</mi> <mo>=</mo> <munder> <mo data-mjx-texclass="OP" movablelimits="true">max</mo> <mi>i</mi> </munder> <msub> <mi>a</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> </math>. Subtracting the maximum prevents exponential overflow, and the result can be used to form softmax probabilities. This assumes at least one finite, valid weight and requires an explicit policy for all-zero, negative, NaN, or infinite inputs. Underflow of very small normalized probabilities is a separate concern from overflow; do not silently equate zero after underflow with mathematically impossible. For log weights <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>1000</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>1001</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>1000</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math>, subtracting <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mn>1001</mn> </math> keeps exponentials bounded while leaving the normalized probabilities unchanged. Prerequisites

This companion appears in Volume 1, The Visual Computing Bible — Volume I: Image Formation, Rendering, GPU Systems and Geometry Queries: Convolution and filter footprints — Convolution and filter footprints Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: XR01 · Latest development: University courses Definition and mechanism Convolution combines shifted values with a weighting kernel; its spectrum multiplies transfer functions. Pixel footprints and boundary policies define what is averaged. A separable Gaussian uses two 1D passes; unpadded DFT filtering wraps circularly. Prerequisites
Continuous signals and discrete samples — Filtering/frequency analysis operates on a declared domain and its samples. Fourier analysis and spectral phase — Frequency and phase reveal transfer, sampling ambiguity and structural loss.
Used by
PSF OTF and MTF Multiscale texture filtering Optical flow and time to contact Edge localization and subpixel contours Template matching and distance transforms PDE fields and discrete Laplacians Attention and visual transformers Learned image features and CNNs ## Recall and next depth
Derive the three-tap filter’s gain and constant preservation. Pending: implementation cost, padding and spatially varying kernels. Written coverage is not a claim of learner mastery or accepted numbered-curriculum progress. Source and navigation Expanded teaching explanation · Independent coverage · Dependency Map University course development Extend the current convolution note from a sliding kernel to image formation and resampling. A pixel integrates incoming image energy over a finite footprint; point sampling is only an approximation to that area integral. Convolution combines nearby values with weights whose spatial support is the kernel footprint, and its Fourier transform describes which spatial frequencies survive. Before reducing resolution, low-pass filtering suppresses frequencies the coarser grid cannot represent. In texture mapping, the screen-to-texture Jacobian maps a nearly square screen pixel to a texture-space parallelogram. If the two singular directions have very different lengths, an isotropic mip level blurs one direction too much; anisotropic filters take extra samples along the long axis. This same footprint reasoning links pixel reconstruction, antialiasing, texture filtering, and sensor blur without treating them as unrelated tricks. Sampling continuous signals and image formation · Image sampling, filtering, and efficient reconstruction · Textures and surface detail. Open Convolution and filter footprints in Volume 1

Appendix.title: Cross-volume companion reference
Appendix.Content:
This companion appears in Volume 2, The Foundations Bible — Volume II: Numerical Methods, Probability, Geometry and Camera Systems: A posteriori error bounds for contractive iteration — A posteriori error bounds for contractive iteration Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 10 · Latest development: Phase 10 Definition and mechanism For a fixed-point iteration <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mi>n</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <mi>G</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mi>n</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math>, suppose <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>G</mi> </math> is a contraction with Lipschitz constant <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>q</mi> <mo><</mo> <mn>1</mn> </math> on a region containing the iterates and its fixed point. Then the remaining error is bounded by the next step divided by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mn>1</mn> <mo>−</mo> <mi>q</mi> </math>: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo data-mjx-texclass="ORD" fence="false" stretchy="false">‖</mo> <msup> <mi>x</mi> <mo>∗</mo> </msup> <mo>−</mo> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mi>n</mi> </msub> <mo data-mjx-texclass="ORD" fence="false" stretchy="false">‖</mo> <mo>≤</mo> <mo data-mjx-texclass="ORD" fence="false" stretchy="false">‖</mo> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mi>n</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msub> <mo>−</mo> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mi>n</mi> </msub> <mo data-mjx-texclass="ORD" fence="false" stretchy="false">‖</mo> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>/</mo> </mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>−</mo> <mi>q</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math>. The assumption is essential; a small step alone does not prove convergence because stagnation or a failed update can also make changes tiny. In implementation, report the contraction evidence or a suitable residual bound and keep failure distinct from success. This turns an observed update into a conditional, checkable estimate rather than a guess. If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>q</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>/</mo> </mrow> <mn>2</mn> </math> and the latest step is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msup> <mn>10</mn> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>−</mo> <mn>6</mn> </mrow> </msup> </math>, this bound is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mn>2</mn> <mo>×</mo> <msup> <mn>10</mn> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>−</mo> <mn>6</mn> </mrow> </msup> </math>, conditional on the contraction proof. Prerequisites
Forward and backward error Conditioning and singularity
Used by

This companion appears in Volume 2, The Foundations Bible — Volume II: Numerical Methods, Probability, Geometry and Camera Systems: Cubic Hermite interpolation — Cubic Hermite interpolation Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 10 · Latest development: Phase 10 Definition and mechanism A cubic Hermite segment is determined by endpoint values and endpoint tangent data. With normalized <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>t</mi> <mo>∈</mo> <mo stretchy="false">[</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo stretchy="false">]</mo> </math>, its four basis polynomials blend the two endpoint positions and two tangents. Tangents are derivatives with respect to the parameter, so physical-time derivatives must be scaled by segment duration: a velocity in units per second is not interchangeable with a tangent per normalized parameter. Hermite curves are useful when a camera path or animation must pass through known positions while exposing direct control over its entry and exit directions. The endpoint constraints determine one cubic polynomial; continuity between adjacent segments still requires compatible endpoint tangents. Prerequisites
Interpolation versus approximation Spline bases and curve evaluation

Appendix.Content:
This companion appears in Volume 2, The Foundations Bible — Volume II: Numerical Methods, Probability, Geometry and Camera Systems: Bézier curves and De Casteljau evaluation — Bézier curves and De Casteljau evaluation Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 10 · Latest development: Phase 10 Definition and mechanism A Bézier curve blends control points with Bernstein basis weights. The weights are nonnegative and sum to one on <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">[</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo stretchy="false">]</mo> </math>, so the curve remains in the control points’ convex hull and reaches its first and last control points at the endpoints. De Casteljau’s repeated linear interpolation evaluates the curve using numerically straightforward convex combinations; the intermediate levels also reveal subdivision geometry. A cubic Bézier’s endpoint tangents depend on its first and last control-polygon edges, so moving a handle changes direction and scale. The convex-hull guarantee applies to the curve parameter interval; extrapolation outside it loses that containment property. Subdivide the curve before tessellation when screen-space curvature changes rapidly; parameter steps alone do not guarantee uniform pixel error. Prerequisites
Interpolation versus approximation Spline bases and curve evaluation

This companion appears in Volume 2, The Foundations Bible — Volume II: Numerical Methods, Probability, Geometry and Camera Systems: Exterior products and geometric algebra — Exterior products and geometric algebra Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: Phase6 · Latest development: Phase6 Definition and mechanism Exterior products represent oriented higher-dimensional elements without forcing them into vectors. A wedge is antisymmetric and bilinear; a bivector has grade two. Euclidean geometric algebra combines inner and exterior products into one product. Higher-dimensional sums of bivectors need not be a single plane. The plane element <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>I</mi> <mo>=</mo> <msub> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mi mathvariant="bold">e</mi> </mrow> <mn>1</mn> </msub> <msub> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mi mathvariant="bold">e</mi> </mrow> <mn>2</mn> </msub> </math> satisfies <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <msup> <mi>I</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msup> <mo>=</mo> <mo>−</mo> <mn>1</mn> </math>, connecting plane rotations to complex-number behavior. Prerequisites

Appendix.Content:
This companion appears in Volume 2, The Foundations Bible — Volume II: Numerical Methods, Probability, Geometry and Camera Systems: Finite differences and step-size balance — Finite differences and step-size balance Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 9 · Latest development: Phase 9 Definition and mechanism Finite differences estimate derivatives from sampled function values. Forward and backward differences use one-sided samples and have first-order truncation error; central differences use samples on both sides and usually have second-order truncation error for smooth functions. Making the step arbitrarily small is not always better: subtractive cancellation and evaluation noise grow as the step shrinks, while truncation error grows when it is too large. The useful step balances these effects and depends on scale, precision, and function noise. Finite differences are valuable for black-box sensitivities and gradient checks, but they are not automatic differentiation and can fail near discontinuities or branch changes. A numerical gradient check should compare directional derivatives, use scale-aware steps, and avoid interpreting one tolerance pass as proof that every derivative path is correct. Prerequisites
Derivative as a local linear map Absolute and relative error

Texture derivatives carry physical stretch. Cleaned TBN frames need normalization, degeneracy checks and a mirrored-UV sign convention. Panel texture derivatives are <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>4</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>3</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math> before normalization. An atan2 expression combines cross magnitude and dot, retaining sine- and cosine-like information. Scale inputs before evaluating to reduce range failures. A signed angle requires a specified oriented plane. Parallel directions give zero, antiparallel directions give <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>π</mi> </math>, and perpendicular directions give <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>π</mi> <mrow data-mjx-texclass="ORD"> <mo>/</mo> </mrow> <mn>2</mn> </math>. Appendix.Content:
This companion appears in Volume 2, The Foundations Bible — Volume II: Numerical Methods, Probability, Geometry and Camera Systems: ODE initial-value problems and stiffness — ODE initial-value problems and stiffness Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 9 · Latest development: Phase 9 Definition and mechanism An ordinary differential equation specifies a state’s rate of change as a function of state and time. An initial-value problem adds the starting state; together they define the trajectory when existence and uniqueness conditions hold. Numerical integration advances approximate states through finite time steps. Stability concerns whether numerical errors remain controlled under repeated updates, not just whether one step is accurate. A stiff system contains modes with very different time scales; explicit methods may require impractically small steps to remain stable even when the visible solution changes slowly. Implicit methods can enlarge the stable step region but require solving equations. Consistency, stability, and convergence are distinct properties. A simulator should choose its step and integrator based on the dynamics, not merely the display frame interval or apparent smoothness of one trajectory. Prerequisites
Definite integrals and the fundamental theorem Eigenvalues and eigenspaces Absolute and relative error
Used by

This companion appears in Volume 1, The Engine Builder's Bible — Volume I: From First Frame to Core Runtime Systems: Object identity and generation handles — Object identity and generation handles Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: C007 · Latest development: C008 Definition and mechanism Copied handles are distinct C++ objects with equal application identities. A validated handle does not certify a previous component borrow; assignment may preserve a C++ slot while changing logical ownership. Object value, identity and address answer different questions. Equal values can belong to different objects; the same address can host successive lifetimes. A logical index/generation handle must be checked against the owning registry’s bounds, occupancy and generation. Counter wrap and registry identity remain policy obligations. Prerequisites
Object construction and storage reuse — Storage reuse creates successive occupants, motivating handles that record the intended generation.

Appendix.title: Cross-volume companion reference
Appendix.Content:
This companion appears in Volume 1, The Engine Builder's Bible — Volume I: From First Frame to Core Runtime Systems: Vulkan synchronization2 and resource transitions — Vulkan synchronization2 and resource transitions Vulkan synchronization is not “put a barrier between two passes.” A dependency has to connect a real producer access to a real consumer access with execution and memory scopes that cover both operations. Vulkan 1.3 includes the synchronization2 model promoted from VK_KHR_synchronization2. It places stage and access masks together in the version-2 barrier structures and uses commands such as vkCmdPipelineBarrier2 and vkQueueSubmit2. Primary references: - https://docs.vulkan.org/guide/latest/extensions/VK_KHR_synchronization2.html - https://docs.vulkan.org/spec/latest/chapters/synchronization.html Producer → consumer reasoning For every hazard, write the transition in words first. Example: A transfer command writes a storage buffer. A later compute shader reads that buffer. The producer execution stage is transfer. The producer access is transfer write. The consumer execution stage is compute shader. The consumer access is shader storage read. An abstract memory barrier therefore needs to cover: source stage = TRANSFER source access = TRANSFER_WRITE destination stage = COMPUTE_SHADER destination access = SHADER_STORAGE_READ. Using ALL_COMMANDS and MEMORY_READ/WRITE everywhere may accidentally work but destroys precision and can hide misunderstanding. Using a destination stage that never performs the consumer access is not made correct by a broad access mask. Image transitions add a layout contract Images have another state dimension: layout. An image memory barrier can both synchronize accesses and transition from oldLayout to newLayout. The old layout must describe the state established by prior use unless the contents are intentionally discarded under the rules that permit that. A render graph therefore needs more than “read” and “write.” For each image subresource it eventually needs:
stage/access usage; required layout; aspect; mip range; array-layer range; queue ownership when queues/families differ.
A whole-image state tracker is a valid early implementation but cannot claim correct independent mip/layer scheduling. Queue submission and timeline semaphores Synchronization2 also modernizes queue submission through VkSubmitInfo2 and related structures. Timeline semaphores carry monotonically increasing integer values and are useful for expressing ordered completion points across submissions. A timeline value is not a memory barrier by itself; the signal/wait operations participate in dependencies whose scopes must still match the work. Native witness now in the repository tools/native/vulkan_sync_smoke.cpp is compiled and executed in the dedicated native graphics workflow on Ubuntu with a Vulkan implementation and validation layer packages. It:
creates a Vulkan 1.3 instance; finds a device exposing synchronization2; creates a queue/device with the feature enabled; records a VkMemoryBarrier2 through vkCmdPipelineBarrier2; submits the command buffer using vkQueueSubmit2; waits for fence completion; fails on validation-layer errors when the layer is available.
That materially raises the evidence level from a CPU-only logical graph. It still does not prove a resource-specific RAW transition, image layout transition, queue-family transfer, timeline protocol, transient aliasing, physical-GPU performance, or current Kairo/Vulkax integration. Each of those needs its own captured witness. Related: GPU workgroups and synchronization, Rendering history validity, Render graph barrier lowering.. Open Vulkan synchronization2 and resource transitions in Volume 1

Appendix.title: Cross-volume companion reference
Appendix.Content:
This companion appears in Volume 1, The Visual Computing Bible — Volume I: Image Formation, Rendering, GPU Systems and Geometry Queries: Spline bases and curve evaluation — Spline bases and curve evaluation Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: University courses · Latest development: University courses Definition and mechanism A spline is a piecewise polynomial curve whose neighboring pieces join under explicit continuity constraints. A cubic Bézier segment uses four control points and Bernstein weights; the weights sum to one, so the curve lies in their convex hull. A B-spline uses local basis functions so moving one control point changes only nearby spans rather than the whole curve. Knots mark where polynomial pieces meet; repeated knots reduce continuity. Catmull–Rom curves interpolate their control points and can be convenient for motion paths, while Bézier curves expose endpoint tangents through their handles. To evaluate a curve, compute basis weights at parameter <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>t</mi> </math> and take their weighted sum of control points. Position, first derivative, and parameterization speed matter separately: even a smooth path may speed up or slow down unless its parameter is adjusted. Prerequisites
Basis coordinates and dimension
Used by
Worlds, Images and Inference Bézier curves and De Casteljau evaluation Cubic Hermite interpolation ## Full teaching explanation
Curves as controllable functions · Animation curves and motion paths. Open Spline bases and curve evaluation in Volume 1

Appendix.title: Cross-volume companion reference
Appendix.Content:
This companion appears in Volume 2, The Foundations Bible — Volume II: Numerical Methods, Probability, Geometry and Camera Systems: Bracketed and open root solvers — Bracketed and open root solvers Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: Phase 10 · Latest development: Phase 10 Definition and mechanism A root solver seeks <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>f</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>x</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>=</mo> <mn>0</mn> </math>. A bracketed method maintains an interval whose endpoints have opposite signs; continuity then guarantees at least one root remains inside, and bisection provides a predictable shrinking error bound. Open methods such as secant and Newton can converge faster near a well-behaved simple root, but they may diverge, encounter a zero derivative, or leave the relevant domain. A safeguarded hybrid uses a bracket for global protection and accepts fast proposals only when they preserve progress. Residual size alone does not certify root accuracy when the root is poorly conditioned, and discontinuous functions do not satisfy the sign-change guarantee. Prerequisites
Algorithmic stability Conditioning and singularity Stable quadratic root evaluation A posteriori error bounds for contractive iteration
Used by
Numerical error budgets
Full teaching explanation
Finding roots with guarantees and convergence checks

This companion appears in Volume 2, The Foundations Bible — Volume II: Numerical Methods, Probability, Geometry and Camera Systems: Gaussian elimination and pivoting — Gaussian elimination and pivoting Equivalent elementary row operations expose pivots and triangular structure while preserving the solution set when applied to the full augmented system. Pivoting avoids zero or dangerously small divisors; it improves the calculation but does not cure an ill-conditioned problem. Use it when: understanding REF/RREF, LU, consistency, rank, and triangular solves. Developed in Phase 8: Elimination turns those geometric questions into auditable row operations on the augmented matrix. Pivots expose rank and free variables; partial pivoting chooses a safer divisor and tracks row exchanges, while residual and growth checks explain why pivoting cannot repair ill-conditioning. elimination steps · pivoting and growth Prerequisites Linear systems and fundamental subspaces, Matrix multiplication and composition order, Conditioning and singularity. Used by LU factorization and reusable solves, Matrix norms and numerical error, Sparse and iterative solvers. This companion appears in Volume 2, The Foundations Bible — Volume II: Numerical Methods, Probability, Geometry and Camera Systems: Unit directions and safe normalization — Unit directions and safe normalization Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: Phase6 · Latest development: Phase6 Definition and mechanism A unit direction is finite, nonzero input scaled to approximate length one. Scale by the largest absolute component before measuring to avoid unnecessary squared overflow or underflow. Zero has no direction; application noise thresholds are distinct from numerical existence. For finite nonzero input, scaled squared length lies between <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mn>1</mn> </math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mn>3</mn> </math>. A vector of huge components can have a computable unit direction even when its original length does not fit. Prerequisites
Norms lengths and induced distances — Lengths and their domains are needed before unit directions or angular measurements. Robust norm and intermediate range — Range-safe scaling avoids losing a valid direction to unnecessary squared intermediates.
Used by

Reflection refraction and shading directions — Builds on this mechanism in the connected geometry story. This companion appears in Volume 2, The Foundations Bible — Volume II: Numerical Methods, Probability, Geometry and Camera Systems: Complex numbers and planar rotations — Complex numbers and planar rotations Curriculum depth: Introduced · First seen: Phase6 · Latest development: Phase6 Definition and mechanism Complex multiplication combines planar rotation and scaling. A unit complex multiplier represents a rotation; its conjugate gives the inverse. A two-component storage tuple is not automatically a rotation. Multiplication by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mi>i</mi> </math> sends <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>x</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>y</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math> to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mo>−</mo> <mi>y</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>x</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </math>. Zero collapses the plane rather than representing any rotation. Prerequisites
Scalars fields and real-number models — Field operations define which scalar multipliers the vector laws may use.

Appendix.title: Cross-volume companion reference
Appendix.Content: This companion appears in Volume 2, The Foundations Bible — Volume II: Numerical Methods, Probability, Geometry and Camera Systems: Matrix norms and numerical error — Matrix norms and numerical error The spectral norm is the largest 2-norm stretch and equals the largest singular value. The Frobenius norm measures aggregate squared entry energy. Residuals, orthogonality errors, and condition numbers need a declared norm and scale; a small residual alone need not imply a sensitive solution is accurate. Use it when: setting scaled tolerances or interpreting numerical diagnostics. Developed in Phase 8: The spectral norm measures worst-case amplification, while the Frobenius norm accumulates squared energy across entries. The chapter uses them to scale residuals, reconstruction errors, and orthogonality defects, and separates backward error in a nearby problem from forward error in the requested answer. norms and scale · residuals and error interpretation Prerequisites Norms lengths and induced distances, Singular value decomposition, Forward and backward error. Used by Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse, Matrix functions, Sparse and iterative solvers. Teaching path: norms and error. A matrix norm can protect a geometry bound A local sphere under a linear transform is generally an ellipsoid. The Frobenius norm times its original radius gives a safe, possibly loose enclosing radius. Taking only the longest matrix column can fail under shear. The culling example derives the bound, demonstrates the shear counterexample, and links its geometric figure. This connects numerical matrix norms to conservative rejection decisions.. Open Matrix norms and numerical error in Volume 2

This companion appears in Volume 2, The Visual Computing Bible — Volume II: Computational Geometry, Vision, Reconstruction and XR: Quantization and compressed weights — Quantization and compressed weights Curriculum depth: Developed · First seen: C001 · Latest development: C006 Definition and mechanism Low-precision values and packed model weights reuse field-width, mask, shift, and bandwidth trade-offs. Quantization maps a larger numeric domain to a smaller discrete set, usually with information loss. Packing stores those discrete codes compactly; dequantization reconstructs approximations. Bit packing alone is lossless for valid codes, whereas quantization changes represented precision. M006 develops affine scales and zero points, local group calibration, offset-coded INT4, one-bit row centroids, metadata overhead and error metrics. Packing preserves discrete codes; quantization deliberately loses information. See the worked five-value group in the continuous story. Prerequisites
Bit packing — Packing places several constrained values into a carrier. Arithmetic policies — A policy states the intended response to an unrepresentable answer: wrap modulo a base, report checked failure, widen storage, clamp to an endpoint, or grow arbitrary precision.
Used by
One-bit centroid quantization — uses this mechanism to define its representation, error or validation contract. Quantization error metrics — uses this mechanism to define its representation, error or validation contract.
Connect later chunks here when they use this concept.
